metadata.title: Backpressure
metadata.description: How to handle backpressure and cancellation when working with the AI SDK

title.children: Tying Stream Laziness to AI Responses

contents.content: This page focuses on understanding back-pressure and cancellation when working with streams. You do not need to know this information to use the AI SDK, but for those interested, it offers a deeper dive on why and how the SDK optimally streams responses.

In the following sections, we'll explore back-pressure and cancellation in the context of a simple example program. We'll discuss the issues that can arise from an eager approach and demonstrate how a lazy approach can resolve them.

contents.heading: back-pressure-and-cancellation-with-streams
contents.content: Let's begin by setting up a simple example program:

contents.heading: back-pressure-and-cancellation-with-streams
contents.content: In this example, we create an async-generator that yields positive integers, a ReadableStream that wraps our integer generator, and a reader which will read values out of our stream. Notice, too, that our integer generator logs out "yielding ${i}", and our reader logs out "read ${value}". Both take an arbitrary amount of time to process data, represented with a 100ms sleep in our generator, and a 1sec sleep in our reader.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: If you were to run this program, you'd notice something funny. We'll see roughly 10 "yield" logs for every "read" log. This might seem obvious, the generator can push values 10x faster than the reader can pull them out. But it represents a problem, our stream has to maintain an ever expanding queue of items that have been pushed in but not pulled out.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: The problem stems from the way we wrap our generator into a stream. Notice the use of for await (…) inside our start handler. This is an eager for-loop, and it is constantly running to get the next value from our generator to be enqueued in our stream. This means our stream does not respect back-pressure, the signal from the consumer to the producer that more values aren't needed yet. We've essentially spawned a thread that will perpetually push more data into the stream, one that runs as fast as possible to push new data immediately. Worse, there's no way to signal to this thread to stop running when we don't need additional data.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: To fix this, ReadableStream allows a pull handler. pull is called every time the consumer attempts to read more data from our stream (if there's no data already queued internally). But it's not enough to just move the for await(…) into pull, we also need to convert from an eager enqueuing to a lazy one. By making these 2 changes, we'll be able to react to the consumer. If they need more data, we can easily produce it, and if they don't, then we don't need to spend any time doing unnecessary work.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: Our createStream is a little more verbose now, but the new code is important. First, we need to manually call our iterator.next() method. This returns a Promise for an object with the type signature { done: boolean, value: T }. If done is true, then we know that our iterator won't yield any more values and we must close the stream (this allows the consumer to know that the stream is also finished producing values). Else, we need to enqueue our newly produced value.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: When we run this program, we see that our "yield" and "read" logs are now paired. We're no longer yielding 10x integers for every read! And, our stream now only needs to maintain 1 item in its internal buffer. We've essentially given control to the consumer, so that it's responsible for producing new values as it needs it. Neato!

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: Let's go back to our initial eager example, with 1 small edit. Now instead of reading 10,000 integers, we're only going to read 3:

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: We're back to yielding 10x the number of values read. But notice now, after we've read 3 values, we're continuing to yield new values. We know that our reader will never read another value, but our stream doesn't! The eager for await (…) will continue forever, loudly enqueuing new values into our stream's buffer and increasing our memory usage until it consumes all available program memory.

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: The fix to this is exactly the same: use pull and manual iteration. By producing values lazily, we tie the lifetime of our integer generator to the lifetime of the reader. Once the reads stop, the yields will stop too:

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: Since the solution is the same as implementing back-pressure, it shows that they're just 2 facets of the same problem: Pushing values into a stream should be done lazily, and doing it eagerly results in expected problems.

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: Now let's imagine you're integrating AIBot service into your product. Users will be able to prompt "count from 1 to infinity", the browser will fetch your AI API endpoint, and your servers connect to AIBot to get a response. But "infinity" is, well, infinite. The response will never end!

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: After a few seconds, the user gets bored and navigates away. Or maybe you're doing local development and a hot-module reload refreshes your page. The browser will have ended its connection to the API endpoint, but will your server end its connection with AIBot?

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: If you used the eager for await (...) approach, then the connection is still running and your server is asking for more and more data from AIBot. Our server spawned a "thread" and there's no signal when we can end the eager pulls. Eventually, the server is going to run out of memory (remember, there's no active fetch connection to read the buffering responses and free them).

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: With the lazy approach, this is taken care of for you. Because the stream will only request new data from AIBot when the consumer requests it, navigating away from the page naturally frees all resources. The fetch connection aborts and the server can clean up the response. The ReadableStream tied to that response can now be garbage collected. When that happens, the connection it holds to AIBot can then be freed.

headings.content: Tying Stream Laziness to AI Responses

metadata.title: Caching
metadata.description: How to handle caching when working with the AI SDK

contents.content: Depending on the type of application you're building, you may want to cache the responses you receive from your AI provider, at least temporarily.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
The recommended approach to caching responses is using language model middleware
and the simulateReadableStream function.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
Language model middleware is a way to enhance the behavior of language models by intercepting and modifying the calls to the language model.
Let's see how you can use language model middleware to cache responses.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
This example uses @upstash/redis to store and retrieve the assistant's
responses but you can use any KV storage provider you would like.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
This middleware caches the raw model response before AI SDK validates
structured output. When using structured output, cache only a response that
has passed your schema validation; otherwise, an invalid response can be
replayed from the cache on later requests.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: LanguageModelV4Middleware has the wrapGenerate and wrapStream wrapping methods, plus the optional transformParams method. wrapGenerate is called when using generateText, while wrapStream is called when using streamText.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: For wrapGenerate, you can cache the response directly. Instead, for wrapStream, you cache an array of the stream parts, which can then be used with simulateReadableStream function to create a simulated ReadableStream that returns the cached response. In this way, the cached response is returned chunk-by-chunk as if it were being generated by the model. You can control the initial delay and delay between chunks by adjusting the initialDelayInMs and chunkDelayInMs parameters of simulateReadableStream.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: You can see a full example of caching with Redis in a Next.js application in our Caching Middleware Recipe.

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Alternatively, each AI SDK Core function has special lifecycle callbacks you can use. The one of interest is likely onEnd, which is called when the generation is complete. This is where you can cache the full response.

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Here's an example of how you can use Upstash Redis and Next.js to cache the OpenAI response for 1 hour:

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Both the cached and the fresh responses use the
text stream protocol,
so use TextStreamChatTransport when calling this route with useChat.

metadata.title: Advanced
metadata.description: Learn how to use advanced functionality within the AI SDK and RSC API.

contents.content: This section covers advanced topics and concepts for the AI SDK and RSC API. Working with LLMs often requires a different mental model compared to traditional software development.
After these concepts, you should have a better understanding of the paradigms behind the AI SDK and RSC API, and how to use them to build more AI applications.

metadata.title: Language Models as Routers
metadata.description: Generative User Interfaces and Language Models as Routers

contents.content: Since language models can render user interfaces as part of their generations, the resulting model generations are referred to as generative user interfaces.
In this section we will learn more about generative user interfaces and their impact on the way AI applications are built.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Generative user interfaces are not deterministic in nature because they depend on the model's generation output. Since these generations are probabilistic in nature, it is possible for every user query to result in a different user interface.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Users expect their experience using your application to be predictable, so non-deterministic user interfaces can sound like a bad idea at first. However, language models can be set up to limit their generations to a particular set of outputs using their ability to call functions.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: When language models are provided with a set of function definitions and instructed to execute any of them based on user query, they do either one of the following things:

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Execute a function that is most relevant to the user query.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Not execute any function if the user query is out of bounds of the set of functions available to them.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: This way, it is possible to ensure that the generations result in deterministic outputs, while the choice a model makes still remains to be probabilistic.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: This emergent ability exhibited by a language model to choose whether a function needs to be executed or not based on a user query is believed to be models emulating "reasoning".

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: As a result, the combination of language models being able to reason which function to execute as well as render user interfaces at the same time gives you the ability to build applications where language models can be used as a router.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Historically, developers had to write routing logic that connected different parts of an application to be navigable by a user and complete a specific task.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: In web applications today, most of the routing logic takes place in the form of routes:

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /login would navigate you to a page with a login form.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /user/john would navigate you to a page with profile details about John.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /api/events?limit=5 would display the five most recent events from an events database.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: While routes help you build web applications that connect different parts of an application into a seamless user experience, it can also be a burden to manage them as the complexity of applications grow.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Next.js has helped reduce complexity in developing with routes by introducing:

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: File-based routing system

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Dynamic routing

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: API routes

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Middleware

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: App router, and so on...

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: With language models becoming better at reasoning, we believe that there is a future where developers only write core application specific components while models take care of routing them based on the user's state in an application.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: With generative user interfaces, the language model decides which user interface to render based on the user's state in the application, giving users the flexibility to interact with your application in a conversational manner instead of navigating through a series of predefined routes.

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: For routes like:

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /profile/[username]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /search?q=[query]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /media/[id]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: that have segments dependent on dynamic data, the language model can generate the correct parameters and render the user interface.

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: For example, when you're in a search application, you can ask the language model to search for artworks from different artists. The language model will call the search function with the artist's name as a parameter and render the search results.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: For actions that require a sequence of steps to be completed by navigating through different routes, the language model can generate the correct sequence of routes to complete in order to fulfill the user's request.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: For example, when you're in a calendar application, you can ask the language model to schedule a happy hour evening with your friends. The language model will then understand your request and will perform the right sequence of tool calls to:

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Lookup your calendar

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Lookup your friends' calendars

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Determine the best time for everyone

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Search for nearby happy hour spots

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Create an event and send out invites to your friends

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Just by defining functions to lookup contacts, pull events from a calendar, and search for nearby locations, the model is able to sequentially navigate the routes for you.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: To learn more, check out these examples using the streamUI function to stream generative user interfaces to the client based on the response from the language model.

metadata.title: Multiple Streamables
metadata.description: Learn to handle multiple streamables in your application.

contents.heading: multiple-streamable-uis
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC APIs allow you to compose and return any number of streamable UIs, along with other data, in a single request. This can be useful when you want to decouple the UI into smaller components and stream them separately.

contents.heading: multiple-streamable-uis
contents.content: The client side code is similar to the previous example, but the tool call will return the new data structure with the weather and forecast UIs. Depending on the speed of getting weather and forecast data, these two components might be updated independently.

contents.heading: nested-streamable-uis
contents.content: You can stream UI components within other UI components. This allows you to create complex UIs that are built up from smaller, reusable components. In the example below, we pass a historyChart streamable as a prop to a StockCard component. The StockCard can render the historyChart streamable, and it will automatically update as the server responds with new data.

metadata.title: Multistep Interfaces
metadata.description: Concepts behind building multistep interfaces

contents.content: Multistep interfaces refer to user interfaces that require multiple independent steps to be executed in order to complete a specific task.
In order to understand multistep interfaces, it is important to understand two concepts:
Tool composition
Application context
Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This is a powerful concept that allows you to break down complex tasks into smaller, more manageable steps.
Application context refers to the state of the application at any given point in time. This includes the user's input, the output of the language model, and any other relevant information.

When designing multistep interfaces, you need to consider how the tools in your application can be composed together to form a coherent user experience as well as how the application context changes as the user progresses through the interface.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: The application context can be thought of as the conversation history between the user and the language model. The richer the context, the more information the model has to generate relevant responses.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: In the context of multistep interfaces, the application context becomes even more important. This is because the user's input in one step may affect the output of the model in the next step.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: For example, consider a meal logging application that helps users track their daily food intake. The language model is provided with the following tools:

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: log_meal takes in parameters like the name of the food, the quantity, and the time of consumption to log a meal.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: delete_meal takes in the name of the meal to be deleted.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: When the user logs a meal, the model generates a response confirming the meal has been logged.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: Now when the user decides to delete the meal, the model should be able to reference the previous step to identify the meal to be deleted.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: In this example, managing the application context is important for the model to generate the correct response. The model needs to have information about the previous actions in order for it to use generate the parameters for the delete_meal tool.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This involves defining the inputs and outputs of each tool, as well as how they interact with each other.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The design of how these tools can be composed together to form a multistep interface is crucial to both the user experience of your application and the model's ability to generate the correct output.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: For example, consider a flight booking assistant that can help users book flights. The assistant can be designed to have the following tools:

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: searchFlights: Searches for flights based on the user's query.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: lookupFlight: Looks up details of a specific flight based on the flight number.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: bookFlight: Books a flight based on the user's selection.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The searchFlights tool is called when the user wants to lookup flights for a specific route. This would typically mean the tool should be able to take in parameters like the origin and destination of the flight.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The lookupFlight tool is called when the user wants to get more details about a specific flight. This would typically mean the tool should be able to take in parameters like the flight number and return information about seat availability.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The bookFlight tool is called when the user decides to book a flight. In order to identify the flight to book, the tool should be able to take in parameters like the flight number, trip date, and passenger details.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: So the conversation between the user and the model could look like this:

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: After lookupFlight returns, the passenger details needed by the bookFlight tool are not yet available in the application context. The model asks the user for those details; once the user supplies the names, the model can call bookFlight.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Looking up passenger information could've been another tool that the model could've called before calling the bookFlight tool assuming that the user is logged into the application. This way, the model does not have to ask the user for the passenger details and can proceed with the booking.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The lookupContacts tool is called before the bookFlight tool to ensure that the passenger details are available in the application context when booking the flight. This way, the model can reduce the number of steps required from the user and use its ability to call tools that populate its context and use that information to complete the booking process.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Now, let's introduce another tool called lookupBooking that can be used to show booking details by taking in the name of the passenger as parameter. This tool can be composed with the existing tools to provide a more complete user experience.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: In this example, the lookupBooking tool is used to provide the user with the status of their wife's upcoming flight. By composing this tool with the existing tools, the model is able to generate a response that includes the booking status and the departure date of the flight without requiring the user to provide additional information.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: As a result, the more tools you design that can be composed together, the more complex and powerful your application can become.

metadata.title: Prompt Engineering
metadata.description: Learn how to engineer prompts for LLMs with the AI SDK

title.children: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?

contents.heading: what-is-a-large-language-model-llm
contents.content: A Large Language Model is essentially a prediction engine that takes a sequence of words as input and aims to predict the most likely sequence to follow. It does this by assigning probabilities to potential next sequences and then selecting one. The model continues to generate sequences until it meets a specified stopping criterion.

contents.heading: what-is-a-large-language-model-llm
contents.content: These models learn by training on massive text corpuses, which means they will be better suited to some use cases than others. For example, a model trained on GitHub data would understand the probabilities of sequences in source code particularly well. However, it's crucial to understand that the generated sequences, while often seeming plausible, can sometimes be random and not grounded in reality. As these models become more accurate, many surprising abilities and applications emerge.

contents.heading: what-is-a-prompt
contents.content: Prompts are the starting points for LLMs. They are the inputs that trigger the model to generate text. The scope of prompt engineering involves not just crafting these prompts but also understanding related concepts such as hidden prompts, tokens, token limits, and the potential for prompt hacking, which includes phenomena like jailbreaks and leaks.

contents.heading: why-is-prompt-engineering-needed
contents.content: Prompt engineering currently plays a pivotal role in shaping the responses of LLMs. It allows us to tweak the model to respond more effectively to a broader range of queries. This includes the use of techniques like semantic search, command grammars, and the ReActive model architecture. The performance, context window, and cost of LLMs varies between models and model providers which adds further constraints to the mix. For example, the GPT-4 model is more expensive than GPT-3.5-turbo and significantly slower, but it can also be more effective at certain tasks. And so, like many things in software engineering, there is a trade-offs between cost and performance.

contents.heading: why-is-prompt-engineering-needed
contents.content: To assist with comparing and tweaking LLMs, we've built an AI playground that allows you to compare the performance of different models side-by-side online. When you're ready, you can even generate code with the AI SDK to quickly use your prompt and your selected model into your own applications.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Imagine you want to build a slogan generator for marketing campaigns. Creating catchy slogans isn't always straightforward!

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: First, you'll need a prompt that makes it clear what you want. Let's start with an instruction. Submit this prompt to generate your first completion.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Not bad! Now, try making your instruction more specific.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Introducing a single descriptive term to our prompt influences the completion. Essentially, crafting your prompt is the means by which you "instruct" or "program" the model.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Clear instructions are key for quality outcomes, but that might not always be enough. Let's try to enhance your instruction further.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: These slogans are fine, but could be even better. It appears the model overlooked the 'live' part in our prompt. Let's change it slightly to generate more appropriate suggestions.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Often, it's beneficial to both demonstrate and tell the model your requirements. Incorporating examples in your prompt can aid in conveying patterns or subtleties. Test this prompt that carries a few examples.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Great! Incorporating examples of expected output for a certain input prompted the model to generate the kind of names we aimed for.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Apart from designing prompts, you can influence completions by tweaking model settings. A crucial setting is the temperature.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: You might have seen that the same prompt, when repeated, yielded the same or nearly the same completions. This happens when your temperature is at 0.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Attempt to re-submit the identical prompt a few times with temperature set to 1.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Notice the difference? With a temperature above 0, the same prompt delivers varied completions each time.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Keep in mind that the model forecasts the text most likely to follow the preceding text. Temperature, a value from 0 to 1, essentially governs the model's confidence level in making these predictions. A lower temperature implies lesser risks, leading to more precise and deterministic completions. A higher temperature yields a broader range of completions.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: For your slogan generator, you might want a large pool of name suggestions. A moderate temperature of 0.6 should serve well.

contents.heading: recommended-resources
contents.content: Prompt Engineering is evolving rapidly, with new methods and research papers surfacing every week. Here are some resources that we've found useful for learning about and experimenting with prompt engineering:

contents.heading: recommended-resources
contents.content: The Vercel AI Playground

contents.heading: recommended-resources
contents.content: Brex Prompt Engineering

contents.heading: recommended-resources
contents.content: Prompt Engineering Guide by Dair AI

Rate limiting helps you protect your APIs from abuse. It involves setting a
maximum threshold on the number of requests a client can make within a
specified timeframe. This simple technique acts as a gatekeeper,
preventing excessive usage that can degrade service performance and incur
unnecessary costs.

metadata.title: Rendering UI with Language Models
metadata.description: Rendering UI with Language Models

title.children: Rendering User Interfaces on the Server

contents.content: Language models generate text, so at first it may seem like you would only need to render text in your application.

Above, the language model is passed a tool called getWeather that returns the weather information as text. However, instead of returning text, if you return a JSON object that represents the weather information, you can use it to render a React component instead.
Now you can use the object returned by the getWeather function to conditionally render a React component <WeatherCard/> that displays the weather information by passing the object as props.
Here's a little preview of what that might look like.
Rendering interfaces as part of language model generations elevates the user experience of your application, allowing people to interact with language models beyond text.
They also make it easier for you to interpret sequential tool calls that take place in multiple steps and help identify and debug where the model reasoned incorrectly.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: To recap, an application has to go through the following steps to render user interfaces as part of model generations:

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The user prompts the language model.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The language model generates a response that includes a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The tool call returns a JSON object that represents the user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The response is sent to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The client receives the response and checks if the latest message was a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: If it was a tool call, the client renders the user interface based on the JSON object returned by the tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: Most applications have multiple tools that are called by the language model, and each tool can return a different user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: For example, a tool that searches for courses can return a list of courses, while a tool that searches for people can return a list of people. As this list grows, the complexity of your application will grow as well and it can become increasingly difficult to manage these user interfaces.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC (@ai-sdk/rsc) takes advantage of RSCs to solve the problem of managing all your React components on the client side, allowing you to render React components on the server and stream them to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: Rather than conditionally rendering user interfaces on the client based on the data returned by the language model, you can directly stream them from the server during a model generation.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The createStreamableUI function belongs to the @ai-sdk/rsc module and creates a stream that can send React components to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: On the server, you render the <WeatherCard/> component with the props passed to it, and then stream it to the client. On the client side, you only need to render the UI that is streamed from the server.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: Now the steps involved are simplified:

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The user prompts the language model.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The language model generates a response that includes a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The tool call renders a React component along with relevant props that represent the user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The response is streamed to the client and rendered directly.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server

This way, all operations from language model generation to UI rendering can be done on the server, while the client only needs to render the UI that is streamed from the server.

metadata.title: Secure URL Fetching
metadata.description: How the AI SDK protects server-side fetches of URLs returned by model providers, and how to harden your deployment further.

title.children: Restrict outbound egress at the network layer

contents.content:
Many providers return a URL in their response body — a generated image,
audio, or video to download, or a polling URL to check job status. The AI SDK
fetches these server-side and returns the result to your code. Because that URL
comes from an external service, a malicious or compromised provider (or anyone
able to tamper with the response) could point it at an internal address such as
a cloud-metadata endpoint (http://169.254.169.254/…), a private host
(http://10.0.0.5/…), or localhost.

To prevent that, the SDK validates every response-supplied URL before fetching
it. This happens automatically inside the provider packages — you don't need to
configure anything.

For authenticated task-status polling, providers can construct the first URL
from the configured API endpoint. The SDK trusts that configured origin for the
initial request, but manually follows and validates every redirect away from it.
MiniMax, Kling AI, and ByteDance video polling use this protected path.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content: When the SDK fetches a URL taken from a provider response, it:

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content:
Rejects private, loopback, and link-local targets — IPv4 (10/8,
172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, CGNAT, multicast, …) and the
equivalent IPv6 ranges, plus localhost and .local. Non-http(s) schemes
are rejected too.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content:
Re-validates every redirect hop — a URL that passes but then redirects to
an internal address is blocked; the redirect is never followed blindly.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content:
Validates DNS at connection time on Node.js — every resolved address is
checked, and the socket is pinned to the validated DNS result so DNS
rebinding cannot introduce a different address between validation and
connection.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content:
Strips risky request headers — proxy-forwarding, cloud-metadata, and
cookie headers are removed before the request.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content:
Drops credentials across origins — caller headers (Authorization,
Cookie, and provider-specific API-key headers alike) are not sent to a host
on a different origin than the provider's; a redirect that crosses origin
drops all of them except the user-agent.

contents.heading: what-the-sdk-protects-against
contents.content: A blocked URL surfaces as a DownloadError.

contents.heading: fetching-untrusted-urls-directly
contents.content:
For custom integrations using @ai-sdk/provider-utils, use fetchUntrustedUrl
when the URL comes from a response or other untrusted input. It validates URLs
and redirects and withholds credentials and unknown custom headers on the first
request unless the URL matches a configured origin:

contents.heading: fetching-untrusted-urls-directly
contents.content:
Here, Authorization is sent only when the initial URL has the same origin as
providerBaseURL. Otherwise, only allowlisted metadata such as Accept,
Range, and User-Agent is sent. A cross-origin redirect drops all caller
headers except User-Agent, and credentials are never reattached on later hops.

contents.heading: fetching-untrusted-urls-directly
contents.content:
credentialedOrigin must come from your configuration, never from the response
URL. It does not disable URL validation. For a configured private endpoint, pass
trustedOrigin as well; if credentialedOrigin is omitted, fetchUntrustedUrl
uses trustedOrigin as the origin allowed to receive credentials. Extra protocol
metadata can be allowed with untrustedFirstHopHeaders: ['x-protocol-version'].
Only list headers that are safe to disclose to any destination; use a configured
origin for credentials.

contents.heading: fetching-untrusted-urls-directly
contents.content:
The existing fetchWithValidatedRedirects helper preserves its first-request
behavior: it sanitizes risky headers but still forwards authentication and
custom headers. Switch to fetchUntrustedUrl to opt into first-request
credential isolation. Existing calls to getFromApi also retain their behavior;
pass credentialedOrigin when fetching response-supplied URLs with credentials.

contents.heading: self-hosted-and-local-endpoints
contents.content:
URLs that are same-origin with the provider endpoint you configured (e.g. a
custom baseURL pointing at a self-hosted or localhost deployment) are
exempt from these checks — they target exactly the host you told the SDK to
talk to. This also applies to task-status polling. Any redirect off that origin
is still validated before the redirected request is sent.

contents.heading: dns-validation-across-runtimes
contents.content:
On Node.js, the default validated download fetch uses node:dns and an
undici connector hook to validate every resolved address at connection time.
The connector uses those exact results, closing both hostname-to-private-IP and
DNS-rebinding bypasses.

contents.heading: dns-validation-across-runtimes
contents.content:
Wrapping or replacing global fetch does not disable this protection: the
default Node.js download transport is independent of global fetch.

contents.heading: dns-validation-across-runtimes
contents.content:
Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, and framework edge runtimes use their platform
fetch, even when they expose a Node-compatible process object.

contents.heading: dns-validation-across-runtimes
contents.content:
If you explicitly inject a custom fetch, it is responsible for equivalent DNS
validation and connection pinning. Other runtimes do not expose Node's
DNS/socket hooks, so server deployments on those runtimes should restrict
network egress to private, loopback, link-local, and cloud-metadata ranges.

contents.heading: hardening-your-deployment
contents.content:
If your server fetches provider-supplied URLs and you want to close the DNS
gaps, use one (ideally both) of these:

contents.heading: restrict-outbound-egress-at-the-network-layer
contents.content:
Deny your server's network egress to 169.254.0.0/16, RFC-1918 ranges, and
loopback. This is the most robust control and is independent of application
code.

contents.heading: harden-an-injected-fetch
contents.content:
The Node.js default is already pinned. If you explicitly inject a custom
fetch, back it with an undici
Agent whose connect.lookup validates the resolved IP and lets the socket
connect only to a safe address — closing both the hostname-to-private and the
DNS-rebinding windows:

contents.heading: harden-an-injected-fetch
contents.content:
The SDK's URL validation and your custom fetch's connect-time pinning are
complementary — keep both.

headings.content: Restrict outbound egress at the network layer

metadata.title: Sequential Generations
metadata.description: Learn how to implement sequential generations ("chains") with the AI SDK

contents.content: When working with the AI SDK, you may want to create sequences of generations (often referred to as "chains" or "pipes"), where the output of one becomes the input for the next. This can be useful for creating more complex AI-powered workflows or for breaking down larger tasks into smaller, more manageable steps.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: In a sequential chain, the output of one generation is directly used as input for the next generation. This allows you to create a series of dependent generations, where each step builds upon the previous one.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: Here's an example of how you can implement sequential actions:

contents.heading: example
contents.content: In this example, we first generate ideas for a blog post, then pick the best idea, and finally create an outline based on that idea. Each step uses the output from the previous step as input for the next generation.

metadata.title: Stopping Streams
metadata.description: Learn how to cancel streams with the AI SDK

contents.content:
Canceling ongoing streams is often needed.
For example, users might want to stop a stream when they realize that the response is not what they want.
The different parts of the AI SDK support canceling streams in different ways.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core
contents.content:
The AI SDK functions have an abortSignal argument that you can use to cancel a stream.
You would use this if you want to cancel a stream from the server side to the LLM API, e.g. by
forwarding the abortSignal from the request.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui
contents.content:
The hooks, e.g. useChat or useCompletion, provide a stop helper function that can be used to cancel a stream.
This aborts the HTTP request from the client. To also stop the model request on the server, your server runtime must propagate the client disconnect to the request's AbortSignal, and your route must forward that signal to the AI SDK Core call as shown above.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui
contents.content:
Stream abort functionality is not compatible with stream resumption. If you're
using resume: true in useChat, the abort functionality will break the
resumption mechanism. Choose either abort or resume functionality, but not
both.

contents.heading: vercel
contents.content: On Vercel, request cancellation is only supported in the Node.js runtime and must be enabled for each function that needs it. Add supportsCancellation to the function's configuration in vercel.json:

contents.heading: vercel
contents.content: With cancellation enabled, calling stop() aborts the client request, Vercel aborts req.signal, and forwarding req.signal as abortSignal cancels the model request.

contents.heading: vercel
contents.content:
Without supportsCancellation, stop() still stops the client-side stream
but the server-side generation may continue.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: When streams are aborted, you may need to perform cleanup operations such as persisting partial results or cleaning up resources. The onAbort callback provides a way to handle these scenarios on the server side.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Unlike onEnd, which is called when a stream completes normally, onAbort is specifically called when a stream is aborted via AbortSignal. This distinction allows you to handle normal completion and aborted streams differently.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content:
For UI message streams (toUIMessageStreamResponse), the onEnd callback
also receives an isAborted parameter that indicates whether the stream was
aborted. This allows you to handle both completion and abort scenarios in a
single callback.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: The onAbort callback receives:

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: steps: Array of all completed steps before the abort occurred

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: This is particularly useful for:

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Persisting partial conversation history to database

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Saving partial progress for later continuation

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Cleaning up server-side resources or connections

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Logging abort events for analytics

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: You can also handle abort events directly in the stream using the abort stream part:

contents.heading: ui-message-streams
contents.content: When using toUIMessageStream, you need to handle stream abortion slightly differently. The onEnd callback receives an isAborted parameter, and you should pass consumeStream to createUIMessageStreamResponse to ensure proper abort handling:

contents.heading: ui-message-streams
contents.content: The consumeStream function is necessary for proper abort handling in UI message streams. It ensures that the stream is properly consumed even when aborted, preventing potential memory leaks or hanging connections.

contents.heading: ui-message-streams
contents.content:
The onEnd callback distinguishes consumer cancellation from an observed
abort. When the consumer cancels the UI message stream before an outcome is
declared, such as during a client disconnect, isCancelled is true,
outcome.status remains 'unknown', and isAborted remains false. When the
stream observes an abort part first, outcome.status is 'aborted',
isAborted is true, and isCancelled is absent. Check both flags when the
same cleanup should run for either case.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC does not currently support stopping streams.

metadata.title: Vercel Deployment Guide
metadata.description: Learn how to deploy an AI application to production on Vercel

contents.content: In this guide, you will deploy an AI application to Vercel using Next.js (App Router).
Vercel is a platform for developers that provides the tools, workflows, and infrastructure you need to build and deploy your web apps faster, without the need for additional configuration.

Vercel allows for automatic deployments on every branch push and merges onto the production branch of your GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket projects. It is a great option for deploying your AI application.

contents.heading: before-you-begin
contents.content: To follow along with this guide, you will need:

contents.heading: before-you-begin
contents.content: a Vercel account

contents.heading: before-you-begin

contents.heading: before-you-begin

contents.heading: before-you-begin
contents.content: This guide will teach you how to deploy the application you built in the Next.js (App Router) quickstart tutorial to Vercel. If you haven’t completed the quickstart guide, you can start with this repo.

contents.heading: commit-changes
contents.content: Vercel offers a powerful git-centered workflow that automatically deploys your application to production every time you push to your repository’s main branch.

contents.heading: commit-changes
contents.content: Before committing your local changes, make sure that you have a .gitignore. Within your .gitignore, ensure that you are excluding your environment variables (.env) and your node modules (node_modules).

contents.heading: commit-changes

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo
contents.content: Navigate to github.com

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo

contents.heading: create-git-repo
contents.content: Scroll down the page and copy the commands under the title "...or push an existing repository from the command line"

contents.heading: create-git-repo
contents.content: Go back to the terminal, paste and then run the commands

contents.heading: create-git-repo
contents.content: Note: if you run into the error "error: remote origin already exists.", this is because your local repository is still linked to the repository you cloned. To "unlink", you can run the following command:

contents.heading: create-git-repo
contents.content: Rerun the code snippet from the previous step.

contents.heading: import-project-in-vercel
contents.content: On the New Project page, under the Import Git Repository section, select the Git provider that you would like to import your project from. Follow the prompts to sign in to your GitHub account.

contents.heading: import-project-in-vercel
contents.content: Once you have signed in, you should see your newly created repository from the previous step in the "Import Git Repository" section. Click the "Import" button next to that project.

contents.heading: add-environment-variables
contents.content: Your application uses environment secrets to store your OpenAI API key using a .env.local file locally in development. To add this API key to your production deployment, expand the "Environment Variables" section and paste in your .env.local file. Vercel will automatically parse your variables and enter them in the appropriate key:value format.

contents.heading: deploy
contents.content: Press the Deploy button. Vercel will create the Project and deploy it based on the chosen configurations.

contents.heading: enjoy-the-confetti
contents.content: To view your deployment, select the Project in the dashboard and then select the Domain. This page is now visible to anyone who has the URL.

contents.heading: considerations
contents.content: When deploying an AI application, there are infrastructure-related considerations to be aware of.

contents.heading: function-duration
contents.content: In most cases, you will call the large language model (LLM) on the server. By default, Vercel serverless functions have a maximum duration of 10 seconds on the Hobby Tier. Depending on your prompt, it can take an LLM more than this limit to complete a response. If the response is not resolved within this limit, the server will throw an error.

contents.heading: function-duration
contents.content: You can specify the maximum duration of your Vercel function using route segment config. To update your maximum duration, add the following route segment config to the top of your route handler or the page which is calling your server action.

contents.heading: function-duration
contents.content: You can increase the max duration to 60 seconds on the Hobby Tier. For other tiers, see the documentation for limits.

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: AI SDK UI helpers such as useChat and useCompletion abort the client request when you call stop(). To propagate that cancellation to a Vercel Function and its model request, you must:

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: Use the Node.js runtime, which is the default for Next.js route handlers.

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: Enable supportsCancellation for the route in vercel.json.

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: Forward the route's req.signal to streamText or generateText as abortSignal.

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: For example, enable cancellation for your chat route:

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: Then forward the request signal to the AI SDK:

contents.heading: request-cancellation
contents.content: Without supportsCancellation, calling stop() closes the client-side stream but does not cancel the Vercel Function or model request. See Stopping Streams for the complete client and server setup.

contents.heading: security-considerations
contents.content: Given the high cost of calling an LLM, it's important to have measures in place that can protect your application from abuse.

contents.heading: rate-limit
contents.content: Rate limiting is a method used to regulate network traffic by defining a maximum number of requests that a client can send to a server within a given time frame.

contents.heading: rate-limit
contents.content: Follow this guide to add rate limiting to your application.

contents.heading: firewall
contents.content: A firewall helps protect your applications and websites from DDoS attacks and unauthorized access.

contents.heading: firewall
contents.content: Vercel Firewall is a set of tools and infrastructure, created specifically with security in mind. It automatically mitigates DDoS attacks and Enterprise teams can get further customization for their site, including dedicated support and custom rules for IP blocking.

metadata.title: Building Agents
metadata.description: Complete guide to creating agents with the ToolLoopAgent.

title.children: Define Agent Behavior with System Instructions

contents.content: The ToolLoopAgent provides a structured way to encapsulate LLM configuration, tools, and behavior into reusable components. It handles the agent loop for you, allowing the LLM to call tools multiple times in sequence to accomplish complex tasks. Define agents once and use them across your application.

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: When building AI applications, you often need to:

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: Reuse configurations - Same model settings, tools, and prompts across different parts of your application

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: Maintain consistency - Ensure the same behavior and capabilities throughout your codebase

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: Simplify API routes - Reduce boilerplate in your endpoints

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: Type safety - Get full TypeScript support for your agent's tools and outputs

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent-class
contents.content: The ToolLoopAgent class provides a single place to define your agent's behavior.

contents.heading: creating-an-agent
contents.content: Define an agent by instantiating the ToolLoopAgent class with your desired configuration:

contents.heading: configuration-options
contents.content: The ToolLoopAgent accepts all the same settings as generateText and streamText. Configure:

contents.heading: tools
contents.content: Provide tools that the agent can use to accomplish tasks:

contents.heading: context-and-agent-state
contents.content:
Use runtimeContext as the agent's shared runtime state. It flows through the
agent loop and is available in prepareStep, lifecycle callbacks, and final
results. If a tool needs server-side values such as credentials, scoped
permissions, or default settings, pass them through toolsContext and declare
them with the tool's contextSchema.

contents.heading: context-and-agent-state
contents.content: Set runtimeContext and toolsContext in the ToolLoopAgent constructor.

contents.heading: context-and-agent-state
contents.content:
For context that changes with each invocation, use callOptionsSchema and
prepareCall. See Configuring Call Options.

contents.heading: context-and-agent-state
contents.content:
Model call settings returned from prepareStep, such as temperature, apply
only to the current step. Later steps use the agent's top-level setting unless
they return another override.

contents.heading: context-and-agent-state
contents.content:
For the full model, including sensitive context filtering and where each context
value is available, see Runtime and Tool
Context.

contents.heading: tools-that-use-experimental-sandboxes
contents.content:
Pass experimental_sandbox when an agent tool needs a command or code execution
environment. The experimental sandbox is a per-call value, so provide it to
generate(), stream(), or the agent UI stream helper that invokes the agent.

contents.heading: tools-that-use-experimental-sandboxes
contents.content:
The experimental sandbox description is not added to the model prompt automatically. Include
it in the prompt or instructions when the model needs to know environment
details. Passing an experimental sandbox does not sandbox the tool itself; the tool must
explicitly delegate operations to the experimental sandbox. See the
Experimental Sandbox section in Tool Calling
for more details.

contents.heading: tools-that-use-experimental-sandboxes
contents.content:
You can also require approval before a tool executes. Configure approval on the
ToolLoopAgent with toolApproval:

contents.heading: tools-that-use-experimental-sandboxes
contents.content:
For manual approvals, automatic approvals and denials, dynamic policy functions,
and useChat integration, see Tool
Approvals.

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: By default, agents run for 20 steps (stopWhen: isStepCount(20)). In each step, the model either generates text or calls a tool. If it generates text, the agent completes. If it calls a tool, the AI SDK executes that tool.

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: You can configure stopWhen differently to allow more steps. After each tool execution, the agent triggers a new generation where the model can call another tool or generate text:

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: Each step represents one generation (which results in either text or a tool call). The loop continues until:

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: A finish reasoning other than tool-calls is returned, or

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: A tool that is invoked does not have an execute function, or

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: A tool call needs approval, or

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: A stop condition is met

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: You can combine multiple conditions:

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: Learn more about loop control and stop conditions.

contents.content: Control how the agent uses tools:

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: You can also force the use of a specific tool:

contents.heading: structured-output
contents.content: Define structured output schemas:

contents.heading: define-agent-behavior-with-system-instructions
contents.content: System instructions define your agent's behavior, personality, and constraints. They set the context for all interactions and guide how the agent responds to user queries and uses tools.

contents.heading: basic-system-instructions
contents.content: Set the agent's role and expertise:

contents.heading: detailed-behavioral-instructions
contents.content: Provide specific guidelines for agent behavior:

contents.heading: constrain-agent-behavior
contents.content: Set boundaries and ensure consistent behavior:

contents.heading: tool-usage-instructions
contents.content: Guide how the agent should use available tools:

contents.heading: format-and-style-instructions
contents.content: Control the output format and communication style:

contents.heading: using-an-agent
contents.content: Once defined, you can use your agent in three ways:

contents.heading: generate-text
contents.content: Use generate() for one-time text generation:

contents.heading: stream-text
contents.content: Use stream() for streaming responses:

contents.heading: respond-to-ui-messages
contents.content: Use createAgentUIStreamResponse() to create API responses for client applications:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Agents provide lifecycle callbacks that let you hook into different phases of the agent execution.
These are useful for logging, observability, debugging, and custom telemetry.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: The available lifecycle callbacks are:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onStart: Called once when the agent operation begins, before any LLM calls. Receives model info, messages, settings, and runtimeContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onStepStart: Called before each step (LLM call). Receives the step number, model, messages being sent, tools, and prior steps.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onToolExecutionStart: Called right before a tool's execute function runs. Receives the tool call object, messages, and toolContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onToolExecutionEnd: Called right after a tool's execute function completes or errors. Receives the tool call, toolExecutionMs, and a toolOutput discriminated union (type: 'tool-result' with output, or type: 'tool-error' with error).

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onStepEnd: Called after each step finishes. Receives step results including usage, performance, finish reason, and tool calls.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: onEnd: Called when all steps are finished and the response is complete. Receives all step results, total usage, and runtimeContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: For the full event data reference, see Lifecycle Callbacks. ToolLoopAgent uses the same generation lifecycle event types for onStart, onStepStart, onToolExecutionStart, onToolExecutionEnd, onStepEnd, and onEnd.

contents.heading: constructor-vs-method-callbacks
contents.content: All lifecycle callbacks can be defined in the constructor for agent-wide tracking, in the generate()/stream() call for per-call tracking, or both. When both are provided, both are called (constructor first, then the method callback):

metadata.title: Configuring Call Options
metadata.description: Pass type-safe runtime inputs to dynamically configure agent behavior.

contents.content: Call options allow you to pass type-safe structured inputs to your agent. Use them to dynamically modify any agent setting based on the specific request.

contents.heading: why-use-call-options
contents.content: When you need agent behavior to change based on runtime inputs:

contents.heading: why-use-call-options
contents.content: Add dynamic context - Inject retrieved documents, user preferences, or session data into prompts

contents.heading: why-use-call-options
contents.content: Select models dynamically - Choose faster or more capable models based on request complexity

contents.heading: why-use-call-options
contents.content: Configure tools per request - Pass user location to search tools or adjust tool behavior

contents.heading: why-use-call-options

metadata.title: Loop Control
metadata.description: Control agent execution with built-in loop management using stopWhen and prepareStep

title.children: Run Up to a Maximum Number of Steps

contents.content: You can control both the execution flow and the settings at each step of the agent loop. The loop continues until:
A finish reasoning other than tool-calls is returned, or
A tool that is invoked does not have an execute function, or
A tool call needs approval, or
A stop condition is met
The AI SDK provides built-in loop control through two parameters: stopWhen for defining stopping conditions and prepareStep for modifying settings (model, tools, messages, and more) between steps.

contents.heading: stop-conditions
contents.content: The stopWhen parameter controls when to stop execution when there are tool results in the last step. By default, ToolLoopAgent stops after 20 steps using isStepCount(20). This default is a safety measure to prevent runaway loops that could result in excessive API calls and costs.

contents.heading: stop-conditions
contents.content: WorkflowAgent does not apply a default step limit. It continues until the model stops calling tools or another natural termination condition is met. Configure an explicit condition such as isStepCount(20) when you need to bound its model calls. See WorkflowAgent Loop Control for details.

contents.heading: stop-conditions
contents.content: When you provide stopWhen, the agent continues executing after tool calls until a stopping condition is met. When the condition is an array, execution stops when any of the conditions are met.

contents.heading: use-built-in-conditions
contents.content: The AI SDK provides several built-in stopping conditions:

contents.heading: use-built-in-conditions
contents.content: isStepCount(count) — stops after a specified number of steps

contents.heading: use-built-in-conditions
contents.content: hasToolCall(...toolNames) — stops when any of the specified tools is called

contents.heading: use-built-in-conditions
contents.content: isLoopFinished() — never triggers, letting the loop run until the agent is naturally finished

contents.heading: run-until-finished
contents.content: If you want a ToolLoopAgent to run until the model naturally stops making tool calls, use isLoopFinished(). This removes its default step limit:

contents.heading: run-until-finished
contents.content:
Use isLoopFinished() with caution. Without a step limit, the agent could
potentially run indefinitely or incur significant costs if the model keeps
making tool calls.

contents.heading: combine-multiple-conditions
contents.content: Combine multiple stopping conditions. The loop stops when it meets any condition:

contents.heading: create-custom-conditions
contents.content: Build custom stopping conditions for specific requirements:

contents.heading: create-custom-conditions
contents.content: Custom conditions receive step information across all steps:

contents.heading: prepare-step
contents.content: The prepareStep callback runs before each step in the loop and defaults to the initial settings if you don't return any changes. Use it to modify settings, manage context, or implement dynamic behavior based on execution history.

contents.heading: prepare-step
contents.content: It receives messages for the current step, plus initialMessages and responseMessages when you need to distinguish the original input from assistant/tool messages accumulated in earlier steps. Treat messages as the loop's current message state: if you return a messages override, that override persists as the base for later steps, together with the response messages from each completed step.

contents.heading: dynamic-model-selection
contents.content: Switch models based on step requirements:

contents.heading: model-call-settings
contents.content:
Override provider-agnostic model call settings for an individual step. This can
be useful when tool-calling steps need more deterministic sampling than the
final response:

contents.heading: model-call-settings
contents.content:
prepareStep can override maxOutputTokens, temperature, topP, topK,
presencePenalty, frequencyPenalty, stopSequences, seed, and
reasoning. These overrides apply only to the current step. When a setting is
omitted or undefined, the top-level value is used for that step. Defined
falsy values such as temperature: 0, seed: 0, and an empty
stopSequences array are preserved.

contents.heading: context-management
contents.content: Long-running agents can accumulate large tool results, reasoning parts, and assistant messages. Use prepareStep to mutate the message state that will be used by later steps. This is useful for compaction, and you decide when compaction should happen.

contents.heading: context-management
contents.content: The messages value contains the messages that will be sent for the current step. When you return a messages override from prepareStep, that changed list becomes the base for later steps. New assistant and tool response messages are appended to it as the loop continues. If you need to rebuild a step from the discrete pieces instead of the persisted message state, use initialMessages for the original input and responseMessages for the model/tool response messages accumulated so far.

contents.heading: context-management
contents.content: The pruneMessages helper provides a built-in way to remove selected messages. You can use it inside prepareStep when you want a simple compaction strategy.

contents.heading: context-management
contents.content: The token estimator above is intentionally simple and only demonstrates one way to decide when to compact. The main point is that prepareStep can return a new messages array, and that array becomes the message state for following steps. The same pattern also works with generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: tool-selection
contents.content: Control which tools are available at each step:

contents.heading: tool-selection
contents.content: You can also force a specific tool to be used:

contents.heading: message-modification
contents.content: Transform messages before sending them to the model. Returned messages carry forward to later steps, so later messages values include your transformed messages plus the assistant/tool response messages from completed steps:

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox-selection
contents.content: Switch the experimental sandbox used for tool execution in a single step:

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox-selection
contents.content:
Unlike runtimeContext and toolsContext, an experimental sandbox returned from prepareStep
only applies to tool execution in that step. Later steps use the top-level
experimental_sandbox unless they return their own experimental sandbox override.

contents.heading: access-step-information
contents.content: Both stopWhen and prepareStep receive detailed information about the current execution:

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: You can force the agent to always use tools by combining toolChoice: 'required' with a done tool that has no execute function. This pattern ensures the agent uses tools for every step and stops only when it explicitly signals completion.

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: Key aspects of this pattern:

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: toolChoice: 'required': Forces the model to call a tool at every step instead of generating text directly. This ensures the agent follows a structured workflow.

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: done tool without execute: A tool that has no execute function acts as a termination signal. When the agent calls this tool, the loop stops because there's no function to execute.

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: Accessing results: The final answer is available in result.staticToolCalls, which contains tool calls that weren't executed.

contents.heading: forced-tool-calling
contents.content: This pattern is useful when you want the agent to always use specific tools for operations (like code execution or data retrieval) rather than attempting to answer directly.

contents.heading: manual-loop-control
contents.content: For scenarios requiring complete control over the agent loop, you can use AI SDK Core functions (generateText and streamText) to implement your own loop management instead of using stopWhen and prepareStep. This approach provides maximum flexibility for complex workflows.
