metadata.title: Memory
metadata.description: Add persistent memory to your agent using provider-defined tools, memory providers, or a custom tool.

contents.content: Memory lets your agent save information and recall it later. Without memory, every conversation starts fresh. With memory, your agent builds context over time, recalls previous interactions, and adapts to the user.

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: You can add memory to your agent with the AI SDK in three ways, each with different tradeoffs:

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Approach

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Effort

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Flexibility

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Provider Lock-in

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Provider-Defined Tools

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Low

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Medium

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Yes

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Memory Providers

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Low

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Low

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Depends on memory provider

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: Custom Tool

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: High

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: High

contents.heading: three-approaches
contents.content: No

contents.heading: provider-defined-tools
contents.content: Provider-defined tools are tools where the provider specifies the tool's inputSchema and description, but you provide the execute function. The model has been trained to use these tools, which can result in better performance compared to custom tools.

contents.heading: anthropic-memory-tool
contents.content: The Anthropic Memory Tool gives Claude a structured interface for managing a /memories directory. Claude reads its memory before starting tasks, creates and updates files as it works, and references them in future conversations.

contents.heading: anthropic-memory-tool
contents.content: The tool receives structured commands (view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename), each with a path scoped to /memories. Your execute function maps these to your storage backend (the filesystem, a database, or any other persistence layer).

contents.heading: anthropic-memory-tool
contents.content: When to use this: you want memory with minimal implementation effort and are already using Anthropic models. The tradeoff is provider lock-in, since this tool only works with Claude.

contents.heading: memory-providers
contents.content: Another approach is to use a provider that has memory built in. These providers wrap an external memory service and expose it through the AI SDK's standard interface. Memory storage, retrieval, and injection happen transparently, and you do not define any tools yourself.

contents.heading: letta
contents.content: Letta provides agents with persistent long-term memory. You create an agent on Letta's platform (cloud or self-hosted), configure its memory there, and use the AI SDK provider to interact with it. Letta's agent runtime handles memory management (core memory, archival memory, recall).

contents.heading: letta
contents.content: You can also use Letta's built-in memory tools alongside custom tools:

contents.heading: letta
contents.content: See the Letta provider documentation for full setup and configuration.

contents.heading: mem0
contents.content: Mem0 adds a memory layer on top of any supported LLM provider. It automatically extracts memories from conversations, stores them, and retrieves relevant ones for future prompts.

contents.heading: mem0
contents.content: Mem0 works across multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Cohere). You can also manage memories explicitly:

contents.heading: mem0
contents.content: See the Mem0 provider documentation for full setup and configuration.

contents.heading: supermemory
contents.content: Supermemory is a long-term memory platform that adds persistent, self-growing memory to your AI applications. It provides tools that handle saving and retrieving memories automatically through semantic search.

contents.heading: supermemory
contents.content: Supermemory works with any AI SDK provider. The tools give the model addMemory and searchMemories operations that handle storage and retrieval.

contents.heading: supermemory
contents.content: See the Supermemory provider documentation for full setup and configuration.

contents.heading: hindsight
contents.content: Hindsight provides agents with persistent memory through five tools: retain, recall, reflect, getMentalModel, and getDocument. It can be self-hosted with Docker or used as a cloud service.

contents.heading: hindsight
contents.content: The bankId identifies the memory store and is typically a user ID. In multi-user apps, call createHindsightTools inside your request handler so each request gets the right bank. Hindsight works with any AI SDK provider.

contents.heading: hindsight
contents.content: See the Hindsight provider documentation for full setup and configuration.

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: @mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory provides MongoDB Atlas-backed persistent memory with five structured tiers: Session, Semantic, Procedural, Episodic, and Scratchpad. Retrieval is powered by Atlas Vector Search using any AI SDK embedding model, with automatic index creation and per-type retention policies.

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: This integration targets AI SDK v6 because it relies on v6 APIs such as ModelMessage, ToolLoopAgent, and isLoopFinished():

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: isLoopFinished() lets the agent keep running until the tool loop naturally finishes, which is useful when memory tools need to read and write before the final response.

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: Session memory supports two modes: tool-driven (the LLM decides when to read/write — good for prototypes) and hook-driven (the runtime persists every turn via prepareCall + onEnd hooks — recommended for production). The other memory tiers (semantic, procedural, episodic, scratchpad) are always LLM-controlled and selective by design.

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: MongoDB memory works with any AI SDK model and embedding provider, with no vendor lock-in beyond MongoDB Atlas.

contents.heading: mongodb
contents.content: When to use memory providers: these providers are a good fit when you want memory without building any storage infrastructure. The tradeoff is that the provider controls memory behavior, so you have less visibility into what gets stored and how it is retrieved. You also take on a dependency on an external service.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: Building your own memory tool from scratch is the most flexible approach. You control the storage format, the interface, and the retrieval logic. This requires the most upfront work but gives you full ownership of how memory works, with no provider lock-in and no external dependencies.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: There are two common patterns:

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: Structured actions: you define explicit operations (view, create, update, search) and handle structured input yourself. Safe by design since you control every operation.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: Bash-backed: you give the model a sandboxed bash environment to compose shell commands (cat, grep, sed, echo) for flexible memory access. More powerful but requires command validation for safety.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: For a full walkthrough of implementing a custom memory tool with a bash-backed interface, AST-based command validation, and filesystem persistence, see the Build a Custom Memory Tool recipe.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: Learn how to build agents with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Agents are large language models (LLMs) that use tools in a loop to accomplish tasks.
These components work together:
LLMs process input and decide the next action
Tools extend capabilities beyond text generation (reading files, calling APIs, writing to databases)
Loop orchestrates execution through:
Context management - Maintaining conversation history and deciding what the model sees (input) at each step
Stopping conditions - Determining when the loop (task) is complete

contents.heading: agent-state-and-context
contents.content:
Agents often need server-side state that should not be placed directly in the
prompt, such as tenant settings, request IDs, feature flags, credentials, or
progress through a task.

contents.heading: agent-state-and-context
contents.content:
Use runtimeContext as the agent's shared runtime state. It flows through the
agent loop, is available in prepareStep and lifecycle callbacks, and can be
updated between steps. Use toolsContext for per-tool values such as API keys
or scoped permissions; each tool receives only its own typed context based on
its contextSchema.

contents.heading: agent-state-and-context
contents.content:
Learn more in Runtime and Tool
Context.

contents.heading: why-use-the-toolloopagent

Use HarnessAgent when you want to run a preconfigured established harness,

The rest of this section focuses on ToolLoopAgent, which is the AI SDK agent

Use @ai-sdk/tui to run a ToolLoopAgent in an interactive terminal UI. It is

metadata.title: Policy-Based Tool Approvals
metadata.description: Author tool authorization rules as code with @ai-sdk/policy-opa and Open Policy Agent.

title.children: Bring in external data and integrations
Roll out safely with shadow mode
Send decisions to your observability platform
Capability scoping at the model boundary
Allow-all when no policy is configured

contents.content: Tool Approvals let you approve or deny tool calls with a function in your agent setup. @ai-sdk/policy-opa moves those rules out of code and into Open Policy Agent (OPA) policies written in .rego.
Use it when you want authorization to be:
Written as a separate, reviewable artifact instead of a function buried in agent setup.
Testable in CI with opa test, independent of the SDK.
Editable without a code deploy (when served from a running OPA instance).
The package sits entirely on top of the public toolApproval callback. Nothing changes on the wire: the same tool-approval-request / tool-approval-response flow as built-in approvals.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: OPA is a general policy engine. If you can express a rule as code over structured input, you can enforce it at the tool boundary. Common categories:

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Security and access: scopes, roles, permissions, tenant isolation, allowlists of tools, hosts, or paths.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Business rules: who can do what, on which resources, under which conditions (for example, payments above a threshold need approval).

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Cost and usage: deny or require approval for calls that exceed a budget, token ceiling, or per-user quota.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Compliance and change control: gate destructive or regulated actions on the right approver, environment, or time window.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: The decision is not limited to the current call's arguments. The policy input also carries messages, the full model and tool-call history for the run, so a rule can factor in what already happened: prior tool calls, the sequence of actions so far, or a running total across the conversation. Examples:

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Require approval once a run has already performed N writes.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Deny a second irreversible action (a push, a delete) in the same conversation.

contents.heading: what-you-can-enforce
contents.content: Track cumulative spend or token usage across steps and stop at a ceiling.

contents.heading: best-fit-deterministic-checks
contents.content: Policy enforcement is strongest when the decision is deterministic and verifiable from structured fields, whether those fields come from the current call or the history in messages. The policy extracts a value and compares it, so the answer is the same every time.

contents.heading: best-fit-deterministic-checks
contents.content: Strong fits: scopes, permissions, numeric thresholds, allowlists, time windows, and history-aware checks like counts, sequences, and running totals.

contents.heading: best-fit-deterministic-checks
contents.content: Weak fits: content-based or semantic filtering such as "do not use bad language" or "block toxic content". These are best-effort, hard to verify, and easy to bypass. Use a dedicated moderation or classification step for them, and keep policy for the deterministic gate around it.

contents.heading: best-fit-deterministic-checks
contents.content: Rule of thumb: if you can point at a field in the input object and write an exact check on it, this is the right tool. If the rule depends on judging free-form meaning, do not lean on policy alone.

contents.heading: install
contents.content: The backends are optional peer dependencies.

contents.heading: install
contents.content: Only the backend you import is loaded.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The policy is consulted before every tool dispatch and maps to one of the standard approval statuses:

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: allow runs the tool.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: deny returns a denied result the model can reason about (no human needed).

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: requires-approval pauses the run and waits for a human tool-approval-response.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: No matching rule normalizes to not-applicable, which the SDK treats as allow. Add default decision := { "decision": "deny" } to your policy to default-deny instead.

contents.heading: writing-the-rego-policy
contents.content: The policy emits a decision object. reason is optional and is surfaced back to the model (for deny) or to the human approver (for requires-approval). A manual approval request exposes it as reason in core results and as approval.requestReason in UI messages.

contents.heading: writing-the-rego-policy
contents.content: Notes:

contents.heading: writing-the-rego-policy
contents.content: The legacy boolean shape ({ "allow": true | false, "reason": "..." }) is also accepted, so existing rules migrate without rewriting.

contents.heading: writing-the-rego-policy
contents.content: The default OPA input shape is { tool: { name }, args, messages, runtimeContext }.

contents.heading: writing-the-rego-policy
contents.content: Override the input shape with toInput:

contents.heading: test-the-policy-in-ci
contents.content: OPA ships its own test framework. These tests run without the SDK, which is the main reason policy-as-code beats policy-in-application-code.

contents.heading: test-the-policy-in-ci
contents.content: Run with opa test policy.rego policy_test.rego.

contents.heading: errors-fail-closed
contents.content: If the backend errors (server unreachable, WASM fault, misbuilt bundle), opaPolicy returns denied with the error message as the reason.

contents.heading: errors-fail-closed
contents.content: If the backend returns a present but unrecognized decision, such as an unknown decision value or a non-boolean legacy allow value, opaPolicy returns denied.

contents.heading: errors-fail-closed
contents.content: The error never rejects out of the callback and never aborts the run.

contents.heading: errors-fail-closed
contents.content: A backend outage blocks the affected call rather than silently allowing it.

contents.heading: errors-fail-closed
contents.content: This is distinct from a rule that returns no match: null or undefined normalizes to not-applicable (allow). Use a default ... deny rule if you want unmatched calls denied too.

contents.heading: option-a-wasm-in-process
contents.content: Compile the .rego to WASM ahead of time:

contents.heading: option-a-wasm-in-process
contents.content: No network call per decision.

contents.heading: option-a-wasm-in-process
contents.content: Good fit when you ship the policy with the app, or fetch it from object storage at startup.

contents.heading: option-a-wasm-in-process
contents.content: Hot-reload means rebuilding the WASM and re-instantiating the client.

contents.heading: option-b-http-running-opa-server
contents.content: One HTTP round-trip per decision.

contents.heading: option-b-http-running-opa-server
contents.content: Good fit when policies change frequently and you want hot-reload without redeploying, or when multiple services share one OPA.

contents.heading: option-b-http-running-opa-server
contents.content: Pass headers for Styra DAS / EOPA authentication.

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Policies are not limited to the tool-call input. OPA can decide based on external data such as role-to-permission mappings, IDP group memberships, entitlement lists, or allowlists, and that data can update without redeploying your app.

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: How OPA sources data is OPA's concern, not this package's. The common approaches:

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Static data at load time: pass data to wasmPolicyClient({ wasm, data }). It is handed to the bundle's setData, so the policy can read it under data.*.

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Bundles: point a running OPA server (the HTTP backend) at a bundle service so it periodically pulls fresh policy and data. Role mappings and IDP groups update without a code deploy.

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Lookups during evaluation: a policy can call out to an external service (for example an IDP or entitlements API) while it evaluates a decision.

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Learn the details from OPA, not here:

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: Policy reference

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: External data (including connecting to an IDP)

contents.heading: bring-in-external-data-and-integrations
contents.content: This package only maps the resulting decision to the SDK's approval status. The input it passes is what your policy combines with whatever data OPA already has.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Do not ship a new policy straight to enforce. The first version almost always denies things you did not mean to. shadow(approval, opts) evaluates the policy and reports the decision via onDecision, but tells the SDK every call is approved until you flip enforce: true.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Recommended rollout:

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Write the policy and test it with opa test.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Wrap it in shadow(...) with enforce: false (the default) and wire onDecision to your logs/metrics.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Run in your real environment. Inspect events where decision.type is denied or user-approval: those are the calls the policy would have changed.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Fix the policy and iterate.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: When the only denied / user-approval events are ones you want, set enforce: true.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: Telemetry semantics:

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: onDecision is fire-and-forget. A slow or throwing logger cannot block or break enforcement, and thrown errors are swallowed.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: The contract is enforcement first, observability second.

contents.heading: roll-out-safely-with-shadow-mode
contents.content: For the opposite (enforcement waits for the audit log), log from inside the underlying toolApproval instead of through shadow.

contents.heading: send-decisions-to-your-observability-platform
contents.content: onDecision is not only for rollout. Keep shadow in place with enforce: true and every decision flows to your logging, metrics, or tracing stack while the policy stays load-bearing.

contents.heading: send-decisions-to-your-observability-platform
contents.content: Each PolicyDecisionEvent carries the tool call, the policy decision (type and reason), enforced, and effective (what the SDK acted on). Compare decision against effective to spot drift.

contents.heading: send-decisions-to-your-observability-platform
contents.content: onDecision is fire-and-forget; see the telemetry semantics under shadow mode.

contents.heading: send-decisions-to-your-observability-platform
contents.content: When you use the HTTP backend, OPA can also emit decision logs natively, shipping every evaluation to a remote service for a full audit trail without any application code.

contents.heading: capability-scoping-at-the-model-boundary
contents.content: opaCapabilityMiddleware enforces policy earlier than toolApproval: before the model is even told a tool exists. This is defense in depth, plus it saves tokens and improves jailbreak rejection.

contents.heading: capability-scoping-at-the-model-boundary
contents.content: The rule at path returns a string[] of allowed tool names, or { tools: string[] }.

contents.heading: capability-scoping-at-the-model-boundary
contents.content: Tools not in the allowlist are dropped before the model sees them.

contents.heading: capability-scoping-at-the-model-boundary
contents.content: Fails closed: on a malformed response or evaluator error, params.tools is set to undefined so the model is told it has no tools. For fail-open, write the fallback in Rego.

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: When tools come from MCP discovery or a plugin registry, you cannot write per-tool rules ahead of time, and any tool you forgot is silently allowed. wrapMcpTools makes the approval total over the discovered surface by routing unmatched tools to a configurable default.

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: Defaults for uncovered tools:

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: 'user-approval' (default): require a human. Good when you trust the source but want a safety net.

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: 'denied': hard allowlist mode. The policy enumerates what is allowed; everything else is rejected.

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: 'approved': allow. Only when the discovery source is fully trusted.

contents.heading: scoping-a-discovered-tool-surface
contents.content: Despite the name, it works on any Record<string, Tool>.

contents.heading: allow-all-when-no-policy-is-configured
contents.content: optionalOpaPolicy returns undefined when client is undefined, which is the same as not passing toolApproval (the SDK approves every call). Useful for local dev or CI where the policy file is absent.

contents.heading: allow-all-when-no-policy-is-configured
contents.content: POLICY_WASM_PATH unset: toolApproval is undefined, all calls allowed, OPA modules never loaded.

contents.heading: allow-all-when-no-policy-is-configured
contents.content: POLICY_WASM_PATH set: policy loads, enforcement on.

contents.heading: allow-all-when-no-policy-is-configured
contents.content: For stricter behavior (refuse to start without a policy), use opaPolicy directly and let the missing bytes throw at startup.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: toolApproval only fires when the model calls a tool directly. A coarse dispatcher tool (a bash tool that can run git push, an HTTP tool, an MCP proxy) lets the model bypass a per-action rule by routing through it.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: The fix lives inside the dispatcher's toolApproval entry: parse the dispatcher input down to a logical (name, args) pair, then evaluate it against the same rule the direct tool uses.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: Guidance:

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: Keep the matching logic in one place: either a shared Rego helper rule (both approvals call opaPolicy with the same path) or a shared TypeScript predicate.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: Deny anything you cannot reduce to a clean invocation. Shell input is adversarial to parse, so "cannot prove it is safe" means deny.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: Honest limitation: this gates dispatch at the model's call boundary. It does not stop a tool that, once approved, performs extra side effects beyond what its input describes. For that, run untrusted execution in an out-of-band sandbox (Vercel Sandbox, Firecracker, containers) and treat the sandbox as the trust boundary.

contents.heading: transitive-enforcement-composite-tools
contents.content: Worked examples for SQL, HTTP, MCP, browser, and shell dispatchers live in the package README.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: The ai-sdk-slackbot example wires this package into a real agent end to end. It shows:

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: Every tool call gated by Rego in policies/decision.rego, editable without touching TypeScript.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: Real tools under policy: a web search scoped to a domain, a weather tool with a city allowlist, and a bash tool restricted to a read-only command allowlist (transitive enforcement).

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: Switching backends with one env var (POLICY_MODE): in-process WASM by default, or a live OPA HTTP server for hot-reloading policies in dev.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: Policy code tested independently with OPA-native tests in policies/decision_test.rego.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content: See policies/ and lib/policy/load.ts for how the policy is loaded and applied.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Everything is exported from the package root, @ai-sdk/policy-opa.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Engine-neutral core:

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: shadow(approval, opts?): wrap any approval so it is evaluated and reported but not enforced until opts.enforce: true. Recommended starting point for any new policy.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: wrapMcpTools(tools, approval, opts?): make an approval total over a discovered tool set. opts.default controls uncovered tools.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: PolicyClient: the evaluate(path, input) interface every backend implements. The seam for non-OPA engines.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Helper types: PolicyDecision, WrappedMcpTools, PolicyDecisionEvent.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: OPA backend and adapters:

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: wasmPolicyClient({ wasm, data? }): async; loads a compiled OPA WASM bundle in-process.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: httpPolicyClient({ url, headers? }): sync; client against a running OPA server.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: opaPolicy({ client, path, toInput? }): returns a toolApproval configuration. Fails closed.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: optionalOpaPolicy({ client, path, toInput? }): like opaPolicy but returns undefined when client is undefined.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: opaCapabilityMiddleware({ client, path, toInput? }): a LanguageModelV4Middleware that narrows params.tools to an allowlist. Fails closed.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: normalizeOpaDecision(result): standalone result normalization, for users who call OPA themselves.

metadata.title: Subagents
metadata.description: Delegate context-heavy tasks to specialized subagents while keeping the main agent focused.

title.children: Rendering Subagents in the UI (with useChat)

contents.content: A subagent is an agent that a parent agent can invoke. The parent delegates work via a tool, and the subagent executes autonomously before returning a result.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Define a subagent with its own model, instructions, and tools

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Create a tool that calls it for the main agent to use

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Subagent runs independently with its own context window

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Return a result (optionally streaming progress to the UI)

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Control what the model sees using toModelOutput to summarize

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Subagents add latency and complexity. Use them when the benefits outweigh the costs:

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Use Subagents When

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Avoid Subagents When

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Tasks require exploring large amounts of tokens

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Tasks are simple and focused

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: You need to parallelize independent research

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Sequential processing suffices

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Context would grow beyond model limits

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: Context stays manageable

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: You want to isolate tool access by capability

contents.heading: when-to-use-subagents
contents.content: All tools can safely coexist

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: Some tasks require exploring large amounts of information—reading files, searching codebases, or researching topics. Running these in the main agent consumes context quickly, making the agent less coherent over time.

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: With subagents, you can:

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: Spin up a dedicated agent that uses hundreds of thousands of tokens

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: Have it return only a focused summary (perhaps 1,000 tokens)

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: Keep your main agent's context clean and coherent

contents.heading: offloading-context-heavy-tasks
contents.content: The subagent does the heavy lifting while the main agent stays focused on orchestration.

contents.heading: parallelizing-independent-work
contents.content: For tasks like exploring a codebase, you can spawn multiple subagents to research different areas simultaneously. Each returns a summary, and the main agent synthesizes the findings—without paying the context cost of all that exploration.

contents.heading: specialized-orchestration
contents.content: A less common but valid pattern is using a main agent purely for orchestration, delegating to specialized subagents for different types of work. For example:

contents.heading: specialized-orchestration
contents.content: An exploration subagent with read-only tools for researching codebases

contents.heading: specialized-orchestration
contents.content: A coding subagent with file editing tools

contents.heading: specialized-orchestration
contents.content: An integration subagent with tools for a specific platform or API

contents.heading: specialized-orchestration
contents.content: This creates a clear separation of concerns, though context offloading and parallelization are the more common motivations for subagents.

contents.heading: basic-subagent-without-streaming
contents.content: The simplest subagent pattern requires no special machinery. Your main agent has a tool that calls another agent in its execute function:

contents.heading: basic-subagent-without-streaming
contents.content: This works well when you don't need to show the subagent's progress in the UI. The tool call blocks until the subagent completes, then returns the final text response.

contents.heading: handling-cancellation
contents.content: When the user cancels a request, the abortSignal propagates to the subagent. Always pass it through to ensure cleanup:

contents.heading: handling-cancellation
contents.content: If you abort the signal, the subagent stops executing and throws an AbortError. The main agent's tool execution fails, which stops the main loop.

contents.heading: handling-cancellation
contents.content: To avoid errors about incomplete tool calls in subsequent messages, use convertToModelMessages with ignoreIncompleteToolCalls:

contents.heading: handling-cancellation
contents.content: This filters out tool calls that don't have corresponding results. Learn more in the convertToModelMessages reference.

contents.heading: streaming-subagent-progress
contents.content: When you want to show incremental progress as the subagent works, use preliminary tool results. This pattern uses a generator function that yields partial updates to the UI.

contents.heading: how-preliminary-tool-results-work
contents.content: Change your execute function from a regular function to an async generator (async function*). Each yield sends a preliminary result to the frontend:

contents.heading: building-the-complete-message
contents.content: Each yield replaces the previous output entirely (it does not append). This means you need a way to accumulate the subagent's response into a complete message that grows over time.

contents.heading: building-the-complete-message
contents.content: The readUIMessageStream utility handles this. It reads each chunk from the stream and builds an ever-growing UIMessage containing all parts received so far:

contents.heading: building-the-complete-message
contents.content: Each yielded message is a complete UIMessage containing all the subagent's parts up to that point (text, tool calls, and tool results). The frontend simply replaces its display with each new message.

contents.heading: controlling-what-the-model-sees
contents.content: Here's where subagents become powerful for context management. The full UIMessage with all the subagent's work is stored in the message history and displayed in the UI. But you can control what the main agent's model actually sees using toModelOutput.

contents.heading: how-it-works-1
contents.content: The toModelOutput function maps the tool's output to the tokens sent to the model:

contents.heading: how-it-works-1
contents.content: With this setup:

contents.heading: how-it-works-1
contents.content: Users see: The full subagent execution—every tool call, every intermediate step

contents.heading: how-it-works-1
contents.content: The model sees: Just the final summary text

contents.heading: how-it-works-1
contents.content: The subagent might use 100,000 tokens exploring and reasoning, but the main agent only consumes the summary. This keeps the main agent coherent and focused.

contents.heading: write-subagent-instructions-for-summarization
contents.content: For toModelOutput to extract a useful summary, your subagent must produce one. Add explicit instructions like this:

contents.heading: write-subagent-instructions-for-summarization
contents.content: Without this instruction, the subagent might not produce a comprehensive summary. It could simply say "Done", leaving toModelOutput with nothing useful to extract.

contents.heading: rendering-subagents-in-the-ui-with-usechat
contents.content: To display streaming progress, check the tool part's state and preliminary flag.

contents.content: State

contents.content: Description

contents.content: Tool input being generated

contents.content: Tool ready to execute

contents.heading: type-safety-for-subagent-output
contents.content: Export types alongside your agents for use in UI components:

contents.heading: render-messages-and-subagent-output
contents.content: This example uses the types defined above to render both the main agent's messages and the subagent's streamed output:

contents.heading: no-tool-approvals-in-subagents
contents.content:
Subagent tools cannot use approval flows such as toolApproval (or the
deprecated needsApproval). All tools must execute automatically without user
confirmation.

contents.heading: subagent-context-is-isolated
contents.content: Each subagent invocation starts with a fresh context window. This is one of the key benefits of subagents: they don't inherit the accumulated context from the main agent, which is exactly what allows them to do heavy exploration without bloating the main conversation.

contents.heading: subagent-context-is-isolated
contents.content: If you need to give a subagent access to the conversation history, the messages are available in the tool's execute function alongside abortSignal:

contents.heading: subagent-context-is-isolated
contents.content: Use this sparingly since passing full history defeats some of the context isolation benefits.

contents.heading: streaming-adds-complexity
contents.content: The basic pattern (no streaming) is simpler to implement and debug. Only add streaming when you need to show real-time progress in the UI.

metadata.title: Terminal UI
metadata.description: Run AI SDK agents in an interactive terminal UI.

contents.content:
The @ai-sdk/tui package lets you run a local ToolLoopAgent or connect to a
remote agent through a ChatTransport in an interactive terminal interface.
It is useful for local development, demos, and internal tools where a terminal
experience is enough and you do not want to build a custom UI.

The terminal UI handles prompt input, streamed assistant responses, markdown
rendering, tool cards, reasoning sections, scrolling, and tool approval prompts.

contents.heading: installation
contents.content: Install @ai-sdk/tui alongside ai and the provider package you use:

contents.heading: running-an-agent
contents.content: Create a ToolLoopAgent and pass it to runAgentTUI:

contents.heading: running-an-agent
contents.content: runAgentTUI runs until the user exits with Esc or Ctrl+C.

contents.heading: connecting-to-a-remote-agent
contents.content:
Pass a ChatTransport instead of an agent to connect the terminal UI to a
remote AI SDK UI message endpoint:

contents.heading: connecting-to-a-remote-agent
contents.content:
The transport controls the endpoint, authentication, request body, and other
remote communication behavior. The terminal UI keeps its internal chat id and
message history private to the transport contract.

contents.heading: sandbox
contents.content:
Pass a sandbox session with the sandbox option when your agent tools need an
execution environment:

contents.heading: sandbox
contents.content:
The terminal UI forwards the sandbox to every agent call as
experimental_sandbox. Tool description functions and tool execute functions
can read it from their options and delegate command or file operations to it.
Add the sandbox description to your agent instructions if the model should know
details such as the working directory, public hostname, or exposed ports.

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content: You can control how tool calls, reasoning, and response statistics are shown:

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content: Settings:

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content:
tools: Controls tool call rendering. Use "full" to show tool input and
output, "collapsed" to show only tool cards, "auto-collapsed" to show the
latest tool expanded until another visible section appears, or "hidden" to
omit tool calls. Defaults to "auto-collapsed".

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content:
reasoning: Controls reasoning rendering. Use "full" to show reasoning,
"collapsed" to show only reasoning cards, "auto-collapsed" to show the
latest reasoning expanded until another visible section appears, or "hidden"
to omit reasoning. Defaults to "auto-collapsed".

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content:
responseStatistics: Use "outputTokensPerSecond" to show output token
throughput or "outputTokenCount" to show output token count. Defaults to
"outputTokensPerSecond".

contents.heading: display-options
contents.content:
contextSize: When provided, the terminal UI shows total token usage as a
percentage of the model context window.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
runAgentTUI supports ToolLoopAgent tool approval flows. When an agent emits a
manual approval request, the terminal UI prompts the user to approve or deny the
tool call before the agent continues.

contents.heading: compatibility
contents.content:
When using the agent option, the agent must be runnable directly from terminal
user input. It must not require per-call options and must not use structured
output, because the terminal UI cannot infer those values from a free-form
prompt. Use a transport for remote agents that need custom request handling.

contents.heading: compatibility
contents.content:
Use agent.generate() or agent.stream() directly for examples or apps that
need fixed prompts, call options, structured output, custom result inspection, or
custom stream processing.

contents.heading: controls

contents.heading: controls

contents.heading: controls
contents.content: PageUp / PageDown: scroll transcript by a full page

metadata.title: Tool Approvals
metadata.description: Add manual and automatic approval flows to ToolLoopAgent tools.

title.children: Use One Policy for All Tools

contents.content: By default, tools with an execute function run automatically when the model calls them. Use toolApproval on ToolLoopAgent to review, approve, or deny selected tool calls before they execute.
toolApproval is useful for tools that can modify data, spend money, execute code, send messages, access private data, or perform any other sensitive action.

toolApproval applies to tools executed by the AI SDK. Provider-executed
tools run provider-side and do not use AI SDK tool approvals.

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: Every approval rule returns one of these statuses, either as a string or as an object with a type field:

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: 'not-applicable': execute the tool normally without approval metadata. This is the default.

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: 'approved': record an automatic approval, then execute the tool.

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: 'denied': record an automatic denial and return a denied tool output.

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: 'user-approval': emit an approval request and wait for an explicit response.

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: For automatic approvals and denials, use the object form when you want to include a reason:

contents.heading: statuses
contents.content: Approval functions can also return undefined, which is treated the same as 'not-applicable'.

contents.heading: require-approval-for-a-tool
contents.content: Use a per-tool map when each tool has a simple policy.

contents.heading: require-approval-for-a-tool
contents.content: When runCommand is called, the agent returns a tool-approval-request instead of executing the tool.

contents.heading: decide-based-on-tool-input
contents.content: Use a per-tool approval function when the decision depends on the parsed tool input. The function receives the typed input plus toolCallId, messages, toolContext, and runtimeContext.

contents.heading: decide-based-on-tool-input
contents.content: In this example, non-admin users are denied automatically, large payments require manual approval, and smaller admin payments execute normally.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: Pass a function directly as toolApproval when approval depends on the full tool call, shared state across tools, or the complete tool set. This is called a GenericToolApprovalFunction.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: The generic function receives:

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: toolCall: the full tool call, including toolName, toolCallId, input, and whether it is dynamic.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: tools: all tools available to the model.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: toolsContext: context for all tools.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: messages: the messages sent to the model for the step that produced the tool call.

contents.heading: use-one-policy-for-all-tools
contents.content: runtimeContext: the call's shared runtime context.

contents.heading: configure-approval-per-request
contents.content: Because toolApproval is an agent setting, you can also return it from prepareCall. This is useful when approval policy depends on call options, tenant policy, or user permissions.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Manual approval requires two calls:

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Call agent.generate() or agent.stream() with toolApproval.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Read the tool-approval-request from the result or UI stream.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Ask the user or your approval system for a decision.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Add a tool-approval-response to the messages.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: Call the agent again with the updated messages.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content: If approved, the tool runs on the second call. If denied, the model receives the denial and can respond without the tool result.

contents.heading: handle-manual-approvals
contents.content:
When a tool execution is denied, consider adding an instruction such as "When
a tool execution is not approved, do not retry it" to prevent repeated
approval requests for the same action.

contents.heading: use-with-usechat
contents.content: When streaming an agent to a chat UI, approval requests appear as tool parts with state: 'approval-requested'. Respond with addToolApprovalResponse.

contents.heading: use-with-usechat
contents.content:
Only call addToolApprovalResponse for manual approvals. Automatic approvals and denials already include approval state in the stream.
When a manual approval status includes a reason, it is available as
part.approval.requestReason. A reason supplied with
addToolApprovalResponse is stored separately as part.approval.reason.

contents.heading: schema-transforms-and-persisted-approvals
contents.content:
Approval requests preserve the original schema input in inputSchemaInput when
it differs from the input presented for approval. Keep this field when persisting
responseMessages or UI messages; the UI message conversion functions preserve it
automatically.

contents.heading: schema-transforms-and-persisted-approvals
contents.content:
On continuation, the SDK reconstructs the transformed input and checks that it
matches the approved input. It never replaces the approved input with a different
value. Older or projected histories that omit the original input are rejected as
invalid tool input if revalidation fails or would change the approved value.

contents.heading: schema-transforms-and-persisted-approvals
contents.content:
The original input is included in persisted messages and UI approval streams,
including fields removed by schema transforms. A transform that removes a field
does not redact it from approval metadata.

contents.heading: trust-model
contents.content: In the standard useChat pattern, the server rebuilds the conversation from the messages the client sends each turn. The server does not persist conversation state between requests. This means the message history is client-controlled input.

contents.heading: trust-model
contents.content: Tool approvals reconstructed from this history are re-validated before execution: the tool input is checked against the tool's schema, and the approval policy is re-evaluated. However, without additional protection, a client that crafts a valid-looking approval for a schema-conforming input can bypass the human-in-the-loop step.

contents.heading: trust-model
contents.content: If your tools perform sensitive operations (modifying data, spending money, calling external APIs, accessing private resources), use experimental_toolApprovalSecret to cryptographically bind approvals to the server that issued them.

contents.heading: signing-approvals-with-experimental_toolapprovalsecret
contents.content: When you provide a secret, the server HMAC-signs each approval request at issuance and verifies the signature when the approval is replayed. A forged or tampered approval is rejected before the tool executes. Configure the secret on ToolLoopAgent (or pass it directly to generateText or streamText).

contents.heading: signing-approvals-with-experimental_toolapprovalsecret
contents.content: The signature binds the approval to the exact tool name, tool call ID, and input arguments. Changing any of these after signing invalidates the approval.

contents.heading: signing-approvals-with-experimental_toolapprovalsecret
contents.content: Every serverless instance that might handle a request needs the same secret, since one instance signs the approval and a different instance may verify it on the next turn.

contents.heading: signing-approvals-with-experimental_toolapprovalsecret

contents.heading: signing-approvals-with-experimental_toolapprovalsecret

WorkflowAgent also supports experimental_toolApprovalSecret. It signs in
a workflow step before writing the durable approval request. Pass an
environment variable reference, such as
{ environmentVariable: 'TOOL_APPROVAL_SECRET' }, so the raw secret is read
only inside signing and verification steps. Only the signature is persisted
and sent to the client.

contents.content: The WorkflowAgent from @ai-sdk/workflow is designed for building durable, resumable agents that run inside a workflow. It provides the same agent loop as the ToolLoopAgent, but adds automatic state persistence, tool schema serialization, and built-in tool approval flows that survive workflow step boundaries.

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: A standard ToolLoopAgent runs entirely in memory — if the process crashes, all progress is lost. For production agents that make multiple tool calls, this creates problems:

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: Statefulness — Long-running agent loops need to persist state across process boundaries

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: Resumability — If a step fails, you want to retry from the last checkpoint, not restart from scratch

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: Human-in-the-loop — Tools that require user approval need to pause the agent and resume later

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: Observability — Each tool call runs as a discrete workflow step, visible in dashboards

contents.heading: why-durable-agents
contents.content: WorkflowAgent solves these by running inside a workflow, where each tool execution is a durable step with automatic retries.

contents.content: For simpler use cases that don't need durability, use ToolLoopAgent from the ai package.

contents.heading: installation
contents.content: @ai-sdk/workflow requires Workflow 5, as well as the ai package and zod peer dependencies. The workflow package provides the Workflow DevKit runtime (getWritable, 'use workflow', 'use step').

contents.heading: creating-a-workflowagent
contents.content: Define an agent by instantiating the WorkflowAgent class with a model, instructions, and tools:

contents.heading: model-resolution
contents.content: The model parameter accepts two forms:

contents.heading: using-the-agent-in-a-workflow
contents.content: WorkflowAgent is designed to run inside a workflow function. The key integration points are:

contents.heading: using-the-agent-in-a-workflow
contents.content: Mark your function with 'use workflow'

contents.heading: using-the-agent-in-a-workflow
contents.content: Pass getWritable() to the agent's stream() method

contents.heading: using-the-agent-in-a-workflow
contents.content: Start the workflow from your API route

contents.heading: message-conversion
contents.content: WorkflowAgent.stream() expects ModelMessage[], not UIMessage[]. When receiving messages from the client (via useChat), convert them first:

contents.heading: writable-streams
contents.content: Unlike ToolLoopAgent where you consume the returned stream, WorkflowAgent writes raw ModelCallStreamPart chunks to a writable stream provided by the workflow runtime via getWritable(). At the response boundary, use createModelCallToUIChunkTransform() to convert these into UIMessageChunk objects for the client:

contents.heading: writable-streams
contents.content:
The transform also forwards reset-step events emitted by WorkflowAgent on
retries.
Clients remove partial parts from the failed model-call step before processing
the retried output.

contents.heading: resumable-streaming-with-workflowchattransport
contents.content: Workflow functions can time out or be interrupted by network failures. WorkflowChatTransport is a ChatTransport implementation that handles these interruptions automatically — it detects when a stream ends without a finish event and reconnects to resume from where it left off.

contents.heading: resumable-streaming-with-workflowchattransport
contents.content: The transport requires your POST endpoint to return an x-workflow-run-id response header, and a GET endpoint at {api}/{runId}/stream for reconnection:

contents.heading: resumable-streaming-with-workflowchattransport
contents.content:
WorkflowChatTransport counts UIMessageChunk objects, while the durable
WorkflowAgent stream stores raw ModelCallStreamPart objects. Replay the raw
stream from index 0 and apply the non-negative UI cursor in
createModelCallToUIChunkTransform() as shown above. Negative start indexes
require a durable stream that already stores UIMessageChunk objects and
cannot be used with this raw-to-UI conversion.

contents.heading: resumable-streaming-with-workflowchattransport
contents.content: For the full API reference, see WorkflowChatTransport.

contents.heading: tools-as-workflow-steps
contents.content: Mark tool execute functions with 'use step' to make them durable workflow steps. This gives each tool call:

contents.heading: tools-as-workflow-steps
contents.content: Automatic retries — Failed tool calls are retried automatically (default: 3 attempts)

contents.heading: tools-as-workflow-steps
contents.content: Persistence — Results survive process restarts

contents.heading: tools-as-workflow-steps
contents.content: Observability — Each tool call appears as a discrete step in the workflow dashboard

contents.heading: tools-as-workflow-steps
contents.content: Tools without 'use step' still work but run as regular in-memory functions without durability guarantees.

contents.heading: tool-approval
contents.content:
For WorkflowAgent, human approval is configured on the tool definition with
needsApproval. This is specific to WorkflowAgent; for generateText,
streamText, and ToolLoopAgent, use toolApproval instead. When a workflow
tool has needsApproval set, the agent pauses and emits an approval request to
the writable stream. The workflow suspends until the user approves or denies:

contents.heading: tool-approval
contents.content: Because the workflow is durable, the approval request survives process restarts — the user can approve hours later and the agent will resume.

contents.heading: signed-tool-approvals
contents.content:
Client-supplied message history can be modified before it is replayed to the
workflow. For tools that perform sensitive operations, configure
experimental_toolApprovalSecret to authenticate approval requests:

contents.heading: signed-tool-approvals
contents.content:
The agent HMAC-signs the approval ID, tool call ID, tool name, and validated
input. When approved message history is replayed, a missing or invalid
signature prevents the tool from executing. The signature is preserved through
the durable model-call stream, createModelCallToUIChunkTransform(),
addToolApprovalResponse(), and convertToModelMessages().

contents.heading: signed-tool-approvals
contents.content:
Use a high-entropy secret of at least 32 bytes and make the same secret
available to every worker that can issue or resume an approval. Keep old keys
available while approvals signed with them are pending; changing the secret
invalidates those pending approvals.

contents.heading: signed-tool-approvals
contents.content:
WorkflowAgent passes only the environment variable name into signing and
verification steps. Each step reads the secret from its local environment, and
the raw value is never included in step arguments, durable stream parts,
callbacks, or telemetry events. Configure the environment variable on every
worker, and do not put the secret value in runtimeContext or toolsContext.

contents.heading: signed-tool-approvals
contents.content:
You can also provide experimental_toolApprovalSecret to agent.stream().
The stream-level value overrides the constructor default.

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content:
Unlike ToolLoopAgent, WorkflowAgent does not apply a default step limit.
When stopWhen is omitted, it continues until the model stops calling tools or
another natural termination condition is met.

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content:
A model that repeatedly calls tools can make an unlimited number of model
calls. Configure an explicit stop condition when you need to bound execution
time and cost.

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content: Control how many steps the agent can take:

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content:
Omitting stopWhen already lets WorkflowAgent continue until it has finished
calling tools. You can make that intent explicit with isLoopFinished():

contents.heading: loop-control
contents.content:
isLoopFinished() is equivalent to omitting stopWhen for WorkflowAgent.
Use it with caution because a model that keeps calling tools can run
indefinitely and incur significant costs. See
isLoopFinished().

contents.heading: structured-output
contents.content: Parse agent responses into typed objects using Output:

contents.heading: configuration-options
contents.content: WorkflowAgent accepts the same generation settings as ToolLoopAgent (temperature, maxOutputTokens, topP, etc.) plus workflow-specific options.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: Pass server-side state through the agent loop without putting it into the prompt. Use these instead of the previous experimental_context option.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: runtimeContext is shared agent state that flows through prepareStep, lifecycle callbacks, and onEnd. Treat it as immutable; return a new value from prepareStep to update it for the current and subsequent steps.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: toolsContext is a per-tool map keyed by tool name. Each tool's execute only sees its own validated entry as context. Tools that declare a contextSchema validate their entry against the schema before execution.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: runtimeContext and toolsContext can also be passed per-call to stream(), where they override the constructor-level defaults.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: Because WorkflowAgent runs inside the Workflow runtime, context values may be persisted and replayed across workflow and step boundaries. Keep runtimeContext, toolsContext, and any context values returned from prepareStep serializable. Use plain data such as strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, plain objects, dates, URLs, maps, sets, and other Workflow-supported structured data. Do not put functions, class instances, symbols, WeakMap, WeakSet, database clients, or SDK clients in context. Pass identifiers or configuration data instead, and recreate non-serializable resources inside step functions.

contents.heading: runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: This differs from ToolLoopAgent, which runs in memory and can carry richer JavaScript values for the lifetime of a single process. With WorkflowAgent, treating context as durable data keeps workflow replay and step execution reliable.

contents.heading: experimental_sandbox
contents.content:
Pass a sandbox session when tools need an execution environment. The sandbox is
available to tool descriptions and execute functions as
experimental_sandbox, and to prepareStep, where you can override it for the
current step:

contents.heading: experimental_sandbox
contents.content:
experimental_sandbox is a live runtime handle, not durable context. Do not
store it in runtimeContext or toolsContext. If a tool runs as a separate
workflow step, pass serializable sandbox identifiers or configuration and
reattach inside that step.

contents.heading: preparecall
contents.content: Called once before the agent loop starts. Use it to transform model, instructions, or other settings based on runtime context:

contents.heading: preparestep
contents.content: Called before each step (LLM call). Use it to modify settings, manage context, or inject messages dynamically:

contents.heading: preparestep
contents.content: Both prepareCall and prepareStep can also be passed per-call in stream().

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Agents provide lifecycle callbacks for logging, observability, and custom telemetry. All callbacks can be defined in the constructor (agent-wide) or in stream() (per-call). When both are provided, both fire (constructor first):

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
For concrete tool sets, WorkflowAgentToolExecutionStartEvent and
WorkflowAgentToolExecutionEndEvent preserve the relationship between each
tool name and its input, context, and output types. TypeScript narrows the
nested toolCall directly, but use Extract or a user-defined type guard when
you need to narrow the correlated toolContext or output fields by tool name.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Tool input callbacks (onInputStart, onInputDelta, and
onInputAvailable) are also preserved by WorkflowAgent. The model call runs
inside a durable step, while callback functions remain in the workflow
context because arbitrary functions cannot cross the step boundary. As a
result, WorkflowAgent records the callback events during the model step and
replays them in order immediately after that step completes, before tool
execution and step lifecycle callbacks. They do not run concurrently with
model generation and cannot provide in-flight cancellation or backpressure.
Each callback receives its tool's toolsContext entry after
contextSchema validation.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
For highly fragmented tool inputs, onInputDelta replay data is part of the
durable model-step result. Only configure onInputDelta when each generated
delta is needed; omit it to avoid retaining delta replay data.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
The deprecated experimental_onStart and experimental_onStepStart names
remain available for backwards compatibility. When both the stable and
experimental name are provided in the same constructor or stream() call, the
stable callback is used.

contents.heading: type-inference
contents.content: Infer the UI message type for type-safe client components:

contents.heading: migrating-from-durableagent
contents.content: WorkflowAgent replaces the Workflow DevKit's DurableAgent. The two share the same core idea — a durable agent loop that runs inside a workflow — but WorkflowAgent moves the class into the AI SDK, tightens typing, and introduces first-class tool approval. If you are using DurableAgent today, follow the steps below to switch.

contents.heading: change-the-import-and-class-name
contents.content: DurableAgent was exported from workflow/ai. WorkflowAgent is exported from @ai-sdk/workflow, alongside its helpers.

contents.heading: change-the-import-and-class-name
contents.content: Install the new package alongside workflow:

contents.heading: write-modelcallstreampart-not-uimessagechunk
contents.content: DurableAgent wrote UIMessageChunk objects directly to the writable returned by getWritable(). WorkflowAgent writes the lower-level ModelCallStreamPart shape and leaves the conversion to a transform at the response boundary. This keeps the durable stream provider-shaped and avoids baking a UI protocol into the workflow payload.

contents.heading: replace-maxsteps-with-stopwhen
contents.content: DurableAgent accepted maxSteps directly. WorkflowAgent uses the AI SDK's shared stopWhen conditions so the same stop logic works across ToolLoopAgent, generateText, and streamText.

contents.heading: replace-maxsteps-with-stopwhen
contents.content: See Loop Control for the full list of stop conditions.

contents.heading: replace-experimental_output-with-output
contents.content: The returned value is now on result.output (previously result.experimental_output).

contents.heading: workflowagent-use-needsapproval-for-human-in-the-loop-tools
contents.content: With DurableAgent, tool approval was implemented by calling a Hook from inside the tool's execute function. WorkflowAgent makes approval a first-class tool property — the agent emits the approval request, suspends the workflow, and resumes automatically when the user responds.

contents.heading: workflowagent-use-needsapproval-for-human-in-the-loop-tools
contents.content:
needsApproval also accepts an async function so you can decide per-input
whether approval is required (see Tool Approval above).

contents.heading: uimessages--collectuimessages-is-gone
contents.content: DurableAgent.stream() returned accumulated uiMessages when collectUIMessages: true was set. WorkflowAgent.stream() returns ModelMessage[] on result.messages instead.

contents.heading: uimessages--collectuimessages-is-gone
contents.content: For persistence, store UIMessage[] as your source of truth and call convertToModelMessages before passing them to the agent — this is the pattern described in Chatbot Message Persistence. There is no built-in ModelMessage → UIMessage conversion, so avoid persisting result.messages as your only copy if you need to render the conversation in the UI later.

contents.heading: non-streaming-generation
contents.content: Use agent.generate() when you need the completed result without streaming:

contents.heading: non-streaming-generation
contents.content: Generation uses the provider's doGenerate() method and the same durable tool loop as streaming. It defaults to a maximum of 20 steps, while stream() remains unbounded unless you set stopWhen. Generation failures reject; stream model errors retain their existing result.error behavior.

contents.heading: non-streaming-generation
contents.content: The generated result uses core's final-step text and all-step content, tool results, warnings, and usage semantics. responseMessages contains generated messages only. output defaults to text and supports constructor or per-call output specifications. End callbacks run before complete-output parsing.

contents.heading: non-streaming-generation
contents.content: Use result getters inside the workflow, then return selected serializable fields through run.returnValue. Returning the whole result class is not supported. See the generate reference for options and remaining differences.

contents.heading: approval-round-trips-without-streaming
contents.content: Both generate() and stream() return approval requests even when no writable is provided. For generation, keep result.responseMessages, display the requested tool and input to the user, then append their decision to the next call:

contents.heading: approval-round-trips-without-streaming
contents.content: Use the approvalId from the returned tool-approval-request and the user's approved decision. Preserve the request signature and original tool-call input when storing the conversation. Configure experimental_toolApprovalSecret with the same environment-variable reference for both invocations. Secrets are resolved inside durable signing and verification steps.

contents.heading: approval-round-trips-without-streaming
contents.content: Local tools execute only after approval validation; denied tools produce an execution-denied result. Provider-executed approvals are forwarded to the provider. Tools that wait on Workflow hooks can also suspend and resume during generation.

contents.heading: deadlines-cancellation-and-replay
contents.content: Inside a workflow, timeout sets an absolute deadline for model calls. Each model step checks it before dispatch, before SDK retry attempts, and after the provider returns. The same deadline remains in effect after a tool suspends and resumes. SDK maxRetries governs model retries; the durable model step does not add another retry layer. Expiration before dispatch rejects with TimeoutError; expiration during SDK retry backoff rejects with AbortError. Neither starts a new retry.

contents.heading: deadlines-cancellation-and-replay
contents.content: A model deadline does not cancel a tool waiting on a Workflow hook. The run can remain suspended after that deadline. Once the hook resumes, any subsequent model call fails before dispatch if the deadline has expired. To stop the suspended run, use the Workflow runtime's run.cancel() API. Cancellation does not undo external side effects that already happened.

contents.heading: deadlines-cancellation-and-replay
contents.content: Workflow reuses completed durable model and tool steps on replay. Put external side effects inside step functions and use the external service's idempotency mechanism where necessary: completed-step replay does not guarantee exactly-once effects for an interrupted attempt.

contents.heading: deadlines-cancellation-and-replay
contents.content: Generated files and result getters are available inside workflow code. Return the data the caller needs, for example:

contents.heading: deadlines-cancellation-and-replay
contents.content: The generated result class itself is not a supported run.returnValue shape. Request and response bodies are omitted unless explicitly enabled with include; available response headers, timestamps, IDs and provider metadata are retained. Workflow uses its existing callback shapes and preparation rules, and reports model response timing rather than complete tool/step timing. It does not implement ToolLoopAgent's callOptionsSchema abstraction or core's live streaming readers and HTTP response helpers.

contents.heading: replace-experimental_context-with-runtimecontext-and-toolscontext
contents.content: WorkflowAgent no longer accepts experimental_context. Split the value into shared agent state (runtimeContext) and per-tool state (toolsContext); each tool's execute then receives only its own validated entry as context. See runtimeContext and toolsContext for the full shape.

contents.heading: everything-else
contents.content: Other options carry over with the same names: prepareStep, onStart, onStepStart, onStepEnd, onEnd, onError, toolChoice, activeTools, timeout, repairToolCall, experimental_sandbox, and the usual generation settings (temperature, maxOutputTokens, topP, …). WorkflowAgent additionally adds prepareCall (runs once before the loop) and the onToolExecutionStart / onToolExecutionEnd lifecycle callbacks documented above. The deprecated experimental_onStart and experimental_onStepStart aliases remain available for backwards compatibility.

metadata.title: Workflow Patterns
metadata.description: Learn workflow patterns for building reliable agents with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Combine the building blocks from the overview with these patterns to add structure and reliability to your agents:
Sequential Processing - Steps executed in order
Parallel Processing - Independent tasks run simultaneously
Evaluation/Feedback Loops - Results checked and improved iteratively
Orchestration - Coordinating multiple components
Routing - Directing work based on context

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Consider these key factors:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Flexibility vs Control - How much freedom does the LLM need vs how tightly you must constrain its actions?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Error Tolerance - What are the consequences of mistakes in your use case?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Cost Considerations - More complex systems typically mean more LLM calls and higher costs

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Maintenance - Simpler architectures are easier to debug and modify

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Start with the simplest approach that meets your needs. Add complexity only when required by:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Breaking down tasks into clear steps

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Adding tools for specific capabilities

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Implementing feedback loops for quality control

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Introducing multiple agents for complex workflows

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Let's look at examples of these patterns in action.

contents.heading: patterns-with-examples
contents.content: These patterns, adapted from Anthropic's guide on building effective agents, serve as building blocks you can combine to create comprehensive workflows. Each pattern addresses specific aspects of task execution. Combine them thoughtfully to build reliable solutions for complex problems.

contents.heading: sequential-processing-chains
contents.content: The simplest workflow pattern executes steps in a predefined order. Each step's output becomes input for the next step, creating a clear chain of operations. Use this pattern for tasks with well-defined sequences, like content generation pipelines or data transformation processes.

contents.heading: routing
contents.content: This pattern lets the model decide which path to take through a workflow based on context and intermediate results. The model acts as an intelligent router, directing the flow of execution between different branches of your workflow. Use this when handling varied inputs that require different processing approaches. In the example below, the first LLM call's results determine the second call's model size and system prompt.

contents.heading: parallel-processing
contents.content: Break down tasks into independent subtasks that execute simultaneously. This pattern uses parallel execution to improve efficiency while maintaining the benefits of structured workflows. For example, analyze multiple documents or process different aspects of a single input concurrently (like code review).

contents.heading: orchestrator-worker
contents.content: A primary model (orchestrator) coordinates the execution of specialized workers. Each worker optimizes for a specific subtask, while the orchestrator maintains overall context and ensures coherent results. This pattern excels at complex tasks requiring different types of expertise or processing.

contents.heading: evaluator-optimizer
contents.content: Add quality control to workflows with dedicated evaluation steps that assess intermediate results. Based on the evaluation, the workflow proceeds, retries with adjusted parameters, or takes corrective action. This creates robust workflows capable of self-improvement and error recovery.

metadata.title: Batch
metadata.description: Learn how to process asynchronous batches with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Batch support is experimental and the API may change in patch releases.

Batches let you submit multiple independent requests for asynchronous
processing. The provider processes the batch in the background, so your
application does not need to keep the request open while the model generates
the results. This is useful for workloads such as classification,
summarization, and content generation that do not need an immediate response.

The batch API supports text generation with type: 'text' and image generation
with type: 'image'.
The AI SDK provides five functions for the batch lifecycle:

experimental_startBatch
submits a batch and returns its initial status and a serializable reference.

experimental_getBatchStatus
retrieves the latest status and request counts.

experimental_getBatchResults
asynchronously iterates over the terminal result for each request.

experimental_cancelBatch
requests cancellation of a batch.

experimental_listBatches
lists batches and their latest statuses.

All five functions are exported from ai. The examples below use aliases so
the shorter names can be used in application code:

Cancellation and listing are optional provider capabilities. Calling either
function with a provider that does not implement it throws an
UnsupportedFunctionalityError. In the cancellation and listing examples
below, provider represents a batch provider that implements the respective
capability.

contents.heading: supported-providers
contents.content:
Batch processing requires a provider that implements the batch interface.
Support is provider- and model-specific. The first-party providers with
support are:
