contents.content: Batch processing

contents.heading: supported-providers
contents.content:
See the provider documentation for the supported models, limits, and native
batch behavior. For example, OpenAI batch support is available through the
Responses API, not openai.chat().

contents.heading: starting-a-batch
contents.content:
Pass a provider and one or more uniquely identified requests to startBatch.
Each text request must specify type: 'text', a model ID, and either a text prompt
or a messages array. Requests can use different model IDs when supported by
the provider. Each request can also use the usual text-generation settings such
as instructions, maxOutputTokens, temperature, topP, topK,
presencePenalty, frequencyPenalty, stopSequences, seed, and reasoning.

contents.heading: starting-a-batch
contents.content:
Tool definitions and tool settings are provided on individual requests. A tool
with the same name must have the same definition in every request that uses it.

contents.heading: starting-a-batch
contents.content:
Request IDs must be non-empty and unique within the batch. They are the link
between an input request and its result. Results are not guaranteed to arrive
in input order, so use the ID rather than an array position when associating a
result with application data.

contents.heading: starting-a-batch
contents.content:
You can pass provider-specific settings at the batch level with
providerOptions, or on an individual request with that request's
providerOptions. Settings supported by the provider can differ between the
two levels. The warnings property on the start result contains warnings about
unsupported settings.

contents.heading: starting-a-batch
contents.content:
The batch reference returned by startBatch is serializable. Persist it
before the process exits if the batch will be completed by another process or
at a later time. When retrieving a batch, pass the same provider. The AI SDK
uses the reference to ensure that a batch is not read through an incompatible
provider.

contents.heading: image-requests
contents.content:
Image requests use the same prompt and generation settings as generateImage:
prompt, n, size, aspectRatio, seed, and providerOptions. A prompt
can also contain input images and a mask for providers that support image
editing. Provider batch endpoints may support only a subset of these options;
unsupported options produce warnings or errors.

contents.heading: image-requests
contents.content:
Successful image items have an images array of GeneratedFile values, plus
image warnings, response metadata, usage, and provider metadata when the
provider supplies them. Successful text items have text and content
properties. Use the type property to narrow mixed results:

contents.heading: batch-tools
contents.content:
Batch text requests support both client-defined tools and provider-defined
tools. Tool definitions are sent with each request that includes them, so the
model can call them independently for each request.

contents.heading: batch-tools
contents.content:
Client-defined tools are definition-only in a batch. Their execute functions
are never invoked, and the AI SDK does not submit tool results or start a
follow-up generation after retrieving a tool call. Pass the same tool set to
getBatchResults to validate and normalize returned tool calls:

contents.heading: batch-tools
contents.content:
Provider-defined tools, such as web search or code execution, can execute on
the provider when supported by that provider's batch API. Their tool calls and
results are returned as normalized content parts. See the provider
documentation for the tools and models available in batches.

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content:
The start result includes the initial status. Use getBatchStatus to retrieve
the latest status while the provider is processing the batch:

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content: The normalized batch status is one of:

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content: pending — the provider is still processing the batch.

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content:
completed — the batch reached a terminal state and results can be
retrieved.

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content:
failed — the batch could not be completed. The error property may
contain additional details.

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content:
Status responses can also include requestCounts, createdAt, expiresAt,
rawStatus, and provider metadata. requestCounts reports the total,
pending, completed, and failed requests known by the provider.

contents.heading: checking-batch-status
contents.content:
For webhook-capable providers, pass webhookUrl to startBatch to
receive a notification when the batch reaches a terminal state. Webhook
support and payloads are provider-specific. The provider pages linked above
describe their webhook behavior; providers that do not support webhooks return
an unsupported warning and continue without one.

contents.heading: cancelling-a-batch
contents.content: Use cancelBatch to ask the provider to stop processing a batch:

contents.heading: cancelling-a-batch
contents.content:
A successful call means that the provider accepted the cancellation request.
It does not guarantee that cancellation has finished or that every pending
request will be cancelled. Use getBatchStatus to retrieve the latest status
after requesting cancellation.

contents.heading: cancelling-a-batch
contents.content:
The result can include provider metadata with additional information from the
cancellation response.

contents.heading: listing-batches
contents.content:
Use listBatches to retrieve batches from the provider. Results are paginated.
Pass the returned nextCursor as cursor to retrieve the next page:

contents.heading: listing-batches
contents.content:
Each item is a serializable batch reference with its latest normalized status,
so it can be passed directly to getBatchStatus, getBatchResults, or
cancelBatch. Cursors are opaque and provider-specific; applications should
store or pass them unchanged rather than inspect their contents.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content:
After the batch is complete, getBatchResults returns an async iterable. Each
item contains the ID and terminal status for one input request:

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content: Successful items include:

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content:
text — the concatenated text content. This can be an empty string when the
result contains no text parts.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content:
content — ordered, normalized content parts, including text, reasoning,
files, sources, tool calls, tool results, and provider content where
supported.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content: finishReason and optional rawFinishReason.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content: usage and optional response metadata.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content: Optional providerMetadata.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content:
Failed, cancelled, and expired items include their id and status. Failed
items include an error; cancelled and expired items may also include one.
One failed request does not necessarily mean that every request in the batch
failed, so handle each item independently.

contents.heading: retrieving-results
contents.content:
Batch retrieval does not run an AI SDK tool loop or invoke client-defined
execute functions. Provider-defined tools may execute on the provider as part
of batch processing. Treat result content and provider metadata as untrusted
model output, and avoid logging it indiscriminately because it can contain
sensitive data.

contents.heading: request-controls
contents.content:
All batch lifecycle functions accept providerOptions, headers, timeout,
and abortSignal for the current operation. getBatchStatus,
getBatchResults, and listBatches also accept maxRetries:

contents.heading: request-controls
contents.content:
maxRetries controls retries for status, result retrieval, and listing. It
does not retry batch creation or cancellation. It defaults to 2; set it to 0
to disable retries.

contents.heading: request-controls
contents.content: abortSignal cancels the current API request.

contents.heading: request-controls
contents.content: timeout limits the current HTTP operation.

contents.heading: request-controls
contents.content:
These controls affect communication with the provider. They do not change the
provider's processing deadline or cancel a batch that has already been
submitted.

metadata.title: Code Mode
metadata.description: Let models orchestrate AI SDK tools with sandboxed JavaScript and TypeScript.

contents.content:
Code mode lets a model write JavaScript or TypeScript that calls your AI SDK
tools. The generated code runs in an isolated QuickJS sandbox and returns a JSON-serializable result.
Instead of calling tools one at a time, a model can use code mode to:
call independent tools concurrently
transform and combine tool results
filter large tool responses before returning them to the model
use JavaScript control flow for multi-step operations
Code mode is provided by the @ai-sdk/code-mode package.

Code mode is experimental and its APIs may change in future releases. It
requires Node.js 22 or newer and is not available in browser or edge runtimes.

contents.heading: using-code-mode-with-generatetext
contents.content:
Define your tools in one tool set and use experimental_toolCallers to select
which tools code mode can call:

contents.heading: using-code-mode-with-generatetext
contents.content:
The keys in experimental_toolCallers are the tools being governed.
The values identify their allowed callers. In this example, getInventory and
getDemand are available through code_mode, but they are not exposed to the
model as directly callable tools. Include DIRECT_TOOL_CALL when a tool should
also be callable directly:

contents.heading: using-code-mode-with-generatetext
contents.content:
Tools without an experimental_toolCallers entry keep their existing direct
tool-calling behavior.

contents.heading: using-code-mode-with-generatetext
contents.content:
The code mode tool description includes TypeScript signatures generated from
the input and output schemas of its allowed tools. Descriptions,
inputExamples, and precise schemas help the model write correct code.

contents.heading: discovering-tools-through-conversation
contents.content:
By default, changing the tools routed through code mode also changes the
provider-visible code_mode tool description. Set toolDiscovery to
'conversation' to keep that tool definition stable and provide the current
host-tool catalog in a user message instead:

contents.heading: discovering-tools-through-conversation
contents.content:
The AI SDK adds a complete code mode capability catalog to the conversation
before calling the model. The catalog contains TypeScript signatures and call
examples for the tools routed through code mode. When the effective tools or
their definitions change in a later step or generation call, the SDK adds a
new catalog that replaces earlier catalogs.

contents.heading: discovering-tools-through-conversation
contents.content:
This mode can improve prompt-cache reuse because the provider-visible tool
definition stays unchanged. Actual cache behavior depends on the model
provider.

contents.heading: discovering-tools-through-conversation
contents.content: For the example above, the model can generate a program like:

contents.heading: discovering-tools-through-conversation
contents.content:
Each provided tool is available through the global tools object. Tool names
that are not valid JavaScript identifiers use bracket notation:

contents.heading: searching-deferred-tools
contents.content:
Use toolSearch() with deferLoading: true to expose tools only when the model
needs them. With toolDiscovery: 'conversation', discovered definitions arrive
in user messages, preserving the tool-definition cache by keeping the
provider-visible code mode tool unchanged. Actual prompt-cache reuse depends on
the provider.

contents.heading: searching-deferred-tools
contents.content:
See Tool Search for direct-calling and code mode
examples.

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: Generated programs support:

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: JavaScript and type-stripped TypeScript

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: top-level await and return

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: standard JavaScript control flow and data transformations

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: Promise.all for concurrent tool calls

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: JSON.parse and JSON.stringify

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content: console.log, console.info, console.debug, and console.error

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content:
Every tool call is asynchronous and must be awaited or otherwise observed.
Returning while tool calls are still detached fails the invocation and aborts
the outstanding work.

contents.heading: writing-code-mode-programs
contents.content:
Programs and tool inputs and outputs cross the sandbox boundary as JSON. Return
only JSON-serializable values. TypeScript support is limited to removing type
syntax; code mode does not perform type checking or provide a full TypeScript
compiler.

contents.heading: direct-execution
contents.content:
Use experimental_runCodeMode when you want to execute a program directly
instead of exposing code mode to a model:

contents.heading: direct-execution
contents.content:
runCodeMode returns the value returned by the program. It uses the same
sandbox and execution limits as the AI SDK tool.

contents.heading: tool-approval
contents.content:
Code mode does not currently integrate with AI SDK tool approval flows. Tool
calls made by generated code are nested inside the code mode invocation, so
they cannot pause the generation and surface a tool approval request to your
application.

contents.heading: tool-approval
contents.content:
Do not expose tools that rely on user approval to code mode. Keep those tools
directly callable by the model instead. If a nested tool requires approval,
the call is rejected rather than executed.

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content:
Every invocation has limits for runtime, memory, source size, results, tool
payloads, console output, and tool calls. Override them with
executionPolicy:

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: The available limits are:

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: timeoutMs: total execution time

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: memoryLimitBytes: QuickJS memory

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxStackSizeBytes: QuickJS stack

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxSourceBytes: generated source code

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxResultBytes: returned result

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxConsoleOutputBytes: combined console output

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxToolInputBytes: input for each tool call

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxToolOutputBytes: output from each tool call

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxBridgeRequests: total tool calls

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content: maxInFlightBridgeRequests: concurrent tool calls

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content:
Use experimental_setMaxWorkers to set a process-wide cap on concurrent code
mode workers:

contents.heading: execution-limits
contents.content:
Without an explicit cap, code mode chooses one based on available memory, up to
32 workers.

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content: Each invocation receives a fresh QuickJS context. Sandboxed code cannot access:

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content: Node.js globals such as process, require, or module

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content: the host file system or module loader

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content: fetch, WebCrypto, or performance APIs

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content: eval or dynamic Function construction

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content:
Network or system access must be implemented in a tool and explicitly provided
to code mode.

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content:
Treat the sandbox as defense in depth. Generated code and tool arguments are
untrusted. Tools execute in your host application, outside the QuickJS
sandbox, and every capability exposed by a provided tool is available to the
generated program. Enforce authorization and validate inputs inside each tool.

contents.heading: isolation-and-tool-access
contents.content:
Tool input schemas are validated before their execute functions run. Abort
signals and AI SDK tool execution context are forwarded to nested tool calls.

metadata.title: Decisions
metadata.description: Decide answers to Choice, Score, and Boolean questions against shared state.

contents.content:
experimental_decide decides answers to named questions against one shared state using
a decision model. State can be a string, JSON object, or JSON array. An array
is one state, not a batch of unrelated inputs.

This API and the decision model specification are experimental and may change
in patch releases. Pass a decision model instance, resolve a model through a
provider registry, or use a string ID. Strings resolve through Vercel AI Gateway
unless you configure a decision-capable default provider.

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: Use a provider's decisionModel factory:

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: Provider

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: Example model

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: TypeSafe AI

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: typeSafeAi.decisionModel('jev-latest')

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: OpenAI

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: openai.decisionModel('gpt-6-luna')

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: Anthropic

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: anthropic.decisionModel('claude-haiku-4-5-20251001')

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: Google

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content: google.decisionModel('gemini-3.5-flash-lite')

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content:
TypeSafe AI's Jev and OpenAI's
Decisions API
supply native Choice, Score, and Boolean decisions. Each question is evaluated
independently. Choice and Score answers include native probability distributions.

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content:
Anthropic and Google adapt structured language-model output for all three types,
evaluating all questions in one prompt. Their Boolean answers contain prompted
estimates of P(true), and Choice and Score answers omit probability distributions.
Select a model that supports the provider's structured-output API and judge quality
against your own labeled examples before choosing a model for a task.

contents.heading: provider-models
contents.content:
The Anthropic and Google language-model adapters request reasoning: 'none' by
default. Each provider maps this setting to its model's reasoning controls. Pass
supported reasoning settings through providerOptions to override this default.
OpenAI decision models use the Decisions endpoint and do not accept Responses
API reasoning options.

contents.heading: model-aliases-and-registries
contents.content:
Use customProvider to give models application-specific names, then register
providers with createProviderRegistry:

contents.heading: model-aliases-and-registries
contents.content:
Registry IDs use providerId:modelId; the separator option changes the
separator. Only the first separator is used, so model IDs can contain it.
Custom aliases take precedence over a fallback provider. A fallback only resolves
unknown model IDs; it does not retry failed decisions or substitute a model
when a question type is unsupported. Registered providers keep their own
credentials and settings. Registry language/image middleware does not wrap
decision models.

contents.heading: default-provider-strings
contents.content:
String IDs use Vercel AI Gateway by default. Configure Gateway authentication
with AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY or Vercel OIDC, then pass a Gateway model ID:

contents.heading: default-provider-strings
contents.content:
To resolve strings through your own provider or aliases, configure the default
provider once at application startup:

contents.heading: default-provider-strings
contents.content:
A direct provider such as typeSafeAi can also be the default; then use its
unprefixed model ID, such as 'jev-latest'. String values in decisionModels
also resolve through this global default. Prefer model instances in aliases to
avoid resolution cycles. Global configuration affects other AI SDK functions
too; avoid changing it per request in a shared process.

contents.heading: default-provider-strings
contents.content:
An explicitly configured default provider must expose a decisionModel
method; Gateway is used only when no default provider is configured. Missing
registry providers throw NoSuchProviderError; missing models or decision
capabilities throw
NoSuchModelError with modelType: 'decisionModel'. Unsupported model versions
throw UnsupportedModelVersionError, including models returned by registries.
The stable ProviderV4 and ProviderRegistryProvider interfaces are unchanged;
keep the inferred registry type, or use Experimental_DecisionProviderRegistry,
to retain its experimental decisionModel method.

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Type

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Criteria

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Answer

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: choice

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: A nonempty map of options to descriptions

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: choice, inferred as a union of option keys; optional probabilities

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: score

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: At least two ordered level descriptions

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Fractional score in [0, levels.length - 1]; optional probabilities

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: boolean

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Optional true and false descriptions

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content: Required probability, the model-estimated probability of true

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content:
Instructions and descriptions can be strings, JSON objects, or JSON arrays.
Descriptions can also be null. Core treats structured descriptions as content;
it does not interpret their keys. Functions, class instances, cycles, undefined
values, and nonfinite numbers are not JSON-compatible.

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content:
Answers retain question IDs and have the same type as their question. When a
Choice distribution is supplied, it includes every option and the selected
choice has maximal probability. Score distributions use string keys for
zero-based level indices, and the score equals the probability-weighted mean.
Without a distribution, a score is the model's estimated position on the rubric.

contents.heading: question-types
contents.content:
Distributions must sum to one, and weighted scores must agree with their
distributions. The default absolute tolerance is 0.000001. Providers that round
their output can declare rounding.probabilityDecimals and
rounding.scoreDecimals (integers from 0 to 15). Validation then also allows half
a unit in the last decimal place per rounded probability or score, accumulated
over the sum or weighted mean. For example, probabilities rounded to two decimal
places can sum to 0.99 even when their unrounded values sum to one. The result
includes this rounding information. Invalid output is rejected; native values
are preserved, never silently normalized.

contents.heading: probabilities-and-confidence
contents.content:
Choice and Score distributions are optional. Boolean probability is required:
0.98 means a strong yes and 0.02 means a strong no. It is not confidence in
either outcome. The SDK does not promise calibration across providers. Structured
language-model adapters prompt the model to estimate P(true); native decision providers return
their API probabilities. Provider-specific confidence statistics belong
in providerMetadata. TypeSafe exposes its separate Choice/Score confidence
statistic at result.providerMetadata?.typesafe?.confidence, keyed by question
ID. It is not the selected option's probability or a portable confidence measure.

contents.heading: probabilities-and-confidence
contents.content:
Check for optional distributions before using them. For example, an application
can route only when a provider supplies a sufficiently high selected-option
probability:

contents.heading: probabilities-and-confidence
contents.content:
Choose Boolean thresholds in application code, using labeled data from the task
rather than assuming that the same threshold behaves identically across providers:

contents.heading: errors-and-cancellation
contents.content:
The model's supportedQuestionTypes are checked before calling the provider.
Any unsupported question fails the entire call with
Experimental_DecisionUnsupportedQuestionTypeError. Successful calls return
an answer for every question; there is no partial success, and Core does not
substitute models automatically.

contents.heading: errors-and-cancellation
contents.content:
Invalid inputs throw InvalidArgumentError. Missing answers, mismatched answer
types, invalid options, scores, or probabilities throw InvalidResponseDataError.
If the model refuses any question, the call throws
Experimental_DecisionRefusalError with the refused question IDs, and is not
retried.
Transient provider failures use the normal retry policy (maxRetries: 2 by
default). Use abortSignal to cancel the decisions request, headers for request headers,
and providerOptions for provider-specific settings.

contents.heading: errors-and-cancellation
contents.content:
The result includes usage, warnings, providerMetadata, and response.
Unknown token counts stay undefined; totalTokens is available only when both
input and output counts are known.

contents.heading: errors-and-cancellation
contents.content: For tests, use Experimental_DecisionMockModelV4 from ai/test.

contents.heading: scope-and-examples
contents.content:
experimental_decide currently returns one complete result for one shared state. It does
not stream answers, perform multilabel classification, or batch unrelated
states. Run separate calls for separate states. Provider support and judgment
quality depend on the chosen model. Core does not choose another model, but a
provider can implement routing through its provider options. For example, AI
Gateway supports conditional decision fallbacks under
providerOptions.gateway.models.

contents.heading: scope-and-examples
contents.content:
Runnable examples are in
examples/ai-functions/src/decide,
including basic examples for TypeSafe, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, model
registries, custom aliases, default-provider strings, and probability-based routing.

contents.heading: related-resources
contents.content:
Explore use cases, implementation guides, and a deployable template for using
Jev from TypeSafe AI with the AI SDK:

contents.heading: related-resources
contents.content: Jev use cases: Explore ideas for applying decisions in your application.

contents.heading: related-resources
contents.content: Classify, route, and score with Jev and AI SDK: Learn how to ask typed questions, route answers using probabilities, and test routing logic with a mock decision model.

contents.heading: related-resources
contents.content: Jev and AI SDK form router guide: Explore form routing with Jev and the AI SDK.

contents.heading: related-resources
contents.content: Jev and AI SDK form router template: Deploy a Next.js application that routes form submissions with Jev and uses a language model fallback for uncertain or failed decisions.

metadata.title: DevTools
metadata.description: Debug and inspect AI SDK applications with DevTools

contents.content:
AI SDK DevTools is intended for local development only. Do not use in
production environments.

AI SDK DevTools gives you full visibility over your AI SDK calls with generateText, streamText, and ToolLoopAgent. It helps you debug and inspect LLM requests, responses, tool calls, and multi-step interactions through a web-based UI.
DevTools is composed of two parts:
Telemetry Integration: Captures runs and steps from your AI SDK calls via the telemetry system
Viewer: A web UI to inspect the captured data

contents.heading: installation
contents.content: Install the DevTools package:

contents.heading: requirements
contents.content: AI SDK v7 (ai@latest)

contents.heading: requirements
contents.content: Node.js compatible runtime

contents.heading: register-the-integration
contents.content: Register DevToolsTelemetry globally so it captures all AI SDK calls:

contents.heading: register-the-integration
contents.content: Telemetry is enabled automatically once an integration is registered — no per-call configuration is needed:

contents.heading: register-the-integration
contents.content: You can also pass the integration to individual calls instead of registering it globally:

contents.heading: launch-the-viewer
contents.content: Start the DevTools viewer:

contents.heading: launch-the-viewer
contents.content: Open http://localhost:4983 to view your AI SDK interactions.

contents.heading: choose-a-viewer-theme
contents.content:
The viewer uses the dark theme by default. Use the theme button in the viewer
header to switch between dark and light themes. Your selection is stored in
your browser and restored the next time you open the viewer at the same origin.

contents.heading: monorepo-usage
contents.content: If you are using a monorepo setup (e.g. Turborepo, Nx), start DevTools from the same workspace where your AI SDK code runs.

contents.heading: monorepo-usage
contents.content: For example, if your API is in apps/api, run:

contents.heading: monorepo-usage
contents.content:
The explicit @latest tag ensures that npx installs an executable copy
instead of selecting a transitive dependency whose binary is not linked into
the workspace.

contents.heading: captured-data
contents.content: DevTools captures the following information from your AI SDK calls:

contents.heading: captured-data
contents.content: Input parameters and prompts: View the complete input sent to your LLM

contents.heading: captured-data
contents.content: Output content and tool calls: Inspect generated text, tool invocations, and tool results

contents.heading: captured-data

contents.heading: media-previews
contents.content:
DevTools recognizes current file content parts as well as the deprecated
image-*, file-*, and media tool-result aliases. Inline image, audio, and
video data is previewed directly, while the captured JSON shape and metadata
remain available for inspection. The viewer displays at most 8 previews per
value, traverses at most 12 nested levels, and embeds inline previews up to 5
MiB. Longer JSON strings are truncated in the viewer to avoid duplicating large
base64 payloads. Binary values in recognized media-bearing fields are persisted
as base64 so they remain previewable; unrelated binary values retain their
normal JSON representation.

contents.heading: media-previews
contents.content: For example, a tool can return media through toModelOutput:

contents.heading: media-previews
contents.content:
Remote http and https media is not loaded automatically. Select Load
preview in the viewer to fetch it with anonymous CORS and no referrer.
Cross-origin browser credentials are omitted, but same-origin browser
credentials may still be included by the browser. URLs containing embedded
usernames or passwords are rejected. Unsupported media, provider references,
malformed values, unsafe URL schemes, and inline values over the preview limit
retain their JSON and metadata fallback without an embedded preview.

contents.heading: media-previews
contents.content: Telemetry is enabled automatically, but AI SDK 7 excludes raw request and response bodies from step results by default. To make them available to DevTools for generateText, enable body retention on the call:

contents.heading: media-previews
contents.content: ToolLoopAgent accepts the same include setting in its constructor. For streamText and ToolLoopAgent.stream(), only the request body can be retained; use include: { requestBody: true }.

contents.heading: runs-and-steps
contents.content: DevTools organizes captured data into runs and steps:

contents.heading: runs-and-steps
contents.content: Run: A complete multi-step AI interaction, grouped by the initial prompt

contents.heading: runs-and-steps
contents.content: Step: A single LLM call within a run (e.g., one generateText or streamText call)

contents.heading: runs-and-steps
contents.content: Multi-step interactions, such as those created by tool calling or agent loops, are grouped together as a single run with multiple steps. Nested sub-agent calls are linked to their parent run, making it easy to trace the full execution tree.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The DevToolsTelemetry integration hooks into the AI SDK telemetry lifecycle to capture all generateText, streamText, generateObject, and streamObject calls. Captured data is stored locally in a JSON file (.devtools/generations.json) and served through a web UI built with Hono and React.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content:
The integration automatically adds .devtools to your .gitignore file.
Verify that .devtools is in your .gitignore to ensure you don't commit
sensitive AI interaction data to your repository.

contents.heading: security-considerations
contents.content: DevTools stores all AI interactions locally in plain text files, including:

contents.heading: security-considerations

contents.heading: security-considerations
contents.content: Only use DevTools in local development environments. Do not enable DevTools in production or when handling sensitive data.

metadata.title: Embeddings
metadata.description: Learn how to embed values with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Embeddings are a way to represent words, phrases, or images as vectors in a high-dimensional space.
In this space, similar words are close to each other, and the distance between words can be used to measure their similarity.

contents.heading: embedding-a-single-value
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embed function to embed single values, which is useful for tasks such as finding similar words
or phrases or clustering text.
You can use it with embeddings models, e.g. openai.embeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.embeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
When loading data, e.g. when preparing a data store for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG),
it is often useful to embed many values at once (batch embedding).

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embedMany function for this purpose.
Similar to embed, you can use it with embeddings models,
e.g. openai.embeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.embeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-similarity
contents.content:
After embedding values, you can calculate the similarity between them using the cosineSimilarity function.
This is useful to e.g. find similar words or phrases in a dataset.
You can also rank and filter related items based on their similarity.

contents.heading: token-usage
contents.content:
Many providers charge based on the number of tokens used to generate embeddings.
Both embed and embedMany provide token usage information in the usage property of the result object:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Embedding model settings can be configured using providerOptions for provider-specific parameters:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Google's gemini-embedding-2 model (also available as gemini-embedding-2-preview) supports multimodal embedding content through providerOptions.google.content. Each entry corresponds to the value at the same index and can contain { text: string }, { inlineData: { mimeType: string; data: string } }, or { fileData: { fileUri: string; mimeType: string } } parts. fileUri can reference remote content such as HTTP URLs or Google Cloud Storage URIs (gs://...).

contents.heading: parallel-requests
contents.content: The embedMany function now supports parallel processing with configurable maxParallelCalls to optimize performance:

contents.heading: retries
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional maxRetries parameter of type number
that you can use to set the maximum number of retries for the embedding process.
It defaults to 2 retries (3 attempts in total). You can set it to 0 to disable retries.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the embedding process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the embedding request.

contents.heading: response-information
contents.content: Both embed and embedMany return response information that includes the raw provider response:

You can enhance embedding models, e.g. to set default values, using
wrapEmbeddingModel and EmbeddingModelMiddleware.

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.description: Learn how to handle errors in the AI SDK Core

title.children: Retrying provider errors after streaming starts

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: Regular errors are thrown and can be handled using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: See Error Types for more information on the different types of errors that may be thrown.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-simple-streams
contents.content:
When errors occur during streams that do not support error chunks,
the error is thrown as a regular error.
You can handle these errors using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-streaming-with-error-support
contents.content:
The stream result supports error parts.
You can handle those parts similar to other parts.
It is recommended to also add a try-catch block for errors that
happen outside of the streaming.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
maxRetries retries failures that happen while starting a model call. To retry
well-formed provider error events received after response streaming has begun,
set streamRetries:

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
Stream retries rerun only the failed model step with the same accumulated
conversation and generation context. Earlier completed steps, including their
tool calls and tool results, are not replayed. Tool input, tool calls, approval
requests, tool callbacks, and client-side tool execution from a failed attempt
are discarded. They are only exposed or executed after an attempt reaches a
successful model-call finish.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
Well-formed provider error events are normalized into
StreamProviderError
instances. The same instance is supplied to onError and, if recovery is not
requested or retries are exhausted, to the error part in the full stream. Use
its isRetryable metadata when deciding whether to request recovery.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
A retry remains part of the same logical step. onStepStart runs once for that
step. onLanguageModelCallStart runs for each provider call attempt, while
onLanguageModelCallEnd runs only for attempts that reach a model-call finish.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
You can also decide dynamically in onError. Set streamRetries explicitly to
enable stream recovery; use 0 when a single retry should only be
callback-directed:

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
Callback-directed recovery is limited to one retry per logical step. When
automatic retries are configured, onError can request one additional retry
after the automatic retry budget is exhausted. This bounds the total number of
recovery calls for a step to streamRetries + 1.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
When streamRetries is omitted, all stream retry behavior is disabled and an
existing logging-only onError callback retains incremental tool streaming.
An onError return value other than { retry: true } keeps its previous
behavior and does not request recovery. Provider error events that are
recovered are not emitted as final error parts.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
Non-tool output emitted before a provider error cannot be retracted. A retried
model step may therefore append repeated or divergent partial text, reasoning,
files, or sources to consumer streams. Open text and reasoning parts are ended
before recovered output begins so UI consumers do not retain them in a
streaming state. Failed-attempt output is excluded from the recovered step
result, structured output parsing, response messages, and subsequent model
steps. Final request and response metadata come from the recovered attempt.
Retries also add latency and may incur additional provider usage and cost.

contents.heading: retrying-provider-errors-after-streaming-starts
contents.content:
Failed-attempt isolation prevents AI SDK client-side tools from executing, but
it cannot undo work already performed by provider-executed tools. Retrying a
step after provider-side work may repeat that work or its cost. Use
idempotency controls for provider-executed side effects.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: When streams are aborted (e.g., via chat stop button), you may want to perform cleanup operations like updating stored messages in your UI. Use the onAbort callback to handle these cases.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback is called when a stream is aborted via AbortSignal, but onEnd is not called. This ensures you can still update your UI state appropriately.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback receives:

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: steps: An array of all completed steps before the abort

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: You can also handle abort events directly in the stream:

headings.content: Handling streaming errors (streaming with error support)
Retrying provider errors after streaming starts

metadata.title: File Uploads
metadata.description: Learn how to upload files and use provider references with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the uploadFile
function to upload files to a provider and get back a ProviderReference that can be
used in subsequent API calls.

In the AI SDK, the uploaded file is identified by a ProviderReference — a
Record<string, string> mapping provider names to provider-specific identifiers.
This concept is used for other provider specific asset references too, such as
uploaded skills.
As a shorthand, you can pass a provider instance directly to api instead of calling .files() explicitly — the SDK will call .files() for you:

contents.heading: supported-file-types
contents.content:
You can upload images, PDFs, text files, and other documents depending on the provider.
The media type is auto-detected from the file bytes when not specified explicitly:

contents.heading: supported-file-types
contents.content: Use the providerReference in a file content part with its media type:

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content:
Some providers accept additional options through providerOptions.
For example, OpenAI requires a purpose field:

contents.heading: streaming-uploads
contents.content:
Providers that support streaming uploads (e.g. OpenAI, xAI) accept a tagged
{ type: 'stream', stream } shape, sending the bytes without buffering the
full file in memory. Providers without streaming support reject stream data
with an UnsupportedFunctionalityError.

contents.heading: streaming-uploads
contents.content:
The provider consumes the stream: any failed upload — including validation
failures before a request is made — cancels it, and it must not be reused. Stream data cannot be sniffed, so mediaType defaults to
application/octet-stream when omitted, and multipart-based providers default
the filename to "blob".

contents.heading: streaming-uploads
contents.content:
Uploads can be cancelled with abortSignal and carry request-specific
headers. Results include byteSize, createdAt, and expiresAt (the
provider-applied retention expiry) when the provider reports them.

contents.heading: provider-references
contents.content:
A ProviderReference is a Record<string, string> that maps provider names to
provider-specific file identifiers:

contents.heading: provider-references
contents.content:
When you pass a ProviderReference as the data or image field of a message content
part, the provider looks up its own file ID from the reference. If the reference doesn't
contain an entry for the current provider, an error is thrown.

contents.heading: multi-provider-usage
contents.content:
If you switch providers mid-conversation (for example, continuing a chat started with
OpenAI using Anthropic), you need to upload the file to both providers and merge the
references:

contents.heading: multi-provider-usage
contents.content:
The merged reference can then be used in messages regardless of which provider processes
the request — each provider will find its own file ID.

metadata.title: Generating Structured Data
metadata.description: Learn how to generate structured data with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
While text generation can be useful, your use case will likely call for generating structured data.
For example, you might want to extract information from text, classify data, or generate synthetic data.

Many language models are capable of generating structured data, often defined as using "JSON modes" or "tools".
However, you need to manually provide schemas and then validate the generated data as LLMs can produce incorrect or incomplete structured data.

The AI SDK standardises structured object generation across model providers
using the output property on generateText
and streamText.
You can use Zod schemas, Valibot, or JSON schemas to specify the shape of the data that you want,
and the AI model will generate data that conforms to that structure.

Structured output generation is part of the generateText and streamText
flow. This means you can combine it with tool calling in the same request.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Use generateText with Output.object() to generate structured data from a prompt.
The schema is also used to validate the generated data, ensuring type safety and correctness.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Structured output generation counts as a step in the AI SDK's multi-turn
execution model (where each model call or tool execution is one step). When
combining with tools, account for this in your stopWhen configuration.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the response property:

contents.heading: stream-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Given the added complexity of returning structured data, model response time can be unacceptable for your interactive use case.
With streamText and output, you can stream the model's structured response as it is generated.

contents.heading: stream-structured-outputs
contents.content: You can consume the structured output on the client with the useObject hook.

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: streamText starts streaming immediately. When errors occur during streaming, they become part of the stream rather than thrown exceptions (to prevent stream crashes).

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: To handle errors, provide an onError callback:

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: For non-streaming error handling with generateText, see the Error Handling section below.

contents.heading: output-types
contents.content: The AI SDK supports multiple ways of specifying the expected structure of generated data via the Output object. You can select from various strategies for structured/text generation and validation.

contents.heading: outputtext
contents.content: Use Output.text() to generate plain text from a model. This option doesn't enforce any schema on the result: you simply receive the model's text as a string. This is the default behavior when no output is specified.

contents.heading: outputobject
contents.content: Use Output.object({ schema }) to generate a structured object based on a schema (for example, a Zod schema). The output is type-validated to ensure the returned result matches the schema.

contents.heading: outputobject
contents.content:
Partial outputs streamed via streamText cannot be validated against your
provided schema, as incomplete data may not yet conform to the expected
structure.

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content:
Use Output.array({ element, minItems, maxItems }) to specify that you expect
an array of typed objects from the model. Each element must conform to the
element schema, and the optional bounds constrain the number of elements.

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content:
minItems and maxItems must be non-negative integers, and minItems cannot
be greater than maxItems. Use the same value for both options to require an
exact length. The bounds are sent to providers as part of the structured output
schema when supported, and the AI SDK independently validates the final output.

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content: When streaming arrays with streamText, you can use elementStream to receive each completed element as it is generated:

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content:
Each element emitted by elementStream is complete and validated against your
element schema. This differs from partialOutputStream, which streams the
entire partial array including incomplete elements. If the model generates
more than maxItems, elementStream errors before emitting the first excess
element. This does not automatically abort provider generation, and the final
output promise rejects.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: Use Output.choice({ options }) when you expect the model to choose from a specific set of string options, such as for classification or fixed-enum answers.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: You can provide any set of string options, and the output will always be a single string value that matches one of the specified options. The AI SDK validates that the result matches one of your options, and will throw if the model returns something invalid.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: This is especially useful for making classification-style generations or forcing valid values for API compatibility.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: Use Output.json() when you want to generate and parse unstructured JSON values from the model, without enforcing a specific schema. This is useful if you want to capture arbitrary objects, flexible structures, or when you want to rely on the model's natural output rather than rigid validation.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: With Output.json, the AI SDK only checks that the response is valid JSON; it doesn't validate the structure or types of the values. If you need schema validation, use the .object or .array outputs instead.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: For more advanced validation or different structures, see the Output API reference.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs-with-tools
contents.content: One of the key advantages of using structured output with generateText and streamText is the ability to combine it with tool calling.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs-with-tools
contents.content:
When using tools with structured output, remember that generating the
structured output counts as a step. Configure stopWhen to allow enough steps
for both tool execution and output generation.

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: You can add .describe("...") to individual schema properties to give the model hints about what each property is for. This helps improve the quality and accuracy of generated structured data:

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Property descriptions are particularly useful for:

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Clarifying ambiguous property names

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Specifying expected formats or conventions

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Providing context for complex nested structures

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: You can optionally specify a name and description for the output. These are used by some providers for additional LLM guidance, e.g. via tool or schema name.

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: This works with all output types that support structured generation:

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.object({ name, description, schema })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.array({ name, description, element, minItems, maxItems })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.choice({ name, description, options })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.json({ name, description })

contents.heading: accessing-reasoning
contents.content: You can access the reasoning used by the language model to generate the object via the reasoningText property on the result. This property contains a string with the model's thought process, if available.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: generateText can report structured output failures in two ways:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
If the model response cannot be parsed or validated against the schema,
generateText rejects with an
AI_NoObjectGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
If generateText returns a result without an output, accessing result.output
throws an
AI_NoOutputGeneratedError.
This can happen when the final step does not finish with a stop reason, for
example when it finishes with tool-calls.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
The output property is a getter, so destructuring it also triggers this
access.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
NoObjectGeneratedError preserves the following information to help you log
the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: text: The text that was generated by the model. This can be the raw text or the tool call text, depending on the object generation mode.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: response: Metadata about the language model response, including response id, timestamp, and model.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: usage: Request token usage.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error (e.g. a JSON parsing error). You can use this for more detailed error handling.

contents.heading: more-examples
contents.content: You can see structured output generation in action using various frameworks in the following examples:

metadata.title: Generating Text
metadata.description: Learn how to generate text with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate text in response to a prompt, which can contain instructions and information to process.
For example, you can ask a model to come up with a recipe, draft an email, or summarize a document.
The AI SDK Core provides two functions to generate text and stream it from LLMs:
generateText: Generates text for a given prompt and model.
streamText: Streams text from a given prompt and model.
Advanced LLM features such as tool calling and structured data generation are built on top of text generation.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can generate text using the generateText function. This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can use more advanced prompts to generate text with more complex instructions and content:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: The result object of generateText contains the generated output and metadata:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in all steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text from the final step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.files: The files that were generated in all steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in all steps (only available for some models).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that were made in all steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The results of the tool calls from all steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.rawFinishReason: The raw reason why the generation finished (from the provider).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.usage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider in all steps (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps, including per-step performance.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.finalStep: Details for the final step, including performance.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.output: The generated structured output using the output specification.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: Each step includes performance with timing and throughput information:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: effectiveOutputTokensPerSecond: Effective output tokens per second, calculated as outputTokens / requestSeconds.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: outputTokensPerSecond: For streaming steps, output tokens per second after the first generated output chunk, calculated as outputTokens / outputStreamSeconds. For generateText, this is undefined.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: inputTokensPerSecond: For streaming steps, input tokens per second before the first generated output chunk, calculated as inputTokens / ttftSeconds. For generateText, this is undefined.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: effectiveTotalTokensPerSecond: Effective total tokens per second, calculated as (inputTokens + outputTokens) / requestSeconds.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: stepTimeMs: Total time spent on the step, including language model response time and tool execution time, in milliseconds.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: responseTimeMs: Time spent waiting for the language model response in milliseconds.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: toolExecutionMs: Time spent executing each client-side tool call in the step in milliseconds, keyed by tool call ID.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: timeToFirstOutputMs: For streaming steps, the time until the first generated output chunk was received in milliseconds. For generateText, this is undefined.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: timeBetweenOutputChunksMs: For streaming steps with at least two output chunks, timing statistics for the gaps between generated output chunks in milliseconds.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the finalStep.response property:

contents.heading: onend-callback
contents.content:
When using generateText, you can provide an onEnd callback that is triggered after the last step is finished (
API Reference
).
It contains the text, usage information, finish reason, messages, steps, total usage, and more:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content:
Experimental callbacks are subject to breaking changes in incremental package
releases.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content:
generateText provides several experimental lifecycle callbacks that let you hook into different phases of the generation process.
These are useful for logging, observability, debugging, and custom telemetry.
Errors thrown inside these callbacks are silently caught and do not break the generation flow.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: The available lifecycle callbacks are:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onStart: Called once when the generateText operation begins, before any LLM calls. Receives model info, messages, settings, and runtimeContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onStepStart: Called before each step (LLM call). Receives the step number, model, messages being sent, tools, and prior steps.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallStart: Called immediately before the provider model call begins. Useful when you want to observe the model invocation separately from later tool execution.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallEnd: Called after the model response has been normalized and parsed, but before any client-side tool execution begins. Receives the model-call content parts, usage, finish reason, and provider metadata.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onToolExecutionStart: Called right before a tool's execute function runs. Receives the tool call object, messages, and toolContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onToolExecutionEnd: Called right after a tool's execute function completes or errors. Receives the tool call object, toolExecutionMs, and a toolOutput discriminated union (type: 'tool-result' with output, or type: 'tool-error' with error).

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onStepEnd: Called after each step finishes. Includes stepNumber (zero-based index of the completed step).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: Depending on your model and prompt, it can take a large language model (LLM) up to a minute to finish generating its response. This delay can be unacceptable for interactive use cases such as chatbots or real-time applications, where users expect immediate responses.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: AI SDK Core provides the streamText function which simplifies streaming text from LLMs:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.textStream is both a ReadableStream and an AsyncIterable.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming and suppresses errors to prevent
server crashes. Use the onError callback to log errors.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
You can use streamText on its own or in combination with AI SDK
UI and AI SDK
RSC.
The result.stream can be passed to several standalone helpers to make the integration into AI SDK UI easier:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: createUIMessageStreamResponse({ stream: toUIMessageStream({ stream: result.stream }) }): Creates a UI Message stream HTTP response (with tool calls etc.) that can be used in a Next.js App Router API route.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse({ stream: toUIMessageStream({ stream: result.stream }), response }): Writes UI Message stream delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: createTextStreamResponse({ stream: toTextStream({ stream: result.stream }) }): Creates a simple text stream HTTP response.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: pipeTextStreamToResponse({ stream: toTextStream({ stream: result.stream }), response }): Writes text delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText is using backpressure and only generates tokens as they are
requested. You need to consume the stream in order for it to finish.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: It also provides several promises that resolve when the stream is finished:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in all steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text from the final step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.finalStep: Details for the final step, including per-step performance.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.files: Files that have been generated by the model in all steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in all steps (only available for some models).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that have been executed in all steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The tool results that have been generated in all steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.rawFinishReason: The raw reason why the generation finished (from the provider).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.usage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.totalUsage: Deprecated. Use result.usage instead.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider in all steps (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps, including per-step performance.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: For streamText, timeToFirstOutputMs is set when the first generated output chunk is received for a step. timeBetweenOutputChunksMs includes min, p10, median, avg, p90, and max when at least two output chunks are received.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming to enable sending data without waiting for the model.
Errors become part of the stream and are not thrown to prevent e.g. servers from crashing.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content: To log errors, you can provide an onError callback that is triggered when an error occurs.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: When using streamText, you can provide an onChunk callback that is triggered for each chunk of the stream.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: It receives all stream part types from stream, including:

streamText provides several experimental lifecycle callbacks that let you hook into different phases of the streaming process.
These are useful for logging, observability, debugging, and custom telemetry.
Errors thrown inside these callbacks are silently caught and do not break the streaming flow.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: The available lifecycle callbacks are:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: onStart: Called once when the streamText operation begins, before any LLM calls. Receives model info, messages, settings, and runtimeContext.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1

contents.heading: stream-property
contents.content:
You can read a stream with all events using the stream property.
This can be useful if you want to implement your own UI or handle the stream in a different way.
Here is an example of how to use the stream property:

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
You can use the experimental_transform option to transform the stream.
This is useful for e.g. filtering, changing, or smoothing the text stream.

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
The transformations are applied before the callbacks are invoked and the promises are resolved.
If you e.g. have a transformation that changes all text to uppercase, the onEnd callback will receive the transformed text.

contents.heading: smoothing-streams
contents.content:
The AI SDK Core provides a smoothStream function that
can be used to smooth out text and reasoning streaming.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also implement your own custom transformations.
The transformation function receives the tools that are available to the model,
and returns a function that is used to transform the stream.
Tools can either be generic or limited to the tools that you are using.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
Here is an example of how to implement a custom transformation that converts
all text to uppercase:

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also stop the stream using the stopStream function.
This is e.g. useful if you want to stop the stream when model guardrails are violated, e.g. by generating inappropriate content.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
When you invoke stopStream, it is important to simulate the finish-step and finish events to guarantee that a well-formed stream is returned
and all callbacks are invoked.

contents.heading: multiple-transformations
contents.content: You can also provide multiple transformations. They are applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Some providers such as Perplexity and
Google include sources in the response.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Currently sources are limited to web pages that ground the response.
You can access them using the sources property of the result.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: Each url source contains the following properties:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: id: The ID of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: url: The URL of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: title: The optional title of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: providerMetadata: Provider metadata for the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use generateText, you can access the sources using the sources property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use streamText, you can access the sources using the stream property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: The sources are also available in the result.sources promise.
