metadata.title: Image Generation
metadata.description: Learn how to generate images with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the generateImage
function to generate images based on a given prompt using an image model.
You can access the image data using the base64 or uint8Array properties:

contents.heading: size-and-aspect-ratio
contents.content: Depending on the model, you can either specify the size or the aspect ratio.

contents.heading: size
contents.content:
The size is specified as a string in the format {width}x{height}.
Models only support a few sizes, and the supported sizes are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio
contents.content:
The aspect ratio is specified as a string in the format {width}:{height}.
Models only support a few aspect ratios, and the supported aspect ratios are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: generateImage also supports generating multiple images at once:

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content:
generateImage will automatically call the model as often as needed (in
parallel) to generate the requested number of images.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: Each image model has an internal limit on how many images it can generate in a single API call. The AI SDK manages this automatically by batching requests appropriately when you request multiple images using the n parameter. By default, the SDK uses provider-documented limits (for example, DALL-E 3 can only generate 1 image per call, while DALL-E 2 supports up to 10).

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: If needed, you can override this behavior using the maxImagesPerCall setting when generating your image. This is particularly useful when working with new or custom models where the default batch size might not be optimal:

contents.heading: checking-image-editing-support
contents.content:
Image model instances can advertise whether they support reference image files
and masks. Check these capabilities before routing an image editing request:

contents.heading: checking-image-editing-support
contents.content:
supportsFileInputs and supportsMaskInputs can be true, false, or
undefined (unknown), and providers may expose any of these values
asynchronously. Treat only true as confirmed support when selecting a model for an edit. File and mask
support are separate because some models accept reference images but do not
accept masks.

contents.heading: checking-image-editing-support
contents.content:
These capabilities describe support for the SDK's standardized image and mask
inputs, including the provider's request mapping. A model name that resembles a
supported family is not sufficient evidence of support. A model may still require
provider-specific options or impose limits on input formats and counts.

contents.heading: checking-image-editing-support
contents.content:
The AI SDK does not automatically reject editing inputs based on these
capabilities. Applications can decide whether to reject the request, ask the
user to choose another model, or use a fallback when support is false or
unknown.

contents.heading: providing-a-seed
contents.content:
You can provide a seed to the generateImage function to control the output of the image generation process.
If supported by the model, the same seed will always produce the same image.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content:
Image models often have provider- or even model-specific settings.
You can pass such settings to the generateImage function
using the providerOptions parameter. The options for the provider
(openai in the example below) become request body properties.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the image generation process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the image generation request.

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content: If the model returns warnings, e.g. for unsupported parameters, they will be available in the warnings property of the response.

contents.heading: provider-metadata
contents.content: Some providers expose metadata for an individual image. It is available directly on the generated image:

contents.heading: provider-metadata
contents.content: The outer key of image.providerMetadata is the provider name. The inner value is the metadata for that image.

contents.heading: underlying-calls
contents.content: When a request is split into multiple provider calls, calls preserves the images, provider metadata, response metadata, warnings, and usage for each call. images and usage remain convenient flattened and aggregate views, respectively.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
When generateImage cannot generate a valid image, it throws a AI_NoImageGeneratedError.
Unclassified empty image responses are retried according to maxRetries before this error is thrown.
Providers can classify terminal empty responses, such as moderation blocks, with isRetryable: false; these responses are not retried.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate an image. It can arise due to the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: calls: Results from the underlying image model calls, including generated images, provider metadata, response metadata, warnings, and usage.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: responses: Metadata about the image model responses, including timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error handling

contents.heading: image-middleware
contents.content:
You can enhance image models, e.g. to set default values or implement logging, using
wrapImageModel and ImageModelV4Middleware.

contents.heading: image-middleware
contents.content: Here is an example that sets a default size when none is provided:

contents.heading: generating-images-with-language-models
contents.content:
Some language models such as Google gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview support multi-modal outputs including images.
With such models, you can access the generated images using the files property of the response.

metadata.title: Lifecycle Callbacks
metadata.description: Observe AI SDK lifecycle events in generateText, streamText, embed, embedMany, rerank, and experimental_decide calls

contents.content:
Event callbacks let you run your own code at important points in an AI SDK call.
You can attach them directly to generateText, streamText, embed, embedMany, rerank, and experimental_decide calls to observe what happened, record usage, debug multi-step generations, and monitor tool execution.
They are especially useful when you want application-specific logic close to the call site:
Log which model, prompt shape, and settings were used for a request.
Record token usage, latency, finish reasons, and warnings for analytics or billing.
Understand how a multi-step tool call moved from model response to tool execution to final answer.
Track tool inputs, tool outputs, execution time, and errors.
Attach your own request, user, tenant, or workflow identifiers through runtimeContext and toolsContext.

For automatic OpenTelemetry instrumentation across your application, use Telemetry.
Use event callbacks when you want to run custom code for a specific AI SDK call.

contents.heading: basic-usage
contents.content: Pass callbacks as options to the AI SDK function you are calling:

contents.heading: basic-usage
contents.content:
Callbacks can be synchronous or asynchronous. If a callback throws, the error is caught internally and the AI SDK call continues.
Because callbacks run as part of the lifecycle, keep them fast or enqueue expensive work in a background system.

contents.heading: request-logging
contents.content:
Use onStart and onEnd to record one application log for the beginning and end of a call.
The callId is available across lifecycle events, so you can correlate logs from the same request.

contents.heading: request-logging
contents.content: This pattern works well for audit logs, internal dashboards, and tracking usage for a particular feature.

contents.heading: measuring-model-performance
contents.content:
onLanguageModelCallEnd runs after a provider response has been normalized and parsed.
For streamText, the event also includes streaming-specific timing data such as time to first output and gaps between output chunks.

contents.heading: measuring-model-performance
contents.content:
Use model-call events when you want to measure provider work specifically.
Use step events when you want timing that includes SDK-managed work such as local tool execution.

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content:
When you use tools with generateText or streamText, a single user request can involve multiple model calls.
Each model call is a step. The model may call a tool in one step, receive the tool result, and then produce a final answer in the next step.

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: This helps answer questions such as:

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: Did the model call a tool or answer directly?

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: How many steps did the request take?

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: Which step used the most tokens?

contents.heading: debugging-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: Did time go to the model response or to local tool execution?

contents.heading: monitoring-tool-execution
contents.content:
Tool execution callbacks run around the tool's execute function.
Use them to record tool usage, latency, successful results, and tool errors.

contents.heading: monitoring-tool-execution
contents.content: toolOutput is a discriminated union. When toolOutput.type is 'tool-result', the output is available on toolOutput.output. When it is 'tool-error', the error is available on toolOutput.error.

contents.heading: observing-embeddings-and-reranking
contents.content:
Embedding and reranking callbacks are simpler: they expose onStart and onEnd around the operation.
This is useful for retrieval pipelines where you want to understand how often you are embedding, how many values you embed, and how reranking changes result sets.

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: generateText and streamText expose the richest lifecycle because they can involve prompts, model calls, tool calls, and multiple steps.

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: A typical single-step generation runs in this order:

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStepStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStepEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: A multi-step generation with local tool execution usually runs like this:

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStepStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onLanguageModelCallEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onToolExecutionStart

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onToolExecutionEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onStepEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: Repeat step callbacks until the stop condition is met

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content: onEnd

contents.heading: generation-lifecycle
contents.content:
onStepStart and onStepEnd describe the full step.
onLanguageModelCallStart and onLanguageModelCallEnd describe only the model call inside that step.
This distinction matters when the step includes local tool execution: the step duration can be longer than the model response duration.

contents.heading: runtime-and-tool-context
contents.content:
Generation and step lifecycle callbacks receive the full runtimeContext and
toolsContext values that flow through the call. Tool-execution callbacks receive
the scoped toolContext for the tool being executed. This makes callbacks useful
for attaching application context without changing prompts or tool inputs.

contents.heading: runtime-and-tool-context
contents.content:
Telemetry integrations can filter runtimeContext and toolsContext before
exporting them. Generation and step callbacks receive the full context
objects; tool-execution callbacks receive scoped tool context. Be careful not
to log secrets or sensitive user data from callbacks.

contents.heading: event-data-reference
contents.content: The exact event data depends on the callback. The tables below summarize the fields you will most commonly use.

contents.heading: onstart
contents.content: Called once before any model calls are made.

contents.heading: onstepstart
contents.content: Called before each step begins.

contents.heading: onlanguagemodelcallstart
contents.content: Called immediately before the provider model call begins.

contents.heading: onlanguagemodelcallend
contents.content: Called after the provider response has been normalized and parsed, before local tool execution begins.

contents.heading: ontoolexecutionstart
contents.content: Called before a local tool's execute function runs.

contents.heading: ontoolexecutionend
contents.content: Called after a local tool's execute function completes or errors.

contents.heading: onstepend
contents.content: Called after each step completes. The event is the full StepResult for that step.

contents.heading: onend
contents.content: Called once when the full generation completes.

contents.heading: embedding-events
contents.content:
embed and embedMany share the same event interfaces.
Use operationId to distinguish 'ai.embed' from 'ai.embedMany'.
For embed, value is a single string. For embedMany, value is an array of strings.

contents.heading: decision-events
contents.content:
Decision callbacks are experimental. Their exported types are
Experimental_DecideStartEvent and Experimental_DecideEndEvent.

contents.heading: onend-3
contents.content: Includes every onStart field plus:

metadata.title: MCP Apps
metadata.description: Learn how to connect to MCP Apps and render interactive tool UIs with the AI SDK.

contents.content: MCP Apps extend Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools with interactive UI resources. The model still calls ordinary MCP tools, but tools can point to a ui:// resource containing HTML that your app renders in a sandboxed iframe.
The AI SDK provides two pieces for building MCP Apps hosts:
@ai-sdk/mcp helpers for advertising MCP Apps support, filtering model-visible and app-visible tools, and reading ui:// resources.
@ai-sdk/react components for rendering the app iframe and bridging MCP Apps JSON-RPC messages.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: An MCP Apps host usually does the following:

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: Connect to the MCP server with MCP Apps client capabilities.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: List tools and split them by MCP Apps visibility.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: Pass only model-visible tools to streamText or generateText.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: Read the app's ui:// resource when a tool part includes MCP App metadata.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: Render the HTML resource in a sandboxed iframe.

contents.heading: host-flow
contents.content: Proxy allowed iframe requests, such as app-visible tools/call, back to the MCP server.

contents.heading: connect-with-mcp-apps-support
contents.content: Use mcpAppClientCapabilities when creating the MCP client. This advertises that your host can render text/html;profile=mcp-app resources.

contents.heading: connect-with-mcp-apps-support
contents.content: Only advertise these capabilities if your host can fetch and render MCP App resources safely.

contents.heading: expose-only-model-visible-tools
contents.content: MCP Apps tools can declare _meta.ui.visibility. Tools with "model" visibility can be passed to the model. Tools with only "app" visibility should be kept for iframe requests and not exposed to the model.

contents.heading: expose-only-model-visible-tools
contents.content: When the model calls an app-backed tool, the MCP client preserves the app metadata on the tool UI part. The React renderer uses that metadata to decide whether a tool part has an MCP App.

contents.heading: read-app-resources
contents.content: Use readMCPAppResource to read and normalize an app resource before sending it to the browser host.

contents.heading: read-app-resources
contents.content: readMCPAppResource verifies the resource uses a ui:// URI, requires the MCP Apps MIME type, decodes text or base64 resource contents, and returns the HTML plus rendering metadata such as CSP and permissions.

contents.heading: proxy-app-visible-tool-calls
contents.content: The iframe cannot connect directly to your MCP server. It sends JSON-RPC messages to your host, and your host decides what is allowed.

contents.heading: proxy-app-visible-tool-calls
contents.content: For app-initiated tool calls, validate that the requested tool is app-visible before calling the MCP server.

contents.heading: proxy-app-visible-tool-calls
contents.content: In production, add any policy and user approval checks your app needs before forwarding iframe requests.

contents.heading: render-with-react
contents.content: In your React chat UI, render normal message parts as usual and pass tool parts to experimental_MCPAppRenderer.

contents.heading: render-with-react
contents.content:
experimental_MCPAppRenderer is experimental and may change in a future
release.

contents.heading: render-with-react
contents.content: For ordinary tools, experimental_MCPAppRenderer renders the provided fallback (or nothing when no fallback is provided). For app-backed tools, it loads the resource, creates the sandbox bridge, sends tool input and result notifications to the iframe, and forwards supported app requests through your handlers.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Treat MCP App HTML as untrusted content. Render it in a sandboxed iframe, ideally through a sandbox proxy route on a separate origin.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Never pass app-only tools to the model. Use splitMCPAppTools and expose only modelVisible tools.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Validate every iframe request on the server before calling client.callTool.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Cache app resources by resourceUri so repeated tool calls do not refetch identical HTML.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Keep tool content and structuredContent useful without the UI, so text-only hosts still work.

contents.heading: best-practices
contents.content: Close short-lived MCP clients when the response or host request finishes.

metadata.title: MCP Events
metadata.description: Understand the MCP webhook events contract and the AI SDK APIs for subscribing, verifying, and receiving events.

contents.content:
MCP events let a server notify your application when something changes, such as
a new document comment. Your MCP client manages the subscription; your webhook
endpoint receives the events.

These APIs are experimental and implement the webhook portion of the MCP
Events design
draft.
Polling and push-stream delivery are not supported.

contents.heading: choose-who-manages-subscriptions
contents.content:
Use experimental_events: { adapter } when a backend manages subscriptions,
webhook delivery and renewal. The adapter exposes managed watch handles and
requires no AI SDK event store. See managed subscriptions.

contents.heading: choose-who-manages-subscriptions
contents.content:
Use experimental_events: { store } when your application directly registers
MCP webhooks, persists their secrets and schedules renewal. The following flow
describes this direct mode. Event catalog discovery works in either mode, and
without either configuration.

contents.heading: how-mcp-events-work
contents.content:
The client sends events/subscribe with the event name, filters, webhook URL,
and signing secret. Optional ttlMs and cursor parameters set the requested
lifetime and replay position.

contents.heading: how-mcp-events-work
contents.content:
The server can send a signed challenge to verify the webhook before accepting
the subscription. After verification, it returns the subscription ID,
refreshBefore, cursor, and truncated.

contents.heading: how-mcp-events-work
contents.content:
As events occur, the server sends signed POST requests to the webhook. The
webhook verifies each signature, handles the event, and acknowledges delivery.

contents.heading: how-mcp-events-work
contents.content:
The client renews the subscription before refreshBefore by sending
events/subscribe with the same identity, or stops it with events/unsubscribe.
Subscriptions with a finite lifetime expire if they are not renewed.

contents.heading: how-mcp-events-work
contents.content:
Your application decides what to do with each event. Deliveries may be duplicated
or reordered, so use the subscription ID and event ID to deduplicate processing.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content:
Create an MCP client with createMCPClient and manage subscriptions through
client.experimental_events. The following methods are experimental:

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: Method

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: Description

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: list()

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: List event names, schemas, and delivery modes with events/list.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: subscribe(options)

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: Save the signing secret, send events/subscribe, and return the subscription result.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: refresh({ id })

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: Renew an existing subscription with events/subscribe.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: unsubscribe({ id })

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content: Send events/unsubscribe and remove the saved subscription after success.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content:
Refresh reuses the saved callback URL, arguments, signing secret, and latest
cursor. Your application schedules renewal before refreshBefore.

contents.heading: using-mcp-events
contents.content:
To receive events, use
experimental_createMCPEventWebhook({ store, onEvent })
as your webhook handler. It handles signed verification challenges, verifies
incoming event signatures, and passes each event directly to your onEvent
callback.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
Both use an application-provided eventStore implementing
Experimental_MCPEventStore. This is an AI SDK storage adapter, not an MCP
protocol primitive. It privately persists subscription identities, callback URLs,
signing secrets, and cursors so both sides can access them. See the
file-store example
for the five methods: get, getById, set, update, and delete. Use shared
durable storage scoped to one MCP server and authenticated principal;
update must atomically merge the supplied fields.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content: First, expose the webhook route. It must be reachable before subscribing.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
The helper verifies signatures and echoes challenges automatically. It invokes
onEvent without exposing the secret, then returns 204 after successful
processing. Processing failures return 503 so the server can retry. In your
app, resolve onEvent only after processing or durably accepting the event.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content: Two optional callbacks handle signed subscription lifecycle messages:

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
onGap({ subscription, messageId, gap }): some events are no longer available
for replay. Reconcile application state or notify the agent. After the callback
succeeds, the helper saves gap.cursor and truncated: true; the subscription
stays active and event delivery continues.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
onTerminated({ subscription, messageId, termination }): the server has ended
the subscription. Inspect termination.error for the reason and notify the
agent. After the callback succeeds, the helper removes the saved subscription.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
State updates also occur when the corresponding callback is omitted. Callback or
storage failures return 503 for retry. Resolve callbacks only after processing
or durable acceptance, and deduplicate by subscription ID and messageId (the
signed webhook-id). The helper does not run or notify an agent automatically.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content: Then subscribe using the same store.

contents.heading: connect-the-webhook-and-client
contents.content:
Before sending the subscription request, the SDK generates and saves
delivery.secret. It appends a mcp_event_subscription query parameter to the
callback URL so the webhook can find that secret even while verification is
pending. Preserve this parameter and pass the raw request body to the handler.

contents.heading: runnable-example
contents.content:
The local example
uses @modelcontextprotocol/server to emit a comment and the AI SDK to subscribe,
verify, and receive it. It needs no model API key. Local HTTP callbacks require
delivery.allowInsecureLocalhost: true; production callbacks use HTTPS.

metadata.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
metadata.description: Learn how to connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and use their tools with AI SDK Core.

contents.content:
The AI SDK supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to access their tools, resources, and prompts.
This enables your AI applications to discover and use capabilities across various services through a standardized interface.

If you're using OpenAI's Responses API, you can also use the built-in
openai.tools.mcp tool, which provides direct MCP server integration without
needing to convert tools. See the OpenAI provider
documentation for details.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: We recommend using HTTP transport (like StreamableHTTPClientTransport) for production deployments. The stdio transport should only be used for connecting to local servers as it cannot be deployed to production environments.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: Create an MCP client using one of the following transport options:

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: HTTP transport (Recommended): Either configure HTTP directly via the client using transport: { type: 'http', ... }, or use MCP's official TypeScript SDK StreamableHTTPClientTransport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: SSE (Server-Sent Events): An alternative HTTP-based transport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: stdio: For local development only. Uses standard input/output streams for local MCP servers

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content:
The AI SDK MCP client supports both legacy initialization-based protocol
versions and stateless MCP 2026-07-28. The built-in stdio transport probes
with server/discover and automatically falls back to the legacy
initialize handshake for older servers. Custom transports can opt into this
negotiation with supportsProtocolVersionDiscovery: true.

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: For production deployments, we recommend using the HTTP transport. You can configure it directly on the client:

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content:
If a legacy MCP server uses Streamable HTTP sessions, you can reattach to a
saved session by restoring both the previous session id and initialize result.
MCP 2026-07-28 is stateless and does not use these options:

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content:
When initialInitializeResult is provided, createMCPClient reuses the cached
initialize metadata and does not send another initialize request. When
onSessionExpired is called, the transport has already cleared the session id
and the request still fails with the underlying HTTP error. Retry by creating a
fresh client without initialSessionId or initialInitializeResult.
Set terminateSessionOnClose to false when closing only the local client but
keeping the MCP session available for a later reattach.

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: Alternatively, you can use StreamableHTTPClientTransport from MCP's official TypeScript SDK:

contents.heading: sse-transport
contents.content: SSE provides an alternative HTTP-based transport option. Configure it with a type and url property. You can also provide an authProvider for OAuth:

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The stdio transport should only be used for local servers.

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The Stdio transport can be imported from either the MCP SDK or the AI SDK:

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content: You can also bring your own transport by implementing the MCPTransport interface for specific requirements not covered by the standard transports.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
The client returned by the createMCPClient function is a
lightweight client intended for use in tool conversion. It currently does not
support all features of the full MCP client, such as automatic session
persistence, resumable streams, and receiving notifications.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
Authorization via OAuth is supported when using the AI SDK MCP HTTP or SSE
transports by providing an authProvider.

contents.heading: shared-oauth-credential-storage
contents.content:
When multiple MCP clients or replicas share OAuth credentials, a rotating refresh
token can be used concurrently. One refresh may save new tokens while another
receives invalid_grant for the old refresh token.

contents.heading: shared-oauth-credential-storage
contents.content:
The optional OAuthClientProvider.invalidateCredentials method receives a
second argument identifying the tokens used by a failed refresh:

contents.heading: shared-oauth-credential-storage
contents.content:
For scope === 'tokens' with a context, delete the credential only if the stored
access and refresh tokens still match context.tokens. The comparison and
deletion must be atomic, using a conditional database operation or a transaction.
If they no longer match, leave the newer tokens in storage. The SDK retries
authorization and reads the stored tokens again.

contents.heading: shared-oauth-credential-storage
contents.content:
The SDK also provides this context when invalidating stored tokens that lack an
authorization server pin. Other invalidations can omit the context.

contents.heading: shared-oauth-credential-storage
contents.content:
If an authorization-code exchange returns invalid_grant, the SDK propagates
the error without invalidating stored credentials or retrying the rejected code.
A rejected authorization code does not indicate that existing access or refresh
tokens are invalid.

contents.heading: oauth-authorization-server-validation
contents.content:
When using MCP OAuth in server-side applications, the MCP server can advertise
the OAuth authorization server to use. If you connect to MCP servers outside
your control, implement validateAuthorizationServerURL on your
authProvider to allow only the authorization server origins you trust:

contents.heading: oauth-authorization-server-validation
contents.content:
This hook is called before the SDK fetches authorization server metadata, so a
rejected URL is not requested. It is optional and does not change existing OAuth
flows unless you implement it.

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
When completing an OAuth authorization callback, pass the callback's iss
parameter to auth as callbackIssuer:

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
When iss is present, it must exactly match the discovered authorization
server issuer. The authorization code is not exchanged when it does not match.

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
Dynamic client registration requests include an OAuth application_type. The
client infers native for loopback, localhost, and custom-scheme redirects,
and web for remote HTTP(S) redirects. You can override this by setting
application_type in the provider's clientMetadata.

contents.heading: dynamic-client-credential-recovery
contents.content:
To let the SDK replace invalid credentials created through dynamic client
registration, implement isClientInformationDynamicallyRegistered on the
OAuth client provider. Return true only when the current client information
came from a dynamic registration response. Persist this provenance alongside
the credentials when the provider is recreated between requests.

contents.heading: dynamic-client-credential-recovery
contents.content:
When this method is omitted or returns false, client information is treated
as pre-registered and is preserved after invalid_client and
unauthorized_client errors. The SDK does not infer provenance from fields such
as redirect_uris, because pre-registered clients can contain the same
metadata as dynamically registered clients.

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
MCP tool calls can fail for transient transport reasons, such as rate limits,
temporary overload, or gateway timeouts. You can opt into automatic retries for
tools/call requests by passing maxRetries when creating the client:

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
Retries are disabled by default. Built-in retry matching is intended for
transient HTTP and network failures only. JSON-RPC application errors, such as
invalid tool arguments, are surfaced immediately without retrying. Successful
MCP tool responses with isError: true are also returned to the model without
retrying.

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
maxRetries applies to tools/call requests, not to client initialization.
The following example identifies potentially transient HTTP initialization
failures using the exported MCPClientError type guard:

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
This example only considers HTTP statuses. A missing statusCode does not
establish that a failure is transient: configuration errors, protocol errors,
and cancelled requests can also lack an HTTP status. Network and timeout
retries require a separate application policy. OAuth errors such as
UnauthorizedError and MCPClientOAuthError are rethrown by this example.

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
Only enable retries for MCP tools where retrying is safe. Retrying
non-idempotent tools, such as tools that send emails or create records, can
duplicate side effects.

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: After initialization, you should close the MCP client based on your usage pattern:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For short-lived usage (e.g., single requests), close the client when the response is finished

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For long-running clients (e.g., command line apps), keep the client open but ensure it's closed when the application terminates

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When streaming responses, you can close the client when the LLM response has finished. For example, when using streamText, you should use the onEnd callback:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When generating responses without streaming, you can use try/finally or cleanup functions in your framework:

contents.heading: using-mcp-tools
contents.content: The client's tools method acts as an adapter between MCP tools and AI SDK tools. It supports two approaches for working with tool schemas:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: With schema discovery, all tools offered by the server are automatically listed, and input parameter types are inferred based on the schemas provided by the server:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: This approach is simpler to implement and automatically stays in sync with server changes. However, you won't have TypeScript type safety during development, and all tools from the server will be loaded

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
MCP servers can describe tool behavior with annotations such as
readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint. The
MCP client exposes these annotations on each tool's metadata.annotations and
on the resulting tool call's toolMetadata.annotations.

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
Annotations are untrusted, server-provided hints. The MCP client does not turn
them into an approval policy automatically. Applications should combine them
with deterministic controls such as tool allowlists, scoped credentials, and
their own toolApproval policy.

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
The following conservative policy allows tools to run automatically only when
the server explicitly marks them as read-only. Tools with readOnlyHint: false
or no readOnlyHint require user approval:

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
See the
local tool annotations example
for a complete annotated MCP server and application-layer approval
configuration. Start the server and client in separate terminals:

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
Ask the client to read, delete, or create a note. The read-only tool executes
immediately. The destructive and unannotated tools prompt for approval; after
you enter y or n, the client sends the decision back and prints the model's
response.

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: For better type safety and control, you can define the tools and their input schemas explicitly in your client code:

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: This approach provides full TypeScript type safety and IDE autocompletion, letting you catch parameter mismatches during development. When you define schemas, the client only pulls the explicitly defined tools, keeping your application focused on the tools it needs

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: When MCP servers return structuredContent (per the MCP specification), you can define an outputSchema to get typed tool results:

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: When outputSchema is provided:

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: The client extracts structuredContent from the tool result

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: The output is validated against your schema at runtime

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: You get full TypeScript type safety for the result

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: If the server doesn't return structuredContent, the client falls back to parsing JSON from the text content. If neither is available or validation fails, an error is thrown.

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: If a server returns structuredContent without the backwards-compatible content field, the client adds a text content block containing the serialized JSON before returning the result. This compatibility behavior handles servers that omit the text mirror recommended by the MCP specification.

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content:
Without outputSchema, the tool returns the raw CallToolResult object
containing content and optional isError fields.

contents.heading: using-mcp-resources
contents.content: According to the MCP specification, resources are application-driven data sources that provide context to the model. Unlike tools (which are model-controlled), your application decides when to fetch and pass resources as context.

contents.heading: using-mcp-resources
contents.content: The MCP client provides three methods for working with resources:

contents.heading: listing-resources
contents.content: List all available resources from the MCP server:

contents.heading: reading-resource-contents
contents.content: Read the contents of a specific resource by its URI:

contents.heading: listing-resource-templates
contents.content: Resource templates are dynamic URI patterns that allow flexible queries. List all available templates:

contents.heading: using-mcp-completions
contents.content:
MCP servers can provide autocompletion suggestions for prompt arguments and
resource template variables when they advertise the completions capability.
Use complete to ask the server for suggestions based on the current partial
argument value:

contents.heading: using-mcp-completions
contents.content:
For resource templates or prompts with multiple arguments, pass already resolved
values through context.arguments:

contents.heading: using-mcp-completions
contents.content:
If the connected server does not advertise capabilities.completions, the
client throws an MCPClientError.

contents.heading: using-mcp-prompts
contents.content: MCP Prompts is an experimental feature and may change in the future.

contents.heading: using-mcp-prompts
contents.content: According to the MCP specification, prompts are user-controlled templates that servers expose for clients to list and retrieve with optional arguments.

contents.heading: getting-a-prompt
contents.content: Retrieve prompt messages, optionally passing arguments defined by the server:

contents.heading: handling-elicitation-requests
contents.content: Elicitation is a mechanism where MCP servers can request additional information from the client during tool execution. For example, a server might need user input to complete a registration form or confirmation for a sensitive operation.

contents.heading: handling-elicitation-requests
contents.content:
It is up to the client application to handle elicitation requests properly.
The MCP client simply surfaces these requests from the server to your
application code.

contents.heading: enabling-elicitation-support
contents.content: To enable elicitation, you need to advertise the capability when creating the MCP client:

contents.heading: registering-an-elicitation-handler
contents.content: Use the onElicitationRequest method to register a handler that will be called when the server requests input:

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: Your handler must return an object with an action field that can be one of:

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'accept': User provided the requested information. Must include content with the data.

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'decline': User chose not to provide the information.

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'cancel': User cancelled the operation entirely.

contents.heading: detecting-tool-definition-drift-rug-pull
contents.content:
An MCP server sends tool definitions (name, description, input schema) when your
app first connects, and you typically review and approve them at that point.
Nothing in the protocol prevents the server from later serving a different
definition for the same tool name — for example a description carrying injected
instructions, or an input schema widened with an extra field. Because the SDK
uses whatever tools you pass on each call, a mutated definition returned by a
later mcpClient.tools() fetch would be used without any comparison to what was
approved. This is the MCP "rug pull"
class of attack.

contents.heading: detecting-tool-definition-drift-rug-pull
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides two functions to pin the approved definitions and detect
changes. fingerprintTools digests the server-controlled, security-relevant
fields of each tool (string description, resolved input schema, and title)
into a stable map of tool name to digest. detectToolDrift diffs two such maps.
Your app owns baseline storage and the response to drift (block, force
re-approval, or alert):

contents.heading: detecting-tool-definition-drift-rug-pull
contents.content:
This detects mutation of a tool's description, input schema, or title — the
prompt-injection and schema-widening vectors. It cannot detect a
behavior/endpoint swap where the name, description, and schema are all
unchanged, because the tool runs remotely on the MCP server and that change is
invisible to the client. Core stays unopinionated: it does not persist
baselines or block calls — those are your app's responsibility.

contents.heading: examples
contents.content: You can see MCP in action in the following examples:

metadata.title: Language Model Middleware
metadata.description: Learn how to use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models

contents.content:
Language model middleware is a way to enhance the behavior of language models
by intercepting and modifying the calls to the language model.

It can be used to add features like guardrails, RAG, caching, and logging
in a language model agnostic way. Such middleware can be developed and
distributed independently from the language models that they are applied to.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
You can use language model middleware with the wrapLanguageModel function.
It takes a language model and a language model middleware and returns a new
language model that incorporates the middleware.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content: The wrapped language model can be used just like any other language model, e.g. in streamText:

contents.heading: multiple-middlewares
contents.content:
You can provide multiple middlewares to the wrapLanguageModel function.
The middlewares will be applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK comes with several built-in middlewares that you can use to configure language models:

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: extractReasoningMiddleware: Extracts reasoning information from the generated text and exposes it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: extractJsonMiddleware: Extracts JSON from text content by stripping markdown code fences. Useful when using Output.object() with models that wrap JSON responses in code blocks.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: simulateStreamingMiddleware: Simulates streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: defaultInstructionsMiddleware: Applies default instructions when a call does not provide its own instructions.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: defaultSettingsMiddleware: Applies default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: addToolInputExamplesMiddleware: Adds tool input examples to tool descriptions for providers that don't natively support the inputExamples property.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
Some providers and models expose reasoning information in the generated text using special tags,
e.g. <think> and </think>.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: The extractReasoningMiddleware function can be used to extract this reasoning information and expose it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: You can then use that enhanced model in functions like generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
The extractReasoningMiddleware function also includes a startWithReasoning option.
When set to true, the reasoning tag will be prepended to the generated text.
This is useful for models that do not include the reasoning tag at the beginning of the response.
For more details, see the DeepSeek R1 guide.

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: Some models wrap JSON responses in markdown code fences (e.g., ```json ... ```) even when you request structured output.

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: The extractJsonMiddleware function strips these code fences from the response, making it compatible with Output.object().

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: You can also provide a custom transform function for models that use different formatting:

contents.heading: simulate-streaming
contents.content:
The simulateStreamingMiddleware function can be used to simulate streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.
This is useful when you want to maintain a consistent streaming interface even when using models that only provide complete responses.

contents.heading: default-settings
contents.content: The defaultSettingsMiddleware function can be used to apply default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: default-instructions
contents.content:
The defaultInstructionsMiddleware function applies instructions to calls that
do not already contain a system message. Instructions provided directly on a
call take precedence over the defaults.

contents.heading: default-instructions
contents.content:
The instructions option also accepts a SystemModelMessage or an array of
SystemModelMessage objects when you need provider options on an instruction.

contents.heading: default-instructions
contents.content:
The middleware treats any system message in the normalized prompt as
call-level instructions and does not add the defaults. Only enable
allowSystemInMessages for trusted message histories, because a system
message in that history can override these defaults.

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content:
The addToolInputExamplesMiddleware function adds tool input examples to tool descriptions.
This is useful for providers that don't natively support the inputExamples property on tools.
The middleware serializes the examples into the tool's description text so models can still benefit from seeing example inputs.

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content: When you define a tool with inputExamples, the middleware will append them to the tool's description:

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content: The tool description will be transformed to:

contents.heading: options
contents.content: prefix (optional): A prefix text to prepend before the examples. Default: 'Input Examples:'.

contents.heading: options
contents.content: format (optional): A custom formatter function for each example. Receives the example object and its index. Default: JSON.stringify(example.input).

contents.heading: options
contents.content: remove (optional): Whether to remove the inputExamples property from the tool after adding them to the description. Default: true.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK provides a Language Model Middleware specification. Community members can develop middleware that adheres to this specification, making it compatible with the AI SDK ecosystem.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: Here are some community middlewares that you can explore:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The Custom tool call parser middleware extends tool call capabilities to models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style tools parameter. This includes many self-hosted and third-party models that lack native function calling features.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content:
Using this middleware on models that support native function calls may result
in unintended performance degradation, so check whether your model supports
native function calls before deciding to use it.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: This middleware enables function calling capabilities by converting function schemas into prompt instructions and parsing the model's responses into structured function calls. It works by transforming the JSON function definitions into natural language instructions the model can understand, then analyzing the generated text to extract function call attempts. This approach allows developers to use the same function calling API across different model providers, even with models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style function calling format, providing a consistent function calling experience regardless of the underlying model implementation.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The @ai-sdk-tool/parser package offers three middleware variants:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: createToolMiddleware: A flexible function for creating custom tool call middleware tailored to specific models

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: hermesToolMiddleware: Ready-to-use middleware for Hermes & Qwen format function calls

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: gemmaToolMiddleware: Pre-configured middleware for Gemma 3 model series function call format

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Here's how you can enable function calls with Gemma models that don't support them natively:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Find more examples at this link.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
Implementing language model middleware is advanced functionality and requires
a solid understanding of the language model
specification.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: You can implement any of the following three function to modify the behavior of the language model:

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: transformParams: Transforms the parameters before they are passed to the language model, for both doGenerate and doStream.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapGenerate: Wraps the doGenerate method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapStream: Wraps the doStream method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
Every LanguageModelV4Middleware object must set
specificationVersion: 'v4'.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: Here are some examples of how to implement language model middleware:

contents.heading: examples
contents.content:
These examples are not meant to be used in production. They are just to show
how you can use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models.

contents.heading: logging
contents.content: This example shows how to log the parameters and generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: caching
contents.content: This example shows how to build a simple cache for the generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content: This example shows how to use RAG as middleware.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content:
Helper functions like getLastUserMessageText and findSources are not part
of the AI SDK. They are just used in this example to illustrate the concept of
RAG.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
Guard rails are a way to ensure that the generated text of a language model call
is safe and appropriate. This example shows how to use guardrails as middleware.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
The streaming example buffers each text block until text-end so matches
split across text-delta chunks cannot leak through. This delays output and
uses memory proportional to the text block size. Do not redact each delta
independently. An incremental implementation must retain every possible
incomplete match, and a fixed-size buffer alone is not safe for unbounded
variable-length patterns.

contents.heading: configuring-per-request-custom-metadata
contents.content: To send and access custom metadata in Middleware, you can use providerOptions. This is useful when building logging middleware where you want to pass additional context like user IDs, timestamps, or other contextual data that can help with tracking and debugging.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: An overview of AI SDK Core.

contents.content:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced programs that can understand, create, and engage with human language on a large scale.
They are trained on vast amounts of written material to recognize patterns in language and predict what might come next in a given piece of text.

AI SDK Core simplifies working with LLMs by offering a standardized way of integrating them into your app - so you can focus on building great AI applications for your users, not waste time on technical details.
For example, here’s how you can generate text with various models using the AI SDK:

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
AI SDK Core has various functions designed for text generation, structured data generation, and tool usage.
These functions take a standardized approach to setting up prompts and settings, making it easier to work with different models.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
generateText: Generates text and tool calls.
This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases such as automation tasks where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
streamText: Stream text and tool calls.
You can use the streamText function for interactive use cases such as chat bots and content streaming.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content: Both generateText and streamText support structured output via the output property (e.g. Output.object(), Output.array()), allowing you to generate typed, schema-validated data for information extraction, synthetic data generation, classification tasks, and streaming generated UIs.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Please check out the AI SDK Core API Reference for more details on each function.

metadata.title: Prompt Engineering
metadata.description: Learn how to develop prompts with AI SDK Core.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When you create prompts that include tools, getting good results can be tricky as the number and complexity of your tools increases.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Here are a few tips to help you get the best results:

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use a model that is strong at tool calling, such as gpt-6-astra or claude-sonnet-5-5. Weaker models will often struggle to call tools effectively and flawlessly.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the number of tools low, e.g. to 5 or less.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the complexity of the tool parameters low. Complex Zod schemas with many nested and optional elements, unions, etc. can be challenging for the model to work with.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use semantically meaningful names for your tools, parameters, parameter properties, etc. The more information you pass to the model, the better it can understand what you want.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Add .describe("...") to your Zod schema properties to give the model hints about what a particular property is for.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When the output of a tool might be unclear to the model and there are dependencies between tools, use the description field of a tool to provide information about the output of the tool execution.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: You can include example input/outputs of tool calls in your prompt to help the model understand how to use the tools. Keep in mind that the tools work with JSON objects, so the examples should use JSON.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: In general, the goal should be to give the model all information it needs in a clear way.

contents.heading: tool--structured-data-schemas
contents.content: The mapping from Zod schemas to LLM inputs (typically JSON schema) is not always straightforward, since the mapping is not one-to-one.

contents.heading: zod-dates
contents.content:
Zod expects JavaScript Date objects, but models return dates as strings.
You can specify and validate the date format using z.string().datetime() or z.string().date(),
and then use a Zod transformer to convert the string to a Date object.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: When working with tools that have optional parameters, you may encounter compatibility issues with certain providers that use strict schema validation.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content:
This is particularly relevant for OpenAI models with structured outputs
(strict mode).

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: For maximum compatibility, optional parameters should use .nullable() instead of .optional():

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: For tool calls and object generation, it's recommended to use temperature: 0 to ensure deterministic and consistent results:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Lower temperature values reduce randomness in model outputs, which is particularly important when the model needs to:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Generate structured data with specific formats

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Make precise tool calls with correct parameters

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Follow strict schemas consistently

contents.heading: inspecting-warnings
contents.content:
Not all providers support all AI SDK features.
Providers either throw exceptions or return warnings when they do not support a feature.
To check if your prompt, tools, and settings are handled correctly by the provider, you can check the call warnings:

contents.heading: request-messages
contents.content:
You can inspect the input messages that were sent to the model for the final step using request.messages.
Set include.requestMessages to true to include these messages in step results.

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content:
You can inspect the raw HTTP request bodies for models that expose them, e.g. OpenAI.
This allows you to inspect the exact payload that is sent to the model provider in the provider-specific way.

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content: Request bodies are available via the finalStep.request.body property of the response:

metadata.title: Provider & Model Management
metadata.description: Learn how to work with multiple providers and models

title.children: Combining Custom Providers, Provider Registry, and Middleware

contents.content:
When you work with multiple providers and models, it is often desirable to manage them in a central place
and access the models through simple string ids.

The AI SDK offers custom providers and
a provider registry for this purpose:

With custom providers, you can pre-configure model settings, provide model name aliases,
and limit the available models.
The provider registry lets you mix multiple providers and access them through simple string ids.
You can mix and match custom providers, the provider registry, and middleware in your application.

contents.heading: custom-providers
contents.content: You can create a custom provider using customProvider.

contents.heading: example-custom-model-settings
contents.content:
You might want to override the default model settings for a provider or provide model name aliases
with pre-configured settings.

contents.heading: example-model-name-alias
contents.content: You can also provide model name aliases, so you can update the model version in one place in the future:

contents.heading: example-limit-available-models
contents.content: You can limit the available models in the system, even if you have multiple providers.

contents.heading: example-files-and-skills-interfaces
contents.content: You can attach a provider's files or skills interface to your custom provider. This allows you to use uploadFile and uploadSkill through the same provider abstraction.

contents.heading: example-files-and-skills-interfaces
contents.content: If no files or skills option is set but a fallbackProvider is configured, the custom provider will inherit those interfaces from the fallback.

contents.heading: provider-registry
contents.content: You can create a provider registry with multiple providers and models using createProviderRegistry.

contents.heading: setup-with-custom-separator
contents.content: By default, the registry uses : as the separator between provider and model IDs. You can customize this separator:

contents.heading: example-use-language-models
contents.content:
You can access language models by using the languageModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-text-embedding-models
contents.content:
You can access text embedding models by using the .embeddingModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-image-models
contents.content:
You can access image models by using the imageModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-video-models
contents.content:
You can access video models by using the videoModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-files-interface
contents.content:
You can access a provider's files interface by calling registry.files(providerId).
This is useful when you want to upload files through a provider in the registry before referencing them in model requests.

contents.heading: example-use-skills-interface
contents.content: You can access a provider's skills interface by calling registry.skills(providerId).

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content:
The central idea of provider management is to set up a file that contains all the providers and models you want to use.
You may want to pre-configure model settings, provide model name aliases, limit the available models, and more.

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: Here is an example that implements the following concepts:

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: pass through gateway with a namespace prefix (here: gateway > *)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: pass through a full provider with a namespace prefix (here: xai > *)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: setup an OpenAI-compatible provider with custom api key and base URL (here: custom > *)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: setup model name aliases (here: anthropic > fast, anthropic > writing, anthropic > reasoning)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: pre-configure model settings (here: anthropic > reasoning)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: validate the provider-specific options (here: AnthropicLanguageModelOptions)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: use a fallback provider (here: anthropic > *)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: limit a provider to certain models without a fallback (here: groq > llama-3.1-8b-instant, groq > qwen/qwen3.6-27b)

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content: define a custom separator for the provider registry (here: >)

contents.heading: global-provider-configuration
contents.content: The AI SDK 5 includes a global provider feature that allows you to specify a model using just a plain model ID string:

contents.heading: global-provider-configuration
contents.content: By default, the global provider is set to the Vercel AI Gateway.

contents.heading: customizing-the-global-provider
contents.content: You can set your own preferred global provider:

contents.heading: customizing-the-global-provider
contents.content: This simplifies provider usage and makes it easier to switch between providers without changing your model references throughout your codebase.

contents.heading: experimental-decision-models
contents.content:
Custom providers accept decisionModels aliases, and registries expose
decisionModel('provider:model'). These methods return model instances for
experimental_decide. Direct string IDs use Gateway by default, or an
explicitly configured default provider with a decisionModel method. Registry
middleware for language and image models does not apply to decision.
See Decisions
for aliases, default-provider configuration, and capability differences.

headings.content: Combining Custom Providers, Provider Registry, and Middleware

metadata.title: Realtime
metadata.description: Learn how to build realtime voice conversations with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
This guide covers legacy token-based, turn-based realtime conversations over
WebSockets. These sessions run in the browser and connect
directly to the provider using a short-lived token that you create on your
server. You can also route the connection through AI Gateway.

For OpenAI Live's continuous JSON/PCM16 WSS relay runtime and application-handled
client delegation, see
experimental_useRealtime.
The typical flow is:
The browser calls your setup endpoint.
Your server creates a short-lived realtime token with experimental_realtime.getToken().
The browser opens a WebSocket connection to the provider or AI Gateway.
The model streams audio, text, and tool calls back to the browser.
Tool calls are handled by your application with onToolCall.

For continuous OpenAI Live conversations, use an application-owned WebSocket
relay or optional WebRTC via api.session. Live uses client delegation: your
application handles delegated work and submits context rather than using the
turn-based tool loop below. See the
experimental_useRealtime reference
for SDP setup, server-owned permissions, capture ownership, and graceful close.

contents.heading: setup-endpoint
contents.content:
Create a setup endpoint that returns a short-lived token for the realtime
provider. This endpoint can also attach tool definitions to the session.

contents.heading: setup-endpoint
contents.content:
In production, authenticate and rate-limit your setup endpoint. It creates
realtime sessions using your server-side API key.

contents.heading: ai-gateway
contents.content:
Use AI Gateway when you want the same
realtime client code to work across supported upstream providers. The Gateway
normalizes realtime events server-side, and the browser still receives only a
short-lived client secret.

contents.heading: ai-gateway
contents.content: Create the short-lived Gateway realtime token from a server-side setup endpoint:

contents.heading: ai-gateway
contents.content: Then use the matching Gateway realtime model in the browser:

contents.heading: ai-gateway
contents.content:
gateway.experimental_realtime.getToken() must run on your server because it
uses your Gateway credential to mint a vcst_ client secret. Creating the
realtime model with gateway.experimental_realtime() is safe in the browser.

contents.heading: ai-gateway
contents.content:
Tool definitions work the same way with AI Gateway: convert AI SDK tools with
experimental_getRealtimeToolDefinitions() in your setup endpoint and return
the definitions alongside the token. The hook includes them in the session
update after the WebSocket opens.

contents.heading: client-session
contents.content:
Use the experimental_useRealtime hook to connect to a realtime model, capture
microphone audio, play model audio, send text messages, and render messages.

contents.heading: client-session
contents.content:
Keep model and session configuration objects stable across renders. Use module
scope as above, or useMemo when configuration depends on props. Replacing either
object replaces the hook's session.

contents.heading: tool-calling
contents.content:
Realtime tool execution is client-driven. The provider sends tool calls over the
WebSocket, and your application handles them with onToolCall. If the result is
available immediately, return it from onToolCall. The SDK sends it back to the
provider as tool output.

contents.heading: tool-calling
contents.content:
For server-backed tools, call an app-specific API endpoint from onToolCall.
Avoid generic "execute tool by name" routes. App-specific endpoints are easier
to secure because they can use your normal authentication, authorization,
validation, and rate limiting rules.

contents.heading: client-tool-handler
contents.content:
You can also submit tool output manually with addToolOutput when the tool
requires user interaction or another asynchronous process:

contents.heading: supported-providers
contents.content: Realtime models are available on providers that expose realtime WebSocket APIs:

contents.heading: supported-providers
contents.content:
You can also route realtime through the AI Gateway, which normalizes the
session so the same client code works across upstream providers:

contents.heading: supported-providers
contents.content:
gateway.experimental_realtime.getToken() mints a short-lived Gateway client
secret on your server. The browser uses that token to open the Gateway
WebSocket; the SDK handles the Gateway-specific WebSocket subprotocols for you.
See the AI Gateway realtime docs
for Gateway-specific token and provider option details.

metadata.title: Reasoning
metadata.description: Learn how to control reasoning across providers with the top-level reasoning parameter.

contents.content: Many language models support an internal "reasoning" phase (sometimes also called "thinking") before producing a response. The AI SDK provides a top-level reasoning parameter on generateText and streamText that controls this behavior across providers with a single, portable setting.

contents.heading: basic-usage
