AI SDK Tools vs MCP Tools

contents.content:
As covered under Foundations, tools are objects that can be called by the model to perform a specific task.
Function tools and dynamic tools contain several core elements:

description: An optional description of the tool that can influence when the tool is picked. It can be a string or a function that derives the description from the tool's context and experimental sandbox.
inputSchema: A Zod schema or a JSON schema that defines the input parameters. The schema is consumed by the LLM, and also used to validate the LLM tool calls.

execute: An optional async function that is called with the inputs from the tool call. It produces a value of type RESULT (generic type). It is optional because you might want to forward tool calls to the client or to a queue instead of executing them in the same process.
strict: (optional, boolean) Enables strict tool calling when supported by the provider

You can use the tool helper function to
infer the types of the execute parameters.
The tools parameter of generateText and streamText is an object that has the tool names as keys and the tools as values:

When a model uses a tool, it is called a "tool call" and the output of the
tool is called a "tool result".

Tool calling is not restricted to only text generation.
You can also use it to render user interfaces (Generative UI).

contents.heading: dynamic-descriptions
contents.content:
Tool descriptions can be fixed strings or functions. Use a function when the
description sent to the model should depend on the current tool context or
experimental sandbox, such as a tenant, project, environment, or workspace.

contents.heading: dynamic-descriptions
contents.content:
The description function is resolved before the tool definition is sent to the
model for each generation step. It receives the matching tool context from
toolsContext and the current experimental_sandbox, if one was provided. If prepareStep
updates toolsContext or experimental_sandbox, the next step uses those updated values.

contents.heading: strict-mode
contents.content:
When enabled, language model providers that support strict tool calling will only generate tool calls that are valid according to your defined inputSchema.
This increases the reliability of tool calling.
However, not all schemas may be supported in strict mode, and what is supported depends on the specific provider.

contents.heading: strict-mode
contents.content: By default, strict mode is disabled. You can enable it per-tool by setting strict: true:

contents.heading: strict-mode
contents.content:
Not all providers or models support strict mode. For those that do not, this
option is ignored.

contents.heading: input-examples
contents.content:
You can specify example inputs for your tools to help guide the model on how input data should be structured.
When supported by providers, input examples can help when JSON schema itself does not fully specify the intended
usage or when there are optional values.

contents.heading: input-examples
contents.content:
Only the Anthropic providers supports tool input examples natively. Other
providers ignore the setting.

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: By default, tools with an execute function run automatically as the model calls them. Configure approval with toolApproval on generateText, streamText, or ToolLoopAgent.

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: toolApproval can be either:

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: A GenericToolApprovalFunction for all tool calls

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: A per-tool map of statuses and/or SingleToolApprovalFunction callbacks (either function may return undefined for the same effect as 'not-applicable')

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: The older needsApproval property on tool() definitions is deprecated. Existing code still works, but new code should move approval logic to toolApproval.

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content:
In the per-tool object form, each key can be one of four statuses, either as a
string or as an object with a type field:

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content: 'not-applicable': the tool is executed without an approval flow. This is the default behavior.

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content: 'approved': record an automatic approval by emitting approval request/response parts in the output, then execute the tool

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content: 'denied': record an automatic denial by emitting approval request/response parts in the output, then surface a denied tool output

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content: 'user-approval': emit an approval request and wait for an explicit response

contents.heading: configure-toolapproval
contents.content:
Object statuses can also include a reason. For automatic approvals and denials,
the reason is emitted on the approval response. For manual approval, the reason
is emitted on the approval request so it can be shown to the approver:

contents.heading: generic-toolapproval-function
contents.content:
Pass a GenericToolApprovalFunction as toolApproval to handle every tool
call in one place. The callback receives toolCall, tools, toolsContext,
messages, and runtimeContext (the same runtimeContext you pass to
generateText or streamText, typed as the second ToolApprovalConfiguration
type parameter; it defaults to Context). It may return undefined for the same effect as 'not-applicable'.

contents.heading: generic-toolapproval-function
contents.content:
The same pattern works for streamText and for toolApproval on
ToolLoopAgent when you need one policy
across all tools.

contents.heading: generic-toolapproval-function
contents.content:
For a per-tool object instead, each key can be a SingleToolApprovalFunction
that receives the tool input and options toolCallId, messages, toolContext
(the same shape as tool execution context, without abortSignal), and
runtimeContext. Return undefined for the same effect as 'not-applicable'.

contents.heading: generic-toolapproval-function
contents.content: This is useful for tools that perform sensitive operations like executing commands, processing payments, modifying data, and more potentially dangerous actions.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: When a tool requires manual approval, generateText and streamText don't pause execution. Instead, they complete and return tool-approval-request parts in the result content. This means the manual approval flow requires two calls to the model: the first returns the approval request, and the second (after receiving the approval response) either executes the tool or informs the model that approval was denied.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content:
Manual approval comes from toolApproval returning 'user-approval'. If the
tool should just execute normally, use 'not-applicable', return undefined
from a GenericToolApprovalFunction or SingleToolApprovalFunction, or omit
the setting entirely. If toolApproval returns 'approved' or 'denied' or
their object forms, the SDK records that decision automatically in the same
generation by emitting approval request/response parts. When you provide a
reason on an automatic approval or denial, that reason is included in the
emitted approval response and can be rendered in the UI.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Here's the manual approval flow:

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Call generateText or streamText with toolApproval

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The model generates a tool call

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The call returns tool-approval-request parts in result.content

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Your app requests approval and collects the user's decision

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Add a tool-approval-response to the messages array

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Call generateText or streamText again with the updated messages

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: If approved, the tool runs and returns a result. If denied, the model sees the denial and responds accordingly.

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content: After calling generateText or streamText, check result.content for tool-approval-request parts:

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content: To respond, create a tool-approval-response and add it to your messages:

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content: Then call generateText or streamText again with the updated messages. If approved, the tool executes. If denied, the model receives the denial and can respond accordingly.

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content:
When the tool should execute without any approval metadata in the output, use
'not-applicable', return undefined from an approval function, or omit toolApproval. Use 'approved', 'denied', or
their object forms only when you want the result to include an automatic
tool-approval-request with isAutomatic: true followed by a
tool-approval-response, so you can inspect or render the decision without
prompting the user again.

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content:
When a tool execution is denied, consider adding a system instruction like
"When a tool execution is not approved, do not retry it" to prevent the model
from attempting the same call again.

contents.heading: handling-approval-requests
contents.content:
Provider-executed tools are executed provider-side without considering the
tool approval setting. toolApproval (and the deprecated needsApproval)
only control tools that the AI SDK executes locally.

contents.heading: dynamic-approval
contents.content:
You can make approval decisions based on tool input by providing an async
function in a per-tool toolApproval object:

contents.heading: dynamic-approval
contents.content:
In this example, only transactions over $1000 require approval. Smaller
transactions execute automatically.

contents.heading: dynamic-approval
contents.content:
You can use a SingleToolApprovalFunction in a per-tool toolApproval object when you want to return
'not-applicable', undefined (equivalent to 'not-applicable'), 'approved', 'denied', or 'user-approval' at call time
instead of defining the default on the tool itself. For automatic approvals and
denials, the callback can also return { type, reason }, for example
{ type: 'denied', reason: 'blocked by policy' }. For decisions that need the full toolCall or
several tools at once, pass a GenericToolApprovalFunction as toolApproval instead
of a per-tool map. The generic function can return undefined the same way.

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval-with-usechat
contents.content: When using useChat, the approval flow is handled through UI state. See Chatbot Tool Usage for details on handling approvals in your UI with addToolApprovalResponse.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: With the stopWhen setting, you can enable multi-step calls in generateText and streamText. When stopWhen is set and the model generates a tool call, the AI SDK will trigger a new generation passing in the tool result until there are no further tool calls or the stopping condition is met.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: The AI SDK provides several built-in stopping conditions:

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: isStepCount(count) — stops after a specified number of steps (default: isStepCount(20))

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: hasToolCall(...toolNames) — stops when any of the specified tools is called

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: isLoopFinished() — never triggers, letting the loop run until naturally finished

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: You can also combine multiple conditions in an array or create custom conditions. See Loop Control for more details.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content:
The stopWhen conditions are only evaluated when the last step contains tool
results.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: By default, when you use generateText or streamText, it triggers a single generation. This works well for many use cases where you can rely on the model's training data to generate a response. However, when you provide tools, the model now has the choice to either generate a normal text response, or generate a tool call. If the model generates a tool call, its generation is complete and that step is finished.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: You may want the model to generate text after the tool has been executed, either to summarize the tool results in the context of the users query. In many cases, you may also want the model to use multiple tools in a single response. This is where multi-step calls come in.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: You can think of multi-step calls in a similar way to a conversation with a human. When you ask a question, if the person does not have the requisite knowledge in their common knowledge (a model's training data), the person may need to look up information (use a tool) before they can provide you with an answer. In the same way, the model may need to call a tool to get the information it needs to answer your question where each generation (tool call or text generation) is a step.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: In the following example, there are two steps:

contents.heading: example
contents.content: Step 1

contents.heading: example
contents.content: The prompt 'What is the weather in San Francisco?' is sent to the model.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: The model generates a tool call.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: The tool call is executed.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: Step 2

contents.heading: example
contents.content: The tool result is sent to the model.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: The model generates a response considering the tool result.

contents.heading: steps
contents.content:
To access intermediate tool calls and results, you can use the steps property in the result object
or the streamText onEnd callback.
It contains all the text, tool calls, tool results, per-step performance, and more from each step.

contents.heading: onstepend-callback
contents.content:
When using generateText or streamText, you can provide an onStepEnd callback that
is triggered when a step is finished,
i.e. all text deltas, tool calls, and tool results for the step are available.
When you have multiple steps, the callback is triggered for each step.

contents.heading: onstepend-callback
contents.content: The callback receives a stepNumber (zero-based) to identify which step just completed:

contents.heading: tool-execution-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
You can use onToolExecutionStart and onToolExecutionEnd to observe tool execution.
These callbacks are called right before and after each tool's execute function, giving you
visibility into tool execution timing, inputs, outputs, and errors:

contents.heading: tool-execution-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Errors thrown inside these callbacks are silently caught and do not break the generation flow.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: The prepareStep callback is called before a step is started.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: It is called with the following parameters:

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: model: The model that was passed into generateText.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: stopWhen: The stopping condition that was passed into generateText.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: stepNumber: The number of the step that is being executed.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: steps: The steps that have been executed so far.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: instructions: The instructions that will be sent to the model for the current step. If prepareStep returns an instructions override, those instructions carry forward as the default for later steps.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: initialInstructions: The instructions that were passed into generateText or streamText.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: messages: The messages that will be sent to the model for the current step. Treat this as the loop's current message state. If prepareStep returns a messages override, those messages carry forward as the base for later steps.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: initialMessages: The messages that were passed into generateText or streamText.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: responseMessages: The accumulated assistant/tool response messages so far, including any tool results generated before the first model step from approved tool calls in the input messages.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: runtimeContext: The runtime context passed via the runtimeContext setting.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: toolsContext: The per-tool context map passed via the toolsContext setting.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: experimental_sandbox: The experimental sandbox passed via the experimental_sandbox setting.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: You can use it to provide different settings for a step, including modifying the input messages.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: If you return instructions, those instructions carry forward to later steps until prepareStep returns another instructions or system override. Use initialInstructions when you need to restore or compare against the top-level instructions from the original call.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: In longer agentic loops, you can use the messages parameter to mutate the message state that will be used by later steps. This is particularly useful for context compaction, and you decide when compaction should happen.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: The messages parameter contains the messages for the current step. By default, this is initialMessages followed by the accumulated responseMessages. If a previous prepareStep returned messages, later steps use those persisted messages plus the response messages from the previous step.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: Use initialMessages when you need the original input messages and responseMessages when you need the discrete assistant/tool response messages from the model so far.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: The pruneMessages helper provides a built-in way to remove selected messages or message parts. You can use it inside prepareStep when you want a simple compaction strategy.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: This example uses an estimated token threshold, but you can use any trigger. The key behavior is that returning messages mutates the message state for later steps.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: Returned message changes persist across steps. If you want to derive each step's messages from the original input plus the discrete response messages instead of the persisted message state, rebuild them from initialMessages and responseMessages each time:

contents.heading: provider-options-for-step-configuration
contents.content: You can use providerOptions in prepareStep to pass provider-specific configuration for each step. This is useful for features like Anthropic's code execution container persistence:

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content:
Adding the generated assistant and tool messages to your conversation history is a common task,
especially if you are using multi-step tool calls.

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content:
Both generateText and streamText have a responseMessages property that you can use to
add the assistant and tool messages to your conversation history.
It is also available in the onEnd callback of streamText.

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content: The responseMessages property contains the accumulated response messages from the call as an array of ModelMessage objects that you can add to your conversation history:

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: AI SDK Core supports dynamic tools for scenarios where tool schemas are not known at compile time. This is useful for:

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools without schemas

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: User-defined functions at runtime

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: Tools loaded from external sources

contents.heading: using-dynamictool
contents.content: The dynamicTool helper creates tools with unknown input/output types:

contents.heading: type-safe-handling
contents.content: When using both static and dynamic tools, use the dynamic flag for type narrowing:

contents.heading: preliminary-tool-results
contents.content:
You can return an AsyncIterable over multiple results.
In this case, the last value from the iterable is the final tool result.

contents.heading: preliminary-tool-results
contents.content:
This can be used in combination with generator functions to e.g. stream status information
during the tool execution:

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content:
You can use the toolChoice setting to influence when a tool is selected.
It supports the following settings:

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: auto (default): the model can choose whether and which tools to call.

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: required: the model must call a tool. It can choose which tool to call.

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: none: the model must not call tools

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: { type: 'tool', toolName: string (typed) }: the model must call the specified tool

contents.heading: tool-execution-options
contents.content: When tools are called, they receive additional options as a second parameter.

contents.heading: tool-call-id
contents.content:
The ID of the tool call is forwarded to the tool execution.
You can use it e.g. when sending tool-call related information with stream data.

contents.heading: messages
contents.content:
The messages that were sent to the language model to initiate the response that contained the tool call are forwarded to the tool execution.
You can access them in the second parameter of the execute function.
In multi-step calls, the messages contain the text, tool calls, and tool results from all previous steps.

contents.heading: abort-signals
contents.content:
The abort signals from generateText and streamText are forwarded to the tool execution.
You can access them in the second parameter of the execute function and e.g. abort long-running computations or forward them to fetch calls inside tools.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
Pass experimental_sandbox to generateText, streamText, or a ToolLoopAgent
call when a tool needs to run commands or code in an execution environment. The experimental sandbox is available to tool description functions and on the second parameter of the tool's execute function.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
This API is experimental and can change in patch releases. Passing an
experimental sandbox does not sandbox the tool itself.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
Tool code still runs wherever your application runs. Only the operations that your tool explicitly delegates to
the experimental sandbox, such as experimental_sandbox.run(...),
run in the experimental sandbox environment.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
The experimental sandbox description is not added to the model prompt automatically. If the model should know about details such as the root directory, exposed ports, or public hostname, include experimental_sandbox.description in your system prompt,
instructions, user-visible context, or a tool description function.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
run also accepts an optional workingDirectory, env, and abortSignal.
Use workingDirectory when a tool needs to run a command from a directory other
than the experimental sandbox implementation's default working directory. Use env
to set environment variables for the command. Forward
abortSignal from the tool execution options so the experimental sandbox can cancel the command if the overall operation is aborted or times out.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content: The AI SDK forwards your experimental sandbox object but does not create or isolate one for you.

contents.heading: experimental-sandbox
contents.content:
The Experimental_SandboxSession interface is only a contract. Its isolation guarantees depend on your implementation or experimental sandbox provider. A local implementation that uses
child_process.exec with a working directory is not a security boundary because
commands can still access paths outside that directory. For untrusted commands
or user-directed coding agents, use a real isolation provider, restrict
available commands, set command timeouts, and combine experimental sandbox usage with tool approval for sensitive actions.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content:
You can pass in arbitrary runtime context from generateText or streamText via the runtimeContext setting.
This runtime context is available in prepareStep.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content: To avoid confusion with prompt context or retrieved context, the docs refer to this feature as runtime context.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content: This is useful for values like tenant information, feature flags, session data, or other server-side state that should influence step preparation without being embedded into the prompt.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content: Tool execution context is now separate. If a tool needs server-side values such as API keys, pass them via toolsContext, keyed by tool name. Each tool then receives only its own typed context value based on its contextSchema.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content:
For the full mental model, examples, lifecycle details, and guidance on choosing
between prompt context, runtime context, and tool context, see
Runtime and Tool Context.

contents.heading: tool-context-telemetry
contents.content:
Tool context often contains server-side values such as API keys, access tokens, or internal identifiers.
Use telemetry.includeToolsContext to include selected top-level context properties in telemetry integrations:

contents.heading: tool-context-telemetry
contents.content:
Telemetry integrations receive the weather tool context as { defaultUnit: 'fahrenheit' }.
Properties set to false or omitted are excluded. If telemetry.includeToolsContext is omitted, no tool context properties are included.

contents.heading: tool-context-telemetry
contents.content:
telemetry.includeToolsContext only filters telemetry integrations. Tool
execution, lifecycle callbacks, and returned results still receive the full
typed tool context. See Runtime and Tool
Context for how tool context
flows through execution and telemetry.

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: The following tool input lifecycle hooks are available:

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputStart: Called when the model starts generating the input (arguments) for the tool call

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputDelta: Called for each chunk of text as the input is streamed

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputAvailable: Called when the complete input is available and validated

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputStart is always called before onInputAvailable, including when using generateText. onInputDelta is only called in streaming contexts (when using streamText).

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
Modularizing your code often requires defining types to ensure type safety and reusability.
To enable this, the AI SDK provides several helper types for tools, tool calls, and tool results.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
You can use them to strongly type your variables, function parameters, and return types
in parts of the code that are not directly related to streamText or generateText.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
Each tool call is typed with ToolCall<NAME extends string, ARGS>, depending
on the tool that has been invoked.
Similarly, the tool results are typed with ToolResult<NAME extends string, ARGS, RESULT>.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
The tools in streamText and generateText are defined as a ToolSet.
The type inference helpers TypedToolCall<TOOLS extends ToolSet>
and TypedToolResult<TOOLS extends ToolSet> can be used to
extract the tool call and tool result types from the tools.

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: The AI SDK has four tool-call related errors:

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: NoSuchToolError: the model tries to call a tool that is not defined in the tools object

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: InvalidToolInputError: the model calls a tool with inputs that do not match the tool's input schema

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: ToolCallRepairError: an error that occurred during tool call repair

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: ToolChoiceViolationError: the generateText response does not satisfy a required or specifically selected tool choice

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: When tool execution fails (errors thrown by your tool's execute function), the AI SDK adds them as tool-error content parts to enable automated LLM roundtrips in multi-step scenarios.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: generateText throws errors for tool schema validation issues and other errors, and can be handled using a try/catch block. Tool execution errors appear as tool-error parts in the result steps:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: Tool execution errors are available in the result steps:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: streamText sends errors as part of the stream result. Tool execution errors appear as tool-error parts, while other errors appear as error parts.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: When using toUIMessageStream, you can pass an onError function to extract the error message from the error part and forward it as part of the stream response:

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
Language models sometimes fail to generate valid tool calls,
especially when the input schema is complex or the model is smaller.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
If you use multiple steps, those failed tool calls will be sent back to the LLM
in the next step to give it an opportunity to fix it.
However, you may want to control how invalid tool calls are repaired without requiring
additional steps that pollute the message history.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
You can use the repairToolCall function to attempt to repair the tool call
with a custom function.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: You can use different strategies to repair the tool call:

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Use a model with structured outputs to generate the inputs.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Send the messages, instructions, and tool schema to a stronger model to generate the inputs.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Provide more specific repair instructions based on which tool was called.

contents.heading: active-tools
contents.content:
Language models can only handle a limited number of tools at a time, depending on the model.
To allow for static typing using a large number of tools and limiting the available tools to the model at the same time,
the AI SDK provides the activeTools property.

contents.heading: active-tools
contents.content:
It is an array of tool names that are currently active.
By default, the value is undefined and all tools are active.

contents.heading: tool-order
contents.content:
Some providers include tool definitions in the cached portion of a request.
If the order of those definitions changes between otherwise similar requests,
the provider may not be able to reuse the cached prefix as effectively.

contents.heading: tool-order
contents.content:
Use toolOrder when you want a stable provider request shape for caching or
debugging. The list can be partial: tools listed in toolOrder are sent first
in that order, and any remaining tools are sent afterwards in alphabetical
order. Tool names are typed from your tools object.

contents.heading: tool-order
contents.content:
toolOrder controls only the order of tool definitions sent to the provider.
It does not force the model to call a tool. Use toolChoice to
control tool selection, and use activeTools when you want to
limit which tools are available. When both activeTools and toolOrder are
provided, activeTools filters the available tools first and toolOrder
orders the remaining tools.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
Multi-modal tool results are experimental and supported by Anthropic, OpenAI,
and Google (Gemini 3 models).

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
For Google Generative AI, use base64 inline-data file parts
({ type: 'file', mediaType, data: { type: 'data', data } }) or base64
data: URLs in URL-style file parts
({ type: 'file', mediaType, data: { type: 'url', url: new URL('data:...') } }).
Remote HTTP(S) URLs in tool-result URL parts are not supported.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
The Google Vertex provider
also supports direct gs:// tool-result file references for Gemini 3 and later
models with supported image and document MIME types. It downloads HTTP(S)
tool-result URLs and sends their contents as inline data.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
In order to send multi-modal tool results, e.g. screenshots, back to the model,
they need to be converted into a specific format.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
AI SDK Core tools have an optional toModelOutput function
that converts the tool result into a content part.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content: Here is an example for converting a screenshot into a content part:

contents.heading: extracting-tools
contents.content:
Once you start having many tools, you might want to extract them into separate files.
The tool helper function is crucial for this, because it ensures correct type inference.

contents.heading: extracting-tools
contents.content: Here is an example of an extracted tool:

contents.heading: mcp-tools
contents.content:
The AI SDK supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to access their tools.
MCP enables your AI applications to discover and use tools across various services through a standardized interface.

contents.heading: mcp-tools
contents.content: For detailed information about MCP tools, including initialization, transport options, and usage patterns, see the MCP Tools documentation.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-tools-vs-mcp-tools
contents.content: In most cases, you should define your own AI SDK tools for production applications. They provide full control, type safety, and optimal performance. MCP tools are best suited for rapid development iteration and scenarios where users bring their own tools.

metadata.title: Transcription
metadata.description: Learn how to transcribe audio with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the transcribe
function to transcribe audio using a transcription model.
The audio property can be a Uint8Array, ArrayBuffer, Buffer, string (base64 encoded audio data), or a URL.
To access the generated transcript:

contents.heading: telemetry
contents.content:
transcribe and experimental_streamTranscribe accept the standard
telemetry option. Registered integrations receive start, end, and error
events with the provider and model, audio byte length and media type, final
transcript, warnings, response metadata, provider metadata, and usage when the
provider reports it. Because streaming transcription is experimental, custom
integrations receive its lifecycle through
experimental_onStreamTranscriptionStart and
experimental_onStreamTranscriptionEnd; errors continue to use onError.
Integrations that wrap or delegate to another telemetry integration must
forward these experimental callbacks explicitly for streaming transcription
to be observed.

contents.heading: telemetry
contents.content:
Raw audio is not included in telemetry events. For streaming transcription,
the final byte length is emitted only after the input stream is consumed and
the transcription finishes. Use recordInputs: false or
recordOutputs: false to prevent integrations from recording sensitive input
or output fields.

contents.heading: telemetry
contents.content:
For URL audio, the downloaded media type is passed to the provider and reported
on successful telemetry events. If downloading or decoding input audio fails,
the start event is still emitted before the correlated error event, but its
audio byte length and media type can be undefined because preparation did not
complete.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content: Use experimental_streamTranscribe when you have live raw audio and need transcript updates before the full audio stream is complete. The function uses transcription models with streaming support; provider options configure provider-specific behavior, but the streaming operation is selected by the function itself.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content:
fullStream is a single-consumer live stream and can only be accessed once.
When you need both stream parts and final results, access fullStream first and
await the result promises while or after consuming it. Accessing a result
promise first consumes the stream internally, so fullStream is no longer
available. This avoids retaining an unbounded replay buffer for live audio.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content: To access the final transcript metadata:

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content: The audio stream must contain raw audio chunks. Uint8Array chunks are raw bytes; string chunks are base64-encoded raw bytes. Always set inputAudioFormat to match the chunks you send.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content:
String model IDs resolve through the global provider (AI Gateway by
default). AI Gateway supports streaming transcription for supported models
(e.g. openai/gpt-realtime-whisper, elevenlabs/eleven-scribe-2-realtime,
xai/grok-stt), so string IDs work:
experimental_streamTranscribe({ model: 'openai/gpt-realtime-whisper', ...
  }). You can also pass a provider model instance (e.g.
openai.transcription('gpt-realtime-whisper')) to stream directly against
the provider.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content:
OpenAI streaming transcription uses openai.transcription('gpt-realtime-whisper').
Cartesia uses cartesia.transcription('ink-2') for streaming-only Ink 2
transcription. ElevenLabs uses
elevenLabs.transcription('scribe_v2_realtime') for Scribe v2 Realtime. Azure
uses azure.transcription('mai-transcribe-2-streaming') for streaming-only
MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming. xAI
uses the same xai.transcription() model for request/response and streaming
transcription; experimental_streamTranscribe selects the provider's
WebSocket STT transport.

contents.heading: streaming-transcription
contents.content: Some providers require WebSocket headers for direct streaming STT. In those runtimes, pass a provider-specific webSocket implementation when creating the provider.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content: Transcription models often have provider or model-specific settings which you can set using the providerOptions parameter.

contents.heading: download-size-limits
contents.content:
When audio is a URL, the SDK downloads the file with a default 2 GiB size limit.
You can customize this using createDownload:

contents.heading: download-size-limits
contents.content: You can also provide a fully custom download function:

contents.heading: download-size-limits
contents.content: If a download exceeds the size limit, a DownloadError is thrown:

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
transcribe accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the transcription process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content: This is particularly useful when combined with URL downloads to prevent long-running requests:

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
transcribe accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the transcription request.

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content: Warnings (e.g. unsupported parameters) are available on the warnings property.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: When transcribe cannot generate a valid transcript, it throws a AI_NoTranscriptGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: This error can arise for any of the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: responses: Metadata about the transcription model responses, including timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error handling.

metadata.title: Translation
metadata.description: Learn how to translate speech with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the
experimental_streamTranslate
function to translate live speech into another language. Translation is a
streaming-only modality: models translate live source audio into
target-language audio and text.

experimental_streamTranslate is built on the speech translation model
specification (Experimental_SpeechTranslationModelV4).

Provider implementations of the speech translation model specification ship
separately. Pass any model instance that implements
Experimental_SpeechTranslationModelV4 — see your provider's documentation
for available translation models.

The audio stream must contain raw audio chunks. Uint8Array chunks are raw
bytes; string chunks are base64-encoded raw bytes. Always set
inputAudioFormat to match the chunks you send.

targetLanguage (and the optional sourceLanguage) are BCP-47-style language
tags (e.g. en, es, fr-CA). Supported values are provider-specific and
validated by the provider.
When sourceLanguage is absent, providers auto-detect the source language.

fullStream is a single-consumer live stream and can only be accessed once.
When you need both stream parts and final results, access fullStream first and
await the result promises while or after consuming it. Accessing a result
promise first consumes the stream internally, so fullStream is no longer
available. This avoids retaining an unbounded replay buffer for live audio.
To access the final translation metadata:

A translation stream is considered successful when at least one audio part
was emitted or the final output text is non-empty. For providers that produce
only audio output, translationText may resolve to an empty string.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: The fullStream yields the following part types:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: audio: a translated audio chunk in the target language.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: output-text-delta: an append-only translated text delta.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content:
output-text-final: final translated text for a provider-defined segment or
utterance.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: source-transcript-delta: an append-only source transcript delta.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content:
source-transcript-partial: non-final source transcript text that may be
revised by later parts.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content:
source-transcript-final: final source transcript text for a
provider-defined segment or utterance.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: raw: raw provider chunks when includeRawChunks is enabled.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: error: stream errors.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content:
Output text is append-only: providers stream output-text-delta parts and
finalize per-utterance with output-text-final. There is no partial/revision
part for output text by design for now.

contents.heading: output-audio-format
contents.content:
Use outputAudioFormat to request a specific audio format for translated
audio chunks. When absent, the provider default output format is used.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content:
Translation models often have provider or model-specific settings which you can
set using the providerOptions parameter.

contents.heading: abort-signals
contents.content: Pass an abortSignal to cancel the translation:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
When experimental_streamTranslate cannot produce a translation — no audio
part was emitted and the final output text is empty, or the stream ends
without a finish event — it errors with a
AI_NoTranslationGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
response: Metadata about the speech translation model response, including
timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error
handling.

metadata.title: Video Generation
metadata.description: Learn how to generate videos with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Video generation is an experimental feature. The API may change in future
versions.

The AI SDK provides the experimental_generateVideo
function to generate videos based on a given prompt using a video model.
You can access the video data using the base64 or uint8Array properties:

contents.heading: aspect-ratio
contents.content:
The aspect ratio is specified as a string in the format {width}:{height}.
Models only support a few aspect ratios, and the supported aspect ratios are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio
contents.content:
Some models also accept 'adaptive', which lets the provider derive the output
ratio from the input media instead of a fixed value. This is typically required
for image-to-video, video editing, and video extension, where the output
inherits the ratio of the input and an explicit ratio is rejected.

contents.heading: resolution
contents.content:
The resolution is specified as a string in the format {width}x{height}.
Models only support specific resolutions, and the supported resolutions are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: duration
contents.content: Some video models support specifying the duration of the generated video in seconds.

contents.heading: frames-per-second-fps
contents.content: Some video models allow you to specify the frames per second for the generated video.

contents.heading: audio-generation
contents.content: Some video models can generate audio alongside the video. Use the generateAudio option to control this:

contents.heading: generating-multiple-videos
contents.content: experimental_generateVideo supports generating multiple videos at once:

contents.heading: generating-multiple-videos
contents.content:
experimental_generateVideo will automatically call the model as often as
needed (in parallel) to generate the requested number of videos.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-videos
contents.content: Each video model has an internal limit on how many videos it can generate in a single API call. The AI SDK manages this automatically by batching requests appropriately when you request multiple videos using the n parameter. Most video models only support generating 1 video per call due to computational cost.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-videos
contents.content: If needed, you can override this behavior using the maxVideosPerCall setting:

contents.heading: image-to-video-generation
contents.content: Some video models support generating videos from an input image. You can provide an image using the prompt object:

contents.heading: image-to-video-generation
contents.content: You can also provide the image as a base64-encoded string or Uint8Array:

contents.heading: first-and-last-frame
contents.content:
Some video models support first-last-frame generation, where you provide the
starting and/or ending frames of the video. Use the frameImages option to pass
role-tagged images in a provider-agnostic way:

contents.heading: reference-inputs
contents.content:
Some video models support reference-to-video generation, where you provide one or
more reference images or videos that the model incorporates into the generated video. Use the inputReferences option to pass
these inputs in a provider-agnostic way:

contents.heading: reference-inputs
contents.content: For URL-based video references, use the object form with an explicit mediaType:

contents.heading: reference-inputs
contents.content:
Providers route each reference by its media type (image vs. video) and emit a
warning when a reference kind is unsupported (for example, providers that accept
only image references warn and ignore a video reference).

contents.heading: providing-a-seed
contents.content:
You can provide a seed to the experimental_generateVideo function to control the output of the video generation process.
If supported by the model, the same seed will always produce the same video.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content:
Video models often have provider- or even model-specific settings.
You can pass such settings to the experimental_generateVideo function
using the providerOptions parameter. The options for the provider
become request body properties.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
experimental_generateVideo accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the video generation process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
Video generation typically takes longer than image generation. Consider using
longer timeouts (60 seconds or more) depending on the model and video length.

contents.heading: polling
contents.content: Video generation is an asynchronous process that can take several minutes to complete. The SDK automatically polls the provider to check if the video is ready. You can configure the polling behavior:

contents.heading: polling
contents.content:
For durable workflows that provide their own sleep primitive, pass it as
poll.delay. The custom delay is used for both polling intervals and webhook
timeouts.

contents.heading: webhooks
contents.content:
For models with native webhook support, pass a webhook factory that returns a
public URL and a promise that resolves when your application receives the
webhook request:

contents.heading: webhooks
contents.content:
createWebhook is an application-specific helper that registers a webhook
listener before returning. Its received promise must resolve with the request
headers and body. The SDK sends url to the provider, waits for received,
and then retrieves the completed video.

contents.heading: webhooks
contents.content:
You can provide poll together with webhook. For models with native webhook
support, poll.timeoutMs limits how long the SDK waits for the notification.
If the model does not support webhooks, the SDK falls back to polling with the
provided interval and timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
experimental_generateVideo accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the video generation request.

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content: If the model returns warnings, e.g. for unsupported parameters, they will be available in the warnings property of the response.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-metadata
contents.content: Some providers expose additional metadata for the result overall or per video.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-metadata
contents.content: The outer key of the returned providerMetadata is the provider name. The inner values are the metadata. A videos key is typically present in the metadata and is an array with the same length as the top level videos key.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-metadata
contents.content: When generating multiple videos with n > 1, you can also access per-call metadata through the responses array:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: When experimental_generateVideo cannot generate a valid video, it throws a AI_NoVideoGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate a video. It can arise due to the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: responses: Metadata about the video model responses, including timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error handling

metadata.title: HarnessAgent
metadata.description: Create and run AI SDK HarnessAgent sessions.

title.children: Basic Sandbox Sessions Without Network Control

contents.content:
HarnessAgent is an AI SDK Agent implementation backed by a harness adapter.
It gives you generate() and stream() methods that return AI SDK-compatible
results while a preconfigured harness powers these results.

contents.heading: installation
contents.content: Install the core harness package, a harness adapter, and a sandbox adapter:

contents.heading: installation
create-an-agent
contents.content:
Construct the agent at module scope. It holds configuration, not a live session.
Live state belongs to HarnessAgentSession.
Create a sandbox session separately and pass it to agent.createSession():

contents.heading: create-an-agent
contents.content:
Set model to select the model that the harness runtime uses. Model identifiers
are specific to each harness. When omitted, the harness uses its default model.
The model is applied per turn, so prepareCall can replace it between turns.

contents.heading: create-an-agent
contents.content:
To use this agent, ensure environment variables with sandbox and harness credentials
are set.

contents.heading: run-a-turn
contents.content: generate() drains the turn and returns a GenerateTextResult.

contents.heading: run-a-turn
contents.content: Use stream() for incremental output:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Configure lifecycle callbacks on HarnessAgent to observe agent calls, model
steps, and tool executions:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Callbacks configured on individual generate() and stream() calls are
invoked in addition to settings callbacks, with settings callbacks invoked
first. Callback errors are ignored and do not change agent execution.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content:
Harness runtimes execute their built-in tools internally. For those tools,
onToolExecutionStart and onToolExecutionEnd describe the logical tool
lifecycle after the runtime reports the result. The callbacks are still
delivered before the tool result is published to the result stream.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content:
Set runtimeContext on HarnessAgent to make application context available to
every turn. Use prepareCall to replace it for each new prompt turn. The
prepared context is available through generate() and stream() and remains
the same during in-memory continuations with continueGenerate() and
continueStream(). Lifecycle callbacks receive the full context, and it is
also available on each result's finalStep.runtimeContext.

contents.heading: runtime-context
contents.content:
Runtime context is excluded from telemetry by default. Use
telemetry.includeRuntimeContext to allowlist individual top-level properties;
only properties set to true are sent to telemetry integrations. Lifecycle
callbacks and results still receive the full context, so avoid storing secrets
that those consumers should not access.

contents.heading: generate-structured-output
contents.content:
Set output when constructing HarnessAgent to require the same typed output
on every turn. The agent converts the output specification to JSON Schema for
the harness adapter, validates the completed response, and returns the parsed
value through result.output.

contents.heading: generate-structured-output
contents.content:
With stream(), read partialOutputStream for incrementally parsed values and
await result.output for the validated final value. Structured data also remains
available as JSON in the normal text and stream surfaces; adapters do not add it
to the finish part.

contents.heading: generate-structured-output
contents.content:
Harness structured output requires a schema. Schema-less Output.json() and
adapters or runtime configurations that cannot enforce the schema throw
HarnessCapabilityUnsupportedError; see the
adapter capability table.

contents.heading: messages-and-history
contents.content:
A harness session owns its native conversation history. When you pass messages
or a message-array prompt, HarnessAgent takes the latest user message as the
fresh input for the turn. It does not replay the full prior conversation into
the harness.

contents.heading: messages-and-history
contents.content:
A trailing tool message is handled differently: tool approval responses and
client-provided tool results continue the unfinished harness turn that produced
the corresponding request or tool call.

contents.heading: messages-and-history
contents.content:
This is different from model calls, where the application usually sends the full
message history. In chat routes, persist and resume the harness session instead
of relying on message replay.

contents.heading: reading-the-runtimes-own-history
contents.content:
The runtime's conversation can grow outside your process — the same
conversation continued interactively in the agent's own CLI, for instance —
and the live event stream never sees those exchanges. Adapters that can reach
their runtime's store expose them through session.readHistory():

contents.heading: reading-the-runtimes-own-history
contents.content:
History reads are adapter-specific; see the adapter capability table before
calling this method.
readHistory() throws HarnessCapabilityUnsupportedError when the adapter
does not implement history reads, and HarnessHistoryUnavailableError when it
does but cannot reach the runtime's store from this environment (for example,
the store lives inside a remote sandbox). A conversation with no recorded
messages yet is not an error; it resolves to an empty messages array.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content: End every session explicitly:

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content: session.destroy() stops the runtime and discards resumability.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content:
session.detach() parks the runtime, returns resume state, and leaves a
supplied sandbox running for a later attach. If the turn is unfinished, the
resume state includes the continuation state.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content:
session.stop() saves resume state, then stops the runtime. If
the turn is unfinished, the resume state includes the continuation state.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content:
session.suspendTurn() is for advanced active-turn continuation across a
process boundary.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content:
session.hasUnfinishedTurn() reports whether the current turn must be
continued or suspended before the session accepts a new prompt.

contents.heading: session-lifecycle
contents.content:
Use destroy() for one-off scripts and tests. Use detach() or stop() for
HTTP routes that need multi-turn continuity.

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
Use callOptionsSchema and prepareCall to derive model, skills,
instructions, tools, and runtimeContext for each new turn. This follows the same
call-options pattern as ToolLoopAgent:

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
prepareCall runs for a new prompt after its custom options have been
validated. Its settings are then fixed for that whole turn. If the turn pauses
for a tool result, approval, stop condition, or process handoff, its
continuation reuses the same settings and does not call prepareCall again.
This prevents settings from changing mid-turn.

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
Changing model does not create a new harness session. Each adapter switches or
reconfigures its runtime before the next prompt while preserving the session's
conversation history.

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
The Codex adapter starts a fresh native Codex thread when its skills,
instructions, or tool catalog changes because codex exec resume retains the
original native thread bootstrap. The harness session remains usable, but prior
native conversation context does not carry across that settings-change boundary.
Turns with unchanged settings continue the existing native thread.

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
Pass abortSignal directly to generate() or stream(); it is already a
per-call setting and is not part of prepareCall. output also stays fixed on
the agent because its response format is tied to the agent's output schema.

contents.heading: change-settings-between-turns
contents.content:
When you pass sandboxSession to agent.createSession(), the caller retains
ownership of that sandbox. session.stop() and session.destroy() still end
the harness runtime but do not stop or destroy the supplied sandbox session.
In this case, the agent does not need a sandbox provider in its constructor.

contents.heading: resuming
contents.content:
Persist the opaque resume state. In this example, the harness sessionId is
chatId, and the sandbox ID is derived from the same known ID. If your
application cannot derive the sandbox ID, persist sandboxSession.id alongside
the harness sessionId and resume state instead. Reattach the sandbox before
asking the agent to resume. When you choose sandboxId on creation, it names a new
live sandbox and never looks one up. Reusing that ID with the creator fails
if the named sandbox exists; only the resume function performs a lookup.

contents.heading: resuming
contents.content:
HarnessAgent validates that the resume state was produced by the same harness
adapter before handing it to the runtime. If the resume state includes an
unfinished turn, call continueStream() or continueGenerate() before sending a
new prompt. The Vercel resume function reattaches whether the sandbox is still
running after detach() or stopped with a restorable snapshot. After
sandboxSession.destroy() deletes it, that ID cannot be resumed.

contents.heading: continue-a-suspended-turn
contents.content:
For advanced workflows that must hand off an active turn across a process
boundary, suspend the turn and persist the continuation state:

contents.heading: continue-a-suspended-turn
contents.content:
When you only have raw continuation state from suspendTurn(), resume with
continueFrom, then continue the turn without sending a new prompt:

contents.heading: continue-a-suspended-turn
contents.content:
Use continueStream() for incremental output, or continueGenerate() to drain
the continued turn and return a GenerateTextResult.

contents.heading: continue-a-suspended-turn
contents.content:
toolsContext and runtimeContext are intentionally not stored in
continuation state because they can contain credentials or non-serializable
host objects. When a suspended turn used context derived by prepareCall,
pass the same values to createSession to rebind them in the process that
continues the turn. After a process resume without rebinding, the continuation
uses the agent's constructor-level runtimeContext and toolsContext.

contents.heading: stop-after-a-harness-step
contents.content:
Use stopWhen to opt into semantic step boundaries. Predicates run after real
harness tool steps that can continue into another model step, and receive the
completed steps from the current invocation. When a predicate matches, the
returned result finishes while the underlying turn remains unfinished. A
terminal text-only step instead consumes the turn's finish event and finishes
naturally.

contents.heading: stop-after-a-harness-step
contents.content:
stopWhen has no default. When omitted, HarnessAgent continues running until
the turn naturally finishes or pauses for host input, preserving the behavior
of agents without step control. Pass one predicate or an array; matching any
predicate finishes the current result slice. Resume a stopped turn with
createSession({ continueFrom }) and continueStream() or
continueGenerate().

contents.heading: prepare-the-sandbox
contents.content: Use sandboxConfig to prepare the sandbox before the harness starts.

contents.heading: prepare-the-sandbox
contents.content:
sandboxConfig.onBootstrap runs during sandbox template creation, after the
harness adapter's own bootstrap and before snapshot-capable providers publish a
snapshot. Use it for expensive setup that should be reused by future sessions.
When you provide onBootstrap, also provide bootstrapHash; change the hash
whenever the bootstrap output should invalidate the reusable snapshot.

contents.heading: prepare-the-sandbox
contents.content:
sandboxConfig.onSession runs after each sandbox session is acquired and its
working directory exists, including resumed sessions. Use it for per-session
files or lightweight configuration.

contents.heading: prepare-the-sandbox
contents.content:
workDir is optional. When provided, it must be relative to the sandbox's
default working directory and is used as the session working directory. Set it
to '.' to use the sandbox's default working directory itself. When omitted,
regular sessions use the default <harnessId>-<sessionId> directory, while
onBootstrap receives the sandbox's default working directory.

contents.heading: prepare-reusable-sandboxes
contents.content:
Use agent.getSandboxTemplate() to resolve one harness's bootstrap recipe and
sandboxConfig.onBootstrap before creating a sandbox. The template's identity
is known before sandbox creation. Vercel persists the prepared snapshot and
creates a live sandbox from it; identical calls reuse that snapshot:

contents.heading: prepare-reusable-sandboxes
contents.content:
For multiple harnesses sharing a caller bootstrap hook, build one template from
all adapters. The last adapter wins for duplicate harnessId values, and the
recipe identities are sorted before hashing. onSession is not part of the
template and runs separately on every acquired session.

contents.heading: prepare-reusable-sandboxes
contents.content:
The derived template includes the source snapshot ID in its cache key, so
repeated calls with the same source and template reuse the prepared snapshot.
Pin mutable Git revisions, image tags, and source URLs when relying on cached
templates. sandboxId names the live sandbox, not its reusable template.
The existing native name option still names the live sandbox; if both are
supplied, their values must match.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: HarnessAgent accepts these main settings:

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: harness: the adapter instance.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
model: optional harness-specific model identifier. When omitted, the
harness uses its default model.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: id: optional stable agent identifier.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
instructions: instructions appended to the runtime's system or developer
prompt when supported, or prepended to the user prompt otherwise.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
headers: additional headers sent with model requests. Headers are fixed at
construction time. authorization, x-api-key, user-agent, and
x-client-app are not allowed.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
callOptionsSchema and prepareCall: validate custom call options and derive
model, skills, instructions, and tools for each new turn.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: output: typed output specification applied to every turn.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
stopWhen: condition(s) for finishing a result slice after a completed
harness tool step that can continue into another model step.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: tools: AI SDK tools executed by the host when the harness calls them.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
runtimeContext: application context forwarded to lifecycle callbacks and
results for every turn; prepareCall can replace it for a new prompt turn.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
activeTools: allowlist of built-in and host-executed tools the harness can
call.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
inactiveTools: denylist of built-in and host-executed tools the harness
cannot call.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: skills: instruction bundles surfaced by the adapter.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: permissionMode: built-in tool permission mode.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: toolApproval: approval status map for host-executed tools.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content: sandboxConfig: sandbox working-directory and lifecycle hook configuration.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
telemetry, debug, and onLog: observability and diagnostics. Use
telemetry.includeRuntimeContext to allowlist runtime context properties for
telemetry.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
Telemetry reports each turn's resolved model, instructions, and active
host-defined tools. Skills are adapter context and do not have a corresponding
AI SDK telemetry field, so they are not included in standard telemetry events.

contents.heading: settings
contents.content:
Adapter-specific settings belong on the adapter factory, for example
createCodex({ reasoningEffort: 'high' }).

contents.heading: custom-sandbox-orchestration
contents.content:
When your application creates and manages sandboxes itself, prepare the network
sandbox session first and then pass that same session to agent.createSession().
The agent does not create the sandbox and does not stop or destroy the
caller-owned sandbox.

contents.heading: basic-sandbox-sessions-without-network-control
contents.content:
The following example demonstrates how the basic-session API works. If your
project can expose a full network sandbox session, passing that session is
strongly recommended. Pass a restricted basic session only when your project
cannot expose the full network session.

contents.heading: basic-sandbox-sessions-without-network-control
contents.content:
A basic sandbox session only exposes filesystem and process APIs. The agent
still leaves the sandbox lifecycle to the caller. For a bridge-backed harness,
configure the bridge port and its externally reachable endpoint on the adapter
because the basic session cannot resolve them.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: Tools for built-in and host-executed tools.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: Skills for reusable instruction bundles.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content:
Harness adapters for adapter-specific
settings.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content:
Workflow utilities for durable
long-running turns.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: UI for useChat integration.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: Learn what AI SDK harnesses are and how they fit into the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK harness abstraction lets you run established agent harnesses through a
single AI SDK surface. A harness is a complete agent runtime, such as Claude
Code, Codex, or Pi. It owns capabilities that are larger than a model call:
workspace access, built-in coding tools, native session state, compaction,
permission flows, and runtime-specific configuration. Harness adapters can run
the runtime in a sandbox, but their execution environments differ by adapter;
review the adapter's runtime location and security guidance before use.

The AI SDK harness abstraction is separate from the provider/model abstraction.
Providers expose models to AI SDK Core functions such as generateText and
streamText. Harnesses expose agent runtimes to HarnessAgent.

Using a harness does not mean giving up customization. HarnessAgent lets you
provide your own instructions, skills, AI SDK tools, permission settings,
sandbox setup hooks, and adapter-specific configuration while preserving the
runtime behavior that makes each harness powerful.

The two abstractions are decoupled, but they use compatible primitives where
possible. Harness output is projected into AI SDK stream and response types, so
surfaces that consume AI SDK model streams can also consume harness streams. For
example, you can pass a HarnessAgent stream to toUIMessageStream and render
it with useChat. The API is designed to feel familiar to AI SDK users, but
harness runtimes have different concepts from lower-level language models.
Configuration follows AI SDK patterns where they fit and diverges where the
harness runtime has different behavior.

Harness packages are experimental. Expect breaking changes between
releases as this early API gets further refined.

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content: Use a harness when you want an existing agent runtime to drive the task:

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content: Coding agents that can inspect and modify a sandboxed workspace.

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content: Agent runtimes with their own built-in tools and permission model.

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content: Multi-turn sessions where the runtime owns conversation history.

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content:
Workflows that should preserve native harness behavior instead of re-creating
it with a tool loop.

contents.heading: when-to-use-a-harness
contents.content:
Use providers and models when you want direct control over the model call, the
tool loop, model settings, structured output, or a custom agent architecture.

contents.heading: core-concepts
contents.content: Harnesses have four primary pieces:

contents.heading: core-concepts
contents.content: HarnessAgent: the AI SDK agent implementation you use in application code.

contents.heading: core-concepts
contents.content:
Harness adapter: the package that connects to a runtime, such as
@ai-sdk/harness-claude-code.

contents.heading: core-concepts
contents.content:
Sandbox provider: the isolated filesystem and process environment where the
harness runs.

contents.heading: core-concepts
contents.content: Session: the live conversation and workspace state for a harness run.

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content:
HarnessAgent.generate() returns an AI SDK GenerateTextResult.
HarnessAgent.stream() returns an AI SDK StreamTextResult.

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: That means you can consume familiar fields:

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: result.text

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: result.stream

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: result.steps

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: result.usage

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content: result.responseMessages

contents.heading: compatible-streams
contents.content:
Harness-specific events are translated into compatible stream parts. Text,
reasoning, tool calls, tool results, usage, and finish reasons use the same AI
SDK shapes where possible. Events without a first-class AI SDK part, such as
workspace file changes and compaction, are surfaced as dynamic
provider-executed tool parts.

contents.heading: sessions-matter
contents.content:
Unlike a language model call, a harness session owns state. The session carries
the harness runtime, sandbox, working directory, native conversation history,
and pending approvals.

contents.heading: sessions-matter
contents.content: Create a session before running turns:

contents.heading: sessions-matter
contents.content:
For server routes, use a stable sessionId and persist the resume state
returned by session.detach() or session.stop().

contents.content: HarnessAgent for the main API.

runtimes.
