metadata.title: Skills
metadata.description: Use skills with AI SDK harnesses.

contents.content:
Skills are reusable instruction bundles that can
be useful for project conventions, workflow guidance, domain-specific procedures,
or any other instructions that should be discoverable by the underlying harness
runtime. You can configure skills for a HarnessAgent or replace them between
completed turns.

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: Pass skills to HarnessAgent with the skills setting:

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: Each skill has:

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: name: stable identifier for the skill.

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: description: short model-facing summary.

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: content: full instruction content.

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content: files: optional additional text files bundled with the skill.

contents.heading: define-skills
contents.content:
Additional files use skill-relative POSIX paths, for example
reference.md, references/codes.md, or templates/config.json. Reference
those paths from content when the agent should read them.

contents.heading: when-to-use-skills
contents.content:
Use skills for reusable instructions that should be available on demand, instead of
always being loaded into the agent's context like regular instructions.

contents.heading: when-to-use-skills
contents.content: Use instructions for broad agent behavior and current-session priorities.

contents.heading: when-to-use-skills
contents.content:
Skills can be changed between completed turns using callOptionsSchema and
prepareCall. See Change Settings Between Turns
for details.

metadata.title: Tools
metadata.description: Use tools with AI SDK harnesses.

contents.content: Harnesses have three tool surfaces:

Built-in tools exposed by the underlying harness runtime, such as file reads,
edits, shell commands, and web search.
AI SDK tools that you pass to HarnessAgent with the tools setting.

External MCP tools configured through the harness adapter's mcpServers
setting.

This page covers harness-specific behavior. For general AI SDK tool concepts,
schemas, tool results, and tool() usage, see Tools.

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content:
Each adapter declares the built-in tools its runtime can call natively.
HarnessAgent merges those built-ins with your host-defined tools and exposes
the combined tool set through agent.tools.

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content:
Built-in calls are executed by the harness runtime, not by your application
process. Stream parts use providerExecuted: true when the runtime already
performed the call.

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: Adapters use common names where possible:

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: read

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: write

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: edit

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: bash

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: grep

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: glob

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content: webSearch

contents.heading: built-in-tools
contents.content:
Some runtimes also expose native tools without a common cross-harness name.
Those appear under their native names.

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content: Pass AI SDK tools to HarnessAgent the same way you do for a ToolLoopAgent:

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content:
When the harness calls weather, HarnessAgent executes the tool in your host
process, then submits the result back to the harness runtime.

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content:
Host-executed tools can declare a contextSchema and receive turn-scoped
context through toolsContext:

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content:
Use prepareCall to replace toolsContext when the value depends on custom
call options. The type of toolsContext follows the tool set: it is rejected
when no tool declares a context schema, required when a tool requires a
context object, and optional when every context object is optional.
HarnessAgent validates each entry against the tool's contextSchema before
execution and exposes the configured map in step results and lifecycle
callbacks.

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content:
Tool context remains host-only and is not serialized into suspended-turn state.
When recreating a session for an unfinished turn, rebind it explicitly:

contents.heading: host-executed-tools
contents.content:
Missing or invalid context fails validation before the host tool executes. The
validation error returned to the harness runtime is intentionally generic so
host-only context values and schema details are not disclosed to the model.

contents.heading: client-side-tools
contents.content:
Omit execute when a browser, user interaction, or another external process
provides the tool result:

contents.heading: client-side-tools
contents.content:
When the harness calls a tool without execute, the returned result slice ends
after the tool-call step while the underlying turn waits for a result.
session.hasUnfinishedTurn() remains true, and session.suspendTurn()
includes the pending tool call in its serializable continuation state.

contents.heading: client-side-tools
contents.content:
In UI flows, pass the model messages produced after addToolOutput to the next
stream() or generate() call. HarnessAgent extracts the trailing tool
result and continues the paused turn automatically.

contents.heading: client-side-tools
contents.content:
For direct agent calls, provide the raw result to continueStream() or
continueGenerate():

contents.heading: client-side-tools
contents.content:
Set isError: true when the external tool failed. To continue in another
process, call suspendTurn(), recreate the session with continueFrom, and
then pass the result to continueStream() or continueGenerate().

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content:
Use activeTools or inactiveTools on HarnessAgent to control which tools the
harness can call. Both settings accept tool names from the combined tool set:
the built-in tools declared by the harness adapter and the AI SDK tools passed
with tools.

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content: activeTools is an allowlist:

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content: inactiveTools is a denylist:

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content:
Pass either activeTools or inactiveTools, not both. The TypeScript settings
type prevents combining them, and HarnessAgent also throws at runtime when
both are specified.

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content:
For host-executed tools, inactive tools are not passed to the underlying
harness runtime. If the runtime still attempts to call one, HarnessAgent
returns an execution-denied tool result.

contents.heading: tool-filtering
contents.content:
For built-in tools, support depends on the harness adapter. Some adapters can
filter built-ins natively. Others enforce filtering through their built-in tool
approval mechanism by denying inactive built-in calls before they execute,
without emitting approval request or response stream parts. Adapters that
support neither mechanism throw when you filter built-in tools.

contents.heading: sandbox-in-tool-execution
contents.content:
Host-executed tools receive the session sandbox through the same
experimental_sandbox execution option used by AI SDK tools elsewhere. The
value is a restricted sandbox session, so tools can read, write, and run
commands without being able to stop the network sandbox or change its network
policy.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
Harnesses distinguish built-in tool permissions from host-executed tool
approvals.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content: Use permissionMode for adapter-native built-ins:

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content: Available values are:

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
allow-all: allow built-in reads, edits, and shell commands. This is the
default.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
allow-edits: allow reads and edits, but request approval for shell commands
when the adapter supports built-in approvals.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
allow-reads: allow reads, but request approval for edits and shell commands
when the adapter supports built-in approvals.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content: Use toolApproval for host-executed tools:

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
toolApproval accepts the same status values as AI SDK tool approval status
objects: not-applicable, approved, user-approval, and denied.

contents.heading: tool-approvals
contents.content:
When approval is required, the stream pauses after a tool-approval-request.
Continue the same session by sending a tool approval response message. In UI
flows, useChat sends those messages for you when you add the approval result.
In direct agent code, pass the approval response as messages on the next
stream() or generate() call.

contents.heading: built-in-approval-support
contents.content:
Most adapters can pause built-in tool calls for approval. Adapters that do not
support it will error if an unsupported tool approval mode is specified.

contents.heading: built-in-approval-support
contents.content:
Host-executed tool approvals are handled by HarnessAgent, so they work across
adapters.

contents.heading: file-changes-and-compaction
contents.content:
Some harness events are not ordinary tool calls. For UI compatibility,
HarnessAgent projects them as dynamic, provider-executed tool parts:

contents.heading: file-changes-and-compaction
contents.content: fileChange: emitted for opaque workspace file mutations.

contents.heading: file-changes-and-compaction
contents.content: compaction: emitted when the runtime compacts context.

contents.heading: file-changes-and-compaction
contents.content: Check part.dynamic before assuming a tool part belongs to your typed tool set.

metadata.title: UI
metadata.description: Use AI SDK harnesses with useChat.

contents.content:
Harness streams are compatible with AI SDK UI message streams. You can use
useChat() on the client and stream HarnessAgent output from a server route.

The important difference from model-based chat routes is session management.
A harness owns its conversation state, so the route should resume or create a
HarnessAgentSession for the chat id instead of replaying the whole UI message
history into a model.

contents.heading: agent
contents.content: Define the HarnessAgent on the server:

contents.heading: session-store
contents.content:
Persist the opaque resume state returned by session.detach(). If the
turn paused for approval or was otherwise interrupted, that resume state carries
the continuation state internally. The chat id can also be the harness
sessionId. Here we derive a stable sandboxId from that known chat id. If
you do not derive one, persist the returned sandboxSession.id separately.

contents.heading: session-store
contents.content:
Use durable storage instead of an in-memory map in production. The creator
always creates a new sandbox and fails on a conflicting sandboxId; only the
resume function reattaches an existing one.

contents.heading: route
contents.content:
Convert UI messages to model messages, run the harness turn, and convert the
result stream back to a UI message stream:

contents.heading: route
contents.content:
Creating the UI message stream before acquiring the session ensures sandbox,
bootstrap, and harness startup failures are sent as UI error parts instead of
becoming generic HTTP errors. getHarnessErrorMessage preserves reviewed,
client-safe harness messages and masks unknown server errors.

contents.heading: route
contents.content:
Do not use createAgentUIStreamResponse directly with HarnessAgent unless you
wrap the agent to inject the required session. HarnessAgent.stream() requires
session on every call.

contents.heading: detach-or-stop
contents.content:
Use session.detach() when you want to park the harness runtime and keep the
sandbox warm for the next request. Bridge-backed adapters can usually reattach
or replay efficiently. If the turn is unfinished, detach() includes the turn
continuation state in the returned resume state.

contents.heading: detach-or-stop
contents.content:
session.stop() saves resume state and stops the harness runtime, but does not
stop a supplied sandbox. The caller owns that network session and should call
its destroy() method when the chat ends, not while a later request needs to
reattach. Preserve the chosen sandboxId across processes.

contents.heading: rendering-harness-parts
contents.content:
Harness output contains the same UI message part shapes used by AI SDK model
streams:

contents.heading: rendering-harness-parts
contents.content: text and reasoning parts for generated content.

contents.heading: rendering-harness-parts
contents.content:
typed tool parts such as tool-bash, tool-read, or a host tool like
tool-weather.

contents.heading: rendering-harness-parts
contents.content:
dynamic-tool parts for dynamic events such as fileChange and
compaction.

contents.heading: rendering-harness-parts
contents.content:
Render typed harness built-ins the same way you render normal AI SDK tool
parts. Check part.state for input-streaming, input-available, and
output-available.

contents.heading: type-safe-tool-parts
contents.content:
Until HarnessAgent session options are part of the base Agent call
parameters, infer UI tools from agent.tools:

contents.heading: type-safe-tool-parts
contents.content: Then use useChat<HarnessMessage>() on the client.

metadata.title: Workflow Utilities
metadata.description: Run HarnessAgent turns as durable Workflow DevKit workflows.

title.children: Defining the Semantic Agent Step Workflow
Starting the Semantic Agent Step Workflow

contents.content:
@ai-sdk/workflow-harness provides helpers for running HarnessAgent turns
inside a workflow.

The package provides a serializable state machine and runners for time-sliced
and semantic agent step turns. You call the appropriate runner from your own
'use workflow' and 'use step' functions.

The core harness and workflow files are framework-independent. The HTTP handlers
shown below use Next.js as one example; adapt them to your runtime and Workflow
SDK integration. If you use Next.js, ensure you have
configured your project for Workflow
before following the examples.

contents.heading: installation
contents.content:
In addition to the workflow specific packages, install the core harness package,
a harness adapter, and a sandbox adapter as shown in
HarnessAgent.

contents.heading: configuring-the-harness-agent
contents.content:
The agent can be configured in the usual way, for the most part. When using
semantic agent steps, set stopWhen to isStepCount(1) so one call to
stream() completes one agent step. Omit it when using time slices.

contents.heading: using-semantic-agent-steps
contents.content:
Semantic agent steps persist the harness turn after each agent step. Configure
the shared agent with the highlighted stopWhen option shown above, then call
runHarnessAgentStep() from a Workflow step.

contents.heading: defining-the-agent-step
contents.content:
Keep the Workflow step in its own module and import the agent dynamically inside
the step body. This keeps the agent, sandbox adapter, and other Node.js
dependencies out of the workflow bundle.

contents.heading: defining-the-semantic-agent-step-workflow
contents.content:
Create the workflow state and keep scheduling agentStep() while the agent has
more work.

contents.heading: defining-the-semantic-agent-step-workflow
contents.content:
This example covers the workflow execution foundation only. For multi-turn
conversations, you must persist the harness session's resumeFrom state
between workflow runs. See Resume Persistence.

contents.heading: defining-the-semantic-agent-step-workflow
contents.content:
Each ready_for_next_step result carries continueFrom, which lets the next
Workflow step continue the same unfinished turn. When the turn finishes,
finalizeHarnessWorkflow() returns its result or throws if the workflow failed.

contents.heading: starting-the-semantic-agent-step-workflow
contents.content:
Start the workflow from server-side code. This Next.js route converts the AI SDK
UI messages, starts agentWorkflow(), and returns the workflow's AI SDK UI
message stream. Passing the converted messages lets HarnessAgent distinguish a
new user turn from tool approval and tool result continuations.

contents.heading: starting-the-semantic-agent-step-workflow
contents.content:
The workflow state sessionId identifies the harness session. The step derives
sandboxId from it before first creating the sandbox and uses that same ID to
reattach on later steps. The state does not serialize a live sandbox. Keep
agent.ts, agent-step.ts, workflow.ts, and the route in separate modules so
the workflow bundle does not include Node-heavy agent, sandbox, or framework
dependencies.

contents.heading: using-time-slices
contents.content:
Time slices persist a long-running harness turn at wall-clock boundaries. Omit
the highlighted stopWhen option from the shared agent, then call
runHarnessAgentTimeSlice() from a Workflow step. It uses a 750-second budget
by default; pass timeSliceSeconds to choose a different budget.

contents.heading: defining-the-time-slice-step
contents.content: As with semantic agent steps, keep the Workflow step in its own module and

contents.heading: defining-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
Create the workflow state and keep scheduling timeSliceStep() while the agent
has more work.

contents.heading: defining-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
This example covers the workflow execution foundation only. For multi-turn
conversations, you must persist the harness session's resumeFrom state
between workflow runs. See Resume Persistence.

contents.heading: defining-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
Each ready_for_next_step result carries continueFrom, which lets the next
Workflow step continue the same unfinished turn. When the turn finishes,
finalizeHarnessWorkflow() returns its result or throws if the workflow failed.

contents.heading: starting-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
Start the workflow from server-side code. As with semantic agent steps, pass the
converted messages so HarnessAgent can distinguish a new user turn from tool
approval and tool result continuations.

contents.heading: starting-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
The workflow state sessionId identifies the harness session. The step derives
sandboxId from it; otherwise, you must persist sandboxSession.id separately
to reattach across steps. Keep
agent.ts, time-slice-step.ts, workflow.ts, and the route in separate
modules so the workflow bundle does not include Node-heavy agent, sandbox, or
framework dependencies.

contents.heading: starting-the-time-sliced-workflow
contents.content:
destroyOnFinish destroys the harness session, but never the supplied sandbox.
The caller can explicitly call sandboxSession.destroy() on the network
session when no later step needs to reattach. Never destroy it at a
time-slice boundary where a subsequent step must resume it.

contents.heading: resume-persistence
contents.content:
Workflow automatically persists the HarnessWorkflowState returned by each
step, including continueFrom, for the duration of the current workflow run.
To continue the native harness session across separate user-turn workflow runs,
persist the opaque resumeFrom state by sessionId.

contents.heading: resume-persistence
contents.content:
The storage implementation is the same for semantic agent steps and time
slices. This example uses Workflow steps because filesystem access must stay out
of the workflow function itself. Use durable storage instead of local files in
production.

contents.heading: resume-persistence
contents.content:
Load the previous resumeFrom state before creating the workflow state, then
persist the updated value after the execution loop. The integration points are
the same for both workflow approaches.

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
The RSC API makes extensive use of Server Actions to power streaming values and UI from the server.

Server Actions are exposed as public, unprotected endpoints. As a result, you should treat Server Actions as you would public-facing API endpoints and ensure that the user is authorized to perform the action before returning any data.

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
Two categories of errors can occur when working with the RSC API: errors while streaming user interfaces and errors while streaming other values.

contents.heading: handling-ui-errors
contents.content: To handle errors while generating UI, the streamableUI object exposes an error() method.

contents.heading: handling-ui-errors
contents.content: With this method, you can catch any error with the stream, and return relevant UI. On the client, you can also use a React Error Boundary to wrap the streamed component and catch any additional errors.

contents.heading: handling-other-errors

metadata.title: Managing Generative UI State
metadata.description: Overview of the AI and UI states

title.children: What is AI and UI State?
Calling Server Actions from the Client

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

State is an essential part of any application. State is particularly important in AI applications as it is passed to large language models (LLMs) on each request to ensure they have the necessary context to produce a great generation. Traditional chatbots are text-based and have a structure that mirrors that of any chat application.
For example, in a chatbot, state is an array of messages where each message has:
id: a unique identifier
role: who sent the message (user/assistant/system/tool)
content: the content of the message
This state can be rendered in the UI and sent to the model without any modifications.

With Generative UI, the model can now return a React component, rather than a plain text message. The client can render that component without issue, but that state can't be sent back to the model because React components aren't serialisable. So, what can you do?
The solution is to split the state in two, where one (AI State) becomes a proxy for the other (UI State).

One way to understand this concept is through a Lego analogy. Imagine a 10,000 piece Lego model that, once built, cannot be easily transported because it is fragile. By taking the model apart, it can be easily transported, and then rebuilt following the steps outlined in the instructions pamphlet. In this way, the instructions pamphlet is a proxy to the physical structure. Similarly, AI State provides a serialisable (JSON) representation of your UI that can be passed back and forth to the model.

contents.heading: what-is-ai-and-ui-state
contents.content: The RSC API simplifies how you manage AI State and UI State, providing a robust way to keep them in sync between your database, server and client.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content: AI State refers to the state of your application in a serialisable format that will be used on the server and can be shared with the language model.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content: For a chat app, the AI State is the conversation history (messages) between the user and the assistant. Components generated by the model would be represented in a JSON format as a tool alongside any necessary props. AI State can also be used to store other values and meta information such as createdAt for each message and chatId for each conversation. The LLM reads this history so it can generate the next message. This state serves as the source of truth for the current application state.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content:
Note: AI state can be accessed/modified from both the server and the
client.

contents.heading: ui-state
contents.content: UI State refers to the state of your application that is rendered on the client. It is a fully client-side state (similar to useState) that can store anything from JavaScript values to React elements. UI state is a list of actual UI elements that are rendered on the client.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: AI SDK RSC simplifies managing AI and UI state across your application by providing several hooks. These hooks are powered by  React context  under the hood.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: Notably, this means you do not have to pass the message history to the server explicitly for each request. You also can access and update your application state in any child component of the context provider. As you begin building multistep generative interfaces, this will be particularly helpful.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: To use @ai-sdk/rsc to manage AI and UI State in your application, you can create a React context using createAI:

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: In this example, you define types for AI State and UI State, respectively.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: Next, wrap your application with your newly created context. With that, you can get and set AI and UI State across your entire application.

contents.heading: reading-ui-state-in-client
contents.content: The UI state can be accessed in Client Components using the useUIState hook provided by the RSC API. The hook returns the current UI state and a function to update the UI state like React's useState.

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-in-client
contents.content: The AI state can be accessed in Client Components using the useAIState hook provided by the RSC API. The hook returns the current AI state.

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-on-server
contents.content: The AI State can be accessed within any Server Action provided to the createAI context using the getAIState function. It returns the current AI state as a read-only value:

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-on-server
contents.content:
Remember, you can only access state within actions that have been passed to
the createAI context within the actions key.

contents.heading: updating-ai-state-on-server
contents.content: The AI State can also be updated from within your Server Action with the getMutableAIState function. This function is similar to getAIState, but it returns the state with methods to read and update it:

contents.heading: updating-ai-state-on-server
contents.content:
It is important to update the AI State with new responses using .update()
and .done() to keep the conversation history in sync.

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content: To call the sendMessage action from the client, you can use the useActions hook. The hook returns all the available Actions that were provided to createAI:

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content: When the user submits a message, the sendMessage action is called with the message content. The response from the action is then added to the UI state, updating the displayed messages.

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content:
Important! Don't forget to update the UI State after you call your Server
Action otherwise the streamed component will not show in the UI.

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content: To learn more, check out this example on managing AI and UI state using @ai-sdk/rsc.

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content: Next, you will learn how you can save and restore state with @ai-sdk/rsc.

Calling Server Actions from the Client

metadata.title: Handling Loading State
metadata.description: Overview of handling loading state with AI SDK RSC

title.children: Handling Loading State on the Client
Streaming Loading State from the Server

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

Given that responses from language models can often take a while to complete, it's crucial to be able to show loading state to users. This provides visual feedback that the system is working on their request and helps maintain a positive user experience.
There are three approaches you can take to handle loading state with the AI SDK RSC:
Managing loading state similar to how you would in a traditional Next.js application. This involves setting a loading state variable in the client and updating it when the response is received.
Streaming loading state from the server to the client. This approach allows you to track loading state on a more granular level and provide more detailed feedback to the user.
Streaming loading component from the server to the client. This approach allows you to stream a React Server Component to the client while awaiting the model's response.

contents.heading: client
contents.content: Let's create a simple Next.js page that will call the generateResponse function when the form is submitted. The function will take in the user's prompt (input) and then generate a response (response). To handle the loading state, use the loading state variable. When the form is submitted, set loading to true, and when the response is received, set it back to false. While the response is being streamed, the input field will be disabled.

contents.heading: server
contents.content: Now let's implement the generateResponse function. Use the streamText function to generate a response to the input.

contents.heading: streaming-loading-state-from-the-server
contents.content: If you are looking to track loading state on a more granular level, you can create a new streamable value to store a custom variable and then read this on the frontend. Let's update the example to create a new streamable value for tracking loading state:

contents.heading: client-1
contents.content: This allows you to provide more detailed feedback about the generation process to your users.

contents.heading: streaming-loading-components-with-streamui
contents.content: If you are using the  streamUI  function, you can stream the loading state to the client in the form of a React component. streamUI supports the usage of  JavaScript generator functions , which allow you to yield some value (in this case a React component) while some other blocking work completes.

contents.heading: server-2
contents.content:
Remember to update the file from .ts to .tsx because you are defining a
React component in the streamUI function.

contents.content: This guide helps you migrate from AI SDK RSC to AI SDK UI.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: The AI SDK has two packages that help you build the frontend for your applications – AI SDK UI and AI SDK RSC.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: We introduced support for using React Server Components (RSC) within the AI SDK to simplify building generative user interfaces for frameworks that support RSC.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: However, given we're pushing the boundaries of this technology, AI SDK RSC currently faces significant limitations that make it unsuitable for stable production use.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: It is not possible to abort a stream using server actions. This will be improved in future releases of React and Next.js (1122).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: When using createStreamableUI and streamUI, components remount on .done(), causing them to flicker (2939).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Many suspense boundaries can lead to crashes (2843).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Using createStreamableUI can lead to quadratic data transfer. You can avoid this using createStreamableValue instead, and rendering the component client-side.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Closed RSC streams cause update issues (3007).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Due to these limitations, AI SDK RSC is marked as experimental, and we do not recommend using it for stable production environments.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: As a result, we strongly recommend migrating to AI SDK UI, which has undergone extensive development to provide a more stable and production grade experience.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: In building v0, we have invested considerable time exploring how to create the best chat experience on the web. AI SDK UI ships with many of these best practices and commonly used patterns like language model middleware, multi-step tool calls, attachments, telemetry, provider registry, and many more. These features have been considerately designed into a neat abstraction that you can use to reliably integrate AI into your applications.

contents.heading: basic-setup
contents.content: The streamUI function executes as part of a server action as illustrated below.

contents.heading: before-call-server-action-and-update-ui-state
contents.content: The chat interface calls the server action. The response is then saved using the useUIState hook.

contents.heading: before-call-server-action-and-update-ui-state
contents.content: The streamUI function combines generating text and rendering the user interface. To migrate to AI SDK UI, you need to separate these concerns – streaming generations with streamText and rendering the UI with useChat.

contents.heading: after-replace-server-action-with-route-handler
contents.content: The streamText function executes as part of a route handler and streams the response to the client. The useChat hook on the client decodes this stream and renders the response within the chat interface.

contents.heading: parallel-tool-calls
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, streamUI does not support parallel tool calls. You will have to use a combination of streamText, createStreamableUI and createStreamableValue.

contents.heading: parallel-tool-calls
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, useChat comes with built-in support for parallel tool calls. You can define multiple tools in the streamText and have them called them in parallel. The useChat hook will then handle the parallel tool calls for you automatically.

contents.heading: multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, streamUI does not support multi-step tool calls. You will have to use a combination of streamText, createStreamableUI and createStreamableValue.

contents.heading: multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, useChat comes with built-in support for multi-step tool calls. You can set stopWhen in the streamText function to define when the model should stop making tool calls. The useChat hook will then handle the multi-step tool calls for you automatically.

contents.heading: generative-user-interfaces
contents.content: The streamUI function uses tools as a way to execute functions based on user input and renders React components based on the function output to go beyond text in the chat interface.

contents.heading: before-render-components-within-the-server-action-and-stream-to-client
contents.content: As mentioned earlier, streamUI generates text and renders the React component in a single server action call.

contents.heading: after-replace-with-route-handler-and-stream-props-data-to-client
contents.content: The streamText function streams the props data as response to the client, while useChat decode the stream as toolInvocations and renders the chat interface.

contents.heading: handling-client-interactions
contents.content: With AI SDK RSC, components streamed to the client can trigger subsequent generations by calling the relevant server action using the useActions hooks. This is possible as long as the component is a descendant of the <AI/> context provider.

contents.heading: after-use-another-chat-hook-with-same-id-from-the-component
contents.content: After switching to AI SDK UI, these messages are synced by initializing the useChat hook in the component with the same id as the parent component.

contents.heading: loading-indicators
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, you can use the initial parameter of streamUI to define the component to display while the generation is in progress.

contents.heading: before-use-loading-to-show-loading-indicator
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, you can use the tool invocation state to show a loading indicator while the tool is executing.

contents.heading: saving-chats
contents.content: Before implementing streamUI as a server action, you should create an <AI/> provider and wrap your application at the root layout to sync the AI and UI states. During initialization, you typically use the onSetAIState callback function to track updates to the AI state and save it to the database when done(...) is called.

contents.heading: after-save-chats-using-callback-function-of-streamtext
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, you will save chats using the onEnd callback function of streamText in your route handler.

contents.heading: restoring-chats
contents.content: When using AI SDK RSC, the useUIState hook contains the UI state of the chat. When restoring a previously saved chat, the UI state needs to be loaded with messages.

contents.heading: restoring-chats
contents.content: Similar to how you typically save chats in AI SDK RSC, you should use the onGetUIState callback function to retrieve the chat from the database, convert it into UI state, and return it to be accessible through useUIState.

contents.heading: before-load-chat-from-database-using-callback-function-of-context-provider
contents.content: AI SDK UI uses the messages field of useChat to store messages. To load messages when useChat is mounted, you should use initialMessages.

contents.heading: before-load-chat-from-database-using-callback-function-of-context-provider
contents.content: As messages are typically loaded from the database, we can use a server actions inside a Page component to fetch an older chat from the database during static generation and pass the messages as props to the <Chat/> component.

contents.heading: streaming-object-generation
contents.content: The createStreamableValue function streams any serializable data from the server to the client. As a result, this function allows you to stream object generations from the server to the client when paired with streamText and Output.

contents.heading: before-read-streamable-value-and-update-object
contents.content: To migrate to AI SDK UI, you should use the useObject hook and implement streamText with Output within your route handler.

After: Replace server action with route handler
After: Update client to use chat hook
Before: Render components within the server action and stream to client
After: Replace with route handler and stream props data to client

Before: Use actions hook to send messages
After: Use another chat hook with same ID from the component
Before: Use loading to show loading indicator
After: Use tool invocation state to show loading indicator

After: Save chats using callback function of streamText

metadata.title: Multistep Interfaces
metadata.description: Overview of Building Multistep Interfaces with AI SDK RSC

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
Multistep interfaces refer to user interfaces that require multiple independent steps to be executed in order to complete a specific task.
For example, if you wanted to build a Generative UI chatbot capable of booking flights, it could have three steps:
Search all flights
Pick flight
Check availability
To build this kind of application you will leverage two concepts, tool composition and application context.

Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This is a powerful concept that allows you to break down complex tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. In the example above, "search all flights", "pick flight", and "check availability" come together to create a holistic "book flight" tool.

Application context refers to the state of the application at any given point in time. This includes the user's input, the output of the language model, and any other relevant information. In the example above, the flight selected in "pick flight" would be used as context necessary to complete the "check availability" task.

contents.content: The turn-by-turn implementation is the simplest form of multistep interfaces. In this implementation, the user and the model take turns during the conversation. For every user input, the model generates a response, and the conversation continues in this turn-by-turn fashion.
