metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: An overview of AI SDK RSC.

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

The @ai-sdk/rsc package is compatible with frameworks that support React
Server Components.

React Server Components (RSC) allow you to write UI that can be rendered on the server and streamed to the client. RSCs enable  Server Actions , a new way to call server-side code directly from the client just like any other function with end-to-end type-safety. This combination opens the door to a new way of building AI applications, allowing the large language model (LLM) to generate and stream UI directly from the server to the client.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: AI SDK RSC has various functions designed to help you build AI-native applications with React Server Components. These functions:

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: Provide abstractions for building Generative UI applications.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: streamUI: calls a model and allows it to respond with React Server Components.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: useUIState: returns the current UI state and a function to update the UI State (like React's useState). UI State is the visual representation of the AI state.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: useAIState: returns the current AI state and a function to update the AI State (like React's useState). The AI state is intended to contain context and information shared with the AI model, such as system messages, function responses, and other relevant data.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: useActions: provides access to your Server Actions from the client. This is particularly useful for building interfaces that require user interactions with the server.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: createAI: creates a client-server context provider that can be used to wrap parts of your application tree to easily manage both UI and AI states of your application.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: Make it simple to work with streamable values between the server and client.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: createStreamableValue: creates a stream that sends values from the server to the client. The value can be any serializable data.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: readStreamableValue: reads a streamable value from the client that was originally created using createStreamableValue.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: createStreamableUI: creates a stream that sends UI from the server to the client.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-functions
contents.content: useStreamableValue: accepts a streamable value created using createStreamableValue and returns the current value, error, and pending state.

contents.heading: templates
contents.content: Check out the following templates to see AI SDK RSC in action.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Please check out the AI SDK RSC API Reference for more details on each function.

metadata.title: Saving and Restoring States
metadata.description: Saving and restoring AI and UI states with onGetUIState and onSetAIState

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

AI SDK RSC provides convenient methods for saving and restoring AI and UI state. This is useful for saving the state of your application after every model generation, and restoring it when the user revisits the generations.

contents.heading: saving-ai-state
contents.content: The AI state can be saved using the onSetAIState callback, which gets called whenever the AI state is updated. In the following example, you save the chat history to a database whenever the generation is marked as done.

contents.heading: restoring-ai-state
contents.content: The AI state can be restored using the initialAIState prop passed to the context provider created by the createAI function. In the following example, you restore the chat history from a database when the component is mounted.

contents.heading: saving-ui-state
contents.content: The UI state cannot be saved directly, since the contents aren't yet serializable. Instead, you can use the AI state as proxy to store details about the UI state and use it to restore the UI state when needed.

contents.heading: restoring-ui-state
contents.content: The UI state can be restored using the AI state as a proxy. In the following example, you restore the chat history from the AI state when the component is mounted. You use the onGetUIState callback to listen for SSR events and restore the UI state.

contents.heading: restoring-ui-state
contents.content: To learn more, check out this example that persists and restores states in your Next.js application.

contents.heading: restoring-ui-state
contents.content: Next, you will learn how you can use @ai-sdk/rsc functions like useActions and useUIState to create interactive, multistep interfaces.

metadata.title: Streaming React Components
metadata.description: Overview of streaming RSCs

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

The RSC API allows you to stream React components from the server to the client with the streamUI function. This is useful when you want to go beyond raw text and stream components to the client in real-time.

Similar to  AI SDK Core  APIs (like  streamText ), streamUI provides a single function to call a model and allow it to respond with React Server Components.
It supports the same model interfaces as AI SDK Core APIs.

contents.heading: concepts
contents.content: To give the model the ability to respond to a user's prompt with a React component, you can leverage tools.

contents.heading: concepts
contents.content:
Remember, tools are like programs you can give to the model, and the model can
decide as and when to use based on the context of the conversation.

contents.heading: concepts
contents.content: With the streamUI function, you provide tools that return React components. With the ability to stream components, the model is akin to a dynamic router that is able to understand the user's intention and display relevant UI.

contents.heading: concepts
contents.content: At a high level, the streamUI works like other AI SDK Core functions: you can provide the model with a prompt or some conversation history and, optionally, some tools. If the model decides, based on the context of the conversation, to call a tool, it will generate a tool call. The streamUI function will then run the respective tool, returning a React component. If the model doesn't have a relevant tool to use, it will return a text generation, which will be passed to the text function, for you to handle (render and return as a React component).

contents.heading: concepts
contents.content: This example calls the streamUI function using OpenAI's gpt-6-astra model, passes a prompt, specifies how the model's plain text response (content) should be rendered, and then provides an empty object for tools. Even though this example does not define any tools, it will stream the model's response as a div rather than plain text.

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content:
Using tools with streamUI is similar to how you use tools with generateText and streamText.
A tool is an object that has:

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content: description: a string telling the model what the tool does and when to use it

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content: inputSchema: a Zod schema describing what the tool needs in order to run

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content: generate: an asynchronous function that will be run if the model calls the tool. This must return a React component

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content: Let's expand the previous example to add a tool.

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content: This tool would be run if the user asks for the weather for their location. If the user hasn't specified a location, the model will ask for it before calling the tool. When the model calls the tool, the generate function will initially return a loading component. This component will show until the awaited call to getWeather is resolved, at which point, the model will stream the <WeatherComponent /> to the user.

contents.heading: adding-a-tool
contents.content:
Note: This example uses a  generator function

(function*), which allows you to pause its execution and return a value,
then resume from where it left off on the next call. This is useful for
handling data streams, as you can fetch and return data from an asynchronous
source like an API, then resume the function to fetch the next chunk when
needed. By yielding values one at a time, generator functions enable efficient
processing of streaming data without blocking the main thread.

contents.heading: using-streamui-with-nextjs
contents.content: Let's see how you can use the example above in a Next.js application.

contents.heading: using-streamui-with-nextjs
contents.content: To use streamUI in a Next.js application, you will need two things:

contents.heading: using-streamui-with-nextjs
contents.content: A Server Action (where you will call streamUI)

contents.heading: using-streamui-with-nextjs
contents.content: A page to call the Server Action and render the resulting components

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content:
Server Actions are server-side functions that you can call directly from the
frontend. For more info, see the
documentation.

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: Create a Server Action at app/actions.tsx and add the following code:

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: The getWeather tool should look familiar as it is identical to the example in the previous section. In order for this tool to work:

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: First define a LoadingComponent, which renders a pulsing div that will show some loading text.

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: Next, define a getWeather function that will timeout for 2 seconds (to simulate fetching the weather externally) before returning the "weather" for a location. Note: you could run any asynchronous TypeScript code here.

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: Finally, define a WeatherComponent which takes in location and weather as props, which are then rendered within a div.

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: Your Server Action is an asynchronous function called streamComponent that takes no inputs, and returns a ReactNode. Within the action, you call the streamUI function, specifying the model (gpt-6-astra), the prompt, the component that should be rendered if the model chooses to return text, and finally, your getWeather tool. Last but not least, you return the resulting component generated by the model with result.value.

contents.heading: step-1-create-a-server-action
contents.content: To call this Server Action and display the resulting React Component, you will need a page.

contents.heading: step-2-create-a-page
contents.content: Create or update your root page (app/page.tsx) with the following code:

contents.heading: step-2-create-a-page
contents.content: This page is first marked as a client component with the "use client"; directive given it will be using hooks and interactivity. On the page, you render a form. When that form is submitted, you call the streamComponent action created in the previous step (just like any other function). The streamComponent action returns a ReactNode that you can then render on the page using React state (setComponent).

contents.heading: going-beyond-a-single-prompt
contents.content: You can now allow the model to respond to your prompt with a React component. However, this example is limited to a static prompt that is set within your Server Action. You could make this example interactive by turning it into a chatbot.

contents.heading: going-beyond-a-single-prompt
contents.content: Learn how to stream React components with the Next.js App Router using streamUI with this example.

metadata.title: Streaming Values
metadata.description: Overview of streaming RSCs

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

The RSC API provides several utility functions to allow you to stream values from the server to the client. This is useful when you need more granular control over what you are streaming and how you are streaming it.

These utilities can also be paired with AI SDK Core
functions like streamText to
easily stream LLM generations from the server to the client.
There are two functions provided by the RSC API that allow you to create streamable values:
createStreamableValue - creates a streamable (serializable) value, with full control over how you create, update, and close the stream.
createStreamableUI - creates a streamable React component, with full control over how you create, update, and close the stream.

contents.heading: createstreamablevalue
contents.content: The RSC API allows you to stream serializable JavaScript values from the server to the client using createStreamableValue, such as strings, numbers, objects, and arrays.

contents.heading: createstreamablevalue
contents.content: This is useful when you want to stream:

contents.heading: createstreamablevalue
contents.content: Text generations from the language model in real-time.

contents.heading: createstreamablevalue
contents.content: Buffer values of image and audio generations from multi-modal models.

contents.heading: createstreamablevalue
contents.content: Progress updates from multi-step agent runs.

contents.heading: creating-a-streamable-value
contents.content: You can import createStreamableValue from @ai-sdk/rsc and use it to create a streamable value.

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-value
contents.content: You can read streamable values on the client using readStreamableValue. It returns an async iterator that yields the value of the streamable as it is updated:

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-value
contents.content: Learn how to stream a text generation (with streamText) using the Next.js App Router and createStreamableValue in this example.

contents.heading: createstreamableui
contents.content: createStreamableUI creates a stream that holds a React component. Unlike AI SDK Core APIs, this function does not call a large language model. Instead, it provides a primitive that can be used to have granular control over streaming a React component.

contents.heading: using-createstreamableui
contents.content: Let's look at how you can use the createStreamableUI function with a Server Action.

contents.heading: using-createstreamableui
contents.content: First, you create a streamable UI with an empty state and then update it with a loading message. After 1 second, you mark the stream as done passing in the actual weather information as its final value. The .value property contains the actual UI that can be sent to the client.

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-ui
contents.content: On the client side, you can call the getWeather Server Action and render the returned UI like any other React component.

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-ui
contents.content: When the button is clicked, the getWeather function is called, and the returned UI is set to the weather state and rendered on the page. Users will see the loading message first and then the actual weather information after 1 second.

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-ui
contents.content: Learn more about handling multiple streams in a single request in the Multiple Streamables guide.

contents.heading: reading-a-streamable-ui
contents.content: Learn more about handling state for more complex use cases with  AI/UI State .

metadata.title: Chatbot Message Persistence
metadata.description: Learn how to store and load chat messages in a chatbot.

contents.content:
Being able to store and load chat messages is crucial for most AI chatbots.
In this guide, we'll show how to implement message persistence with useChat and streamText.

This guide does not cover authorization, error handling, or other real-world
considerations. It is intended to be a simple example of how to implement
message persistence.

contents.heading: starting-a-new-chat
contents.content:
When the user navigates to the chat page without providing a chat ID,
we need to create a new chat and redirect to the chat page with the new chat ID.

contents.heading: starting-a-new-chat
contents.content:
Our example chat store implementation uses files to store the chat messages.
In a real-world application, you would use a database or a cloud storage service,
and get the chat ID from the database.
That being said, the function interfaces are designed to be easily replaced with other implementations.

contents.heading: starting-a-new-chat
contents.content:
The chat ID can come from the URL or the request body, so validate it as an
opaque token before using it in a file path. The resolved path check ensures the
file stays inside the intended .chats directory.

contents.heading: loading-an-existing-chat
contents.content: When the user navigates to the chat page with a chat ID, we need to load the chat messages from storage.

contents.heading: loading-an-existing-chat
contents.content: The loadChat function in our file-based chat store is implemented as follows:

contents.heading: validating-messages-on-the-server
contents.content: When processing messages on the server that contain tool calls, custom metadata, or data parts, you should validate them using validateUIMessages before sending them to the model.

contents.heading: persisting-streaming-tool-input
contents.content:
An input-streaming tool part includes rawInput while tool arguments are
still arriving. Persist the complete UI message, including this field, so a
resumed stream can append later tool-input deltas to the exact text received
before the interruption. AI SDK updates rawInput as each delta arrives and
removes it when the tool input becomes available.

contents.heading: migrating-deprecated-tool-rawinput
contents.content:
Older persisted tool parts in the output-error state may contain rawInput.
This field is deprecated and will be removed in the next major version. Store
tool arguments in input instead. AI SDK emits a deprecation warning when
validateUIMessages, safeValidateUIMessages, or convertToModelMessages
encounters a defined rawInput value. UI stream processing also warns when it
reconstructs a static output-error part with rawInput.

contents.heading: migrating-deprecated-tool-rawinput
contents.content:
Migrate each legacy part by copying rawInput to input when input is
null or undefined, then remove rawInput. This preserves the current
backward-compatible conversion behavior:

contents.heading: validation-with-tools
contents.content: When your messages include tool calls, validate them against your tool definitions:

contents.heading: handling-validation-errors
contents.content: Handle validation errors gracefully when messages from the database don't match current schemas:

contents.heading: displaying-the-chat
contents.content: Once messages are loaded from storage, you can display them in your chat UI. Here's how to set up the page component and the chat display:

contents.heading: displaying-the-chat
contents.content: The chat component uses the useChat hook to manage the conversation:

contents.heading: storing-messages
contents.content: useChat sends the chat id and the messages to the backend.

contents.heading: storing-messages
contents.content:
The useChat message format is different from the ModelMessage format. The
useChat message format is designed for frontend display, and contains
additional fields such as id and createdAt. We recommend storing the
messages in the useChat message format.

contents.heading: storing-messages
contents.content:
When loading messages from storage that contain tools, metadata, or custom data
parts, validate them using validateUIMessages before processing (see the
validation section above).

contents.heading: storing-messages
contents.content:
Storing messages is done in the onEnd callback of the toUIMessageStream function.
onEnd receives the complete messages including the new AI response as UIMessage[].

contents.heading: storing-messages
contents.content:
The actual storage of the messages is done in the saveChat function, which in
our file-based chat store is implemented as follows:

contents.heading: message-ids
contents.content:
In addition to a chat ID, each message has an ID.
You can use this message ID to e.g. manipulate individual messages.

contents.heading: client-side-vs-server-side-id-generation
contents.content: By default, message IDs are generated client-side:

contents.heading: client-side-vs-server-side-id-generation
contents.content: User message IDs are generated by the useChat hook on the client

contents.heading: client-side-vs-server-side-id-generation
contents.content:
AI response message IDs are also generated by useChat on the client, unless
the server sends one in the stream (see below)

contents.heading: client-side-vs-server-side-id-generation
contents.content:
For applications without persistence, client-side ID generation works perfectly.
However, for persistence, you should use IDs that are stable before messages
are stored to ensure consistency across sessions and prevent ID conflicts when
messages are restored.

contents.heading: client-side-vs-server-side-id-generation
contents.content:
The server-side options below control IDs for generated assistant response
messages. User message IDs are created by useChat before the request is sent
to your API route, so keep those client-generated IDs when saving incoming
request messages, or generate and persist your own user message IDs before
sending/storing them.

contents.heading: setting-up-server-side-id-generation
contents.content:
When implementing persistence, you have two options for generating server-side
IDs for assistant response messages:

contents.heading: setting-up-server-side-id-generation
contents.content: Using generateMessageId in toUIMessageStream

contents.heading: setting-up-server-side-id-generation
contents.content: Setting IDs in your start message part with createUIMessageStream

contents.heading: option-1-using-generatemessageid-in-touimessagestream
contents.content: You can control the ID format by providing ID generators using createIdGenerator():

contents.heading: option-2-setting-ids-with-createuimessagestream
contents.content: Alternatively, you can use createUIMessageStream to control the message ID by writing a start message part:

contents.heading: option-2-setting-ids-with-createuimessagestream
contents.content: For client-side applications that don't require persistence, you can still customize client-side ID generation:

contents.heading: sending-only-the-last-message
contents.content:
Once you have implemented message persistence, you might want to send only the last message to the server.
This reduces the amount of data sent to the server on each request and can improve performance.

contents.heading: sending-only-the-last-message
contents.content:
To achieve this, you can provide a prepareSendMessagesRequest function to the transport.
This function receives the messages and the chat ID, and returns the request body to be sent to the server.

contents.heading: sending-only-the-last-message
contents.content: On the server, you can then load the previous messages and append the new message to the previous messages. If your messages contain tools, metadata, or custom data parts, you should validate them:

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content:
By default, the AI SDK streamText function uses backpressure to the language model provider to prevent
the consumption of tokens that are not yet requested.

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content:
However, this means that when the client disconnects, e.g. by closing the browser tab or because of a network issue,
the stream from the LLM will be aborted and the conversation may end up in a broken state.

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content:
Assuming that you have a storage solution in place, you can use the consumeStream method to consume the stream on the backend,
and then save the result as usual.
consumeStream effectively removes the backpressure,
meaning that the result is stored even when the client has already disconnected.

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content: When the client reloads the page after a disconnect, the chat will be restored from the storage solution.

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content:
In production applications, you would also track the state of the request (in
progress, complete) in your stored messages and use it on the client to cover
the case where the client reloads the page after a disconnection, but the
streaming is not yet complete.

contents.heading: handling-client-disconnects
contents.content: For more robust handling of disconnects, you may want to add resumability on disconnects. Check out the Chatbot Resume Streams documentation to learn more.

metadata.title: Chatbot Resume Streams
metadata.description: Learn how to resume chatbot streams after client disconnects.

title.children: Client-side: send the current assistant message
Server-side: stop the active work and clear the stream

contents.content: useChat supports resuming ongoing streams after page reloads. Use this feature to build applications with long-running generations.

In a resumable stream setup, client-side aborts are treated as disconnects.
Closing a tab, refreshing the page, or calling stop() only closes the
current HTTP connection and should not cancel the underlying generation. To
let users stop generation, add a dedicated stop endpoint that persists the
partial response, cancels the active work, and clears the active stream. See
Stop an Active Resumable Stream and
troubleshooting for
more details.

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Stream resumption requires persistence for messages and active streams in your application. The AI SDK provides tools to connect to storage, but you need to set up the storage yourself.

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: The AI SDK provides:

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: A resume option in useChat that automatically reconnects to active streams

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Access to the outgoing stream through the consumeSseStream callback

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Automatic HTTP requests to your resume endpoints

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: You build:

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Storage to track which stream belongs to each chat

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Redis to store the UIMessage stream

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Two API endpoints: POST to create streams, GET to resume them

contents.heading: how-stream-resumption-works
contents.content: Integration with resumable-stream to manage Redis storage

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: To implement resumable streams in your chat application, you need:

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: The resumable-stream package - Handles the publisher/subscriber mechanism for streams

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: A Redis instance - Stores stream data (e.g. Redis through Vercel)

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: A persistence layer - Tracks which stream ID is active for each chat (e.g. database)

contents.heading: client-side-enable-stream-resumption
contents.content: Use the resume option in the useChat hook to enable stream resumption. When resume is true, the hook automatically attempts to reconnect to any active stream for the chat on mount:

contents.heading: client-side-enable-stream-resumption
contents.content:
You must send the chat ID with each request (see
prepareSendMessagesRequest).

contents.heading: client-side-enable-stream-resumption
contents.content: When you enable resume, the useChat hook makes a GET request to /api/chat/[id]/stream on mount to check for and resume any active streams.

contents.heading: client-side-enable-stream-resumption
contents.content:
The default transport URL-encodes the chat ID as a single path segment. IDs equal
to . or .. are rejected with an InvalidArgumentError because URL parsers
interpret them as path traversal segments.

contents.heading: client-side-enable-stream-resumption
contents.content: Let's start by creating the POST handler to create the resumable stream.

contents.heading: create-the-post-handler
contents.content: The POST handler creates resumable streams using the consumeSseStream callback:

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content: Create a GET handler at /api/chat/[id]/stream that:

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content: Reads the chat ID from the route params

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content: Loads the chat data to check for an active stream

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content: Returns 204 (No Content) if no stream is active

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content: Resumes the existing stream if one is found

contents.heading: implement-the-get-handler
contents.content:
The after function from Next.js allows work to continue after the response
has been sent. This ensures that the resumable stream persists in Redis even
after the initial response is returned to the client, enabling reconnection
later.

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: The diagram above shows the complete lifecycle of a resumable stream:

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: Stream creation: When you send a new message, the POST handler uses streamText to generate the response. The consumeSseStream callback creates a resumable stream with a unique ID and stores it in Redis through the resumable-stream package

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: Stream tracking: Your persistence layer saves the activeStreamId in the chat data

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: Client reconnection: When the client reconnects (page reload), the resume option triggers a GET request to /api/chat/[id]/stream

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: Stream recovery: The GET handler checks for an activeStreamId and uses resumeExistingStream to reconnect. If no active stream exists, it returns a 204 (No Content) response

contents.heading: request-lifecycle
contents.content: Completion cleanup: When the stream finishes, the onEnd callback clears the activeStreamId by setting it to null

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content: By default, the useChat hook makes a GET request to /api/chat/[id]/stream when resuming. Customize this endpoint, credentials, and headers, using the prepareReconnectToStreamRequest option in DefaultChatTransport:

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content:
The callback receives the original, unencoded ID. Its returned api URL is used
verbatim, so encode and validate any ID you include in a custom URL yourself.

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content: This lets you:

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content: Match your existing API route structure

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content: Add query parameters or custom paths

contents.heading: customize-the-resume-endpoint
contents.content: Integrate with different backend architectures

contents.heading: stop-an-active-resumable-stream
contents.content: useChat includes a stop() function that aborts the current client request. In a resumable stream setup, that abort is a disconnect signal, not a request to stop generation.

contents.heading: stop-an-active-resumable-stream
contents.content: Stream resumption lets a client reconnect to an active stream after the original connection closes. To make that possible, the server keeps the stream running even when no client is actively consuming it. If the user refreshes the page, closes the tab, loses their connection, or navigates away, the client can reconnect later with resumeStream().

contents.heading: stop-an-active-resumable-stream
contents.content: Because of this, a client-side abort (e.g. closing the page or refreshing) only closes the current HTTP connection. It is not a request to cancel the underlying work. If your stop button only calls stop(), the model request, background job, workflow, or stream writer can continue running, and the client can reconnect to the same active stream.

contents.heading: stop-an-active-resumable-stream
contents.content: To support an explicit stop button, create a dedicated stop endpoint. The endpoint should accept the current assistant message from the client, persist that partial response, cancel the work that is producing the stream, and clear the active stream record for the chat.

contents.heading: stop-an-active-resumable-stream
contents.content: Stream resumption also needs your application to store a reference from the chat to the stream that can be resumed. This guide calls that reference activeStreamId. The resume endpoint uses it to find the stream to reconnect to. The stop endpoint uses the same value to find the work to cancel, and to avoid clearing a newer stream that may have started while the stop request was in flight.

contents.heading: client-side-send-the-current-assistant-message
contents.content: The chat setup is the same as the resumable stream setup above. To add stop behavior, send the latest partial assistant message to your stop endpoint before stopping the local chat stream.

contents.heading: client-side-send-the-current-assistant-message
contents.content: When the client knows the active stream ID, include it in the request. This lets the server ignore stale stop requests that arrive after a newer stream has already started.

contents.heading: client-side-send-the-current-assistant-message
contents.content: The stop request tells your server to cancel the active work. chat.stop() stops the local client from reading more chunks.

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: The stop endpoint should:

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: Load the chat and read its activeStreamId

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: Persist the assistant snapshot if one was sent

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: Cancel the work that is producing the stream

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: Clear activeStreamId only if it still points to the same stream

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: markStreamAsStopped and cancelActiveWork depend on your backend. In a Redis-backed resumable stream setup, you might close the stored stream and abort the model request that is writing to it. In a workflow setup, you might cancel the workflow run that owns the stream. In a job queue setup, you might cancel the job or write a cancellation flag that the job checks.

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: The activeStreamId can identify replay state, producer state, or both. If those are separate in your system, store enough information with the chat to cancel the producer that writes to the stream.

contents.heading: server-side-stop-the-active-work-and-clear-the-stream
contents.content: Persist the assistant snapshot as an insert or merge. Avoid overwriting a newer server-written message with an older client snapshot.

contents.heading: keep-navigation-separate-from-stop
contents.content: Do not call the stop endpoint from route cleanup code. Route cleanup is a disconnect, not an explicit stop. The active stream should remain resumable when the user refreshes the page or navigates away.

contents.heading: keep-navigation-separate-from-stop
contents.content: Only call the stop endpoint for an explicit user action, such as pressing a stop button.

contents.heading: keep-navigation-separate-from-stop
contents.content: After a user stops a stream, avoid automatic reconnect attempts for that chat until the user sends another message or explicitly retries. Otherwise the client can reconnect before cancellation has finished.

contents.heading: important-considerations
contents.content: Stream expiration: Streams in Redis expire after a set time (configurable in the resumable-stream package)

contents.heading: important-considerations
contents.content: Multiple clients: Multiple clients can connect to the same stream simultaneously

contents.heading: important-considerations
contents.content: Error handling: When no active stream exists, the GET handler returns a 204 (No Content) status code

contents.heading: important-considerations
contents.content: Security: Ensure proper authentication and authorization for both creating and resuming streams

contents.heading: important-considerations
contents.content: Race conditions: Clear the activeStreamId when starting a new stream to prevent resuming outdated streams

headings.content: Client-side: send the current assistant message
Server-side: stop the active work and clear the stream

metadata.title: Chatbot Tool Usage
metadata.description: Learn how to use tools with the useChat hook.

contents.content:
With useChat and streamText, you can use tools in your chatbot application.
The AI SDK supports three tool execution patterns in this context:
Automatically executed server-side tools
Automatically executed client-side tools
Tools that require user interaction, such as confirmation dialogs
The flow is as follows:
The user enters a message in the chat UI.
The message is sent to the API route.
In your server side route, the language model generates tool calls during the streamText call.
All tool calls are forwarded to the client.
Server-side tools are executed using their execute method and their results are forwarded to the client.

Client-side tools that should be automatically executed are handled with the onToolCall callback.
You must call addToolOutput to provide the tool result.

Client-side tool that require user interactions can be displayed in the UI.
The tool calls and results are available as tool invocation parts in the parts property of the last assistant message.
When the user interaction is done, addToolOutput can be used to add the tool result to the chat.

The chat can be configured to automatically submit when all tool results are available using sendAutomaticallyWhen.
This triggers another iteration of this flow.

The tool calls and tool executions are integrated into the assistant message as typed tool parts.
A tool part is at first a tool call, and then it becomes a tool result when the tool is executed.
The tool result contains all information about the tool call as well as the result of the tool execution.

Tool result submission can be configured using the sendAutomaticallyWhen
option. You can use the lastAssistantMessageIsCompleteWithToolCalls helper
to automatically submit when all tool results are available. This simplifies
the client-side code while still allowing full control when needed.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: In this example, we'll use three tools:

contents.heading: example
contents.content: getWeatherInformation: An automatically executed server-side tool that returns the weather in a given city.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: askForConfirmation: A user-interaction client-side tool that asks the user for confirmation.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: getLocation: An automatically executed client-side tool that returns a random city.

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content:
The client-side page uses the useChat hook to create a chatbot application with real-time message streaming.
Tool calls are displayed in the chat UI as typed tool parts.
Please make sure to render the messages using the parts property of the message.

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content: There are three things worth mentioning:

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content:
The onToolCall callback is used to handle client-side tools that should be automatically executed.
In this example, the getLocation tool is a client-side tool that returns a random city.
You call addToolOutput to provide the result (without await to avoid potential deadlocks).

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content:
Always check if (toolCall.dynamic) first in your onToolCall handler.
Without this check, TypeScript will throw an error like: Type 'string' is
  not assignable to type '"toolName1" | "toolName2"' when you try to use
toolCall.toolName in addToolOutput.

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content: The sendAutomaticallyWhen option with lastAssistantMessageIsCompleteWithToolCalls helper automatically submits when all tool results are available.

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content:
The parts array of assistant messages contains tool parts with typed names like tool-askForConfirmation.
The client-side tool askForConfirmation is displayed in the UI.
It asks the user for confirmation and displays the result once the user confirms or denies the execution.
The result is added to the chat using addToolOutput with the tool parameter for type safety.

contents.heading: client-side-page
contents.content:
Typed tool parts also include the approval-requested, approval-responded,
and output-denied states. Include these states when handling part.state
exhaustively, even when a tool does not require approval. See
Tool execution approval for a complete approval UI.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Sometimes an error may occur during client-side tool execution. Use the addToolOutput method with a state of output-error and errorText value instead of output to record the error.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
When rendering messages, use isToolOutputErrorUIPart to identify failed
static and dynamic tool parts without checking the tool state directly:

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: Tool execution approval lets you require user confirmation before a server-side tool runs. Unlike client-side tools that execute in the browser, tools with approval still execute on the server—but only after the user approves.

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: Use tool execution approval when you want to:

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: Confirm sensitive operations (payments, deletions, external API calls)

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: Let users review tool inputs before execution

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: Add human oversight to automated workflows

contents.heading: tool-execution-approval
contents.content: For tools that need to run in the browser (updating UI state, accessing browser APIs), use client-side tools instead.

contents.heading: server-setup
contents.content:
Enable approval with toolApproval on streamText. The older
needsApproval property on tools is deprecated. See Tool Execution Approval for configuration options including dynamic approval based on input.

contents.heading: client-side-approval-ui
contents.content:
When a tool requires manual approval, the tool part state is
approval-requested. Automatic approvals and denials also flow through the
same approval states, but they set part.approval.isAutomatic === true, so you
can render the status without calling addToolApprovalResponse. Automatic
approval decisions can also include part.approval.reason.

contents.heading: client-side-approval-ui
contents.content:
Call addToolApprovalResponse only for manual approvals. Automatic approval
decisions already arrive in the UI stream as approval-requested and
approval-responded states, and denied executions continue to output-denied.
If you return a reason from an automatic approval or denial, it is available
as part.approval.reason.
For manual approval requests, the reason for requiring approval is available as
part.approval.requestReason. It remains separate from an optional response
reason supplied to addToolApprovalResponse.

contents.heading: client-side-approval-ui
contents.content:
Approval request chunks can also include an approvalDescriptor with opaque
application-specific metadata. UI message processing exposes it as
part.approval.descriptor in the approval-requested state and preserves it in
subsequent approval-bearing states, including approval-responded. This lets
clients render or persist server-computed approval metadata without using it to
determine whether the tool was approved.

contents.heading: securing-approvals-for-sensitive-tools
contents.content: In the useChat pattern, the client sends the full message history to the server each turn. Without additional protection, a modified client could fabricate an approval response. For tools that perform sensitive operations, add experimental_toolApprovalSecret to your streamText call so the server cryptographically verifies that it issued the approval:

contents.heading: securing-approvals-for-sensitive-tools
contents.content: See Security Considerations for setup details.

contents.heading: auto-submit-after-approval
contents.content:
If nothing happens after you approve a tool execution, make sure you either
call sendMessage manually or configure sendAutomaticallyWhen on the
useChat hook.

contents.heading: auto-submit-after-approval
contents.content: Use lastAssistantMessageIsCompleteWithApprovalResponses to automatically continue the conversation after approvals:

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: When using dynamic tools (tools with unknown types at compile time), the UI parts use a generic dynamic-tool type instead of specific tool types:

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: Dynamic tools are useful when integrating with:

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools without schemas

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: User-defined functions loaded at runtime

contents.heading: dynamic-tools
contents.content: External tool providers

contents.heading: tool-call-streaming
contents.content: Tool call streaming is enabled by default in AI SDK 5.0, allowing you to stream tool calls while they are being generated. This provides a better user experience by showing tool inputs as they are generated in real-time.

contents.heading: tool-call-streaming
contents.content:
With tool call streaming enabled, partial tool calls are streamed as part of the data stream.
They are available through the useChat hook.
The typed tool parts of assistant messages will also contain partial tool calls.
You can use the state property of the tool part to render the correct UI.

contents.heading: step-start-parts
contents.content:
When you are using multi-step tool calls, the AI SDK will add step start parts to the assistant messages.
If you want to display boundaries between tool calls, you can use the step-start parts as follows:

contents.heading: server-side-multi-step-calls
contents.content:
You can also use multi-step calls on the server-side with streamText.
This works when all invoked tools have an execute function on the server side.

contents.heading: errors
contents.content:
Language models can make errors when calling tools.
By default, these errors are masked for security reasons, and show up as "An error occurred" in the UI.

contents.heading: errors
contents.content:
Tool execution errors marked providerExecuted: true bypass this masking and the
UI stream's onError callback. String errors pass through unchanged; other error
values are serialized with JSON.stringify. The original error data is needed
when converting persisted UI messages back into model messages, for example to
preserve Anthropic tool error codes. Harness runtime tool errors also retain
their original messages. The callback still handles invalid tool calls and
stream errors, regardless of whether a tool is provider-executed.

contents.heading: errors
contents.content:
To customize masked errors, pass onError to toUIMessageStream. This callback
does not redact provider-executed tool execution errors sent to the client.

contents.heading: errors
contents.content: In case you are using createUIMessageResponse, you can use the onError function when calling toUIMessageResponse:

metadata.title: Chatbot
metadata.description: Learn how to use the useChat hook.

title.children: Setting custom body fields per request

contents.content: The useChat hook makes it effortless to create a conversational user interface for your chatbot application. It enables the streaming of chat messages from your AI provider, manages the chat state, and updates the UI automatically as new messages arrive.
To summarize, the useChat hook provides the following features:
Message Streaming: All the messages from the AI provider are streamed to the chat UI in real-time.
Managed States: The hook manages the states for input, messages, status, error and more for you.
Seamless Integration: Easily integrate your chat AI into any design or layout with minimal effort.

In this guide, you will learn how to use the useChat hook to create a chatbot application with real-time message streaming.
Check out our chatbot with tools guide to learn how to use tools in your chatbot.
Let's start with the following example first.

contents.heading: example
contents.content:
The UI messages have a new parts property that contains the message parts.
We recommend rendering the messages using the parts property instead of the
content property. The parts property supports different message types,
including text, tool invocation, and tool result, and allows for more flexible
and complex chat UIs.

contents.heading: example
contents.content:
In the Page component, the useChat hook will request to your AI provider endpoint whenever the user sends a message using sendMessage.
The messages are then streamed back in real-time and displayed in the chat UI.

contents.heading: example
contents.content:
This enables a seamless chat experience where the user can see the AI response as soon as it is available,
without having to wait for the entire response to be received.

contents.heading: customized-ui
contents.content: useChat also provides ways to manage the chat message states via code, show status, and update messages without being triggered by user interactions.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: The useChat hook returns a status. It has the following possible values:

contents.heading: status
contents.content: submitted: The message has been sent to the API and we're awaiting the start of the response stream.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: streaming: The response is actively streaming in from the API, receiving chunks of data.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: ready: The full response has been received and processed; a new user message can be submitted.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: error: An error occurred during the API request, preventing successful completion.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: You can use status for e.g. the following purposes:

contents.heading: status
contents.content: To show a loading spinner while the chatbot is processing the user's message.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: To show a "Stop" button to abort the current message.

contents.heading: status
contents.content: To disable the submit button.

contents.heading: error-state
contents.content:
Similarly, the error state reflects the error object thrown during the fetch request.
It can be used to display an error message, disable the submit button, or show a retry button:

contents.heading: error-state
contents.content:
We recommend showing a generic error message to the user, such as "Something
went wrong." This is a good practice to avoid leaking information from the
server.

contents.heading: error-state
contents.content: Please also see the error handling guide for more information.

contents.heading: modify-messages
contents.content: Sometimes, you may want to directly modify some existing messages. For example, a delete button can be added to each message to allow users to remove them from the chat history.

contents.heading: modify-messages
contents.content: The setMessages function can help you achieve these tasks:

contents.heading: modify-messages
contents.content: You can think of messages and setMessages as a pair of state and setState in React.

contents.heading: cancellation-and-regeneration
contents.content: It's also a common use case to abort the response message while it's still streaming back from the AI provider. You can do this by calling the stop function returned by the useChat hook.

contents.heading: cancellation-and-regeneration
contents.content: When the user clicks the "Stop" button, the fetch request will be aborted. This avoids consuming unnecessary resources and improves the UX of your chatbot application.

contents.heading: cancellation-and-regeneration
contents.content: Similarly, you can also request the AI provider to reprocess the last message by calling the regenerate function returned by the useChat hook:

contents.heading: cancellation-and-regeneration
contents.content: When the user clicks the "Regenerate" button, the AI provider will regenerate the last message and replace the current one correspondingly.

contents.heading: throttling-ui-updates
contents.content:
By default, useChat publishes message updates as each chunk is processed.
React may batch multiple updates into a single render.
React and Vue applications can throttle reactive message updates with the throttle option.
Stream processing and event callbacks remain immediate, and the latest messages are published before the chat enters a terminal ready or error status.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: useChat provides optional event callbacks that you can use to handle different stages of the chatbot lifecycle:

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: onFinish: Called when the assistant response is completed. The event includes the response message, all messages, and flags for abort, disconnect, and errors.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: onError: Called when an error occurs during the fetch request.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: onData: Called whenever a data part is received.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: These callbacks can be used to trigger additional actions, such as logging, analytics, or custom UI updates.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: It's worth noting that you can abort the processing by throwing an error in the onData callback. This will trigger the onError callback and stop the message from being appended to the chat UI. This can be useful for handling unexpected responses from the AI provider.

contents.heading: custom-headers-body-and-credentials
contents.content: By default, the useChat hook sends an HTTP POST request to the /api/chat endpoint with the message list as the request body. You can customize the request in two ways:

contents.heading: hook-level-configuration-applied-to-all-requests
contents.content: You can configure transport-level options that will be applied to all requests made by the hook:

contents.heading: dynamic-hook-level-configuration
contents.content: You can also provide functions that return configuration values. This is useful for authentication tokens that need to be refreshed, or for configuration that depends on runtime conditions:

contents.heading: dynamic-hook-level-configuration
contents.content:
For component state that changes over time, use useRef to store the current
value and reference ref.current in your configuration function, or prefer
request-level options (see next section) for better reliability.

contents.heading: request-level-configuration-recommended
contents.content:
Recommended: Use request-level options for better flexibility and control.
Request-level options take precedence over hook-level options and allow you to
customize each request individually.

contents.heading: request-level-configuration-recommended
contents.content: The request-level options are merged with hook-level options, with request-level options taking precedence. On your server side, you can handle the request with this additional information.

contents.heading: setting-custom-body-fields-per-request
contents.content:
You can configure custom body fields on a per-request basis using the second parameter of the sendMessage function.
This is useful if you want to pass in additional information to your backend that is not part of the message list.

contents.heading: setting-custom-body-fields-per-request
contents.content: You can retrieve these custom fields on your server side by destructuring the request body:

contents.heading: message-metadata
contents.content: You can attach custom metadata to messages for tracking information like timestamps, model details, and token usage.

contents.heading: message-metadata
contents.content: For complete examples with type safety and advanced use cases, see the Message Metadata documentation.

contents.heading: transport-configuration
contents.content: You can configure custom transport behavior using the transport option to customize how messages are sent to your API:

contents.heading: transport-configuration
contents.content: The corresponding API route receives the custom request format:

contents.heading: advanced-trigger-based-routing
contents.content: For more complex scenarios like message regeneration, you can use trigger-based routing:

contents.heading: advanced-trigger-based-routing
contents.content: The corresponding API route would handle different triggers:

contents.heading: advanced-trigger-based-routing
contents.content: To learn more about building custom transports, refer to the Transport API documentation.

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: For scenarios where you want to communicate directly with an Agent without going through HTTP, you can use DirectChatTransport. This is useful for:

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: Server-side rendering scenarios

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: Testing without network

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: Single-process applications

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: The DirectChatTransport invokes the agent's stream() method directly, converting UI messages to model messages and streaming the response back as UI message chunks.

contents.heading: direct-agent-transport
contents.content: For more details, see the DirectChatTransport reference.

contents.heading: controlling-the-response-stream
contents.content: With streamText, you can control how error messages and usage information are sent back to the client.

contents.heading: error-messages
contents.content:
By default, the error message is masked for security reasons.
The default error message is "An error occurred."

contents.heading: error-messages
contents.content:
Tool execution errors marked providerExecuted: true are an exception. They
bypass the UI stream's onError callback: strings are forwarded unchanged, and
other error values are serialized with JSON.stringify. This preserves provider
error codes when chat history is converted back into model messages, as well as
error messages from harness runtimes. Stream errors and invalid tool calls still
use onError, even for provider-executed tools. Do not rely on this callback to
redact provider-executed tool execution errors before they reach the client.

contents.heading: error-messages
contents.content: You can forward error messages or send your own error message by providing an onError function:

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Track token consumption and resource usage with message metadata:

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Define a custom metadata type with usage fields (optional, for type safety)

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Attach usage data using messageMetadata in your response

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Display usage metrics in your UI components

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Usage data is attached as metadata to messages and becomes available once the model completes its response generation.

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: Then, on the client, you can access the message-level metadata.

contents.heading: usage-information
contents.content: You can also access your metadata from the onFinish callback of useChat:

contents.heading: text-streams
contents.content: useChat can handle plain text streams by setting the streamProtocol option to text:

contents.heading: text-streams
contents.content:
This configuration also works with other backend servers that stream plain text.
Check out the stream protocol guide for more information.

contents.heading: text-streams
contents.content:
When using TextStreamChatTransport, tool calls, usage information and finish
reasons are not available.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
Some models such as DeepSeek deepseek-r1
and Anthropic claude-sonnet-5-5 support reasoning tokens.
These tokens are typically sent before the message content.
You can forward them to the client with the sendReasoning option:

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: On the client side, you can access the reasoning parts of the message object.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Reasoning parts have a text property that contains the reasoning content.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
Some models may also produce files as part of reasoning (e.g. images).
These are available as reasoning-file parts (ReasoningFileUIPart) with
mediaType and url properties, similar to regular file parts.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Some providers such as Perplexity and
Google include sources in the response.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: You can forward sources to the client with the sendSources option. This example uses the Perplexity Agent API's fast preset to search the web. Install @ai-sdk/perplexity and set PERPLEXITY_API_KEY in your environment:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
On the client side, you can access source parts of the message object.
There are two types of sources: source-url for web pages and source-document for documents.
Here is an example that renders both types of sources:

contents.heading: image-generation
contents.content:
Some models such as Google gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview support image generation.
When images are generated, they are exposed as files to the client.
On the client side, you can access file parts of the message object
and render them as images.

contents.heading: attachments
contents.content: The useChat hook supports sending file attachments along with a message as well as rendering them on the client. This can be useful for building applications that involve sending images, files, or other media content to the AI provider.

contents.heading: attachments
contents.content: There are two ways to send files with a message: using a FileList object from file inputs or using an array of file objects.

contents.heading: filelist
contents.content: By using FileList, you can send multiple files as attachments along with a message using the file input element. The useChat hook will automatically convert them into data URLs and send them to the AI provider.

contents.heading: filelist
contents.content:
Currently, only image/* and text/* content types get automatically
converted into multi-modal content
parts. You will need to handle other
content types manually.

contents.heading: file-objects
contents.content: You can also send files as objects along with a message. This can be useful for sending pre-uploaded files or data URLs.

contents.heading: file-objects
contents.content:
Files generated as part of model reasoning are available as reasoning-file
parts (ReasoningFileUIPart) with the same mediaType and url properties.

contents.heading: type-inference-for-tools
contents.content: When working with tools in TypeScript, AI SDK UI provides type inference helpers to ensure type safety for your tool inputs and outputs.

contents.heading: inferuitool
contents.content: The InferUITool type helper infers the input and output types of a single tool for use in UI messages:

contents.heading: inferuitools
contents.content: The InferUITools type helper infers the input and output types of a ToolSet:

contents.heading: using-inferred-types
contents.content: You can use these inferred types to create a custom UIMessage type and pass it to various AI SDK UI functions:

contents.heading: using-inferred-types
contents.content: Pass the custom type to useChat or createUIMessageStream:

contents.heading: using-inferred-types
contents.content: This provides full type safety for tool inputs and outputs on the client and server.

metadata.title: Completion
metadata.description: Learn how to use the useCompletion hook.

contents.content: The useCompletion hook allows you to create a user interface to handle text completions in your application. It enables the streaming of text completions from your AI provider, manages the state for chat input, and updates the UI automatically as new messages are received.
The useCompletion hook is now part of the @ai-sdk/react package.
In this guide, you will learn how to use the useCompletion hook in your application to generate text completions and stream them in real-time to your users.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: In the Page component, the useCompletion hook will request to your AI provider endpoint whenever the user submits a message. The completion is then streamed back in real-time and displayed in the UI.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: This enables a seamless text completion experience where the user can see the AI response as soon as it is available, without having to wait for the entire response to be received.

contents.heading: customized-ui
contents.content: useCompletion also provides ways to manage the prompt via code, show loading and error states, and update messages without being triggered by user interactions.

contents.heading: loading-and-error-states
contents.content: To show a loading spinner while the chatbot is processing the user's message, you can use the isLoading state returned by the useCompletion hook:

contents.heading: loading-and-error-states
contents.content: Similarly, the error state reflects the error object thrown during the fetch request. It can be used to display an error message, or show a toast notification:

contents.heading: controlled-input
contents.content: In the initial example, we have handleSubmit and handleInputChange callbacks that manage the input changes and form submissions. These are handy for common use cases, but you can also use uncontrolled APIs for more advanced scenarios such as form validation or customized components.

contents.heading: controlled-input
contents.content: The following example demonstrates how to use more granular APIs like setInput with your custom input and submit button components:

contents.heading: cancelation
contents.content: It's also a common use case to abort the response message while it's still streaming back from the AI provider. You can do this by calling the stop function returned by the useCompletion hook.

contents.heading: cancelation
contents.content: When the user clicks the "Stop" button, the fetch request will be aborted. This avoids consuming unnecessary resources and improves the UX of your application.

contents.heading: throttling-ui-updates
contents.content:
By default, the useCompletion hook will trigger a render every time a new chunk is received.
You can throttle the UI updates with the throttle option.

contents.heading: event-callbacks
contents.content: useCompletion also provides optional event callbacks that you can use to handle different stages of the chatbot lifecycle. These callbacks can be used to trigger additional actions, such as logging, analytics, or custom UI updates.

contents.heading: configure-request-options
contents.content: By default, the useCompletion hook sends an HTTP POST request to the /api/completion endpoint with the prompt as part of the request body. You can customize the request by passing additional options to the useCompletion hook:

contents.heading: configure-request-options
contents.content: In this example, the useCompletion hook sends a POST request to the /api/custom-completion endpoint with the specified headers, additional body fields, and credentials for that fetch request. On your server side, you can handle the request with these additional information.

contents.heading: configure-request-options
contents.content:
You can provide a type for the additional body fields. The type applies to
both the body configured on the hook and the body passed to complete:

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.description: Learn how to handle errors in the AI SDK UI

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content:
The AI SDK shows warnings when something might not work as expected.
These warnings help you fix problems before they cause errors.

contents.heading: when-warnings-appear
contents.content:
Warnings use Node.js process.emitWarning when available and console.warn in
browser/edge runtimes. They appear when:

contents.heading: when-warnings-appear
contents.content: Unsupported features: You use a feature or setting that is not supported by the AI model (e.g., certain options or parameters).

contents.heading: when-warnings-appear
contents.content: Compatibility warnings: A feature is used in a compatibility mode, which might work differently or less optimally than intended.

contents.heading: when-warnings-appear
contents.content: Deprecations: You use a deprecated API, option, or message format.

contents.heading: when-warnings-appear
contents.content: Other warnings: The AI model reports another type of issue, such as general problems or advisory messages.

contents.heading: warning-messages
contents.content: All warnings include "AI SDK Warning" so you can easily find them. For example:

contents.heading: turning-off-warnings
contents.content: By default, warnings are shown in the console. You can control this behavior:

contents.heading: turn-off-all-warnings
contents.content: Set a global variable to turn off warnings completely:

contents.heading: custom-warning-handler
contents.content:
You can also provide your own function to handle warnings.
It receives a list of warnings and optional provider and model ids. Custom
handlers receive every warning, including repeated deprecations.

contents.heading: deprecation-warnings
contents.content:
The default logger emits each deprecation code once per loaded SDK instance.
In Node.js, these warnings have the type DeprecationWarning and a stable
AISDK_DEP_* code, available as warning.code on process.on('warning', handler).
Browser/edge console messages include the code in brackets.

Run Node.js with --throw-deprecation to fail on deprecated usage,
--no-deprecation to suppress deprecations, or --trace-deprecation for stack
traces. These flags affect all DeprecationWarnings, rather than individual
codes, and apply only to the default Node.js logger.

contents.heading: error-helper-object
contents.content:
Each AI SDK UI hook also returns an error object that you can use to render the error in your UI.
You can use the error object to show an error message, disable the submit button, or show a retry button.

contents.heading: error-helper-object
contents.content:
We recommend showing a generic error message to the user, such as "Something
went wrong." This is a good practice to avoid leaking information from the
server.

contents.heading: alternative-replace-the-failed-message
contents.content:
Alternatively, you can write a custom submit handler that replaces the failed
user message with new input. If the assistant response started streaming before
the error, remove both the partial assistant response and its user message.

contents.heading: error-handling-callback
contents.content:
Errors can be processed by passing an onError callback function as an option to the useChat or useCompletion hooks.
The callback function receives an error object as an argument.

AI SDK-created client errors use exported error classes with marker-based

For AI SDK UI requests, APICallError.requestBodyValues is undefined so

You might want to create errors for testing.

metadata.title: Generative User Interfaces
metadata.description: Learn how to build Generative UI with AI SDK UI.

title.children: Build a Generative UI Chat Interface

contents.content: Generative user interfaces (generative UI) is the process of allowing a large language model (LLM) to go beyond text and "generate UI". This creates a more engaging and AI-native experience for users.

At the core of generative UI are  tools , which are functions you provide to the model to perform specialized tasks like getting the weather in a location. The model can decide when and how to use these tools based on the context of the conversation.
Generative UI is the process of connecting the results of a tool call to a React component. Here's how it works:
You provide the model with a prompt or conversation history, along with a set of tools.
Based on the context, the model may decide to call a tool.
If a tool is called, it will execute and return data.
This data can then be passed to a React component for rendering.
By passing the tool results to React components, you can create a generative UI experience that's more engaging and adaptive to your needs.

This tool will return simulated data after a 2-second delay. In a real-world application, you would replace this simulation with an actual API call to a weather service.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: An overview of AI SDK UI.

contents.content: AI SDK UI is designed to help you build interactive chat, completion, and assistant applications with ease. It is a framework-agnostic toolkit, streamlining the integration of advanced AI functionalities into your applications.

AI SDK UI provides robust abstractions that simplify the complex tasks of managing chat streams and UI updates on the frontend, enabling you to develop dynamic AI-driven interfaces more efficiently. With three main hooks — useChat, useCompletion, and useObject — you can incorporate real-time chat capabilities, text completions, streamed JSON, and interactive assistant features into your app.
useChat offers real-time streaming of chat messages and manages message, loading, and error state. Manage input state in your component for seamless integration into any UI design.
useCompletion enables you to handle text completions in your applications, managing the prompt input and automatically updating the UI as new completions are streamed.
useObject is a hook that allows you to consume streamed JSON objects, providing a simple way to handle and display structured data in your application.
These hooks are designed to reduce the complexity and time required to implement AI interactions, letting you focus on creating exceptional user experiences.

contents.content:
AI SDK UI functions such as useChat and useCompletion support both text streams and data streams.
The stream protocol defines how the data is streamed to the frontend on top of the HTTP protocol.
This page describes both protocols and how to use them in the backend and frontend.

You can use this information to develop custom backends and frontends for your use case, e.g.,
to provide compatible API endpoints that are implemented in a different language such as Python.
For instance, here's an example using FastAPI as a backend.

A text stream contains chunks in plain text, that are streamed to the frontend.
Each chunk is then appended together to form a full text response.
