OpenAI conversations. You can also set store: false; the provider will
serialize the complete call and screenshot result into each follow-up request.

contents.heading: computer-tool
contents.content:
Run computer use in an isolated browser or VM. Restrict reachable domains,
accounts, credentials, environment variables, and file-system access. Treat
on-screen content as untrusted prompt-injection input, require confirmation
immediately before consequential actions, and avoid exposing sensitive
information in screenshots.

contents.heading: local-shell-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI responses API support the local shell tool for Codex models through the openai.tools.localShell tool.
Local shell is a tool that allows agents to run shell commands locally on a machine you or the user provides.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports the shell tool through the openai.tools.shell tool.
The shell tool allows running bash commands and interacting with a command line.
The model proposes shell commands; your integration executes them and returns the outputs.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content:
Running arbitrary shell commands can be dangerous. Always sandbox execution or
add strict allow-/deny-lists before forwarding a command to the system shell.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content: The shell tool supports three environment modes that control where commands are executed:

contents.heading: local-execution-default
contents.content: When no environment is specified (or type: 'local' is used), commands are executed locally via your execute callback:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: Set environment.type to 'containerAuto' to run commands in an OpenAI-hosted container. No execute callback is needed — OpenAI handles execution server-side:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: The containerAuto environment supports:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: fileIds string[] - File IDs to make available in the container

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: memoryLimit '1g' | '4g' | '16g' | '64g' - Memory limit for the container

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: networkPolicy - Network access policy:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: { type: 'disabled' } — no network access

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: { type: 'allowlist', allowedDomains: string[], domainSecrets?: Array<{ domain, name, value }> } — allow specific domains with optional secrets

contents.heading: existing-container-reference
contents.content: Set environment.type to 'containerReference' to use an existing container by ID:

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: For local execution (default or type: 'local'), your execute function must return an output array with results for each command:

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: stdout string - Standard output from the command

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: stderr string - Standard error from the command

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: outcome - Either { type: 'timeout' } or { type: 'exit', exitCode: number }

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Skills are versioned bundles of files with a SKILL.md manifest that extend the shell tool's capabilities. They can be attached to both containerAuto and local environments.

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Container skills support two formats — by reference (for skills uploaded to OpenAI) or inline (as a base64-encoded zip):

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Local skills point to a directory on disk containing a SKILL.md file:

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: For more details on creating skills, see the OpenAI Skills documentation.

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports the apply patch tool for GPT-5.1 models through the openai.tools.applyPatch tool.
The apply patch tool lets the model create, update, and delete files in your codebase using structured diffs.
Instead of just suggesting edits, the model emits patch operations that your application applies and reports back on,
enabling iterative, multi-step code editing workflows.

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: Your execute function must return:

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: status 'completed' | 'failed' - Whether the patch was applied successfully

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: output string (optional) - Human-readable log text (e.g., results or error messages)

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content:
Tool search allows the model to dynamically search for and load tools into context as needed,
rather than loading all tool definitions up front. This can reduce token usage, cost, and latency
when you have many tools. Mark the tools you want to make searchable with deferLoading: true
in their providerOptions.

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: There are two execution modes:

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: Server-executed (hosted): OpenAI searches across the deferred tools declared in the request and returns the loaded subset in the same response. No extra round-trip is needed.

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: Client-executed: The model emits a tool_search_call, your application performs the lookup, and you return the matching tools via the execute callback.

contents.heading: server-executed-hosted-tool-search
contents.content:
Use hosted tool search when the candidate tools are already known at request time.
Add openai.tools.toolSearch() with no arguments and mark your tools with deferLoading: true:

contents.heading: server-executed-hosted-tool-search
contents.content:
In hosted mode, the model internally searches the deferred tools, loads the relevant ones, and
proceeds to call them — all within a single response. The tool_search_call and
tool_search_output items appear in the response with execution: 'server' and call_id: null.

contents.heading: namespaces
contents.content:
Use providerOptions.openai.namespace to group related function tools for OpenAI.
The SDK keeps each tool executable as a normal AI SDK tool, but serializes grouped
tools as OpenAI namespace entries in the request:

contents.heading: namespaces
contents.content:
Tools in the same namespace must use the same namespace name and description.
For best results with tool search, keep namespace descriptions concise and put
detailed usage guidance on the individual function tools.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content:
Use client-executed tool search when tool discovery depends on runtime state — for example,
tools that vary per tenant, project, or external system. Pass execution: 'client' along with
a description, parameters schema, and an execute callback:

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: In client mode, the flow spans two steps:

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: Step 1: The model emits a tool_search_call with execution: 'client' and a non-null call_id. The SDK calls your execute callback with the search arguments. Your callback returns the discovered tools.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: Step 2: The SDK sends the tool_search_output (with the matching call_id) back to the model. The model can now call the loaded tools as normal function calls.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: For more details, see the OpenAI Tool Search documentation.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports
custom tools
through the openai.tools.customTool tool.
Custom tools return a raw string instead of JSON, optionally constrained to a grammar
(regex or Lark syntax). This makes them useful for generating structured text like
SQL queries, code snippets, or any output that must match a specific pattern.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: Custom tools also work with streamText:

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: The custom tool can be configured with:

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: description string (optional) - A description of what the tool does, to help the model understand when to use it.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: format object (optional) - The output format constraint. Omit for unconstrained text output.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: type 'grammar' | 'text' - The format type. Use 'grammar' for constrained output or 'text' for explicit unconstrained text.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: syntax 'regex' | 'lark' - (grammar only) The grammar syntax. Use 'regex' for regular expression patterns or 'lark' for Lark parser grammar.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: definition string - (grammar only) The grammar definition string (a regex pattern or Lark grammar).

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: execute function (optional) - An async function that receives the raw string input and returns a string result. Enables multi-turn tool calling.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
The allowedTools provider option restricts which of the tools you declared the model is allowed to
call, while still sending the full tools list to OpenAI. Because the tools list stays byte-identical
across requests, the prompt cache is preserved — unlike activeTools, which removes tools from the
request and invalidates the cache whenever the allow-list changes.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content: allowedTools is only supported by the Responses API, and it overrides the request-level toolChoice.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
toolNames string[] - The tools the model may call, named as you declared them in tools. For
provider-defined tools you may also use the canonical OpenAI name (for example web_search).

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
mode 'auto' | 'required' (optional) - 'auto' (default) lets the model pick one of the allowed
tools or answer with a message; 'required' forces it to call at least one of them.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
Both function tools and provider-defined tools can be allow-listed, including web search, file search,
image generation, code interpreter, computer, apply patch, shell, programmatic tool calling, custom
tools, and MCP servers.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
If a name matches both a tool you declared and the canonical OpenAI name of a different tool, the tool
you declared under that name wins, and a warning reports the ambiguity. If several tools share the same
canonical name — two MCP servers, for example — that name is ambiguous, so it is dropped with a warning;
name those tools as you declared them instead.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
Three kinds of tools cannot be allow-listed, because OpenAI's allowed_tools
only sees the eagerly-loaded tool list: the tool search tool,
tools marked with deferLoading, and tools grouped into a namespace. Naming
one of these in allowedTools removes it from the allow-list and emits a
warning; if that leaves no tools at all, the request fails with an error
instead of silently sending no restriction.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
An MCP server is allow-listed as a whole: the entry carries the server label,
so every tool on that server is callable. To restrict which tools on a server
the model may call, use the MCP tool's own allowedTools argument.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports Image inputs for appropriate models.
You can pass Image files as part of the message content using the file type with an image media type:

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content:
The model will have access to the image and will respond to questions about it.
The image should be passed using the data field.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of an image.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports reading PDF files.
You can pass PDF files as part of the message content using the file type:

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of a pdf.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content:
The model will have access to the contents of the PDF file and
respond to questions about it.
The PDF file should be passed using the data field,
and the mediaType should be set to 'application/pdf'.

contents.heading: structured-outputs
contents.content: The OpenAI Responses API supports structured outputs. You can use generateText or streamText with Output to enforce structured outputs.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: When using the OpenAI Responses API, the SDK attaches OpenAI-specific metadata to output parts via providerMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
This metadata can be used on the client side for tasks such as rendering citations or downloading files generated by the Code Interpreter.
To enable type-safe handling of this metadata, the AI SDK exports dedicated TypeScript types.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: For text parts, when part.type === 'text', the providerMetadata is provided in the form of OpenaiResponsesTextProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: This metadata includes the following fields:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
itemId
The ID of the output item in the Responses API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
annotations (optional)
An array of annotation objects generated by the model.
If no annotations are present, this property itself may be omitted (undefined).

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: Each element in annotations is a discriminated union with a required type field. Supported types include, for example:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: url_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: container_file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: file_path

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
These annotations directly correspond to the annotation objects defined by the Responses API and can be used for inline reference rendering or output analysis.
For details, see the official OpenAI documentation:
Responses API – output text annotations.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
When implementing file downloads for files generated by the Code Interpreter,
the container_id and file_id available in providerMetadata can be used
to retrieve the file content. For details, see the Retrieve container file
content
API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content:
When using the OpenAI Responses API, reasoning output parts can include provider metadata.
To handle this metadata in a type-safe way, use OpenaiResponsesReasoningProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: For reasoning parts, when part.type === 'reasoning', the providerMetadata is provided in the form of OpenaiResponsesReasoningProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: This metadata includes the following fields:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: itemIdThe ID of the reasoning item in the Responses API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: reasoningEncryptedContent (optional)Encrypted reasoning content (only returned when requested via include: ['reasoning.encrypted_content']).

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: For source document parts, when part.type === 'source' and sourceType === 'document', the providerMetadata is provided as OpenaiResponsesSourceDocumentProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: This metadata is also a discriminated union with a required type field. Supported types include:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: container_file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: file_path

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: Each type includes the identifiers required to work with the referenced resource, such as fileId and containerId.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content:
Annotations in text parts follow the OpenAI Responses API specification and
therefore use snake_case properties (e.g. file_id, container_id). In
contrast, providerMetadata for source document parts is normalized by the
SDK to camelCase (e.g. fileId, containerId). Fields that depend on the
original text content, such as start_index and end_index, are omitted, as
are fields like filename that are directly available on the source object.

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content: The OpenAI Responses API supports server-side context compaction. When enabled, the server automatically compresses conversation context when token usage crosses a configured threshold. This is useful for long-running conversations or agent loops where you want to stay within token limits without manually managing context.

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content: The compaction item returned by the server is opaque and encrypted — it carries forward key prior state and reasoning into the next turn using fewer tokens. The AI SDK handles this automatically: compaction items are returned as text parts with special providerMetadata, and when passed back in subsequent requests they are sent as compaction input items.

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content: Configuration:

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content: type — Must be 'compaction'

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content: compactThreshold — The token count at which compaction is triggered. When the rendered input token count crosses this threshold, the server runs a compaction pass before continuing inference.

contents.heading: compaction-1
contents.content:
Server-side compaction is ZDR-friendly when you set store: false on your
requests.

contents.heading: explicit-compaction
contents.content:
For Responses-compatible endpoints that support explicit compaction, set
compactionTrigger: true. The provider appends the required
{ type: 'compaction_trigger' } request control after all converted messages
and input items.

contents.heading: explicit-compaction
contents.content:
This is distinct from contextManagement, which configures automatic,
threshold-based compaction. When omitted or false, compactionTrigger does
not add an input item. The resulting compaction output uses the existing
openai.compaction custom part representation. Endpoint and model support can
vary.

contents.heading: detecting-compaction-in-streams
contents.content: When using streamText, you can detect compaction by checking the providerMetadata on text-start and text-end events:

contents.heading: compaction-in-ui-applications
contents.content: When using useChat or other UI hooks, compaction items appear as text parts with providerMetadata. You can detect and style them differently in your UI:

contents.heading: compaction-in-ui-applications
contents.content: The metadata includes the following fields:

contents.heading: compaction-in-ui-applications
contents.content: type — Always 'compaction'

contents.heading: compaction-in-ui-applications
contents.content: itemId string — The ID of the compaction item in the Responses API

contents.heading: compaction-in-ui-applications
contents.content: encryptedContent string (optional) — The encrypted compaction state. This is automatically sent back to the API when the message is included in subsequent requests.

contents.heading: batch
contents.content: Batch support is experimental and the API may change in patch releases.

contents.heading: batch
contents.content:
The OpenAI provider supports asynchronous text generation through the Batch
API. Pass the OpenAI
provider to the AI SDK's Batch API for
the complete workflow, including polling, persistence, and result handling.

contents.heading: batch
contents.content:
Each request specifies its type and model. OpenAI requires every text
request in a batch to use the same model and throws before submission when the
models differ.

contents.heading: webhooks
contents.content:
The OpenAI Batch API does not support per-batch webhooks. When you provide a
webhookUrl, the provider returns an unsupported warning and starts the batch
without a webhook.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the OpenAI chat API using the .chat() factory method.
The first argument is the model id, e.g. gpt-6-astra.
The OpenAI chat models support tool calls and some have multi-modal capabilities.
Use this factory when a custom baseURL points at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
that implements Chat Completions but not the Responses API.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
OpenAI chat models support also some model specific provider options that are not part of the standard call settings.
You can pass them in the providerOptions argument:

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: The following optional provider options are available for OpenAI chat models:

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: logitBias Record<number, number>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Modifies the likelihood of specified tokens appearing in the completion.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Accepts a JSON object that maps tokens (specified by their token ID in
the GPT tokenizer) to an associated bias value from -100 to 100. You
can use this tokenizer tool to convert text to token IDs. Mathematically,
the bias is added to the logits generated by the model prior to sampling.
The exact effect will vary per model, but values between -1 and 1 should
decrease or increase likelihood of selection; values like -100 or 100
should result in a ban or exclusive selection of the relevant token.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: As an example, you can pass {"50256": -100} to prevent the token from being generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: logprobs boolean | number

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Return the log probabilities of the tokens. Including logprobs will increase
the response size and can slow down response times. However, it can
be useful to better understand how the model is behaving.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Setting to true will return the log probabilities of the tokens that
were generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Setting to a number will return the log probabilities of the top n
tokens that were generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: parallelToolCalls boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help OpenAI to
monitor and detect abuse. Learn more.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: reasoningEffort 'none' | 'minimal' | 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Reasoning effort for reasoning models. Defaults to medium. If you use
providerOptions to set the reasoningEffort option, this
model setting will be ignored.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Supported reasoning efforts vary by model. GPT-5.6 supports 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh', and 'max'.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: maxCompletionTokens number

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Maximum number of completion tokens to generate. Useful for reasoning models.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: store boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Whether to enable persistence in Responses API.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: metadata Record<string, string>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Metadata to associate with the request.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: prediction Record<string, any>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Parameters for prediction mode.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: serviceTier 'auto' | 'flex' | 'priority' | 'fast' | 'ultrafast' | 'default'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Service tier for the request. Set to 'flex' for 50% cheaper processing
at the cost of increased latency (available for o3, o4-mini, and gpt-5 models).
Set to 'priority' for faster processing with Enterprise access (available for gpt-4, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o3, o4-mini; gpt-5-nano is not supported).
'fast' is OpenAI's newer name for the 'priority' tier; the two are interchangeable, and responses from
gpt-5.6 and earlier report serviceTier: 'priority' for either.
Set to 'ultrafast' for access-controlled Ultrafast processing (available only for gpt-5.6-sol).

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Defaults to 'auto'.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: strictJsonSchema boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Whether to use strict JSON schema validation.
Defaults to true.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: textVerbosity 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Controls the verbosity of the model's responses. Lower values will result in more concise responses, while higher values will result in more verbose responses.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheKey string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: A cache key for manual prompt caching control. Used by OpenAI to cache responses for similar requests to optimize your cache hit rates.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheOptions object

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Configures prompt caching for GPT-5.6 and later models. mode can be 'implicit' or 'explicit', and ttl currently only supports '30m'. In explicit mode, only content blocks marked with a prompt cache breakpoint are cached.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheRetention 'in_memory' | '24h'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: The legacy retention policy for models before GPT-5.6. Set to '24h' to enable extended prompt caching on supported models. For GPT-5.6 and later models, use promptCacheOptions.ttl instead.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: safetyIdentifier string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: A stable identifier used to help detect users of your application that may be violating OpenAI's usage policies. The IDs should be a string that uniquely identifies each user.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: systemMessageMode 'system' | 'developer' | 'remove'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Override the system message mode for this model. If not specified, the mode is automatically determined based on the model. system uses the 'system' role for system messages (default for most models); developer uses the 'developer' role (used by reasoning models); remove removes system messages entirely.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: forceReasoning boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Force treating this model as a reasoning model. This is useful for "stealth" reasoning models (e.g. via a custom baseURL) where the model ID is not recognized by the SDK's allowlist. When enabled, the SDK applies reasoning-model parameter compatibility rules and defaults systemMessageMode to developer unless overridden.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
OpenAI has introduced the o1,o3, and o4 series of reasoning models.
Currently, o4-mini, o3, o3-mini, and o1 are available via both the chat and responses APIs. The
model gpt-5.1-codex-mini is available only via the responses API.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Reasoning models currently only generate text, have several limitations, and are only supported using generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: They support additional settings and response metadata:

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can use providerOptions to set

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: the reasoningEffort option (or alternatively the reasoningEffort model setting), which determines the amount of reasoning the model performs.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can use the response usage to access the number of reasoning tokens that the model generated via usage.outputTokenDetails.reasoningTokens.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
System messages are automatically converted to OpenAI developer messages for
reasoning models when supported.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can control how system messages are handled by providerOptions systemMessageMode:

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: developer: treat the prompt as a developer message (default for reasoning models).

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: system: keep the system message as a system-level instruction.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: remove: remove the system message from the messages.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
Reasoning models require additional runtime inference to complete their
reasoning phase before generating a response. This introduces longer latency
compared to other models.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
maxOutputTokens is automatically mapped to max_completion_tokens for
reasoning models.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Strict structured outputs are enabled by default.
You can disable them by setting the strictJsonSchema option to false.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI structured outputs have several
limitations,
in particular around the supported schemas,
and are therefore opt-in.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
For example, optional schema properties are not supported.
You need to change Zod .nullish() and .optional() to .nullable().

contents.heading: logprobs
contents.content:
OpenAI provides logprobs information for completion/chat models.
You can access it in the providerMetadata object.

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content:
The OpenAI Chat API supports Image inputs for appropriate models.
You can pass Image files as part of the message content using the file type with an image media type:

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content:
The model will have access to the image and will respond to questions about it.
The image should be passed using the data field.

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of an image.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content:
The OpenAI Chat API supports reading PDF files.
You can pass PDF files as part of the message content using the file type:

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content:
The model will have access to the contents of the PDF file and
respond to questions about it.
The PDF file should be passed using the data field,
and the mediaType should be set to 'application/pdf'.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of a PDF.

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI supports predicted outputs for gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini.
Predicted outputs help you reduce latency by allowing you to specify a base text that the model should modify.
You can enable predicted outputs by adding the prediction option to the providerOptions.openai object:

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI provides usage information for predicted outputs (acceptedPredictionTokens and rejectedPredictionTokens).
You can access it in the providerMetadata object.

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI Predicted Outputs have several
limitations,
e.g. unsupported API parameters and no tool calling support.

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content: You can use the openai provider option to set the image input detail to high, low, original, or auto:

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content: For GPT-5.6, original preserves the input dimensions without resizing to a patch budget or pixel-dimension limit. auto and an omitted detail setting use the same sizing behavior as original, which can increase input token usage for large images.

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content:
Because the UIMessage type (used by AI SDK UI hooks like useChat) does not
support the providerOptions property, you can use convertToModelMessages
first before passing the messages to functions like generateText or
streamText. For more details on providerOptions usage, see
here.

contents.heading: distillation
contents.content:
OpenAI supports model distillation for some models.
If you want to store a generation for use in the distillation process, you can add the store option to the providerOptions.openai object.
This will save the generation to the OpenAI platform for later use in distillation.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content:
OpenAI has introduced Prompt Caching for supported models
including gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content:
Prompt caching is automatically enabled for these models, when the prompt is 1024 tokens or longer. It does
not need to be explicitly enabled.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: You can use the response usage to access the number of prompt tokens that were a cache hit via usage.inputTokenDetails.cacheReadTokens.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For GPT-5.6 and later models, usage.inputTokenDetails.cacheWriteTokens reports tokens written to the cache.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For GPT-5.6 and later models, promptCacheOptions.ttl sets a minimum cache lifetime of 30 minutes. Earlier models generally retain in-memory prefixes for 5-10 minutes of inactivity, up to one hour.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: To improve cache hit rates, you can manually control caching using the promptCacheKey option:

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: GPT-5.6 and later models support explicit cache breakpoints on text, image, and file content blocks. Set a request-level cache key and mark the end of each reusable prefix with promptCacheBreakpoint:

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: In 'implicit' mode, OpenAI places an automatic breakpoint on the latest message and also honors explicit breakpoints. In 'explicit' mode, only marked content blocks are eligible for caching; a request without any explicit breakpoint does not use prompt caching.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For models before GPT-5.6 that support extended caching, you can keep cached prefixes active for up to 24 hours:

contents.heading: audio-input
contents.content: With the gpt-4o-audio-preview model, you can pass audio files to the model.

contents.heading: audio-input
contents.content:
The gpt-4o-audio-preview model is currently in preview and requires at least
some audio inputs. It will not work with non-audio data.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the OpenAI completions API using the .completion() factory method.
The first argument is the model id.
Currently only gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct is supported.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
OpenAI completion models support also some model specific settings that are not part of the standard call settings.
You can pass them as an options argument:

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: The following optional provider options are available for OpenAI completion models:

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: echo: boolean

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: Echo back the prompt in addition to the completion.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: logitBias Record<number, number>

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: Modifies the likelihood of specified tokens appearing in the completion.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Accepts a JSON object that maps tokens (specified by their token ID in
the GPT tokenizer) to an associated bias value from -100 to 100. You
can use this tokenizer tool to convert text to token IDs. Mathematically,
the bias is added to the logits generated by the model prior to sampling.
The exact effect will vary per model, but values between -1 and 1 should
decrease or increase likelihood of selection; values like -100 or 100
should result in a ban or exclusive selection of the relevant token.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
As an example, you can pass {"50256": -100} to prevent the <|endoftext|>
token from being generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: logprobs boolean | number

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Return the log probabilities of the tokens. Including logprobs will increase
the response size and can slow down response times. However, it can
be useful to better understand how the model is behaving.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Setting to true will return the log probabilities of the tokens that
were generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Setting to a number will return the log probabilities of the top n
tokens that were generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: suffix string

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: The suffix that comes after a completion of inserted text.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
Use .experimental_realtime() for both OpenAI Realtime
and OpenAI Live models.

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
The OpenAI-only api option accepts 'live' or 'realtime' and takes precedence
over model-ID selection. Without it, the known gpt-live-1 ID uses Live and other
IDs retain the Realtime default. The provider does not switch APIs after a failed
request. Both model implementations use the existing experimental realtime interface.

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
Live supports browser WSS sessions through an application-owned relay with client
delegation, using experimental_useRealtime for the browser runtime, and optional
browser-direct WebRTC. Your application owns the agent and tool execution; Live
delegations do not invoke onToolCall. For a low-level server adapter, obtain server-only connection
settings with liveModel.getServerWebSocketConfig() and serialize commands with
liveModel.serializeClientEvent(). Create one parser per connection with
liveModel.createServerEventParser() and pass incoming JSON to the returned
function. It returns arrays of normalized events and retains each original event
in raw.

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
For a token-based Realtime API session, create a short-lived token on your
server with openai.experimental_realtime.getToken():

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
Live does not use Realtime client-secret minting. Calling getToken for a known
Live model or with api: 'live' rejects before a mint request. Live's WebSocket
connection authenticates on a trusted server; keep the provider API key out of
browser code. The API selector chooses a protocol, not a different authentication
capability for the same model.

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
Browser authentication to an application-owned relay is separate from OpenAI
authentication. Protect that relay with your application's session or short-lived
credential; an origin check alone is not user authentication. The relay uses its
server-held OpenAI key upstream. Selecting a Live model does not make the Realtime
client-secret endpoint compatible with the Live API.

contents.heading: realtime-models
contents.content:
For browser-direct Live WebRTC, an authenticated application endpoint performs the
SDP exchange through liveModel.doCreateWebRTCSession({ sdp, sessionConfig, abortSignal })
using the server's project key. The browser receives the
session connection answer, not the project key or a Realtime client secret. This
setup endpoint still needs application authentication. See the
experimental_useRealtime reference
for the api.session setup contract and the runnable example.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
Configure Live-specific settings through sessionConfig.providerOptions.openai,
typed with Experimental_OpenAIRealtimeModelLiveOptions. For example:

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
delegation: use { type: 'client' } for application-owned work. Omission or
null also selects client mode. Other delegation modes are unsupported.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content: input: prior text messages with developer, user or assistant roles.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
voice: an authorized custom voice reference { id }, mutually exclusive with
the ordinary sessionConfig.voice string.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
store: requests provider-side session storage; availability depends on the
OpenAI project configuration.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
client.dataChannel: WebRTC startup permission policy with
allowedClientEvents and allowedServerEvents. Set it on the application server,
not from trusted-looking browser input. Omission retains the provider default;
[] allows none and 'all' allows all. Response event selectors use
{ type: 'response.event', responseEvent: 'response.completed' } to select
native nested events, which remain raw custom events rather than managed SDK
responses. Keep readiness, errors, and terminal usage observable for
the session features your application enables.

contents.heading: live-session-options
contents.content:
Send the initial WebSocket configuration with session-start; WebRTC starts the
session during SDP setup and negotiates audio formats through SDP. Live startup settings are
immutable: session-update is rejected. Use input-audio-mute and
input-audio-unmute for remote input processing; these commands do not release the
local microphone. Return application context through
context-append, using the opaque delegationId from delegation-created, or
null for context without a delegation. Its providerOptions.openai.channel
accepts instructions, thinking (the default), or commentary.

contents.heading: live-session-options
live-session-options
contents.content:
For the browser integration, see the
experimental_useRealtime reference.
It covers the JSON/PCM16 WebSocket relay runtime, optional WebRTC setup and permission
policy, microphone and playback ownership, session.delegations, sendEvent for
application context, and close() for bounded finalization. Use wss: for production
relays. Continuous conversation semantics do not imply browser support for every
provider codec or transport. The Realtime guide covers
legacy token-based, turn-based sessions.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the OpenAI transcription API
using the .transcription() factory method.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content: The first argument is the model id e.g. gpt-4o-transcribe.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content: You can also pass additional provider-specific options using the providerOptions argument. For example, supplying the input language in ISO-639-1 (e.g. en) format will improve accuracy and latency.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content: To get word-level timestamps, specify the granularity:

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize identifies speakers in a recording. It defaults to
the diarized_json response format and automatic chunking:

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content: The following provider options are available:

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
timestampGranularities string[]
The granularity of the timestamps in the transcription.
Defaults to ['segment'].
Possible values are ['word'], ['segment'], and ['word', 'segment'].
Note: There is no additional latency for segment timestamps, but generating word timestamps incurs additional latency.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
language string
The language of the input audio. Supplying the input language in ISO-639-1 format (e.g. 'en') will improve accuracy and latency.
Optional.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
prompt string
An optional text to guide the model's style or continue a previous audio segment. The prompt should match the audio language.
Optional.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
temperature number
The sampling temperature, between 0 and 1. Higher values like 0.8 will make the output more random, while lower values like 0.2 will make it more focused and deterministic. If set to 0, the model will use log probability to automatically increase the temperature until certain thresholds are hit.
Defaults to 0.
Optional.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
include string[]
Additional information to include in the transcription response.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
responseFormat 'json' | 'verbose_json' | 'diarized_json'
The format of the transcription response. gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize defaults to diarized_json.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
chunkingStrategy 'auto' | object
Controls how the audio is split into chunks. gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize defaults to 'auto'; provide this option to override the default. The object form configures OpenAI server-side VAD with type: 'server_vad' and optional threshold, prefixPaddingMs, and silenceDurationMs fields.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
streaming object
Options for streaming transcription models such as gpt-realtime-whisper.
Use with experimental_streamTranscribe.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
delay 'minimal' | 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh'
Latency/accuracy tradeoff for realtime transcription.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:
include string[]
Additional fields to include in realtime transcription events, such as item.input_audio_transcription.logprobs.

Create an experimental decision model with openai.decisionModel(modelId).
It uses the native Decisions API
to answer Choice, Score, and Boolean questions with gpt-6-luna.

contents.heading: decision-models
contents.content:
Scores are probability-weighted fractional positions on the ordered rubric, starting
at zero. Choice labels are returned exactly as supplied. Choice and Score answers
include probability distributions. Boolean questions use the API's predicate
primitive and return P(true). Apply thresholds in application code, for example
answers.requestsRefund.probability >= 0.5.

contents.heading: decision-models
contents.content:
Structured state, instructions, and criterion descriptions are serialized as JSON
text. Score levels receive zero-based index labels. Non-null Boolean criteria are
appended to predicate instructions under Criteria for true: and Criteria for false:.
String criteria are passed through; structured criteria are serialized as JSON text.

contents.heading: decision-models
contents.content:
The factory respects createOpenAI settings, including custom fetch and base URL.
Set providerOptions.openai.safetyIdentifier to an opaque end-user identifier for
safety monitoring (up to 128 characters). For example:

contents.heading: decision-models
contents.content:
Import OpenAIDecisionModelOptions from @ai-sdk/openai when using the type above.
Other OpenAI options are unsupported and produce warnings. Native confidence
values are available in providerMetadata.openai.confidence, keyed by question ID.
Input and output token counts are available in usage. The full native token usage
(including cache, reasoning, and total counts) is preserved in
providerMetadata.openai.usage. Response headers, the returned model ID, and the
raw response body are preserved. If OpenAI refuses a question, the entire call
throws InvalidResponseDataError with the question name and the raw response in
error.data. Invalid answers also fail the entire decision.
See Decisions.

contents.heading: decision-models
contents.content:
Decision models can also be accessed through customProvider aliases or
createProviderRegistry().decisionModel('provider:model'). Direct string IDs
use Gateway by default, or an explicitly configured default provider with an
decisionModel method. See
model aliases and registries.

Supported native tools are web_search, fetch_url, people_search,

Search and fetch results are exposed as AI SDK sources. Other native tool traces,
including finance, sandbox, and MCP results, are available in response.body
and raw stream chunks (include: { rawChunks: true }). They are not exposed as
AI SDK client tool calls. Accounts with zero data retention may reject
file-capable tools such as finance_search and sandbox.

contents.heading: migrating-from-v4-sonar-to-v5-agent-api
contents.content:
The Agent API has no equivalent for Sonar PDF or video inputs, image or video
results, search_language_filter, or stream_mode. Related questions require
prompting or structured output. Remove these options during migration.

contents.heading: migrating-from-v4-sonar-to-v5-agent-api
contents.content:
Language requests now use /v1/agent. Custom baseURL proxies must route that
path. Raw responses and streams use the Agent API's typed output and SSE event
formats, and Perplexity provider metadata, usage, cost, and source identifiers
can differ. The embeddings API is unchanged.

contents.heading: migrating-from-v4-sonar-to-v5-agent-api
contents.content:
For PDF inputs, extract the document text before sending it to the Agent API,
or choose another provider that supports PDF input. Move image/video retrieval
and language-filtered search to a separate service if your application requires
those features. Rework consumers of raw Sonar stream events for typed Agent
events. See Perplexity's migration
guide
for the full API-level comparison.

metadata.title: QuiverAI
metadata.description: Learn how to use QuiverAI models with the AI SDK.

contents.content: QuiverAI provides Arrow language models that can reason about and create SVG documents, plus native SVG generation, vectorization, editing, and animation endpoints. The AI SDK provider exposes Arrow 2 through generateText and streamText and exposes image operations through generateImage.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The QuiverAI provider is available via the @ai-sdk/quiverai module. You can install it with

contents.heading: provider-instance

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: If you need a customized setup, you can import createQuiverAI and create a provider instance with your settings:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the QuiverAI provider instance:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Use a different URL prefix for API calls, e.g. to use proxy servers.
The default prefix is https://api.quiver.ai/v1. It also reads QUIVERAI_BASE_URL from the environment.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: apiKey string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
API key that is sent as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.
It defaults to the QUIVERAI_API_KEY environment variable.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Custom headers to include in the requests.

contents.heading: provider-instance

contents.heading: provider-instance

Custom fetch implementation.
You can use it as a middleware to intercept requests,
or to provide a custom fetch implementation for e.g. testing.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
Create an Arrow language model by calling the provider or using
.languageModel():

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
The language-model factory supports arrow-2 and arrow-2-telos through
QuiverAI's stateless POST /v1/responses endpoint.

contents.heading: reasoning-options
contents.content: Configure QuiverAI reasoning through providerOptions.quiverai:

contents.heading: reasoning-options
contents.content: reasoningEffort 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh'

contents.heading: reasoning-options
contents.content: reasoningSummary 'auto'

contents.heading: reasoning-options
contents.content:
The provider does not request encrypted reasoning. During tool loops it replays
the full conversation, matching tool calls and results, and opaque reasoning
item IDs in order without resending private reasoning text or encrypted
reasoning state.

contents.heading: caller-executed-tools
contents.content:
Standard AI SDK tools are sent as Responses API function tools and execute in
your application. Use a bounded loop because each step performs another model
request:

contents.heading: caller-executed-tools
contents.content: QuiverAI custom tools return raw strings and are also executed by the caller:

contents.heading: caller-executed-tools
contents.content: Hosted tools, including legacy quiver:* tools, are not supported.

contents.heading: responses-api-limitations
contents.content:
Requests are stateless. The provider does not enable response storage or
response-ID continuation.

contents.heading: responses-api-limitations
contents.content:
QuiverAI currently documents text response format for this endpoint.
Structured-output settings are omitted and reported in warnings.

contents.heading: responses-api-limitations
contents.content: Streaming tool calls are assembled completely before application execution.

contents.heading: responses-api-limitations
contents.content:
Abort signals, custom headers, and custom fetch implementations are
forwarded to the Responses request.

contents.heading: language-model-usage
contents.content:
result.usage and streaming finish events include input, cache-read,
cache-write, text-output, and reasoning token counts when returned by QuiverAI.

contents.heading: image-models

You can create QuiverAI image models using the .image() factory method.
For more on image generation with the AI SDK see generateImage().

contents.heading: basic-usage
contents.content: QuiverAI returns SVG documents. The generated SVG bytes are available through result.image.uint8Array (or result.images when generating multiple).

contents.content: Maximum number of output tokens. Arrow 2 and Arrow 2 Telos accept 1-65536. The provider retains its legacy validation bound of 131072 for other model IDs; the API may enforce a lower model-specific limit.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: referenceImages Array<{ url: string } | { base64: string }>

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Up to four optional reference images for SVG editing. URL references must use HTTP or HTTPS. Base64 references must decode to PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, or SVG data. Use prepareQuiverAIImageReference to convert binary, data URL, or URL inputs into this JSON-safe provider option shape.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: maxReviewSteps number (0-5)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Maximum number of edit review and redo steps after the initial edit.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: orchestratorMaxOutputTokens number (1-65536)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Optional provider orchestrator token budget for SVG editing.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: shallowMaxOutputTokens number (1-65536)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Optional provider shallow edit token budget for SVG editing.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: autoCrop boolean

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: When vectorizing, automatically crop the input image. Only used with operation: 'vectorize'.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: targetSize number (128-4096)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: When vectorizing, target canvas size in pixels. Only used with operation: 'vectorize'.

contents.heading: reference-images
contents.content: Pass reference images through prompt.images:

contents.heading: reference-images
contents.content: arrow-1 and arrow-1.1 accept up to 4 reference images. arrow-1.1-max accepts up to 16. For Arrow 2 and other model IDs, the provider allows the endpoint maximum of 16 references and lets the API enforce any lower model-specific limit.

contents.heading: vectorizing-a-raster-image
contents.content: Set operation to vectorize and pass a single image in prompt.images:

contents.heading: vectorizing-a-raster-image
contents.content: Vectorization returns one SVG per API request. To request multiple vectorizations with n, also set maxImagesPerCall: 1 so generateImage splits them into separate calls.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Set operation to edit, put exactly one source SVG in prompt.images, and provide the edit instruction in prompt.text:

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: The source SVG can be an HTTP/HTTPS URL, binary data such as a Buffer or Uint8Array, a base64 string, or an SVG data URL. Binary and base64 sources are validated as complete UTF-8 SVG documents and sent to QuiverAI as base64 SVG sources. Remote source URLs are fetched by QuiverAI and must resolve to an SVG.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Edit reference images are separate from the source SVG. Put them in providerOptions.quiverai.referenceImages, not prompt.images. Direct provider-option values use { url } or { base64 }; prepareQuiverAIImageReference converts an HTTP/HTTPS URL, URL, Uint8Array, ArrayBuffer, base64 string, or supported image data URL to that JSON-safe shape.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: SVG editing has these validation constraints:

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: The model must be arrow-2 or arrow-2-telos, and the API key's live model catalog must include the svg_edit operation.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: prompt.images must contain exactly one source SVG.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: prompt.text is required, must not be blank, and must contain at most 4000 characters.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Binary source SVGs must be complete UTF-8 SVG documents no larger than 200000 bytes.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: At most four reference images are accepted. Inline references can contain up to 12582912 decoded bytes.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Editing returns exactly one SVG per API request. To request multiple edits with n, set maxImagesPerCall: 1 so generateImage splits them into separate calls.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Masks and generation/vectorization-only provider options are rejected for edits.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: Edit-only provider options are rejected for generation, vectorization, and animation.

contents.heading: editing-an-svg
contents.content: The edited SVG is returned as bytes in result.image.uint8Array.

contents.heading: animating-an-svg
contents.content: Arrow 2 and Arrow 2 Telos can animate an existing SVG. Set operation to animate and pass exactly one source SVG in prompt.images. The text instruction is optional; omit text to let QuiverAI choose an animation.

contents.heading: animating-an-svg
contents.content: The animation source can be an HTTP or HTTPS URL, SVG bytes, raw base64, or an image/svg+xml base64 data URL. Local file inputs are inspected before the request and rejected when they do not contain SVG data. Remote URLs are validated for their scheme and fetched and validated by QuiverAI.

contents.heading: animating-an-svg
contents.content: Animation returns an animated SVG as bytes in image.uint8Array. When QuiverAI returns timing information, the per-image metadata includes loopPeriodMs and openingAnimationMs; either timing value can be null.

contents.heading: animating-an-svg
contents.content: Animation requests must use arrow-2 or arrow-2-telos, contain exactly one source SVG, omit masks, and produce one result per provider request. To request multiple animations with n, set maxImagesPerCall: 1 so generateImage splits them into separate calls. Animation supports temperature, reasoningEffort, and maxOutputTokens; generation-only and vectorization-only provider options are rejected.

contents.heading: animating-an-svg
contents.content: Source SVGs, text instructions, and remote source URLs are sent to QuiverAI. Animated SVG is active document content. Sanitize it or render it in an isolated context before embedding output from an untrusted source inline in a page.

contents.heading: billing-and-usage
contents.content: Arrow 2 models return measured token counts in result.usage. Fixed-credit models may return compatibility token counts of zero; their credit charge is available in result.providerMetadata?.quiverai?.credits when supplied by the API.

contents.heading: billing-and-usage
contents.content: Model availability and supported operations depend on your organization and API key permissions. Consult QuiverAI's model catalog for current capabilities and billing.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: maxWaitTimeInSeconds number - Maximum time in seconds to wait for the prediction to complete in sync mode. By default, Replicate uses sync mode with a 60-second timeout. contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: pollIntervalMillis number - Interval in milliseconds between polling attempts when a prediction does not complete within the synchronous wait duration. Defaults to 500 milliseconds.

contents.heading: provider-options

metadata.description: Learn how to use the Topaz Labs provider for the AI SDK.

contents.content: The Topaz Labs provider contains support for Topaz Labs' image and video enhancement models.

Topaz models enhance media you supply. They upscale, denoise, sharpen and restore an existing image or video. They do not generate media from a text prompt, so the input file is the required part of the request and a text prompt is ignored.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The Topaz Labs provider is available in the @ai-sdk/topaz module. You can install it with

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can import the default provider instance topaz from @ai-sdk/topaz:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the Topaz Labs provider instance:

It defaults to the TOPAZ_API_KEY environment variable.

Use a different URL prefix for API calls, e.g. to use proxy servers.

contents.heading: image-models
contents.content: The image to enhance (JPEG, PNG or TIFF) is passed through the prompt's images. The Topaz image API is asynchronous: the provider submits the job, polls until it finishes, and downloads the result, so generateImage resolves with the enhanced image.

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: enhancementStrength 'low' | 'medium' | 'high': how aggressively to enhance. Defaults to high.

contents.heading: image-provider-options

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: grainSize number: grain particle size, 1 to 5. Defaults to 1.

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: grainStrength number: grain effect strength, 0 to 1. Defaults to 0.5.

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: inputWidth / inputHeight number: input dimensions in pixels. Topaz infers these from the upload when omitted.

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: outputWidth / outputHeight number: output dimensions in pixels, 1 to 32000. These take precedence over the dimensions derived from size.

contents.content: The source provider option describes the input video. The AI SDK does not inspect media files, so the values come from your side:

contents.heading: source-metadata

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: audioTransfer ('Copy' | 'Convert' | 'None', default Copy), audioCodec ('AAC' | 'AC3' | 'PCM', default AAC), audioBitrate.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: videoEncoder ('AV1' | 'H264' | 'H265' | 'ProRes' | 'VP9', Topaz defaults to H265), videoProfile, videoBitrate, dynamicCompressionLevel ('Low' | 'Mid' | 'High').

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: container ('mp4' | 'mov' | 'mkv' | 'avi' | 'webm'): defaults to the input container when it is mov or mkv, otherwise mp4. ProRes always produces mov, AV1 and VP9 always produce mp4.

contents.content: cropToFit: center-crop to the output dimensions.

contents.content: filter Record<string, unknown>: escape hatch merged into the model's filter entry, overriding the typed options below.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: Proteus filter settings: videoType, auto, fieldOrder, focusFixLevel, compression, details, prenoise, noise, halo, preblur, blur, grain, grainSigma, grainSize, grainType, recoverOriginalDetailValue.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: Starlight Precise filter settings: sharpness, videoBitDepth, videoCodec, videoProfile, watermark.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: See the Proteus and Starlight Precise 2.6 references for the accepted ranges, and Create Video Request for the accepted encoder and profile combinations.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: A non-empty prompt, aspectRatio, seed, duration, generateAudio, frameImages and n greater than 1 are not supported and produce warnings.

contents.heading: long-running-operations
contents.content: Video enhancement takes minutes, so Topaz video models implement the AI SDK's async operation protocol. generateVideo polls to completion, and long clips can exceed its default 10 minute timeout, so raise poll.timeoutMs when needed. Use experimental_startVideo when you would rather persist the operation and check its status later:

contents.heading: long-running-operations
contents.content: If the upload fails after the request is created, the provider cancels the Topaz request so any reserved credits are refunded.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: Topaz estimates the cost of a video request in credits as a [lowerBound, upperBound] range and bills the lower bound.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: The start result's providerMetadata.topaz contains the requestId and, when Topaz could estimate the cost at request time, estimatedCredits. Topaz can do that when source metadata is set. It is informational only: the completed status carries the billed value.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: The completed status's providerMetadata.topaz contains:

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: requestId string: the Topaz request id.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: credits number: the credits Topaz bills for the request (the lower bound of its final estimate).

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: estimatedCredits [number, number]: the final cost range.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: outputSize string: the size of the enhanced video.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: expiresAt number: when the download URL expires, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

contents.heading: video-provider-metadata
contents.content: A failed request reports Topaz's errorCode (for example CREDIT_DIFFERENCE when Topaz's estimate after reading the video diverged from the first one, in which case it refunds the credits) in both the error message and providerMetadata.topaz.errorCode.

The TypeSafe provider supports the experimental decision
API with native Choice, Score, and Boolean answers. It sends all questions in one

Use jev-latest or another TypeSafe model ID. The response includes the actual

contents.heading: decision
contents.content:
State, instructions, and descriptions accept JSON objects and arrays in addition
to strings. Descriptions may be null. Boolean true/false criteria are optional.
The SDK uses the neutral name boolean and maps it to TypeSafe's noul field.

contents.heading: rounded-values-and-confidence
contents.content:
TypeSafe returns scores and probabilities rounded to two decimal places.
result.rounding reports this precision so the SDK can account for rounding when
checking distribution sums and weighted means. The returned values are preserved
unchanged; rounding means probabilities may not add up to exactly one.

contents.heading: rounded-values-and-confidence
contents.content:
Confidence is a separate TypeSafe statistic, available under
result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence[questionId] for Choice and Score
answers. Boolean probability always means P(true), not confidence in either
outcome. Choose decision thresholds in application code.

contents.heading: errors-and-retries
contents.content:
Provider failures use APICallError, including validation and authentication
errors. Core retries transient failures such as 429 and 529 according to
maxRetries (default: 2). abortSignal, request headers, and custom fetch are
forwarded. There is no provider-side retry loop.

contents.heading: errors-and-retries
contents.content:
No provider-specific options are currently defined. Unknown entries under
providerOptions.typesafe produce unsupported-option warnings. Language,
embedding, and image model factories throw NoSuchModelError.

contents.heading: errors-and-retries
contents.content:
Decision models support workflow serialization. A custom fetch function is not
serialized; restored models use the default fetch implementation.

metadata.description: Learn how to use xAI Grok and Imagine.

contents.content: The xAI Grok provider contains language model support for the xAI API.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content:
The xAI Grok provider is available via the @ai-sdk/xai module. You can
install it with

contents.content: You can import the default provider instance xai from @ai-sdk/xai:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
If you need a customized setup, you can import createXai from @ai-sdk/xai
and create a provider instance with your settings:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the xAI provider instance:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: baseURL string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Use a different URL prefix for API calls, e.g. to use proxy servers.
The default prefix is https://api.x.ai/v1.

contents.heading: provider-instance

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
API key that is being sent using the Authorization header. It defaults to
the XAI_API_KEY environment variable.

contents.heading: provider-instance
