metadata.title: Workflow Patterns
metadata.description: Learn workflow patterns for building reliable agents with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Combine the building blocks from the overview with these patterns to add structure and reliability to your agents:
Sequential Processing - Steps executed in order
Parallel Processing - Independent tasks run simultaneously
Evaluation/Feedback Loops - Results checked and improved iteratively
Orchestration - Coordinating multiple components
Routing - Directing work based on context

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Consider these key factors:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Flexibility vs Control - How much freedom does the LLM need vs how tightly you must constrain its actions?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Error Tolerance - What are the consequences of mistakes in your use case?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Cost Considerations - More complex systems typically mean more LLM calls and higher costs

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Maintenance - Simpler architectures are easier to debug and modify

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Start with the simplest approach that meets your needs. Add complexity only when required by:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Breaking down tasks into clear steps

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Adding tools for specific capabilities

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Implementing feedback loops for quality control

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Introducing multiple agents for complex workflows

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Let's look at examples of these patterns in action.

contents.heading: patterns-with-examples
contents.content: These patterns, adapted from Anthropic's guide on building effective agents, serve as building blocks you can combine to create comprehensive workflows. Each pattern addresses specific aspects of task execution. Combine them thoughtfully to build reliable solutions for complex problems.

contents.heading: sequential-processing-chains
contents.content: The simplest workflow pattern executes steps in a predefined order. Each step's output becomes input for the next step, creating a clear chain of operations. Use this pattern for tasks with well-defined sequences, like content generation pipelines or data transformation processes.

contents.heading: routing
contents.content: This pattern lets the model decide which path to take through a workflow based on context and intermediate results. The model acts as an intelligent router, directing the flow of execution between different branches of your workflow. Use this when handling varied inputs that require different processing approaches. In the example below, the first LLM call's results determine the second call's model size and system prompt.

contents.heading: parallel-processing
contents.content: Break down tasks into independent subtasks that execute simultaneously. This pattern uses parallel execution to improve efficiency while maintaining the benefits of structured workflows. For example, analyze multiple documents or process different aspects of a single input concurrently (like code review).

contents.heading: orchestrator-worker
contents.content: A primary model (orchestrator) coordinates the execution of specialized workers. Each worker optimizes for a specific subtask, while the orchestrator maintains overall context and ensures coherent results. This pattern excels at complex tasks requiring different types of expertise or processing.

contents.heading: evaluator-optimizer
contents.content: Add quality control to workflows with dedicated evaluation steps that assess intermediate results. Based on the evaluation, the workflow proceeds, retries with adjusted parameters, or takes corrective action. This creates robust workflows capable of self-improvement and error recovery.

metadata.title: DevTools
metadata.description: Debug and inspect AI SDK applications with DevTools

contents.content:
AI SDK DevTools is experimental and intended for local development only. Do
not use in production environments.

AI SDK DevTools gives you full visibility over your AI SDK calls with generateText, streamText, and ToolLoopAgent. It helps you debug and inspect LLM requests, responses, tool calls, and multi-step interactions through a web-based UI.
DevTools is composed of two parts:
Middleware: Captures runs and steps from your AI SDK calls
Viewer: A web UI to inspect the captured data

metadata.title: Embeddings
metadata.description: Learn how to embed values with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Embeddings are a way to represent words, phrases, or images as vectors in a high-dimensional space.
In this space, similar words are close to each other, and the distance between words can be used to measure their similarity.

contents.heading: embedding-a-single-value
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embed function to embed single values, which is useful for tasks such as finding similar words
or phrases or clustering text.
You can use it with embeddings models, e.g. openai.embeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.embeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
When loading data, e.g. when preparing a data store for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG),
it is often useful to embed many values at once (batch embedding).

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embedMany function for this purpose.
Similar to embed, you can use it with embeddings models,
e.g. openai.embeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.embeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-similarity
contents.content:
After embedding values, you can calculate the similarity between them using the cosineSimilarity function.
This is useful to e.g. find similar words or phrases in a dataset.
You can also rank and filter related items based on their similarity.

contents.heading: token-usage
contents.content:
Many providers charge based on the number of tokens used to generate embeddings.
Both embed and embedMany provide token usage information in the usage property of the result object:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Embedding model settings can be configured using providerOptions for provider-specific parameters:

contents.heading: parallel-requests
contents.content: The embedMany function now supports parallel processing with configurable maxParallelCalls to optimize performance:

contents.heading: retries
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional maxRetries parameter of type number
that you can use to set the maximum number of retries for the embedding process.
It defaults to 2 retries (3 attempts in total). You can set it to 0 to disable retries.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the embedding process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the embedding request.

contents.content: Both embed and embedMany return response information that includes the raw provider response:

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.description: Learn how to handle errors in the AI SDK Core

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: Regular errors are thrown and can be handled using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: See Error Types for more information on the different types of errors that may be thrown.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-simple-streams
contents.content:
When errors occur during streams that do not support error chunks,
the error is thrown as a regular error.
You can handle these errors using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-streaming-with-error-support
contents.content:
Full streams support error parts.
You can handle those parts similar to other parts.
It is recommended to also add a try-catch block for errors that
happen outside of the streaming.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: When streams are aborted (e.g., via chat stop button), you may want to perform cleanup operations like updating stored messages in your UI. Use the onAbort callback to handle these cases.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback is called when a stream is aborted via AbortSignal, but onFinish is not called. This ensures you can still update your UI state appropriately.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback receives:

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: steps: An array of all completed steps before the abort

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: You can also handle abort events directly in the stream:

headings.content: Handling streaming errors (streaming with error support)

metadata.title: Event Callbacks
metadata.description: Subscribe to lifecycle events in generateText and streamText calls

contents.content: The AI SDK provides per-call event callbacks that you can pass to generateText and streamText to observe lifecycle events. This is useful for building observability tools, logging systems, analytics, and debugging utilities.

contents.heading: basic-usage
contents.content: Pass callbacks directly to generateText or streamText:

contents.heading: experimental_onstart
contents.content: Called when the generation operation begins, before any LLM calls are made.

contents.heading: experimental_onstepstart
contents.content: Called before each step (LLM call) begins. Useful for tracking multi-step generations.

contents.heading: experimental_ontoolcallstart
contents.content: Called before a tool's execute function runs.

contents.heading: experimental_ontoolcallfinish
contents.content: Called after a tool's execute function completes or errors. Uses a discriminated union on the success field.

contents.heading: onstepfinish
contents.content: Called after each step (LLM call) completes. Provides the full StepResult.

contents.heading: onfinish
contents.content: Called when the entire generation completes (all steps finished). Includes aggregated data.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Errors thrown inside callbacks are caught and do not break the generation flow. This ensures that monitoring code cannot disrupt your application:

metadata.title: Generating Structured Data
metadata.description: Learn how to generate structured data with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
While text generation can be useful, your use case will likely call for generating structured data.
For example, you might want to extract information from text, classify data, or generate synthetic data.

Many language models are capable of generating structured data, often defined as using "JSON modes" or "tools".
However, you need to manually provide schemas and then validate the generated data as LLMs can produce incorrect or incomplete structured data.

The AI SDK standardises structured object generation across model providers
using the output property on generateText
and streamText.
You can use Zod schemas, Valibot, or JSON schemas to specify the shape of the data that you want,
and the AI model will generate data that conforms to that structure.

Structured output generation is part of the generateText and streamText
flow. This means you can combine it with tool calling in the same request.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Use generateText with Output.object() to generate structured data from a prompt.
The schema is also used to validate the generated data, ensuring type safety and correctness.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Structured output generation counts as a step in the AI SDK's multi-turn
execution model (where each model call or tool execution is one step). When
combining with tools, account for this in your stopWhen configuration.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the response property:

contents.heading: stream-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Given the added complexity of returning structured data, model response time can be unacceptable for your interactive use case.
With streamText and output, you can stream the model's structured response as it is generated.

contents.heading: stream-structured-outputs
contents.content: You can consume the structured output on the client with the useObject hook.

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: streamText starts streaming immediately. When errors occur during streaming, they become part of the stream rather than thrown exceptions (to prevent stream crashes).

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: To handle errors, provide an onError callback:

contents.heading: error-handling-in-streams
contents.content: For non-streaming error handling with generateText, see the Error Handling section below.

contents.heading: output-types
contents.content: The AI SDK supports multiple ways of specifying the expected structure of generated data via the Output object. You can select from various strategies for structured/text generation and validation.

contents.heading: outputtext
contents.content: Use Output.text() to generate plain text from a model. This option doesn't enforce any schema on the result: you simply receive the model's text as a string. This is the default behavior when no output is specified.

contents.heading: outputobject
contents.content: Use Output.object({ schema }) to generate a structured object based on a schema (for example, a Zod schema). The output is type-validated to ensure the returned result matches the schema.

contents.heading: outputobject
contents.content:
Partial outputs streamed via streamText cannot be validated against your
provided schema, as incomplete data may not yet conform to the expected
structure.

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content: Use Output.array({ element }) to specify that you expect an array of typed objects from the model, where each element should conform to a schema (defined in the element property).

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content: When streaming arrays with streamText, you can use elementStream to receive each completed element as it is generated:

contents.heading: outputarray
contents.content:
Each element emitted by elementStream is complete and validated against your
element schema. This differs from partialOutputStream, which streams the
entire partial array including incomplete elements.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: Use Output.choice({ options }) when you expect the model to choose from a specific set of string options, such as for classification or fixed-enum answers.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: You can provide any set of string options, and the output will always be a single string value that matches one of the specified options. The AI SDK validates that the result matches one of your options, and will throw if the model returns something invalid.

contents.heading: outputchoice
contents.content: This is especially useful for making classification-style generations or forcing valid values for API compatibility.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: Use Output.json() when you want to generate and parse unstructured JSON values from the model, without enforcing a specific schema. This is useful if you want to capture arbitrary objects, flexible structures, or when you want to rely on the model's natural output rather than rigid validation.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: With Output.json, the AI SDK only checks that the response is valid JSON; it doesn't validate the structure or types of the values. If you need schema validation, use the .object or .array outputs instead.

contents.heading: outputjson
contents.content: For more advanced validation or different structures, see the Output API reference.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs-with-tools
contents.content: One of the key advantages of using structured output with generateText and streamText is the ability to combine it with tool calling.

contents.heading: generating-structured-outputs-with-tools
contents.content:
When using tools with structured output, remember that generating the
structured output counts as a step. Configure stopWhen to allow enough steps
for both tool execution and output generation.

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: You can add .describe("...") to individual schema properties to give the model hints about what each property is for. This helps improve the quality and accuracy of generated structured data:

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Property descriptions are particularly useful for:

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Clarifying ambiguous property names

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Specifying expected formats or conventions

contents.heading: property-descriptions
contents.content: Providing context for complex nested structures

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: You can optionally specify a name and description for the output. These are used by some providers for additional LLM guidance, e.g. via tool or schema name.

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: This works with all output types that support structured generation:

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.object({ name, description, schema })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.array({ name, description, element })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.choice({ name, description, options })

contents.heading: output-name-and-description
contents.content: Output.json({ name, description })

contents.heading: accessing-reasoning
contents.content: You can access the reasoning used by the language model to generate the object via the reasoning property on the result. This property contains a string with the model's thought process, if available.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: generateText can report structured output failures in two ways:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
If the model response cannot be parsed or validated against the schema,
generateText rejects with an
AI_NoObjectGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
If generateText returns a result without an output, accessing result.output
throws an
AI_NoOutputGeneratedError.
This can happen when the final step does not finish with a stop reason, for
example when it finishes with tool-calls.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
The output property is a getter, so destructuring it also triggers this
access.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
NoObjectGeneratedError preserves the following information to help you log
the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: text: The text that was generated by the model. This can be the raw text or the tool call text, depending on the object generation mode.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: response: Metadata about the language model response, including response id, timestamp, and model.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: usage: Request token usage.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error (e.g. a JSON parsing error). You can use this for more detailed error handling.

contents.heading: more-examples
contents.content: You can see structured output generation in action using various frameworks in the following examples:

metadata.title: Generating Text
metadata.description: Learn how to generate text with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate text in response to a prompt, which can contain instructions and information to process.
For example, you can ask a model to come up with a recipe, draft an email, or summarize a document.
The AI SDK Core provides two functions to generate text and stream it from LLMs:
generateText: Generates text for a given prompt and model.
streamText: Streams text from a given prompt and model.
Advanced LLM features such as tool calling and structured data generation are built on top of text generation.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can generate text using the generateText function. This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can use more advanced prompts to generate text with more complex instructions and content:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: The result object of generateText contains several promises that resolve when all required data is available:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.reasoning: The full reasoning that the model has generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.reasoningText: The reasoning text of the model (only available for some models).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.files: The files that were generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in the last step (only available for some models).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that were made in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The results of the tool calls from the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.rawFinishReason: The raw reason why the generation finished (from the provider).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.usage: The usage of the model during the final step of text generation.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.totalUsage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.request: Additional request information.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.response: Additional response information, including response messages and body.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.providerMetadata: Additional provider-specific metadata.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.output: The generated structured output using the output specification.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the response property:

contents.heading: onfinish-callback
contents.content:
When using generateText, you can provide an onFinish callback that is triggered after the last step is finished (
API Reference
).
It contains the text, usage information, finish reason, messages, steps, total usage, and more:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content:
Experimental callbacks are subject to breaking changes in incremental package
releases.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content:
generateText provides several experimental lifecycle callbacks that let you hook into different phases of the generation process.
These are useful for logging, observability, debugging, and custom telemetry.
Errors thrown inside these callbacks are silently caught and do not break the generation flow.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: The available lifecycle callbacks are:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: experimental_onStart: Called once when the generateText operation begins, before any LLM calls. Receives model info, prompt, settings, and telemetry metadata.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: experimental_onStepStart: Called before each step (LLM call). Receives the step number, model, prompt messages being sent, tools, and prior steps.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: experimental_onToolCallStart: Called right before a tool's execute function runs. Receives the tool name, call ID, and input.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: experimental_onToolCallFinish: Called right after a tool's execute function completes or errors. Receives the tool name, call ID, input, output (or undefined on error), error (or undefined on success), and durationMs.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental
contents.content: onStepFinish: Called after each step finishes. Now also includes stepNumber (zero-based index of the completed step).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: Depending on your model and prompt, it can take a large language model (LLM) up to a minute to finish generating its response. This delay can be unacceptable for interactive use cases such as chatbots or real-time applications, where users expect immediate responses.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: AI SDK Core provides the streamText function which simplifies streaming text from LLMs:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.textStream is both a ReadableStream and an AsyncIterable.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming and suppresses errors to prevent
server crashes. Use the onError callback to log errors.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
You can use streamText on its own or in combination with AI SDK
UI and AI SDK
RSC.
The result object contains several helper functions to make the integration into AI SDK UI easier:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toUIMessageStreamResponse(): Creates a UI Message stream HTTP response (with tool calls etc.) that can be used in a Next.js App Router API route.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse(): Writes UI Message stream delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toTextStreamResponse(): Creates a simple text stream HTTP response.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.pipeTextStreamToResponse(): Writes text delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText is using backpressure and only generates tokens as they are
requested. You need to consume the stream in order for it to finish.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: It also provides several promises that resolve when the stream is finished:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.reasoning: The full reasoning that the model has generated.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.reasoningText: The reasoning text of the model (only available for some models).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.files: Files that have been generated by the model in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in the last step (only available for some models).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that have been executed in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The tool results that have been generated in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.rawFinishReason: The raw reason why the generation finished (from the provider).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.usage: The usage of the model during the final step of text generation.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.totalUsage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.request: Additional request information from the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.response: Additional response information from the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.providerMetadata: Additional provider-specific metadata from the last step.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming to enable sending data without waiting for the model.
Errors become part of the stream and are not thrown to prevent e.g. servers from crashing.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content: To log errors, you can provide an onError callback that is triggered when an error occurs.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: When using streamText, you can provide an onChunk callback that is triggered for each chunk of the stream.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: It receives the following chunk types:

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: text

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: reasoning

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: source

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-call

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-input-start

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-input-delta

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-result

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: raw

contents.heading: onfinish-callback-1
contents.content:
When using streamText, you can provide an onFinish callback that is triggered when the stream is finished (
API Reference
).
It contains the text, usage information, finish reason, messages, steps, total usage, and more:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content:
Experimental callbacks are subject to breaking changes in incremental package
releases.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content:
streamText provides several experimental lifecycle callbacks that let you hook into different phases of the streaming process.
These are useful for logging, observability, debugging, and custom telemetry.
Errors thrown inside these callbacks are silently caught and do not break the streaming flow.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: The available lifecycle callbacks are:

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: experimental_onStart: Called once when the streamText operation begins, before any LLM calls. Receives model info, prompt, settings, and telemetry metadata.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: experimental_onStepStart: Called before each step (LLM call). Receives the step number, model, messages being sent, tools, and prior steps.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: experimental_onToolCallStart: Called right before a tool's execute function runs. Receives the tool call object, messages, and context.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: experimental_onToolCallFinish: Called right after a tool's execute function completes or errors. Receives the tool call object, durationMs, and a discriminated union with success/output or success/error.

contents.heading: lifecycle-callbacks-experimental-1
contents.content: onStepFinish: Called after each step finishes. Receives the finish reason, usage, and other step details.

contents.heading: fullstream-property
contents.content:
You can read a stream with all events using the fullStream property.
This can be useful if you want to implement your own UI or handle the stream in a different way.
Here is an example of how to use the fullStream property:

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
You can use the experimental_transform option to transform the stream.
This is useful for e.g. filtering, changing, or smoothing the text stream.

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
The transformations are applied before the callbacks are invoked and the promises are resolved.
If you e.g. have a transformation that changes all text to uppercase, the onFinish callback will receive the transformed text.

contents.heading: smoothing-streams
contents.content:
The AI SDK Core provides a smoothStream function that
can be used to smooth out text and reasoning streaming.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also implement your own custom transformations.
The transformation function receives the tools that are available to the model,
and returns a function that is used to transform the stream.
Tools can either be generic or limited to the tools that you are using.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
Here is an example of how to implement a custom transformation that converts
all text to uppercase:

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also stop the stream using the stopStream function.
This is e.g. useful if you want to stop the stream when model guardrails are violated, e.g. by generating inappropriate content.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
When you invoke stopStream, it is important to simulate the finish-step and finish events to guarantee that a well-formed stream is returned
and all callbacks are invoked.

contents.heading: multiple-transformations
contents.content: You can also provide multiple transformations. They are applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Some providers such as Perplexity and
Google Generative AI include sources in the response.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Currently sources are limited to web pages that ground the response.
You can access them using the sources property of the result.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: Each url source contains the following properties:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: id: The ID of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: url: The URL of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: title: The optional title of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: providerMetadata: Provider metadata for the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use generateText, you can access the sources using the sources property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use streamText, you can access the sources using the fullStream property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: The sources are also available in the result.sources promise.

contents.heading: examples
contents.content: You can see generateText and streamText in action using various frameworks in the following examples:

metadata.title: Image Generation
metadata.description: Learn how to generate images with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the generateImage
function to generate images based on a given prompt using an image model.
You can access the image data using the base64 or uint8Array properties:

contents.heading: size-and-aspect-ratio
contents.content: Depending on the model, you can either specify the size or the aspect ratio.

contents.heading: size
contents.content:
The size is specified as a string in the format {width}x{height}.
Models only support a few sizes, and the supported sizes are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio
contents.content:
The aspect ratio is specified as a string in the format {width}:{height}.
Models only support a few aspect ratios, and the supported aspect ratios are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: generateImage also supports generating multiple images at once:

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content:
generateImage will automatically call the model as often as needed (in
parallel) to generate the requested number of images.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: Each image model has an internal limit on how many images it can generate in a single API call. The AI SDK manages this automatically by batching requests appropriately when you request multiple images using the n parameter. By default, the SDK uses provider-documented limits (for example, DALL-E 3 can only generate 1 image per call, while DALL-E 2 supports up to 10).

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: If needed, you can override this behavior using the maxImagesPerCall setting when generating your image. This is particularly useful when working with new or custom models where the default batch size might not be optimal:

contents.heading: providing-a-seed
contents.content:
You can provide a seed to the generateImage function to control the output of the image generation process.
If supported by the model, the same seed will always produce the same image.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content:
Image models often have provider- or even model-specific settings.
You can pass such settings to the generateImage function
using the providerOptions parameter. The options for the provider
(openai in the example below) become request body properties.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the image generation process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the image generation request.

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content: If the model returns warnings, e.g. for unsupported parameters, they will be available in the warnings property of the response.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-meta-data
contents.content: Some providers expose additional meta data for the result overall or per image.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-meta-data
contents.content: The outer key of the returned providerMetadata is the provider name. The inner values are the metadata. An images key is always present in the metadata and is an array with the same length as the top level images key.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
When generateImage cannot generate a valid image, it throws a AI_NoImageGeneratedError.
Unclassified empty image responses are retried according to maxRetries before this error is thrown.
Providers can classify terminal empty responses, such as moderation blocks, with isRetryable: false; these responses are not retried.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate an image. It can arise due to the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: responses: Metadata about the image model responses, including timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error handling

contents.heading: image-middleware
contents.content:
You can enhance image models, e.g. to set default values or implement logging, using
wrapImageModel and ImageModelV3Middleware.

contents.heading: image-middleware
contents.content: Here is an example that sets a default size when none is provided:

contents.heading: generating-images-with-language-models
contents.content:
Some language models such as Google gemini-2.5-flash-image support multi-modal outputs including images.
With such models, you can access the generated images using the files property of the response.

metadata.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
metadata.description: Learn how to connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and use their tools with AI SDK Core.

contents.content:
The AI SDK supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to access their tools, resources, and prompts.
This enables your AI applications to discover and use capabilities across various services through a standardized interface.

If you're using OpenAI's Responses API, you can also use the built-in
openai.tools.mcp tool, which provides direct MCP server integration without
needing to convert tools. See the OpenAI provider
documentation for details.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: We recommend using HTTP transport (like StreamableHTTPClientTransport) for production deployments. The stdio transport should only be used for connecting to local servers as it cannot be deployed to production environments.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: Create an MCP client using one of the following transport options:

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: HTTP transport (Recommended): Either configure HTTP directly via the client using transport: { type: 'http', ... }, or use MCP's official TypeScript SDK StreamableHTTPClientTransport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: SSE (Server-Sent Events): An alternative HTTP-based transport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: stdio: For local development only. Uses standard input/output streams for local MCP servers

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: For production deployments, we recommend using the HTTP transport. You can configure it directly on the client:

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: Alternatively, you can use StreamableHTTPClientTransport from MCP's official TypeScript SDK:

contents.heading: sse-transport
contents.content: SSE provides an alternative HTTP-based transport option. Configure it with a type and url property. You can also provide an authProvider for OAuth:

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The stdio transport should only be used for local servers.

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The Stdio transport can be imported from either the MCP SDK or the AI SDK:

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content: You can also bring your own transport by implementing the MCPTransport interface for specific requirements not covered by the standard transports.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
The client returned by the createMCPClient function is a
lightweight client intended for use in tool conversion. It currently does not
support all features of the full MCP client, such as: session
management, resumable streams, and receiving notifications.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
Authorization via OAuth is supported when using the AI SDK MCP HTTP or SSE
transports by providing an authProvider.

contents.heading: oauth-authorization-server-validation
contents.content:
When using MCP OAuth in server-side applications, the MCP server can advertise
the OAuth authorization server to use. If you connect to MCP servers outside
your control, implement validateAuthorizationServerURL on your
authProvider to allow only the authorization server origins you trust:

contents.heading: oauth-authorization-server-validation
contents.content:
This hook is called before the SDK fetches authorization server metadata, so a
rejected URL is not requested. It is optional and does not change existing OAuth
flows unless you implement it.

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
When completing an OAuth authorization callback, pass the callback's iss
parameter to auth as callbackIssuer:

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
When iss is present, it must exactly match the discovered authorization
server issuer. The authorization code is not exchanged when it does not match.

contents.heading: oauth-callback-issuer-validation
contents.content:
Dynamic client registration requests include an OAuth application_type. The
client infers native for loopback, localhost, and custom-scheme redirects,
and web for remote HTTP(S) redirects. You can override this by setting
application_type in the provider's clientMetadata.

contents.heading: dynamic-client-credential-recovery
contents.content:
To let the SDK replace invalid credentials created through dynamic client
registration, implement isClientInformationDynamicallyRegistered on the
OAuth client provider. Return true only when the current client information
came from a dynamic registration response. Persist this provenance alongside
the credentials when the provider is recreated between requests.

contents.heading: dynamic-client-credential-recovery
contents.content:
When this method is omitted or returns false, client information is treated
as pre-registered and is preserved after invalid_client and
unauthorized_client errors. The SDK does not infer provenance from fields such
as redirect_uris, because pre-registered clients can contain the same
metadata as dynamically registered clients.

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
MCP tool calls can fail for transient transport reasons, such as rate limits,
temporary overload, or gateway timeouts. You can opt into automatic retries for
tools/call requests by passing maxRetries when creating the client:

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
Retries are disabled by default. Built-in retry matching is intended for
transient HTTP and network failures only. JSON-RPC application errors, such as
invalid tool arguments, are surfaced immediately without retrying. Successful
MCP tool responses with isError: true are also returned to the model without
retrying.

contents.heading: retrying-transient-tool-failures
contents.content:
Only enable retries for MCP tools where retrying is safe. Retrying
non-idempotent tools, such as tools that send emails or create records, can
duplicate side effects.

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: After initialization, you should close the MCP client based on your usage pattern:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For short-lived usage (e.g., single requests), close the client when the response is finished

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For long-running clients (e.g., command line apps), keep the client open but ensure it's closed when the application terminates

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When streaming responses, you can close the client when the LLM response has finished. For example, when using streamText, you should use the onFinish callback:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When generating responses without streaming, you can use try/finally or cleanup functions in your framework:

contents.heading: using-mcp-tools
contents.content: The client's tools method acts as an adapter between MCP tools and AI SDK tools. It supports two approaches for working with tool schemas:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: With schema discovery, all tools offered by the server are automatically listed, and input parameter types are inferred based on the schemas provided by the server:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: This approach is simpler to implement and automatically stays in sync with server changes. However, you won't have TypeScript type safety during development, and all tools from the server will be loaded

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
MCP servers can describe tool behavior with annotations such as
readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint. The
MCP client exposes these annotations on each tool's metadata.annotations and
on the resulting tool call's toolMetadata.annotations.

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
Annotations are untrusted, server-provided hints. The MCP client does not turn
them into an approval policy automatically. Applications should combine them
with deterministic controls such as tool allowlists, scoped credentials, and
their own needsApproval
policy.

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
The following conservative policy allows tools to run automatically only when
the server explicitly marks them as read-only. Tools with readOnlyHint: false
or no readOnlyHint require user approval:

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
See the
local tool annotations example
for a complete annotated MCP server and application-layer approval
configuration. Start the server and client in separate terminals:

contents.heading: tool-annotations-and-approval
contents.content:
Ask the client to read, delete, or create a note. The read-only tool executes
immediately. The destructive and unannotated tools prompt for approval; after
you enter y or n, the client sends the decision back and prints the model's
response.

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: For better type safety and control, you can define the tools and their input schemas explicitly in your client code:

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: This approach provides full TypeScript type safety and IDE autocompletion, letting you catch parameter mismatches during development. When you define schemas, the client only pulls the explicitly defined tools, keeping your application focused on the tools it needs

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: When MCP servers return structuredContent (per the MCP specification), you can define an outputSchema to get typed tool results:

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: When outputSchema is provided:

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs
contents.content: The client extracts structuredContent from the tool result

contents.heading: typed-tool-outputs

Without outputSchema, the tool returns the raw CallToolResult object
containing content and optional isError fields.

contents.content: According to the MCP specification, resources are application-driven data sources that provide context to the model. Unlike tools (which are model-controlled), your application decides when to fetch and pass resources as context.

contents.content:
MCP servers can provide autocompletion suggestions for prompt arguments and
resource template variables when they advertise the completions capability.
Use complete to ask the server for suggestions based on the current partial
argument value:

For resource templates or prompts with multiple arguments, pass already resolved

contents.content: Elicitation is a mechanism where MCP servers can request additional information from the client during tool execution. For example, a server might need user input to complete a registration form or confirmation for a sensitive operation.

contents.heading: handling-elicitation-requests

It is up to the client application to handle elicitation requests properly.

metadata.title: Language Model Middleware
metadata.description: Learn how to use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models

contents.content:
Language model middleware is a way to enhance the behavior of language models
by intercepting and modifying the calls to the language model.

It can be used to add features like guardrails, RAG, caching, and logging
in a language model agnostic way. Such middleware can be developed and
distributed independently from the language models that they are applied to.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
You can use language model middleware with the wrapLanguageModel function.
It takes a language model and a language model middleware and returns a new
language model that incorporates the middleware.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content: The wrapped language model can be used just like any other language model, e.g. in streamText:

contents.heading: multiple-middlewares
contents.content:
You can provide multiple middlewares to the wrapLanguageModel function.
The middlewares will be applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK comes with several built-in middlewares that you can use to configure language models:

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: extractReasoningMiddleware: Extracts reasoning information from the generated text and exposes it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: extractJsonMiddleware: Extracts JSON from text content by stripping markdown code fences. Useful when using Output.object() with models that wrap JSON responses in code blocks.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: simulateStreamingMiddleware: Simulates streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: defaultSettingsMiddleware: Applies default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: addToolInputExamplesMiddleware: Adds tool input examples to tool descriptions for providers that don't natively support the inputExamples property.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
Some providers and models expose reasoning information in the generated text using special tags,
e.g. <think> and </think>.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: The extractReasoningMiddleware function can be used to extract this reasoning information and expose it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: You can then use that enhanced model in functions like generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
The extractReasoningMiddleware function also includes a startWithReasoning option.
When set to true, the reasoning tag will be prepended to the generated text.
This is useful for models that do not include the reasoning tag at the beginning of the response.
For more details, see the DeepSeek R1 guide.

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: Some models wrap JSON responses in markdown code fences (e.g., ```json ... ```) even when you request structured output.

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: The extractJsonMiddleware function strips these code fences from the response, making it compatible with Output.object().

contents.heading: extract-json
contents.content: You can also provide a custom transform function for models that use different formatting:

contents.heading: simulate-streaming
contents.content:
The simulateStreamingMiddleware function can be used to simulate streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.
This is useful when you want to maintain a consistent streaming interface even when using models that only provide complete responses.

contents.heading: default-settings
contents.content: The defaultSettingsMiddleware function can be used to apply default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content:
The addToolInputExamplesMiddleware function adds tool input examples to tool descriptions.
This is useful for providers that don't natively support the inputExamples property on tools.
The middleware serializes the examples into the tool's description text so models can still benefit from seeing example inputs.

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content: When you define a tool with inputExamples, the middleware will append them to the tool's description:

contents.heading: add-tool-input-examples
contents.content: The tool description will be transformed to:

contents.heading: options
contents.content: prefix (optional): A prefix text to prepend before the examples. Default: 'Input Examples:'.

contents.heading: options
contents.content: format (optional): A custom formatter function for each example. Receives the example object and its index. Default: JSON.stringify(example.input).

contents.heading: options
contents.content: remove (optional): Whether to remove the inputExamples property from the tool after adding them to the description. Default: true.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK provides a Language Model Middleware specification. Community members can develop middleware that adheres to this specification, making it compatible with the AI SDK ecosystem.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: Here are some community middlewares that you can explore:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The Custom tool call parser middleware extends tool call capabilities to models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style tools parameter. This includes many self-hosted and third-party models that lack native function calling features.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content:
Using this middleware on models that support native function calls may result
in unintended performance degradation, so check whether your model supports
native function calls before deciding to use it.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: This middleware enables function calling capabilities by converting function schemas into prompt instructions and parsing the model's responses into structured function calls. It works by transforming the JSON function definitions into natural language instructions the model can understand, then analyzing the generated text to extract function call attempts. This approach allows developers to use the same function calling API across different model providers, even with models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style function calling format, providing a consistent function calling experience regardless of the underlying model implementation.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The @ai-sdk-tool/parser package offers three middleware variants:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: createToolMiddleware: A flexible function for creating custom tool call middleware tailored to specific models

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: hermesToolMiddleware: Ready-to-use middleware for Hermes & Qwen format function calls

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: gemmaToolMiddleware: Pre-configured middleware for Gemma 3 model series function call format

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Here's how you can enable function calls with Gemma models that don't support them natively:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Find more examples at this link.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
Implementing language model middleware is advanced functionality and requires
a solid understanding of the language model
specification.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: You can implement any of the following three function to modify the behavior of the language model:

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: transformParams: Transforms the parameters before they are passed to the language model, for both doGenerate and doStream.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapGenerate: Wraps the doGenerate method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapStream: Wraps the doStream method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
Every LanguageModelV3Middleware object must set
specificationVersion: 'v3'.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: Here are some examples of how to implement language model middleware:

contents.heading: examples
contents.content:
These examples are not meant to be used in production. They are just to show
how you can use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models.

contents.heading: logging
contents.content: This example shows how to log the parameters and generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: caching
contents.content: This example shows how to build a simple cache for the generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content: This example shows how to use RAG as middleware.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content:
Helper functions like getLastUserMessageText and findSources are not part
of the AI SDK. They are just used in this example to illustrate the concept of
RAG.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
Guard rails are a way to ensure that the generated text of a language model call
is safe and appropriate. This example shows how to use guardrails as middleware.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
The streaming example buffers each text block until text-end so matches
split across text-delta chunks cannot leak through. This delays output and
uses memory proportional to the text block size. Do not redact each delta
independently. An incremental implementation must retain every possible
incomplete match, and a fixed-size buffer alone is not safe for unbounded
variable-length patterns.

contents.heading: configuring-per-request-custom-metadata
contents.content: To send and access custom metadata in Middleware, you can use providerOptions. This is useful when building logging middleware where you want to pass additional context like user IDs, timestamps, or other contextual data that can help with tracking and debugging.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: An overview of AI SDK Core.

contents.content:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced programs that can understand, create, and engage with human language on a large scale.
They are trained on vast amounts of written material to recognize patterns in language and predict what might come next in a given piece of text.

AI SDK Core simplifies working with LLMs by offering a standardized way of integrating them into your app - so you can focus on building great AI applications for your users, not waste time on technical details.
For example, here’s how you can generate text with various models using the AI SDK:

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
AI SDK Core has various functions designed for text generation, structured data generation, and tool usage.
These functions take a standardized approach to setting up prompts and settings, making it easier to work with different models.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
generateText: Generates text and tool calls.
This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases such as automation tasks where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
streamText: Stream text and tool calls.
You can use the streamText function for interactive use cases such as chat bots and content streaming.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content: Both generateText and streamText support structured output via the output property (e.g. Output.object(), Output.array()), allowing you to generate typed, schema-validated data for information extraction, synthetic data generation, classification tasks, and streaming generated UIs.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Please check out the AI SDK Core API Reference for more details on each function.

metadata.title: Prompt Engineering
metadata.description: Learn how to develop prompts with AI SDK Core.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When you create prompts that include tools, getting good results can be tricky as the number and complexity of your tools increases.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Here are a few tips to help you get the best results:

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use a model that is strong at tool calling, such as gpt-5 or gpt-4.1. Weaker models will often struggle to call tools effectively and flawlessly.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the number of tools low, e.g. to 5 or less.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the complexity of the tool parameters low. Complex Zod schemas with many nested and optional elements, unions, etc. can be challenging for the model to work with.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use semantically meaningful names for your tools, parameters, parameter properties, etc. The more information you pass to the model, the better it can understand what you want.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Add .describe("...") to your Zod schema properties to give the model hints about what a particular property is for.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When the output of a tool might be unclear to the model and there are dependencies between tools, use the description field of a tool to provide information about the output of the tool execution.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: You can include example input/outputs of tool calls in your prompt to help the model understand how to use the tools. Keep in mind that the tools work with JSON objects, so the examples should use JSON.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: In general, the goal should be to give the model all information it needs in a clear way.

contents.heading: tool--structured-data-schemas
contents.content: The mapping from Zod schemas to LLM inputs (typically JSON schema) is not always straightforward, since the mapping is not one-to-one.

contents.heading: zod-dates
contents.content:
Zod expects JavaScript Date objects, but models return dates as strings.
You can specify and validate the date format using z.string().datetime() or z.string().date(),
and then use a Zod transformer to convert the string to a Date object.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: When working with tools that have optional parameters, you may encounter compatibility issues with certain providers that use strict schema validation.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content:
This is particularly relevant for OpenAI models with structured outputs
(strict mode).

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: For maximum compatibility, optional parameters should use .nullable() instead of .optional():

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: For tool calls and object generation, it's recommended to use temperature: 0 to ensure deterministic and consistent results:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Lower temperature values reduce randomness in model outputs, which is particularly important when the model needs to:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Generate structured data with specific formats

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Make precise tool calls with correct parameters

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Follow strict schemas consistently

contents.heading: inspecting-warnings
contents.content:
Not all providers support all AI SDK features.
Providers either throw exceptions or return warnings when they do not support a feature.
To check if your prompt, tools, and settings are handled correctly by the provider, you can check the call warnings:

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content:
You can inspect the raw HTTP request bodies for models that expose them, e.g. OpenAI.
This allows you to inspect the exact payload that is sent to the model provider in the provider-specific way.

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content: Request bodies are available via the request.body property of the response:

metadata.title: Provider & Model Management
metadata.description: Learn how to work with multiple providers and models

title.children: Combining Custom Providers, Provider Registry, and Middleware

contents.content:
When you work with multiple providers and models, it is often desirable to manage them in a central place
and access the models through simple string ids.

The AI SDK offers custom providers and
a provider registry for this purpose:

With custom providers, you can pre-configure model settings, provide model name aliases,
and limit the available models.
The provider registry lets you mix multiple providers and access them through simple string ids.
You can mix and match custom providers, the provider registry, and middleware in your application.

contents.content: You can create a custom provider using customProvider.

You might want to override the default model settings for a provider or provide model name aliases
with pre-configured settings.

metadata.title: Reranking
metadata.description: Learn how to rerank documents with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Reranking is a technique used to improve search relevance by reordering a set of documents based on their relevance to a query.
Unlike embedding-based similarity search, reranking models are specifically trained to understand the relationship between queries and documents,
often producing more accurate relevance scores.

contents.heading: reranking-documents
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the rerank function to rerank documents based on their relevance to a query.
You can use it with reranking models, e.g. cohere.reranking('rerank-v3.5') or bedrock.reranking('cohere.rerank-v3-5:0').

contents.heading: working-with-object-documents
contents.content: Reranking also supports structured documents (JSON objects), making it ideal for searching through databases, emails, or other structured content:

contents.heading: understanding-the-results
contents.content: The rerank function returns a comprehensive result object:

contents.heading: understanding-the-results
contents.content: Each item in the ranking array contains:

contents.heading: understanding-the-results
contents.content: originalIndex: Position in the original documents array

contents.heading: understanding-the-results
contents.content: score: Relevance score (typically 0-1, where higher is more relevant)

contents.heading: understanding-the-results
contents.content: document: The original document

contents.heading: top-n-results
contents.content: Use topN to limit the number of results returned. This is useful for retrieving only the most relevant documents:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Reranking model settings can be configured using providerOptions for provider-specific parameters:

contents.heading: retries
contents.content:
The rerank function accepts an optional maxRetries parameter of type number
that you can use to set the maximum number of retries for the reranking process.
It defaults to 2 retries (3 attempts in total). You can set it to 0 to disable retries.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
The rerank function accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the reranking process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
The rerank function accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the reranking request.

metadata.title: Settings
metadata.description: Learn how to configure the AI SDK.

title.children: Example: Combined total and step timeout
Example: Per-chunk timeout for streaming (streamText only)

contents.content: Large language models (LLMs) typically provide settings to augment their output.
All AI SDK functions support the following common settings in addition to the model, the prompt, and additional provider-specific settings:

Some providers do not support all common settings. If you use a setting with a
provider that does not support it, a warning will be generated. You can check
the warnings property in the result object to see if any warnings were
generated.

contents.heading: maxoutputtokens
contents.content: Maximum number of tokens to generate.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content: Temperature setting.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means almost deterministic results, and higher values mean more randomness.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content: It is recommended to set either temperature or topP, but not both.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content: Nucleus sampling.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, nucleus sampling is a number between 0 and 1.
E.g. 0.1 would mean that only tokens with the top 10% probability mass are considered.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content: It is recommended to set either temperature or topP, but not both.

contents.heading: topk
contents.content: Only sample from the top K options for each subsequent token.

contents.heading: topk
contents.content:
Used to remove "long tail" low probability responses.
Recommended for advanced use cases only. You usually only need to use temperature.

contents.heading: presencepenalty
contents.content: The presence penalty affects the likelihood of the model to repeat information that is already in the prompt.

contents.heading: presencepenalty
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means no penalty.

contents.heading: frequencypenalty
contents.content: The frequency penalty affects the likelihood of the model to repeatedly use the same words or phrases.

contents.heading: frequencypenalty
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means no penalty.

contents.heading: stopsequences
contents.content: The stop sequences to use for stopping the text generation.

contents.heading: stopsequences
contents.content:
If set, the model will stop generating text when one of the stop sequences is generated.
Providers may have limits on the number of stop sequences.

contents.heading: seed
contents.content:
It is the seed (integer) to use for random sampling.
If set and supported by the model, calls will generate deterministic results.

contents.heading: maxretries
contents.content: Maximum number of retries. Set to 0 to disable retries. Default: 2.

contents.heading: abortsignal
contents.content: An optional abort signal that can be used to cancel the call.

contents.heading: abortsignal
contents.content:
The abort signal can e.g. be forwarded from a user interface to cancel the call,
or to define a timeout using AbortSignal.timeout.

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: An optional timeout in milliseconds. The call will be aborted if it takes longer than the specified duration.

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: This is a convenience parameter that creates an abort signal internally. It can be used alongside abortSignal - if both are provided, the call will abort when either condition is met.

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: You can specify the timeout either as a number (milliseconds) or as an object with totalMs, stepMs, and/or chunkMs properties:

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: totalMs: The total timeout for the entire call including all steps.

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: stepMs: The timeout for each individual step (LLM call). This is useful for multi-step generations where you want to limit the time spent on each step independently.

contents.heading: timeout
contents.content: chunkMs: The timeout between stream chunks (streaming only). The call will abort if no new chunk is received within this duration. This is useful for detecting stalled streams.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content: Additional HTTP headers to be sent with the request. Only applicable for HTTP-based providers.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content:
You can use the request headers to provide additional information to the provider,
depending on what the provider supports. For example, some observability providers support
headers such as Prompt-Id.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content:
The headers setting is for request-specific headers. You can also set
headers in the provider configuration. These headers will be sent with every
request made by the provider.
