contents.content:
Prompts are instructions that you give a large language model (LLM) to tell it what to do.
It's like when you ask someone for directions; the clearer your question, the better the directions you'll get.

Many LLM providers offer complex interfaces for specifying prompts. They involve different roles and message types.
While these interfaces are powerful, they can be hard to use and understand.
In order to simplify prompting, the AI SDK supports text, message, and system prompts.

contents.heading: text-prompts
contents.content:
Text prompts are strings.
They are ideal for simple generation use cases,
e.g. repeatedly generating content for variants of the same prompt text.

contents.heading: text-prompts
contents.content:
You can set text prompts using the prompt property made available by AI SDK functions like streamText or generateText.
You can structure the text in any way and inject variables, e.g. using a template literal.

contents.heading: text-prompts
contents.content: You can also use template literals to provide dynamic data to your prompt.

contents.heading: system-prompts
contents.content:
System prompts are the initial set of instructions given to models that help guide and constrain the models' behaviors and responses.
You can set system prompts using the system property.
System prompts work with both the prompt and the messages properties.
System messages in prompt or messages are allowed by default with a warning; use the system property for system instructions, set allowSystemInMessages: true when you need to send existing message histories that contain system messages, or set allowSystemInMessages: false to reject them.

contents.heading: system-prompts
contents.content:
System messages in prompt or messages can create a prompt injection
attack risk, where users can override or set the system prompt by injecting
system messages. Ideally, provide system instructions through the system
option instead. Set allowSystemInMessages: true to suppress the warning, or
allowSystemInMessages: false to throw an error.

contents.heading: message-prompts
contents.content:
A message prompt is an array of user, assistant, and tool messages.
They are great for chat interfaces and more complex, multi-modal prompts.
You can use the messages property to set message prompts.

contents.heading: message-prompts
contents.content: Each message has a role and a content property. The content can either be text (for user and assistant messages), or an array of relevant parts (data) for that message type.

contents.heading: message-prompts
contents.content: Instead of sending a text in the content property, you can send an array of parts that includes a mix of text and other content parts.

contents.heading: message-prompts
contents.content:
Not all language models support all message and content types. For example,
some models might not be capable of handling multi-modal inputs or tool
messages. Learn more about the capabilities of select
models.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: You can pass through additional provider-specific metadata to enable provider-specific functionality at 3 levels.

contents.heading: function-call-level
contents.content: Functions like streamText or generateText accept a providerOptions property.

contents.heading: function-call-level
contents.content: Adding provider options at the function call level should be used when you do not need granular control over where the provider options are applied.

contents.heading: message-level
contents.content: For granular control over applying provider options at the message level, you can pass providerOptions to the message object:

contents.heading: message-part-level
contents.content: Certain provider-specific options require configuration at the message part level:

contents.heading: message-part-level
contents.content:
AI SDK UI hooks like useChat return
arrays of UIMessage objects, which do not support provider options. We
recommend using the
convertToModelMessages
function to convert UIMessage objects to
ModelMessage objects before
applying or appending message(s) or message parts with providerOptions.

contents.heading: text-parts
contents.content: Text content is the most common type of content. It is a string that is passed to the model.

contents.heading: text-parts
contents.content:
If you only need to send text content in a message, the content property can be a string,
but you can also use it to send multiple content parts.

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: User messages can include image parts. An image can be one of the following:

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: base64-encoded image:

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: string with base-64 encoded content

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: data URL string, e.g. data:image/png;base64,...

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: binary image:

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: ArrayBuffer

contents.content: Buffer

contents.content: http(s) URL string, e.g. https://example.com/image.png

contents.heading: image-parts
contents.content: URL object, e.g. new URL('https://example.com/image.png')

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content:
Only a few providers and models currently support file parts: Google
Generative AI, Google
Vertex AI,
OpenAI (for wav and mp3 audio with
gpt-4o-audio-preview), Anthropic,
OpenAI (for pdf).

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: User messages can include file parts. A file can be one of the following:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: base64-encoded file:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: string with base-64 encoded content

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: data URL string, e.g. data:image/png;base64,...

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: binary data:

contents.heading: file-parts

contents.content: Buffer

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: URL:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: http(s) URL string, e.g. https://example.com/some.pdf

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: URL object, e.g. new URL('https://example.com/some.pdf')

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: You need to specify the MIME type of the file you are sending.

contents.heading: custom-download-function-experimental
contents.content: You can use custom download functions to implement throttling, retries, authentication, caching, and more.

contents.heading: custom-download-function-experimental
contents.content: The default download implementation automatically downloads files in parallel when they are not supported by the model.

contents.heading: custom-download-function-experimental
contents.content: Custom download function can be passed via the experimental_download property:

contents.heading: custom-download-function-experimental
contents.content:
The experimental_download option is experimental and may change in future
releases.

contents.heading: assistant-messages
contents.content:
Assistant messages are messages that have a role of assistant.
They are typically previous responses from the assistant
and can contain text, reasoning, and tool call parts.

contents.heading: example-assistant-message-with-file-content
contents.content:
This content part is for model-generated files. Only a few models support
this, and only for file types that they can generate.

contents.heading: tool-messages
contents.content:
Tools (also known as function calling) are programs
that you can provide an LLM to extend its built-in functionality. This can be
anything from calling an external API to calling functions within your UI.
Learn more about Tools in the next section.

contents.heading: tool-messages
contents.content:
For models that support tool calls, assistant messages can contain tool call parts, and tool messages can contain tool output parts.
A single assistant message can call multiple tools, and a single tool message can contain multiple tool results.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
Tool results can be multi-part and multi-modal, e.g. a text and an image.
You can use output: { type: 'content', value: [...] } to specify multi-part tool results.

contents.heading: system-messages
contents.content:
System messages are messages that are sent to the model before the user messages to guide the assistant's behavior.
You can alternatively use the system property.

title.children: Using Provider Options with the AI Gateway

contents.content: Provider options let you pass provider-specific configuration that goes beyond the standard settings shared by all providers. They are set via the providerOptions property on functions like generateText and streamText.

Provider options are namespaced by the provider name (e.g. openai, anthropic) so you can even include options for multiple providers in the same call — only the options matching the active provider are used. See Prompts: Provider Options for details on applying options at the message and message-part level.

metadata.title: Providers and Models
metadata.description: Learn about the providers and models available in the AI SDK.

contents.content: Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic (providers) offer access to a range of large language models (LLMs) with differing strengths and capabilities through their own APIs.
Each provider typically has its own unique method for interfacing with their models, complicating the process of switching providers and increasing the risk of vendor lock-in.

To solve these challenges, AI SDK Core offers a standardized approach to interacting with LLMs through a language model specification that abstracts differences between providers. This unified interface allows you to switch between providers with ease while using the same API for all providers.
Here is an overview of the AI SDK Provider Architecture:

metadata.title: Streaming
metadata.description: Why use streaming for AI applications?

contents.content: Streaming conversational text UIs (like ChatGPT) have gained massive popularity over the past few months. This section explores the benefits and drawbacks of streaming and blocking interfaces.

Large language models (LLMs) are extremely powerful. However, when generating long outputs, they can be very slow compared to the latency you're likely used to. If you try to build a traditional blocking UI, your users might easily find themselves staring at loading spinners for 5, 10, even up to 40s waiting for the entire LLM response to be generated. This can lead to a poor user experience, especially in conversational applications like chatbots. Streaming UIs can help mitigate this issue by displaying parts of the response as they become available.

contents.heading: real-world-examples
contents.content: Here are 2 examples that illustrate how streaming UIs can improve user experiences in a real-world setting – the first uses a blocking UI, while the second uses a streaming UI.

contents.heading: streaming-ui
contents.content: As you can see, the streaming UI is able to start displaying the response much faster than the blocking UI. This is because the blocking UI has to wait for the entire response to be generated before it can display anything, while the streaming UI can display parts of the response as they become available.

contents.heading: streaming-ui
contents.content: While streaming interfaces can greatly enhance user experiences, especially with larger language models, they aren't always necessary or beneficial. If you can achieve your desired functionality using a smaller, faster model without resorting to streaming, this route can often lead to simpler and more manageable development processes.

contents.heading: streaming-ui
contents.content: However, regardless of the speed of your model, the AI SDK is designed to make implementing streaming UIs as simple as possible. In the example below, we stream text generation in under 10 lines of code using the SDK's streamText function:

contents.heading: streaming-ui
contents.content: For an introduction to streaming UIs and the AI SDK, check out our Getting Started guides.

metadata.title: Tools
metadata.description: Learn about tools with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
While large language models (LLMs) have incredible generation capabilities,
they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather).

Tools are actions that an LLM can invoke.
The results of these actions can be reported back to the LLM to be considered in the next response.

For example, when you ask an LLM for the "weather in London", and there is a weather tool available, it could call a tool
with London as the argument. The tool would then fetch the weather data and return it to the LLM. The LLM can then use this
information in its response.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content:
A tool is an object that can be called by the model to perform a specific task.
You can use tools with generateText
and streamText by passing one or more tools to the tools parameter.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content: A tool consists of three properties:

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content: description: An optional description of the tool that can influence when the tool is picked.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content: inputSchema: A Zod schema or a JSON schema that defines the input required for the tool to run. The schema is consumed by the LLM, and also used to validate the LLM tool calls.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content: execute: An optional async function that is called with the arguments from the tool call.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content:
streamUI uses UI generator tools with a generate function that can return
React components.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content:
If the LLM decides to use a tool, it will generate a tool call.
Tools with an execute function are run automatically when these calls are generated.
The output of the tool calls are returned using tool result objects.

contents.heading: what-is-a-tool
contents.content:
You can automatically pass tool results back to the LLM
using multi-step calls with streamText and generateText.

contents.heading: types-of-tools
contents.content: The AI SDK supports three types of tools, each with different trade-offs:

contents.heading: custom-tools
contents.content: Custom tools are tools you define entirely yourself, including the description, input schema, and execute function. They are provider-agnostic and give you full control.

contents.heading: custom-tools
contents.content: When to use: When you need full control, want provider portability, or are implementing application-specific functionality.

contents.heading: provider-defined-tools
contents.content: Provider-defined tools are tools where the provider specifies the tool's inputSchema and description, but you provide the execute function. These are sometimes called "client tools" because execution happens on your side.

contents.heading: provider-defined-tools
contents.content: Examples include Anthropic's bash and text_editor tools. The model has been specifically trained to use these tools effectively, which can result in better performance for supported tasks.

contents.heading: provider-defined-tools
contents.content: When to use: When the provider offers a tool the model is trained to use well, and you want better performance for that specific task.

contents.heading: provider-executed-tools
contents.content: Provider-executed tools are tools that run entirely on the provider's servers. You configure them, but the provider handles execution. These are sometimes called "server-side tools".

contents.heading: provider-executed-tools
contents.content: Examples include OpenAI's web search and Anthropic's code execution. These provide out-of-the-box functionality without requiring you to set up infrastructure.

contents.heading: provider-executed-tools
contents.content: When to use: When you want powerful functionality (like web search or sandboxed code execution) without managing the infrastructure yourself.

metadata.title: Coding Agents
metadata.description: Learn how to set up the AI SDK for use with coding agents, including installing skills, accessing bundled docs, and using DevTools.

contents.content: This page explains how to get the most out of the AI SDK when working inside a coding agent (such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, or any other AI-assisted development environment).

contents.heading: install-the-ai-sdk-skill
contents.content: The fastest way to give your coding agent deep knowledge of the AI SDK is to install the official AI SDK skill. Skills are lightweight markdown files that load specialized instructions into your agent's context on demand — so your agent knows exactly how to use the SDK without you needing to explain it.

contents.heading: install-the-ai-sdk-skill
contents.content: Install the AI SDK skill using npx skills add:

contents.heading: install-the-ai-sdk-skill
contents.content: This installs the skill into your agent's specific skills directory (e.g., .claude/skills, .codex/skills). If you select more than one agent, the CLI creates symlinks so each agent can discover the skill. Use -a to specify agents directly — for example, -a amp installs into the universal .agents/skills directory. Use -y for non-interactive installation.

contents.heading: install-the-ai-sdk-skill
contents.content: Once installed, any agent that supports the Agent Skills format will automatically discover and load the skill when working on AI SDK tasks.

contents.heading: install-the-ai-sdk-skill
contents.content:
Agent Skills use progressive disclosure: your agent loads only the skill's
name and description at startup. The full instructions are only pulled into
context when the task calls for it, keeping your agent fast and focused.

contents.heading: docs-and-source-code-in-node_modules
contents.content: Once you've installed the ai package, you already have the full AI SDK documentation and source code available locally inside node_modules. Your coding agent can read these directly — no internet access required.

contents.heading: docs-and-source-code-in-node_modules
contents.content: Install the ai package if you haven't already:

contents.heading: docs-and-source-code-in-node_modules
contents.content: After installation, your agent can reference the bundled source code and documentation at paths like:

contents.heading: docs-and-source-code-in-node_modules
contents.content: This means your agent can look up accurate API signatures, implementations, and usage examples directly from the installed package — ensuring it always uses the version of the SDK that's actually installed in your project.

contents.heading: install-devtools
contents.content: AI SDK DevTools gives you full visibility into your AI SDK calls during development. It captures LLM requests, responses, tool calls, token usage, and multi-step interactions, and displays them in a local web UI.

contents.heading: install-devtools
contents.content:
AI SDK DevTools is experimental and intended for local development only. Do
not use in production environments.

contents.heading: install-devtools
contents.content: Install the DevTools package:

contents.heading: add-the-middleware
contents.content: Wrap your language model with the DevTools middleware using wrapLanguageModel:

contents.heading: add-the-middleware
contents.content: Use the wrapped model with any AI SDK Core function:

contents.heading: launch-the-viewer
contents.content: Start the DevTools viewer in a separate terminal:

contents.heading: launch-the-viewer
contents.content: Open http://localhost:4983 to inspect your AI SDK interactions in real time.

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: DevTools captures and displays the following for every call:

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: Input parameters and prompts — the complete input sent to your LLM

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: Output content and tool calls — generated text and tool invocations

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: Token usage and timing — resource consumption and latency per step

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: Raw provider data — complete request and response payloads

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: For multi-step agent interactions, DevTools groups everything into runs (a complete interaction) and steps (each individual LLM call within it), making it easy to trace exactly what your agent did and why.

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: You can also log tool results directly in code during development:

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content: The onStepFinish callback fires after each LLM step and prints any tool results to your terminal — useful for quick debugging without opening the DevTools UI.

contents.heading: inspecting-tool-calls-and-outputs
contents.content:
DevTools stores all AI interactions in a local .devtools/generations.json
file. It automatically adds .devtools to your .gitignore to prevent
committing sensitive interaction data.

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: Learn about Agent Skills to understand the full skill format.

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: Read the DevTools reference for a complete list of captured data and configuration options.

contents.heading: where-to-next

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: While large language models (LLMs) have incredible generation capabilities, they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather). This is where tools come in.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: Tools are actions that an LLM can invoke. The results of these actions can be reported back to the LLM to be considered in the next response.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: For example, if a user asks about the current weather, without tools, the model would only be able to provide general information based on its training data. But with a weather tool, it can fetch and provide up-to-date, location-specific weather information.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: Let's enhance your chatbot by adding a simple weather tool.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route

contents.content: In this updated code:

contents.content: You define a tools object with a weather tool. This tool:

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content: Has a description that helps the model understand when to use it.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content: Defines inputSchema using a Zod schema, specifying that it requires a location string to execute this tool. The model will attempt to extract this input from the context of the conversation. If it can't, it will ask the user for the missing information.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content: Defines an execute function that simulates getting weather data (in this case, it returns a random temperature). This is an asynchronous function running on the server so you can fetch real data from an external API.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content: Now your chatbot can "fetch" weather information for any location the user asks about. When the model determines it needs to use the weather tool, it will generate a tool call with the necessary input. The execute function will then be automatically run, and the tool output will be added to the messages as a tool message.

effect.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content: Notice the blank response in the UI? This is because instead of generating a text response, the model generated a tool call. You can access the tool call and subsequent tool result on the client via the tool-weather part of the message.parts array.

contents.heading: update-your-api-route
contents.content:
Tool parts are always named tool-{toolName}, where {toolName} is the key
you used when defining the tool. In this case, since we defined the tool as
weather, the part type is tool-weather.

contents.heading: update-the-ui

contents.heading: update-the-ui

contents.heading: enabling-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: You may have noticed that while the tool results are visible in the chat interface, the model isn't using this information to answer your original query. This is because once the model generates a tool call, it has technically completed its generation.

contents.heading: enabling-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: To solve this, you can enable multi-step tool calls using stopWhen. By default, stopWhen is set to stepCountIs(1), which means generation stops after the first step when there are tool results. By changing this condition, you can allow the model to automatically send tool results back to itself to trigger additional generations until your specified stopping condition is met. In this case, you want the model to continue generating so it can use the weather tool results to answer your original question.

contents.content: The AI SDK is a powerful toolkit for building AI applications. This page will help you pick the right tools for your requirements.
Let’s start with a quick overview of the AI SDK, which is comprised of three parts:
AI SDK Core: A unified, provider agnostic API for generating text, structured objects, and tool calls with LLMs.
AI SDK UI: A set of framework-agnostic hooks for building chat and generative user interfaces.
AI SDK RSC: Stream generative user interfaces with React Server Components (RSC). Development is currently experimental and we recommend using AI SDK UI.

contents.heading: choosing-the-right-tool-for-your-environment
contents.content: When deciding which part of the AI SDK to use, your first consideration should be the environment and existing stack you are working with. Different components of the SDK are tailored to specific frameworks and environments.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content:
React Server Components
(RSCs) provide a new approach to building React applications that allow components
to render on the server, fetch data directly, and stream the results to the client,
reducing bundle size and improving performance. They also introduce a new way to
call server-side functions from anywhere in your application called Server Actions.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: AI SDK RSC provides a number of utilities that allow you to stream values and UI directly from the server to the client. However, it's important to be aware of current limitations:

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: Cancellation: currently, it is not possible to abort a stream using Server Actions. This will be improved in future releases of React and Next.js.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: Increased Data Transfer: using createStreamableUI can lead to quadratic data transfer (quadratic to the length of generated text). You can avoid this using  createStreamableValue  instead, and rendering the component client-side.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: Re-mounting Issue During Streaming: when using createStreamableUI, components re-mount on .done(), causing flickering.

contents.heading: when-to-use-ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: Given these limitations, we recommend using AI SDK UI for production applications.

Unlike in React, where hooks are rerun any time their containing component is invalidated, code in the script block of a Svelte component is only run once when the component is created.
This means that, if you want arguments to your class to be reactive, you need to make sure you pass a reference into the class, rather than a value:

contents.heading: arguments-to-classes-arent-reactive-by-default
contents.content: Keep in mind that this normally doesn't matter; most parameters you'll pass into the Chat class are static (for example, you typically wouldn't expect your onError handler to change).

contents.heading: you-cant-destructure-class-properties
contents.content: In vanilla JavaScript, destructuring class properties copies them by value and "disconnects" them from their class instance:

contents.heading: you-cant-destructure-class-properties
contents.content: The same is true of classes in Svelte:

contents.heading: instance-synchronization-requires-context
contents.content:
In React, hook instances with the same id are synchronized -- so two instances of useChat will have the same messages, status, etc. if they have the same id.
For most use cases, you probably don't need this behavior -- but if you do, you can create a context in your root layout file using createAIContext:

metadata.title: TanStack Start
metadata.description: Learn how to build your first agent with the AI SDK and TanStack Start.

title.children: Configure your AI Gateway API key

contents.content: The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript library designed to help developers build AI-powered applications.

In this quickstart tutorial, you'll build a simple agent with a streaming chat user interface. Along the way, you'll learn key concepts and techniques that are fundamental to using the AI SDK in your own projects.
If you are unfamiliar with the concepts of Prompt Engineering and HTTP Streaming, you can optionally read these documents first.

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: To follow this quickstart, you'll need:

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: Node.js 18+ and pnpm installed on your local development machine.

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: A  Vercel AI Gateway  API key.

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: If you haven't obtained your Vercel AI Gateway API key, you can do so by signing up on the Vercel website.

contents.heading: create-your-application
contents.content: Start by creating a new TanStack Start application. This command will create a new directory named my-ai-app and set up a basic TanStack Start application inside it.

contents.heading: create-your-application
contents.content: Navigate to the newly created directory:

contents.heading: install-dependencies
contents.content: Install ai and @ai-sdk/react, the AI package and AI SDK's React hooks. The AI SDK's  Vercel AI Gateway provider  ships with the ai package. You'll also install zod, a schema validation library used for defining tool inputs.

contents.heading: install-dependencies
contents.content:
This guide uses the Vercel AI Gateway provider so you can access hundreds of
models from different providers with one API key, but you can switch to any
provider or model by installing its package. Check out available AI SDK
providers for more information.

contents.heading: configure-your-ai-gateway-api-key
contents.content: Create a .env file in your project root and add your AI Gateway API key. This key authenticates your application with Vercel AI Gateway.

contents.heading: configure-your-ai-gateway-api-key
contents.content: Edit the .env file:

contents.heading: configure-your-ai-gateway-api-key
contents.content: Replace xxxxxxxxx with your actual Vercel AI Gateway API key.

contents.heading: configure-your-ai-gateway-api-key
contents.content:
The AI SDK's Vercel AI Gateway Provider will default to using the
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY environment variable.

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: Create a route handler, src/routes/api/chat.ts and add the following code:

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: Let's take a look at what is happening in this code:

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: Define an asynchronous POST request handler using TanStack Start's server routes and extract messages from the body of the request. The messages variable contains a history of the conversation between you and the chatbot and provides the chatbot with the necessary context to make the next generation. The messages are of UIMessage type, which are designed for use in application UI - they contain the entire message history and associated metadata like timestamps.

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: Call streamText, which is imported from the ai package. This function accepts a configuration object that contains a model provider and messages (defined in step 1). You can pass additional settings to further customize the model's behavior. The messages key expects a ModelMessage[] array. This type is different from UIMessage in that it does not include metadata, such as timestamps or sender information. To convert between these types, we use the convertToModelMessages function, which strips the UI-specific metadata and transforms the UIMessage[] array into the ModelMessage[] format that the model expects.

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: The streamText function returns a StreamTextResult. This result object contains the  toUIMessageStreamResponse  function which converts the result to a streamed response object.

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: Finally, return the result to the client to stream the response.

contents.heading: create-a-route-handler
contents.content: This Route Handler creates a POST request endpoint at /api/chat.

contents.heading: choosing-a-provider
contents.content: The AI SDK supports dozens of model providers through first-party, OpenAI-compatible, and  community  packages.

contents.heading: choosing-a-provider
contents.content: This quickstart uses the Vercel AI Gateway provider, which is the default global provider. This means you can access models using a simple string in the model configuration:

contents.heading: choosing-a-provider
contents.content: You can also explicitly import and use the gateway provider in two other equivalent ways:

contents.heading: using-other-providers
contents.content: To use a different provider, install its package and create a provider instance. For example, to use OpenAI directly:

contents.heading: updating-the-global-provider
contents.content: You can change the default global provider so string model references use your preferred provider everywhere in your application. Learn more about provider management.

contents.heading: updating-the-global-provider
contents.content: Pick the approach that best matches how you want to manage providers across your application.

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: Now that you have a Route Handler that can query an LLM, it's time to setup your frontend. The AI SDK's  UI  package abstracts the complexity of a chat interface into one hook, useChat.

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: Update your index route (src/routes/index.tsx) with the following code to show a list of chat messages and provide a user message input:

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: This page utilizes the useChat hook, which will, by default, use the POST API route you created earlier (/api/chat). The hook provides functions and state for handling user input and form submission. The useChat hook provides multiple utility functions and state variables:

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: messages - the current chat messages (an array of objects with id, role, and parts properties).

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: sendMessage - a function to send a message to the chat API.

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: The component uses local state (useState) to manage the input field value, and handles form submission by calling sendMessage with the input text and then clearing the input field.

contents.heading: wire-up-the-ui
contents.content: The LLM's response is accessed through the message parts array. Each message contains an ordered array of parts that represents everything the model generated in its response. These parts can include plain text, reasoning tokens, and more that you will see later. The parts array preserves the sequence of the model's outputs, allowing you to display or process each component in the order it was generated.

contents.heading: running-your-application
contents.content: With that, you have built everything you need for your chatbot! To start your application, use the command:

contents.heading: running-your-application
contents.content: Head to your browser and open http://localhost:3000. You should see an input field. Test it out by entering a message and see the AI chatbot respond in real-time! The AI SDK makes it fast and easy to build AI chat interfaces with TanStack Start.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: While large language models (LLMs) have incredible generation capabilities, they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather). This is where tools come in.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: Tools are actions that an LLM can invoke. The results of these actions can be reported back to the LLM to be considered in the next response.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: For example, if a user asks about the current weather, without tools, the model would only be able to provide general information based on its training data. But with a weather tool, it can fetch and provide up-to-date, location-specific weather information.

contents.heading: enhance-your-chatbot-with-tools
contents.content: Let's enhance your chatbot by adding a simple weather tool.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Modify your src/routes/api/chat.ts file to include the new weather tool:

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: In this updated code:

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: You import the tool function from the ai package and z from zod for schema validation.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: You define a tools object with a weather tool. This tool:

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Has a description that helps the model understand when to use it.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Defines inputSchema using a Zod schema, specifying that it requires a location string to execute this tool. The model will attempt to extract this input from the context of the conversation. If it can't, it will ask the user for the missing information.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Defines an execute function that simulates getting weather data (in this case, it returns a random temperature). This is an asynchronous function running on the server so you can fetch real data from an external API.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Now your chatbot can "fetch" weather information for any location the user asks about. When the model determines it needs to use the weather tool, it will generate a tool call with the necessary input. The execute function will then be automatically run, and the tool output will be added to the messages as a tool message.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Try asking something like "What's the weather in New York?" and see how the model uses the new tool.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content: Notice the blank response in the UI? This is because instead of generating a text response, the model generated a tool call. You can access the tool call and subsequent tool result on the client via the tool-weather part of the message.parts array.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler
contents.content:
Tool parts are always named tool-{toolName}, where {toolName} is the key
you used when defining the tool. In this case, since we defined the tool as
weather, the part type is tool-weather.

contents.heading: update-the-ui
contents.content: To display the tool invocation in your UI, update your src/routes/index.tsx file:

contents.heading: update-the-ui
contents.content: With this change, you're updating the UI to handle different message parts. For text parts, you display the text content as before. For weather tool invocations, you display a JSON representation of the tool call and its result.

contents.heading: update-the-ui
contents.content: Now, when you ask about the weather, you'll see the tool call and its result displayed in your chat interface.

contents.heading: enabling-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: You may have noticed that while the tool is now visible in the chat interface, the model isn't using this information to answer your original query. This is because once the model generates a tool call, it has technically completed its generation.

contents.heading: enabling-multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: To solve this, you can enable multi-step tool calls using stopWhen. By default, stopWhen is set to stepCountIs(1), which means generation stops after the first step when there are tool results. By changing this condition, you can allow the model to automatically send tool results back to itself to trigger additional generations until your specified stopping condition is met. In this case, you want the model to continue generating so it can use the weather tool results to answer your original question.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler-1
contents.content: Modify your src/routes/api/chat.ts file to include the stopWhen condition:

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler-1
contents.content: In this updated code, you set stopWhen to be when stepCountIs(5), allowing the model to use up to 5 "steps" for any given generation.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler-1
contents.content: Head back to the browser and ask about the weather in a location. You should now see the model using the weather tool results to answer your question.

contents.heading: update-your-route-handler-1
contents.content: By setting stopWhen: stepCountIs(5), you're allowing the model to use up to 5 "steps" for any given generation. This enables more complex interactions and allows the model to gather and process information over several steps if needed. You can see this in action by adding another tool to convert the temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

contents.heading: add-another-tool
contents.content: Update your src/routes/api/chat.ts file to add a new tool to convert the temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius:

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: update your src/routes/index.tsx file to render the new temperature conversion tool:

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: This update handles the new tool-convertFahrenheitToCelsius part type, displaying the temperature conversion tool calls and results in the UI.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: Now, when you ask "What's the weather in New York in celsius?", you should see a more complete interaction:

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: The model will call the weather tool for New York.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: You'll see the tool output displayed.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: It will then call the temperature conversion tool to convert the temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: The model will then use that information to provide a natural language response about the weather in New York.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: This multi-step approach allows the model to gather information and use it to provide more accurate and contextual responses, making your chatbot considerably more useful.

contents.heading: update-your-frontend
contents.content: This simple example demonstrates how tools can expand your model's capabilities. You can create more complex tools to integrate with real APIs, databases, or any other external systems, allowing the model to access and process real-world data in real-time. Tools bridge the gap between the model's knowledge cutoff and current information.

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: You've built an AI chatbot using the AI SDK! From here, you have several paths to explore:

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: To learn more about the AI SDK, read through the documentation.

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: If you're interested in diving deeper with guides, check out the RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) and multi-modal chatbot guides.

contents.heading: where-to-next
contents.content: To jumpstart your first AI project, explore available templates.

contents.heading: ai-sdk

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: The release of AI SDK 3.1 introduces several new features that improve the way you build AI applications with the SDK:

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: AI SDK Core, a brand new unified API for interacting with large language models (LLMs).

contents.heading: next-steps

contents.heading: migrating-from-legacy-providers-to-ai-sdk-core

contents.heading: migrating-from-legacy-providers-to-ai-sdk-core
contents.content: In the following Route Handler, you use the OpenAI SDK to query their model. You then pipe that response into the OpenAIStream function which returns a ReadableStream that you can pass to the client using a new StreamingTextResponse.

contents.heading: migrating-from-legacy-providers-to-ai-sdk-core
contents.content: With AI SDK Core you have a unified API for any provider that implements the AI SDK Language Model Specification.

contents.heading: migrating-from-legacy-providers-to-ai-sdk-core
contents.content: Let’s take a look at the example above, but refactored to utilize the AI SDK Core API alongside the AI SDK OpenAI provider. In this example, you import the LLM function you want to use from the ai package, import the OpenAI provider from @ai-sdk/openai, and then you call the model and return the response using the toDataStreamResponse() helper function.

contents.heading: migrating-from-render-to-streamui
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC API was launched as part of version 3.0. This API introduced the render function, a helper function to create streamable UIs with OpenAI models. With the new AI SDK Core API, it became possible to make streamable UIs possible with any compatible provider.

contents.heading: migrating-from-render-to-streamui
contents.content: The following example Server Action uses the render function using the model provider directly from OpenAI. You first create an OpenAI provider instance with the OpenAI SDK. Then, you pass it to the provider key of the render function alongside a tool that returns a React Server Component, defined in the render key of the tool.

contents.heading: migrating-from-render-to-streamui
contents.content: With the new streamUI function, you can now use any compatible AI SDK provider. In this example, you import the AI SDK OpenAI provider. Then, you pass it to the model key of the new streamUI function. Finally, you declare a tool and return a React Server Component, defined in the generate key of the tool.

contents.content:
Check out the AI SDK 3.3 release blog
post for more information about
the release.
No breaking changes in this release.

The following changelog encompasses all changes made in the 3.2.x series,
introducing significant improvements and new features across the AI SDK and its associated libraries:

contents.heading: open-telemetry-support
contents.content: Added experimental OpenTelemetry support for all AI SDK Core functions, enabling better observability and tracing capabilities.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Introduced the experimental useObject hook (for React) that can be used in conjunction with streamObject on the backend to enable seamless streaming of structured data.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Enhanced useChat with experimental support for attachments and streaming tool calls, providing more versatile chat functionalities.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Patched useChat to prevent empty submissions, improving the quality of user interactions by ensuring that only intended inputs are processed.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Fix useChat's reload function, now correctly sending data, body, and headers.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Implemented setThreadId helper for useAssistant, simplifying thread management.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Documented the stream data protocol for useChat and useCompletion, allowing developers to use these functions with any backend. The stream data protocol also enables the use of custom frontends with streamText.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Added support for custom fetch functions and request body customization, offering greater control over API interactions.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui-improvements
contents.content: Added onFinish to useChat hook for access to token usage and finish reason.

contents.heading: core-enhancements
contents.content: Implemented support for sending custom request headers, enabling more tailored API requests.

contents.heading: core-enhancements
contents.content: Added raw JSON schema support alongside existing Zod support, providing more options for schema and data validation.

contents.heading: core-enhancements
contents.content: Introduced usage information for embed and embedMany functions, offering insights into token usage.

contents.heading: core-enhancements
contents.content: Added support for additional settings including stopSequences and topK, allowing for finer control over text generation.

contents.heading: core-enhancements
contents.content: Provided access to information for all steps on generateText, providing access to intermediate tool calls and results.

contents.heading: new-providers
contents.content: AWS Bedrock provider.

contents.heading: provider-improvements
contents.content: Enhanced existing providers including Anthropic, Google, Azure, and OpenAI with various improvements and bug fixes.

contents.heading: provider-improvements
contents.content: Upgraded the LangChain adapter with StreamEvent v2 support and introduced the toDataStreamResponse function, enabling conversion of LangChain output streams to data stream responses.

contents.heading: provider-improvements
contents.content: Added legacy function calling support to the OpenAI provider.

contents.heading: provider-improvements
contents.content: Updated Mistral AI provider with fixes and improvements for tool calling support.

contents.heading: ui-framework-support-expansion
contents.content: SolidJS: Updated useChat and useCompletion to achieve feature parity with React implementations.

contents.heading: ui-framework-support-expansion
contents.content: Vue.js: Introduced useAssistant hook.

contents.heading: ui-framework-support-expansion
contents.content: Vue.js / Nuxt: Updated examples to showcase latest features and best practices.

contents.heading: ui-framework-support-expansion
contents.content: Svelte: Added tool calling support to useChat.

contents.heading: fixes-and-improvements
contents.content: Resolved various issues across different components of the SDK, including race conditions, error handling, and state management.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides Codemod transformations to help upgrade your codebase when a
feature is deprecated, removed, or otherwise changed.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
Codemods are transformations that run on your codebase programmatically. They
allow you to easily apply many changes without having to manually go through
every file.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
Codemods are intended as a tool to help you with the upgrade process. They may
not cover all of the changes you need to make. You may need to make additional
changes manually.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
You can run all codemods provided as part of the 4.0 upgrade process by running
the following command from the root of your project:

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content: To run only the v4 codemods:

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content: Individual codemods can be run by specifying the name of the codemod:

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content: For example, to run a specific v4 codemod:

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
See also the table of codemods. In addition, the latest set of
codemods can be found in the
@ai-sdk/codemod
repository.

contents.heading: removed-baseurl-option
contents.content: The baseUrl option has been removed from all providers. Please use the baseURL option instead.

contents.heading: removed-anthropic-facade
contents.content:
The Anthropic facade has been removed from the Anthropic provider.
Please use the anthropic object or the createAnthropic function instead.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting
contents.content:
The model specific topK setting has been removed from the Anthropic provider.
You can use the standard topK setting instead.

contents.heading: removed-google-facade
contents.content:
The Google facade has been removed from the Google Generative AI provider.
Please use the google object or the createGoogleGenerativeAI function instead.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting-1
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting-1
contents.content:
The model-specific topK setting has been removed from the Google Generative AI provider.
You can use the standard topK setting instead.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting-2
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-topk-setting-2
contents.content:
The model-specific topK setting has been removed from the Google Vertex provider.
You can use the standard topK setting instead.

contents.heading: removed-mistral-facade
contents.content:
The Mistral facade has been removed from the Mistral provider.
Please use the mistral object or the createMistral function instead.

contents.heading: removed-openai-facade
contents.content:
The OpenAI facade has been removed from the OpenAI provider.
Please use the openai object or the createOpenAI function instead.

contents.heading: removed-toaistream
contents.content:
The toAIStream function has been removed from the LangChain adapter.
Please use the toDataStream function instead.

contents.heading: streamtext-returns-immediately
contents.content:
Instead of returning a Promise, the streamText function now returns immediately.
It is not necessary to await the result of streamText.

contents.heading: streamobject-returns-immediately
contents.content:
Instead of returning a Promise, the streamObject function now returns immediately.
It is not necessary to await the result of streamObject.

contents.heading: remove-roundtrips
contents.content:
The maxToolRoundtrips and maxAutomaticRoundtrips options have been removed from the generateText and streamText functions.
Please use the maxSteps option instead.

contents.heading: remove-roundtrips
contents.content:
The roundtrips property has been removed from the GenerateTextResult type.
Please use the steps property instead.

contents.heading: removed-nanoid-export
contents.content: The nanoid export has been removed. Please use generateId instead.

contents.heading: increased-default-size-of-generated-ids
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: increased-default-size-of-generated-ids
contents.content:
The generateId function now
generates 16-character IDs. The previous default was 7 characters.

contents.heading: increased-default-size-of-generated-ids
contents.content:
This might e.g. require updating your database schema if you limit the length of
IDs.

contents.heading: removed-experimentalmessage-types
contents.content: The following types have been removed:

contents.heading: removed-experimentalmessage-types
contents.content: ExperimentalMessage (use ModelMessage instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimentalmessage-types
contents.content: ExperimentalUserMessage (use CoreUserMessage instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimentalmessage-types
contents.content: ExperimentalAssistantMessage (use CoreAssistantMessage instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimentalmessage-types
contents.content: ExperimentalToolMessage (use CoreToolMessage instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimentaltool-type
contents.content: The ExperimentalTool type has been removed. Please use the CoreTool type instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental-ai-function-exports
contents.content: The following exports have been removed:

contents.heading: removed-experimental-ai-function-exports
contents.content: experimental_generateText (use generateText instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimental-ai-function-exports
contents.content: experimental_streamText (use streamText instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimental-ai-function-exports
contents.content: experimental_generateObject (use generateObject instead)

contents.heading: removed-experimental-ai-function-exports
contents.content: experimental_streamObject (use streamObject instead)

contents.heading: removed-ai-stream-related-methods-from-streamtext
contents.content: The following methods have been removed from the streamText result:

contents.heading: removed-ai-stream-related-methods-from-streamtext
contents.content: toAIStream

contents.heading: removed-ai-stream-related-methods-from-streamtext
contents.content: pipeAIStreamToResponse

contents.heading: removed-ai-stream-related-methods-from-streamtext
contents.content: toAIStreamResponse

contents.heading: removed-ai-stream-related-methods-from-streamtext
contents.content: Use the toDataStream, pipeDataStreamToResponse, and toDataStreamResponse functions instead.

contents.heading: renamed-formatstreampart-to-formatdatastreampart
contents.content: The formatStreamPart function has been renamed to formatDataStreamPart.

contents.heading: renamed-parsestreampart-to-parsedatastreampart
contents.content: The parseStreamPart function has been renamed to parseDataStreamPart.

contents.heading: renamed-tokenusage-completiontokenusage-and-embeddingtokenusage-types
contents.content:
The TokenUsage, CompletionTokenUsage and EmbeddingTokenUsage types have
been renamed to LanguageModelUsage (for the first two) and
EmbeddingModelUsage (for the last).

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: The following telemetry data values have been removed:

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: ai.finishReason (now in ai.response.finishReason)

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: ai.result.object (now in ai.response.object)

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: ai.result.text (now in ai.response.text)

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: ai.result.toolCalls (now in ai.response.toolCalls)

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: ai.stream.msToFirstChunk (now in ai.response.msToFirstChunk)

contents.heading: removed-deprecated-telemetry-data
contents.content: This change will apply to observability providers and any scripts or automation that you use for processing telemetry data.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_provider-experimental_providerregistry-and-experimental_modelregistry
contents.content:
The experimental_Provider interface, experimental_ProviderRegistry interface, and experimental_ModelRegistry interface have been removed.
Please use the Provider interface instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_provider-experimental_providerregistry-and-experimental_modelregistry
contents.content:
The model registry is not available any more. Please register
providers instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_createmodelregistry-function
contents.content:
The experimental_createModelRegistry function has been removed.
Please use the experimental_createProviderRegistry function instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_createmodelregistry-function
contents.content:
The model registry is not available any more. Please register
providers instead.

contents.heading: removed-rawresponse-from-results
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-rawresponse-from-results
contents.content:
The rawResponse property has been removed from the generateText, streamText, generateObject, and streamObject results.
You can use the response property instead.

contents.heading: removed-init-option-from-pipedatastreamtoresponse-and-todatastreamresponse
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-init-option-from-pipedatastreamtoresponse-and-todatastreamresponse
contents.content:
The init option has been removed from the pipeDataStreamToResponse and toDataStreamResponse functions.
You can set the values from init directly into the options object.

contents.heading: removed-responsemessages-from-generatetext-and-streamtext
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-responsemessages-from-generatetext-and-streamtext
contents.content:
The responseMessages property has been removed from the generateText and streamText results.
This includes the onFinish callback.
Please use the response.messages property instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_continuationsteps-option
contents.content:
The experimental_continuationSteps option has been removed from the generateText function.
Please use the experimental_continueSteps option instead.

contents.heading: removed-languagemodelresponsemetadatawithheaders-type
contents.content:
The LanguageModelResponseMetadataWithHeaders type has been removed.
Please use the LanguageModelResponseMetadata type instead.

contents.heading: changed-streamtext-warnings-result-to-promise
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: changed-streamtext-warnings-result-to-promise
contents.content: The warnings property of the StreamTextResult type is now a Promise.

contents.heading: changed-streamobject-warnings-result-to-promise
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: changed-streamobject-warnings-result-to-promise
contents.content: The warnings property of the StreamObjectResult type is now a Promise.

contents.heading: renamed-simulatereadablestream-values-to-chunks
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: renamed-simulatereadablestream-values-to-chunks
contents.content: The simulateReadableStream function from ai/test has been renamed to chunks.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc-changes
contents.content:
There are no codemods available for the changes in this section. Please review
and update your code manually.

contents.heading: removed-render-function
contents.content:
The AI SDK RSC 3.0 render function has been removed.
Please use the streamUI function instead or switch to AI SDK UI.

contents.heading: removed-svelte-vue-and-solidjs-exports
contents.content:
This codemod only operates on .ts and .tsx files. If you have code in
files with other suffixes, please review and update your code manually.

contents.heading: removed-svelte-vue-and-solidjs-exports
contents.content:
The ai package no longer exports Svelte, Vue, and SolidJS UI integrations.
You need to install the @ai-sdk/svelte, @ai-sdk/vue, and @ai-sdk/solid packages directly.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_streamdata
contents.content:
The experimental_StreamData export has been removed.
Please use the StreamData export instead.

contents.heading: usechat-hook
contents.content:
There are no codemods available for the changes in this section. Please review
and update your code manually.

contents.heading: removed-streammode-setting
contents.content:
The streamMode options has been removed from the useChat hook.
Please use the streamProtocol parameter instead.

contents.heading: replaced-roundtrip-setting-with-maxsteps
contents.content: The following options have been removed from the useChat hook:

contents.heading: replaced-roundtrip-setting-with-maxsteps
contents.content: experimental_maxAutomaticRoundtrips

contents.heading: replaced-roundtrip-setting-with-maxsteps
contents.content: maxAutomaticRoundtrips

contents.heading: replaced-roundtrip-setting-with-maxsteps
contents.content: maxToolRoundtrips

contents.heading: replaced-roundtrip-setting-with-maxsteps
contents.content:
Please use the maxSteps option instead.
The value of maxSteps is equal to roundtrips + 1.

contents.heading: removed-options-setting
contents.content:
The options parameter in the useChat hook has been removed.
Please use the headers and body parameters instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_addtoolresult-method
contents.content:
The experimental_addToolResult method has been removed from the useChat hook.
Please use the addToolResult method instead.

contents.heading: changed-default-value-of-keeplastmessageonerror-to-true-and-deprecated-the-option
contents.content:
The keepLastMessageOnError option has been changed to default to true.
The option will be removed in the next major release.

contents.heading: usecompletion-hook
contents.content:
There are no codemods available for the changes in this section. Please review
and update your code manually.

contents.heading: removed-streammode-setting-1
contents.content:
The streamMode options has been removed from the useCompletion hook.
Please use the streamProtocol parameter instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_useassistant-export
contents.content:
The experimental_useAssistant export has been removed from the useAssistant hook.
Please use the useAssistant hook directly instead.

contents.heading: removed-threadid-and-messageid-from-assistantresponse
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-threadid-and-messageid-from-assistantresponse
contents.content:
The threadId and messageId parameters have been removed from the AssistantResponse function.
Please use the threadId and messageId variables from the outer scope instead.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_assistantresponse-export
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-experimental_assistantresponse-export
contents.content:
The experimental_AssistantResponse export has been removed.
Please use the AssistantResponse function directly instead.

contents.heading: experimental_useobject-hook
contents.content:
There are no codemods available for the changes in this section. Please review
and update your code manually.

contents.heading: experimental_useobject-hook
contents.content:
The setInput helper has been removed from the experimental_useObject hook.
Please use the submit helper instead.

contents.heading: removed-isxxxerror-static-methods
contents.content:
The isXXXError static methods have been removed from AI SDK errors.
Please use the isInstance method of the corresponding error class instead.

contents.heading: removed-tojson-method
contents.content:
There is no codemod available for this change. Please review and update your
code manually.

contents.heading: removed-tojson-method
contents.content: The toJSON method has been removed from AI SDK errors.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-2x-legacy-changes
contents.content:
There are no codemods available for the changes in this section. Please review
and update your code manually.

contents.heading: removed-2x-legacy-providers
contents.content: Legacy providers from AI SDK 2.x have been removed. Please use the new AI SDK provider architecture instead.

contents.heading: removed-2x-legacy-function-and-tool-calling
contents.content:
The legacy function_call and tools options have been removed from useChat and Message.
The name property from the Message type has been removed.
Please use the AI SDK Core tool calling instead.

contents.heading: removed-2x-prompt-helpers
contents.content: Prompt helpers for constructing message prompts are no longer needed with the AI SDK provider architecture and have been removed.

contents.heading: removed-2x-aistream
contents.content:
The AIStream function and related exports have been removed.
Please use the streamText function and its toDataStream() method instead.

contents.heading: removed-2x-streamingtextresponse
contents.content:
The StreamingTextResponse function has been removed.
Please use the streamText function and its toDataStreamResponse() method instead.

contents.heading: removed-2x-streamtoresponse
contents.content:
The streamToResponse function has been removed.
Please use the streamText function and its pipeDataStreamToResponse() method instead.

contents.heading: removed-2x-rsc-tokens-streaming
contents.content:
The legacy Tokens RSC streaming from 2.x has been removed.
Tokens were implemented prior to AI SDK RSC and are no longer needed.

contents.heading: ui-message-parts
contents.content:
In AI SDK 4.2, we've redesigned how useChat handles model outputs with message parts and multiple steps.
This is a significant improvement that simplifies rendering complex, multi-modal AI responses in your UI.

contents.heading: whats-changed
contents.content:
Assistant messages with tool calling now get combined into a single message with multiple parts, rather than creating separate messages for each step.
This change addresses two key developments in AI applications:

contents.heading: whats-changed
contents.content: Diverse Output Types: Models now generate more than just text; they produce reasoning steps, sources, and tool calls.

contents.heading: whats-changed
contents.content: Interleaved Outputs: In multi-step agent use-cases, these different output types are frequently interleaved.

contents.heading: benefits-of-the-new-approach
contents.content:
Previously, useChat stored different output types separately, which made it challenging to maintain the correct sequence in your UI when these elements were interleaved in a response,
and led to multiple consecutive assistant messages when there were tool calls. For example:

contents.heading: benefits-of-the-new-approach
contents.content: This structure was limiting. The new message parts approach replaces separate properties with an ordered array that preserves the exact sequence:

contents.heading: migration
contents.content:
Existing applications using the previous message format will need to update their UI components to handle the new parts array.
The fields from the previous format are still available for backward compatibility, but we recommend migrating to the new format for better support of multi-modal and multi-step interactions.

metadata.title: Migrate Your Data to AI SDK 5.0
metadata.description: Learn how to migrate your persisted messages and chat data from AI SDK 4.x to 5.0.

title.children: Phase 1: Get Your App Working (Runtime Conversion)
Step 1: Create V5 Schema Alongside V4
Step 2: Implement Dual-Write for New Messages
Step 6: Write to V5 Schema Only

contents.content: AI SDK 5.0 introduces changes to the message structure and persistence patterns. Unlike code migrations that can often be automated with codemods, data migration depends on your specific persistence approach, database schema, and application requirements.

This guide helps you get your application working with AI SDK 5.0 first using a runtime conversion layer. This allows you to update your app immediately without database migrations blocking you. You can then migrate your data schema at your own pace.

contents.heading: recommended-migration-process
contents.content: Follow this two-phase approach for a safe migration:

contents.heading: phase-1-get-your-app-working-runtime-conversion
contents.content: Goal: Update your application to AI SDK 5.0 without touching your database.

contents.heading: phase-1-get-your-app-working-runtime-conversion
contents.content: Update the rest of your application code to AI SDK 5.0 (see the main migration guide)

contents.heading: phase-1-get-your-app-working-runtime-conversion
contents.content: Your database schema remains unchanged during Phase 1. You're only adding a conversion layer that transforms messages at runtime.

contents.heading: phase-1-get-your-app-working-runtime-conversion
contents.content: Timeline: Can be completed in hours or days.

contents.heading: phase-2-migrate-to-v5-schema-recommended
contents.content: Goal: Migrate your data to a v5-compatible schema, eliminating the runtime conversion overhead.

contents.heading: phase-2-migrate-to-v5-schema-recommended

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides Codemod transformations to help upgrade your codebase when a
feature is deprecated, removed, or otherwise changed.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
Codemods are transformations that run on your codebase automatically. They
allow you to easily apply many changes without having to manually go through
every file.

contents.heading: codemods
contents.content:
Codemods are intended as a tool to help you with the upgrade process. They may
not cover all of the changes you need to make. You may need to make additional
changes manually.
