Defaults to false.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: The Open Responses provider instance is a function that you can invoke to create a language model:

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
You can use Open Responses models with the generateText and streamText functions,
and they support structured data generation with Output
(see AI SDK Core).

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Stop sequences, topK, and seed are not supported and are ignored with warnings.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Image inputs are supported for user messages with file parts using image media types.

metadata.title: OpenAI
metadata.description: Learn how to use the OpenAI provider for the AI SDK.

title.children: Typed providerMetadata in Source Document Parts

contents.content: The OpenAI provider contains language model support for the OpenAI responses, chat, and completion APIs, as well as embedding model support for the OpenAI embeddings API.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The OpenAI provider is available in the @ai-sdk/openai module. You can install it with

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can import the default provider instance openai from @ai-sdk/openai:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: If you need a customized setup, you can import createOpenAI from @ai-sdk/openai and create a provider instance with your settings:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the OpenAI provider instance:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: baseURL string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Use a different URL prefix for API calls, e.g. to use proxy servers.
It defaults to the OPENAI_BASE_URL environment variable, and then to
https://api.openai.com/v1.
The default OpenAI model factory (openai('model-id')) uses the Responses
API. If your custom base URL only supports the Chat Completions API, create
chat models with openai.chat('model-id') instead, or use the
OpenAI-compatible provider.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: apiKey string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
API key that is being sent using the Authorization header.
It defaults to the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: name string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
The provider name. You can set this when using OpenAI compatible providers
to change the model provider property. Defaults to openai.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: organization string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: OpenAI Organization.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: project string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: OpenAI project.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: headers Record<string,string>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Custom headers to include in the requests.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: fetch (input: RequestInfo, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Custom fetch implementation.
Defaults to the global fetch function.
You can use it as a middleware to intercept requests,
or to provide a custom fetch implementation for e.g. testing.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: The OpenAI provider instance is a function that you can invoke to create a language model:

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
It automatically selects the correct API based on the model id.
You can also pass additional settings in the second argument:

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
The available options depend on the API that's automatically chosen for the model (see below).
If you want to explicitly select a specific model API, you can use .responses, .chat, or .completion.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
Since AI SDK 5, the OpenAI responses API is called by default (unless you
specify e.g. 'openai.chat')

contents.heading: example
contents.content: You can use OpenAI language models to generate text with the generateText function:

contents.heading: example
contents.content:
OpenAI language models can also be used in the streamText function
and support structured data generation with Output
(see AI SDK Core).

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: You can use the OpenAI responses API with the openai(modelId) or openai.responses(modelId) factory methods. It is the default API that is used by the OpenAI provider (since AI SDK 5).

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
Further configuration can be done using OpenAI provider options.
You can validate the provider options using the OpenAILanguageModelResponsesOptions type.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: The following provider options are available:

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
parallelToolCalls boolean
Whether to use parallel tool calls. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: store boolean

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: Whether to store the generation. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: passThroughUnsupportedFiles boolean

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: Whether to pass through non-image file types as generic input files. Defaults to false, which restricts inline file inputs to images and PDFs. Enable this when the target OpenAI Responses model supports additional file media types.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
maxToolCalls integer
The maximum number of total calls to built-in tools that can be processed in a response.
This maximum number applies across all built-in tool calls, not per individual tool.
Any further attempts to call a tool by the model will be ignored.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
metadata Record<string, string>
Additional metadata to store with the generation.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
conversation string
The ID of the OpenAI Conversation to continue.
You must create a conversation first via the OpenAI API.
Cannot be used in conjunction with previousResponseId.
Defaults to undefined.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
previousResponseId string
The ID of the previous response. You can use it to continue a conversation. Defaults to undefined.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
instructions string
Instructions for the model.
They can be used to change the system or developer message when continuing a conversation using the previousResponseId option.
Defaults to undefined.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
logprobs boolean | number
Return the log probabilities of the tokens. Including logprobs will increase the response size and can slow down response times. However, it can be useful to better understand how the model is behaving. Setting to true returns the log probabilities of the tokens that were generated. Setting to a number (1-20) returns the log probabilities of the top n tokens that were generated.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
user string
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help OpenAI to monitor and detect abuse. Defaults to undefined.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningEffort 'none' | 'minimal' | 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'
Reasoning effort for reasoning models. Defaults to medium. If you use providerOptions to set the reasoningEffort option, this model setting will be ignored.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
Supported reasoning efforts vary by model. GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 support 'none',
'low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh', and 'max'. GPT-6 Astra does not
support 'none'.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
GPT-6 and later models do not support temperature, topP, logprobs, or
the legacy promptCacheRetention option. The provider removes these settings
and returns a warning. Use the Responses API for GPT-6 tool calling.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningEffortUpdate 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'
Updates the reasoning effort for GPT-6 and later models starting with the
current response without changing the request-level effort. Use this with
previousResponseId to preserve the original prompt prefix for caching.
Configuration updates require standard, single-agent mode and cannot be
combined with automatic truncation.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningMode 'standard' | 'pro'
Controls how much model work GPT-5.6 performs before returning a final answer. 'standard' is the default. Use 'pro' for difficult tasks where quality matters more than latency and token usage.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningContext 'auto' | 'current_turn' | 'all_turns'
Controls which available reasoning items GPT-5.6 can reuse. 'auto' uses the model default, 'current_turn' excludes reasoning from earlier turns, and 'all_turns' makes compatible earlier reasoning available. The effective context is returned as providerMetadata.openai.reasoningContext.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningSummary 'auto' | 'detailed'
Controls whether the model returns its reasoning process. Set to 'auto' for a condensed summary, 'detailed' for more comprehensive reasoning. Defaults to undefined (no reasoning summaries). When enabled, reasoning summaries appear in the stream as events with type 'reasoning' and in non-streaming responses within the reasoning field.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
strictJsonSchema boolean
Whether to use strict JSON schema validation. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
OpenAI structured outputs have several
limitations,
in particular around the supported
schemas,
and are therefore opt-in. For example, optional schema properties are not
supported. You need to change Zod .nullish() and .optional() to
.nullable().

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
serviceTier 'auto' | 'flex' | 'priority' | 'fast' | 'default'
Service tier for the request. Set to 'flex' for 50% cheaper processing
at the cost of increased latency (available for o3, o4-mini, and gpt-5 models).
Set to 'priority' for faster processing with Enterprise access (available for gpt-4, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o3, o4-mini; gpt-5-nano is not supported).
'fast' is OpenAI's newer name for the 'priority' tier; the two are interchangeable, and responses from
gpt-5.6 and earlier report serviceTier: 'priority' for either.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: Defaults to 'auto'.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
textVerbosity 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'
Controls the verbosity of the model's response. Lower values result in more concise responses,
while higher values result in more verbose responses. Defaults to 'medium'.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
include Array<string>
Specifies additional content to include in the response. Supported values:
['file_search_call.results'] for including file search results in responses.
['message.output_text.logprobs'] for logprobs.
Defaults to undefined.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
truncation string
The truncation strategy to use for the model response.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: Auto: If the input to this Response exceeds the model's context window size, the model will truncate the response to fit the context window by dropping items from the beginning of the conversation.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: disabled (default): If the input size will exceed the context window size for a model, the request will fail with a 400 error.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
promptCacheKey string
A cache key for manual prompt caching control. Used by OpenAI to cache responses for similar requests to optimize your cache hit rates.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
promptCacheOptions object
Configures prompt caching for GPT-5.6 and later models. mode can be 'implicit' or 'explicit', and ttl currently only supports '30m'. In explicit mode, only content blocks marked with a prompt cache breakpoint are cached.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
promptCacheRetention 'in_memory' | '24h'
The legacy retention policy for models before GPT-5.6. Set to '24h' to enable extended prompt caching on supported models. For GPT-5.6 and later models, use promptCacheOptions.ttl instead.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
safetyIdentifier string
A stable identifier used to help detect users of your application that may be violating OpenAI's usage policies. The IDs should be a string that uniquely identifies each user.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
systemMessageMode 'system' | 'developer' | 'remove'
Controls the role of the system message when making requests. By default (when omitted), for models that support reasoning the system message is automatically converted to a developer message. Setting systemMessageMode to system passes the system message as a system-level instruction; developer passes it as a developer message; remove omits the system message from the request.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
forceReasoning boolean
Force treating this model as a reasoning model. This is useful for "stealth" reasoning models (e.g. via a custom baseURL) where the model ID is not recognized by the SDK's allowlist. When enabled, the SDK applies reasoning-model parameter compatibility rules and defaults systemMessageMode to developer unless overridden.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: The OpenAI responses provider also returns provider-specific metadata:

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: For Responses models, you can type this metadata using OpenaiResponsesProviderMetadata:

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content: The following OpenAI-specific metadata may be returned:

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
responseId string | null | undefined
The ID of the response. Can be used to continue a conversation.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
logprobs (optional)
Log probabilities of output tokens (when enabled).

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
serviceTier (optional)
Service tier information returned by the API.

contents.heading: responses-models
contents.content:
reasoningContext (optional)
Effective persisted-reasoning context returned by GPT-5.6 ('current_turn' or 'all_turns').

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
You can increase reasoning effort for difficult work or reduce it for routine
follow-ups while preserving the conversation prefix for prompt caching:

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
Set the initial effort with request-level providerOptions.openai.reasoningEffort and keep that setting
unchanged throughout the conversation.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
For later changes, add a message-level reasoningEffortUpdate before the next
user message, following
OpenAI's configuration update guidance.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
The new effort applies until another update changes it. When sending conversation
history in messages, include earlier effort updates along with the other messages.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
Represent an update as an empty system message with
providerOptions.openai.reasoningEffortUpdate.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
Set allowSystemInMessages: true to explicitly allow these trusted system messages
and suppress the warning for system messages in messages.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
In this example, the conversation starts at low effort and switches to high
effort for the follow-up. Both requests keep providerOptions.openai.reasoningEffort: 'low'.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses provider sends each message-level effort update as a
configuration_update input item.

contents.heading: changing-reasoning-effort-mid-conversation
contents.content: Message-level updates also work with streamText and previousResponseId.

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: Effort updates are supported on GPT-6-family models with these settings:

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: Setting

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: Required value

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: reasoningMode

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: 'standard' (default)

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: truncation

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: 'disabled' (default)

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: Each update must use exactly content: ''.

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content:
Updates cannot be consecutive, even with the same effort. This also applies
across the boundary with history referenced by previousResponseId or
conversation.

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content: Requests that violate these restrictions are rejected.

contents.heading: restrictions
contents.content:
Effort update messages are sent even if systemMessageMode is set to
remove.

contents.heading: request-level-update-option
contents.content:
The request-level providerOptions.openai.reasoningEffortUpdate option is a
convenience that prepends a configuration update to the input. When using
message-level updates, omit this option.

contents.heading: request-level-update-option
contents.content:
The request-level option continues to warn and omit updates for unsupported
models or configurations.

contents.heading: reasoning-output
contents.content: For reasoning models like gpt-5, you can enable reasoning summaries to see the model's thought process. Different models support different summarizers—for example, o4-mini supports detailed summaries. Set reasoningSummary: "auto" to automatically receive the richest level available.

contents.heading: reasoning-output
contents.content: For non-streaming calls with generateText, the reasoning summaries are available in the reasoning field of the response:

contents.heading: reasoning-output
contents.content: Learn more about reasoning summaries in the OpenAI documentation.

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content:
OpenAI's WebSocket API keeps a persistent connection open, which can significantly
reduce Time-to-First-Byte (TTFB) in agentic workflows with many tool calls.
After the initial connection, subsequent requests skip TCP/TLS/HTTP negotiation entirely.

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content:
The ai-sdk-openai-websocket-fetch
package provides a drop-in fetch replacement that routes streaming requests
through a persistent WebSocket connection.

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content: Pass the WebSocket fetch to createOpenAI via the fetch option:

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content:
The first request will be slower because it must establish the WebSocket connection
(DNS + TCP + TLS + WebSocket upgrade). After that, subsequent steps in a
multi-step tool-calling loop reuse the open connection, resulting in lower TTFB
per step.

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content:
The WebSocket transport only routes streaming requests to the OpenAI Responses
API (POST /responses with stream: true) through the WebSocket. All other
requests (non-streaming, embeddings, etc.) fall through to the standard
fetch implementation.

contents.heading: websocket-transport
contents.content:
You can see a live side-by-side comparison of HTTP vs WebSocket streaming performance
in the demo app.

contents.heading: verbosity-control
contents.content: You can control the length and detail of model responses using the textVerbosity parameter:

contents.heading: verbosity-control
contents.content: The textVerbosity parameter scales output length without changing the underlying prompt:

contents.heading: verbosity-control
contents.content: 'low': Produces terse, minimal responses

contents.heading: verbosity-control
contents.content: 'medium': Balanced detail (default)

contents.heading: verbosity-control
contents.content: 'high': Verbose responses with comprehensive detail

contents.heading: namespaced-function-calls
contents.content:
OpenAI supports grouping related function tools into
namespaces.
When the Responses API returns a function_call with a namespace, the OpenAI provider
exposes this value on the generated tool-call part as
providerMetadata.openai.namespace.

contents.heading: namespaced-function-calls
contents.content:
When using streamText, the namespace is available on the tool-input-end event and on
the final tool-call event:

contents.heading: namespaced-function-calls
contents.content:
If you persist or reconstruct messages for later turns, preserve the OpenAI provider
metadata on tool-call parts. The SDK uses providerMetadata.openai.namespace or
providerOptions.openai.namespace to round-trip the namespace back to OpenAI on
subsequent requests.

contents.heading: async-tool-calling
contents.content:
GPT-6 Astra and later Responses models support
async tool calling.
An async tool lets the model continue generating independent output after issuing
the call instead of waiting for its result. Your application still executes the
tool and sends its result in a later request using the original tool call ID.

contents.heading: async-tool-calling
contents.content: Enable async calling on a function tool with providerOptions.openai.async:

contents.heading: async-tool-calling
contents.content:
The generated tool call exposes the provider marker as
providerMetadata.openai.async. Use providerMetadata.openai.responseId as the
next request's previousResponseId, and submit the result in a tool message with
the original toolCallId.

contents.heading: async-tool-calling
contents.content:
With streamText, OpenAI can continue streaming text after the completed
tool-call part. Use the tool's onInputAvailable callback to start work as soon
as that part arrives. If execute returns the same already-running promise, tool
execution overlaps the rest of the model stream. Omit execute when the job
should outlive the current generation and submit its result in a later request.

contents.heading: async-tool-calling
contents.content:
Async calling applies to directly called function and custom tools. It does not
apply to hosted tools.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: The OpenAI responses API supports web search through the openai.tools.webSearch tool.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: The web search tool supports the following configuration options:

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: externalWebAccess boolean - Whether to use external web access for fetching live content. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: searchContextSize 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' - Controls the amount of context used for the search. Higher values provide more comprehensive results but may have higher latency and cost.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: userLocation - Optional location information to provide geographically relevant results. Includes type (always 'approximate'), country, city, region, and timezone.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: filters - Optional filter configuration to restrict search results.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: allowedDomains string[] - Up to 100 allowed domains for the search.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: blockedDomains string[] - Up to 100 blocked domains for the search.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: Omit the HTTP or HTTPS prefix from domain filters. Subdomains of configured domains are automatically included or excluded.

contents.heading: web-search-tool
contents.content: For detailed information on configuration options see the OpenAI Web Search Tool documentation.

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: The OpenAI responses API supports file search through the openai.tools.fileSearch tool.

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: You can force the use of the file search tool by setting the toolChoice parameter to { type: 'tool', toolName: 'file_search' }.

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: The file search tool supports filtering with both comparison and compound filters:

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: Comparison filters - Filter by a single attribute:

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: eq - Equal to

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: ne - Not equal to

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: gt - Greater than

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: gte - Greater than or equal to

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: lt - Less than

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: lte - Less than or equal to

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: in - Value is in array

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: nin - Value is not in array

contents.heading: file-search-tool
contents.content: Compound filters - Combine multiple filters with and or or:

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content:
OpenAI's Responses API supports multi-modal image generation as a provider-defined tool.
Availability is restricted to specific models (for example, gpt-5 variants).

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content: You can use the image tool with either generateText or streamText:

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content:
When you set store: false, then previously generated images will not be
accessible by the model. We recommend using the image generation tool without
setting store: false.

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content:
To use xhigh or max quality, select gpt-image-2.5-flare or
gpt-image-2.5-sunburst as the image generation tool's model:

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content:
For complete details on model availability, image quality controls, supported sizes, and tool-specific parameters,
refer to the OpenAI documentation:

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content: Image generation overview and models: OpenAI Image Generation

contents.heading: image-generation-tool
contents.content: Image generation tool parameters (background, size, quality, format, etc.): Image Generation Tool Options

contents.heading: code-interpreter-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI responses API supports the code interpreter tool through the openai.tools.codeInterpreter tool.
This allows models to write and execute Python code.

contents.heading: code-interpreter-tool
contents.content: The code interpreter tool can be configured with:

contents.heading: code-interpreter-tool
contents.content: container: Either a container ID string or an object with fileIds to specify uploaded files that should be available to the code interpreter

contents.heading: code-interpreter-tool
contents.content:
When working with files generated by the Code Interpreter, reference
information can be obtained from both annotations in Text
Parts and providerMetadata in
Source Document Parts.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: The OpenAI responses API supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through the openai.tools.mcp tool. This allows models to call tools exposed by remote MCP servers or service connectors.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: The MCP tool can be configured with:

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: serverLabel string (required)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: A label to identify the MCP server. This label is used in tool calls to distinguish between multiple MCP servers.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: serverUrl string (required if connectorId is not provided)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: The URL for the MCP server. Either serverUrl or connectorId must be provided.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: connectorId string (required if serverUrl is not provided)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: Identifier for a service connector. Either serverUrl or connectorId must be provided.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: serverDescription string (optional)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: Optional description of the MCP server that helps the model understand its purpose.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: allowedTools string[] | object (optional)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: Controls which tools from the MCP server are available. Can be:

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: An array of tool names: ['tool1', 'tool2']

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: An object with filters:

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: authorization string (optional)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: OAuth access token for authenticating with the MCP server or connector.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: headers Record<string, string> (optional)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: Optional HTTP headers to include in requests to the MCP server.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: requireApproval 'always' | 'never' | object (optional)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: Controls which MCP tool calls require user approval before execution. Can be:

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: 'always': All MCP tool calls require approval

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: 'never': No MCP tool calls require approval (default)

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: An object with filters:

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content: When approval is required, the model will return a tool-approval-request content part that you can use to prompt the user for approval. See Human in the Loop for more details on implementing approval workflows.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content:
When requireApproval is not set, tool calls are approved by default. Be sure
to connect to only trusted MCP servers, who you trust to share your data with.

contents.heading: mcp-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI MCP tool is different from the general MCP client approach
documented in MCP Tools. The OpenAI MCP tool is
a built-in provider-defined tool that allows OpenAI models to directly connect
to MCP servers, while the general MCP client requires you to convert MCP tools
to AI SDK tools first.

contents.heading: local-shell-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI responses API support the local shell tool for Codex models through the openai.tools.localShell tool.
Local shell is a tool that allows agents to run shell commands locally on a machine you or the user provides.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports the shell tool through the openai.tools.shell tool.
The shell tool allows running bash commands and interacting with a command line.
The model proposes shell commands; your integration executes them and returns the outputs.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content:
Running arbitrary shell commands can be dangerous. Always sandbox execution or
add strict allow-/deny-lists before forwarding a command to the system shell.

contents.heading: shell-tool
contents.content: The shell tool supports three environment modes that control where commands are executed:

contents.heading: local-execution-default
contents.content: When no environment is specified (or type: 'local' is used), commands are executed locally via your execute callback:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: Set environment.type to 'containerAuto' to run commands in an OpenAI-hosted container. No execute callback is needed — OpenAI handles execution server-side:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: The containerAuto environment supports:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: fileIds string[] - File IDs to make available in the container

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: memoryLimit '1g' | '4g' | '16g' | '64g' - Memory limit for the container

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: networkPolicy - Network access policy:

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: { type: 'disabled' } — no network access

contents.heading: hosted-container-auto
contents.content: { type: 'allowlist', allowedDomains: string[], domainSecrets?: Array<{ domain, name, value }> } — allow specific domains with optional secrets

contents.heading: existing-container-reference
contents.content: Set environment.type to 'containerReference' to use an existing container by ID:

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: For local execution (default or type: 'local'), your execute function must return an output array with results for each command:

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: stdout string - Standard output from the command

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: stderr string - Standard error from the command

contents.heading: execute-callback
contents.content: outcome - Either { type: 'timeout' } or { type: 'exit', exitCode: number }

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Skills are versioned bundles of files with a SKILL.md manifest that extend the shell tool's capabilities. They can be attached to both containerAuto and local environments.

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Container skills support two formats — by reference (for skills uploaded to OpenAI) or inline (as a base64-encoded zip):

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: Local skills point to a directory on disk containing a SKILL.md file:

contents.heading: skills
contents.content: For more details on creating skills, see the OpenAI Skills documentation.

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports the apply patch tool for GPT-5.1 models through the openai.tools.applyPatch tool.
The apply patch tool lets the model create, update, and delete files in your codebase using structured diffs.
Instead of just suggesting edits, the model emits patch operations that your application applies and reports back on,
enabling iterative, multi-step code editing workflows.

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: Your execute function must return:

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: status 'completed' | 'failed' - Whether the patch was applied successfully

contents.heading: apply-patch-tool
contents.content: output string (optional) - Human-readable log text (e.g., results or error messages)

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content:
Tool search allows the model to dynamically search for and load tools into context as needed,
rather than loading all tool definitions up front. This can reduce token usage, cost, and latency
when you have many tools. Mark the tools you want to make searchable with deferLoading: true
in their providerOptions.

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: There are two execution modes:

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: Server-executed (hosted): OpenAI searches across the deferred tools declared in the request and returns the loaded subset in the same response. No extra round-trip is needed.

contents.heading: tool-search
contents.content: Client-executed: The model emits a tool_search_call, your application performs the lookup, and you return the matching tools via the execute callback.

contents.heading: server-executed-hosted-tool-search
contents.content:
Use hosted tool search when the candidate tools are already known at request time.
Add openai.tools.toolSearch() with no arguments and mark your tools with deferLoading: true:

contents.heading: server-executed-hosted-tool-search
contents.content:
In hosted mode, the model internally searches the deferred tools, loads the relevant ones, and
proceeds to call them — all within a single response. The tool_search_call and
tool_search_output items appear in the response with execution: 'server' and call_id: null.

contents.heading: namespaces
contents.content:
Use providerOptions.openai.namespace to group related function tools for OpenAI.
The SDK keeps each tool executable as a normal AI SDK tool, but serializes grouped
tools as OpenAI namespace entries in the request:

contents.heading: namespaces
contents.content:
Tools in the same namespace must use the same namespace name and description.
For best results with tool search, keep namespace descriptions concise and put
detailed usage guidance on the individual function tools.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content:
Use client-executed tool search when tool discovery depends on runtime state — for example,
tools that vary per tenant, project, or external system. Pass execution: 'client' along with
a description, parameters schema, and an execute callback:

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: In client mode, the flow spans two steps:

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: Step 1: The model emits a tool_search_call with execution: 'client' and a non-null call_id. The SDK calls your execute callback with the search arguments. Your callback returns the discovered tools.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: Step 2: The SDK sends the tool_search_output (with the matching call_id) back to the model. The model can now call the loaded tools as normal function calls.

contents.heading: client-executed-tool-search
contents.content: For more details, see the OpenAI Tool Search documentation.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports
custom tools
through the openai.tools.customTool tool.
Custom tools return a raw string instead of JSON, optionally constrained to a grammar
(regex or Lark syntax). This makes them useful for generating structured text like
SQL queries, code snippets, or any output that must match a specific pattern.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: Custom tools also work with streamText:

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: The custom tool can be configured with:

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: name string (required) - The name of the custom tool. Used to identify the tool in tool calls.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: description string (optional) - A description of what the tool does, to help the model understand when to use it.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: format object (optional) - The output format constraint. Omit for unconstrained text output.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: type 'grammar' | 'text' - The format type. Use 'grammar' for constrained output or 'text' for explicit unconstrained text.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: syntax 'regex' | 'lark' - (grammar only) The grammar syntax. Use 'regex' for regular expression patterns or 'lark' for Lark parser grammar.

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: definition string - (grammar only) The grammar definition string (a regex pattern or Lark grammar).

contents.heading: custom-tool
contents.content: execute function (optional) - An async function that receives the raw string input and returns a string result. Enables multi-turn tool calling.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
The allowedTools provider option restricts which of the tools you declared the model is allowed to
call, while still sending the full tools list to OpenAI. Because the tools list stays byte-identical
across requests, the prompt cache is preserved — unlike activeTools, which removes tools from the
request and invalidates the cache whenever the allow-list changes.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content: allowedTools is only supported by the Responses API, and it overrides the request-level toolChoice.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
toolNames string[] - The tools the model may call, named as you declared them in tools. For
provider-defined tools you may also use the canonical OpenAI name (for example web_search).

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
mode 'auto' | 'required' (optional) - 'auto' (default) lets the model pick one of the allowed
tools or answer with a message; 'required' forces it to call at least one of them.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
Both function tools and provider-defined tools can be allow-listed, including web search, file search,
image generation, code interpreter, apply patch, shell, custom tools, and MCP servers.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
If a name matches both a tool you declared and the canonical OpenAI name of a different tool, the tool
you declared under that name wins, and a warning reports the ambiguity. If several tools share the same
canonical name — two MCP servers, for example — that name is ambiguous, so it is dropped with a warning;
name those tools as you declared them instead.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
Three kinds of tools cannot be allow-listed, because OpenAI's allowed_tools
only sees the eagerly-loaded tool list: the tool search tool,
tools marked with deferLoading, and tools grouped into a namespace. Naming
one of these in allowedTools removes it from the allow-list and emits a
warning; if that leaves no tools at all, the request fails with an error
instead of silently sending no restriction.

contents.heading: restricting-callable-tools
contents.content:
An MCP server is allow-listed as a whole: the entry carries the server label,
so every tool on that server is callable. To restrict which tools on a server
the model may call, use the MCP tool's own allowedTools argument.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports Image inputs for appropriate models.
You can pass Image files as part of the message content using the 'image' type:

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content:
The model will have access to the image and will respond to questions about it.
The image should be passed using the image field.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: image-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of an image.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content:
The OpenAI Responses API supports reading PDF files.
You can pass PDF files as part of the message content using the file type:

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of a pdf.

contents.heading: pdf-inputs
contents.content:
The model will have access to the contents of the PDF file and
respond to questions about it.
The PDF file should be passed using the data field,
and the mediaType should be set to 'application/pdf'.

contents.heading: structured-outputs
contents.content: The OpenAI Responses API supports structured outputs. You can use generateText or streamText with Output to enforce structured outputs.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: When using the OpenAI Responses API, the SDK attaches OpenAI-specific metadata to output parts via providerMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
This metadata can be used on the client side for tasks such as rendering citations or downloading files generated by the Code Interpreter.
To enable type-safe handling of this metadata, the AI SDK exports dedicated TypeScript types.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: For text parts, when part.type === 'text', the providerMetadata is provided in the form of OpenaiResponsesTextProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: This metadata includes the following fields:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
itemId
The ID of the output item in the Responses API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
annotations (optional)
An array of annotation objects generated by the model.
If no annotations are present, this property itself may be omitted (undefined).

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: Each element in annotations is a discriminated union with a required type field. Supported types include, for example:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: url_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: container_file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content: file_path

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
These annotations directly correspond to the annotation objects defined by the Responses API and can be used for inline reference rendering or output analysis.
For details, see the official OpenAI documentation:
Responses API – output text annotations.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-text-parts
contents.content:
When implementing file downloads for files generated by the Code Interpreter,
the container_id and file_id available in providerMetadata can be used
to retrieve the file content. For details, see the Retrieve container file
content
API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content:
When using the OpenAI Responses API, reasoning output parts can include provider metadata.
To handle this metadata in a type-safe way, use OpenaiResponsesReasoningProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: For reasoning parts, when part.type === 'reasoning', the providerMetadata is provided in the form of OpenaiResponsesReasoningProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: This metadata includes the following fields:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: itemIdThe ID of the reasoning item in the Responses API.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-reasoning-parts
contents.content: reasoningEncryptedContent (optional)Encrypted reasoning content (only returned when requested via include: ['reasoning.encrypted_content']).

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: For source document parts, when part.type === 'source' and sourceType === 'document', the providerMetadata is provided as OpenaiResponsesSourceDocumentProviderMetadata.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: This metadata is also a discriminated union with a required type field. Supported types include:

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: container_file_citation

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: file_path

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content: Each type includes the identifiers required to work with the referenced resource, such as fileId and containerId.

contents.heading: typed-providermetadata-in-source-document-parts
contents.content:
Annotations in text parts follow the OpenAI Responses API specification and
therefore use snake_case properties (e.g. file_id, container_id). In
contrast, providerMetadata for source document parts is normalized by the
SDK to camelCase (e.g. fileId, containerId). Fields that depend on the
original text content, such as start_index and end_index, are omitted, as
are fields like filename that are directly available on the source object.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the OpenAI chat API using the .chat() factory method.
The first argument is the model id, e.g. gpt-4.
The OpenAI chat models support tool calls and some have multi-modal capabilities.
Use this factory when a custom baseURL points at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
that implements Chat Completions but not the Responses API.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
OpenAI chat models support also some model specific provider options that are not part of the standard call settings.
You can pass them in the providerOptions argument:

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: The following optional provider options are available for OpenAI chat models:

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: logitBias Record<number, number>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Modifies the likelihood of specified tokens appearing in the completion.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Accepts a JSON object that maps tokens (specified by their token ID in
the GPT tokenizer) to an associated bias value from -100 to 100. You
can use this tokenizer tool to convert text to token IDs. Mathematically,
the bias is added to the logits generated by the model prior to sampling.
The exact effect will vary per model, but values between -1 and 1 should
decrease or increase likelihood of selection; values like -100 or 100
should result in a ban or exclusive selection of the relevant token.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: As an example, you can pass {"50256": -100} to prevent the token from being generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: logprobs boolean | number

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Return the log probabilities of the tokens. Including logprobs will increase
the response size and can slow down response times. However, it can
be useful to better understand how the model is behaving.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Setting to true will return the log probabilities of the tokens that
were generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Setting to a number will return the log probabilities of the top n
tokens that were generated.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: parallelToolCalls boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help OpenAI to
monitor and detect abuse. Learn more.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: reasoningEffort 'none' | 'minimal' | 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Reasoning effort for reasoning models. Defaults to medium. If you use
providerOptions to set the reasoningEffort option, this
model setting will be ignored.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Supported reasoning efforts vary by model. GPT-5.6 supports 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh', and 'max'.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: maxCompletionTokens number

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Maximum number of completion tokens to generate. Useful for reasoning models.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: store boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Whether to enable persistence in Responses API.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: metadata Record<string, string>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Metadata to associate with the request.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: prediction Record<string, any>

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Parameters for prediction mode.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: serviceTier 'auto' | 'flex' | 'priority' | 'fast' | 'default'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Service tier for the request. Set to 'flex' for 50% cheaper processing
at the cost of increased latency (available for o3, o4-mini, and gpt-5 models).
Set to 'priority' for faster processing with Enterprise access (available for gpt-4, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o3, o4-mini; gpt-5-nano is not supported).
'fast' is OpenAI's newer name for the 'priority' tier; the two are interchangeable, and responses from
gpt-5.6 and earlier report serviceTier: 'priority' for either.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Defaults to 'auto'.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: strictJsonSchema boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content:
Whether to use strict JSON schema validation.
Defaults to true.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: textVerbosity 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Controls the verbosity of the model's responses. Lower values will result in more concise responses, while higher values will result in more verbose responses.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheKey string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: A cache key for manual prompt caching control. Used by OpenAI to cache responses for similar requests to optimize your cache hit rates.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheOptions object

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Configures prompt caching for GPT-5.6 and later models. mode can be 'implicit' or 'explicit', and ttl currently only supports '30m'. In explicit mode, only content blocks marked with a prompt cache breakpoint are cached.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: promptCacheRetention 'in_memory' | '24h'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: The legacy retention policy for models before GPT-5.6. Set to '24h' to enable extended prompt caching on supported models. For GPT-5.6 and later models, use promptCacheOptions.ttl instead.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: safetyIdentifier string

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: A stable identifier used to help detect users of your application that may be violating OpenAI's usage policies. The IDs should be a string that uniquely identifies each user.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: systemMessageMode 'system' | 'developer' | 'remove'

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Override the system message mode for this model. If not specified, the mode is automatically determined based on the model. system uses the 'system' role for system messages (default for most models); developer uses the 'developer' role (used by reasoning models); remove removes system messages entirely.

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: forceReasoning boolean

contents.heading: chat-models
contents.content: Force treating this model as a reasoning model. This is useful for "stealth" reasoning models (e.g. via a custom baseURL) where the model ID is not recognized by the SDK's allowlist. When enabled, the SDK applies reasoning-model parameter compatibility rules and defaults systemMessageMode to developer unless overridden.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
OpenAI has introduced the o1,o3, and o4 series of reasoning models.
Currently, o4-mini, o3, o3-mini, and o1 are available via both the chat and responses APIs. The
model gpt-5.1-codex-mini is available only via the responses API.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Reasoning models currently only generate text, have several limitations, and are only supported using generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: They support additional settings and response metadata:

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can use providerOptions to set

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: the reasoningEffort option (or alternatively the reasoningEffort model setting), which determines the amount of reasoning the model performs.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can use response providerMetadata to access the number of reasoning tokens that the model generated.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
System messages are automatically converted to OpenAI developer messages for
reasoning models when supported.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: You can control how system messages are handled by providerOptions systemMessageMode:

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: developer: treat the prompt as a developer message (default for reasoning models).

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: system: keep the system message as a system-level instruction.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: remove: remove the system message from the messages.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
Reasoning models require additional runtime inference to complete their
reasoning phase before generating a response. This introduces longer latency
compared to other models.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content:
maxOutputTokens is automatically mapped to max_completion_tokens for
reasoning models.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
Strict structured outputs are enabled by default.
You can disable them by setting the strictJsonSchema option to false.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI structured outputs have several
limitations,
in particular around the supported schemas,
and are therefore opt-in.

contents.heading: strict-structured-outputs
contents.content:
For example, optional schema properties are not supported.
You need to change Zod .nullish() and .optional() to .nullable().

contents.heading: logprobs
contents.content:
OpenAI provides logprobs information for completion/chat models.
You can access it in the providerMetadata object.

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content:
The OpenAI Chat API supports Image inputs for appropriate models.
You can pass Image files as part of the message content using the 'image' type:

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content:
The model will have access to the image and will respond to questions about it.
The image should be passed using the image field.

contents.heading: image-support
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of an image.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content:
The OpenAI Chat API supports reading PDF files.
You can pass PDF files as part of the message content using the file type:

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content:
The model will have access to the contents of the PDF file and
respond to questions about it.
The PDF file should be passed using the data field,
and the mediaType should be set to 'application/pdf'.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content: You can also pass a file-id from the OpenAI Files API.

contents.heading: pdf-support
contents.content: You can also pass the URL of a PDF.

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI supports predicted outputs for gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini.
Predicted outputs help you reduce latency by allowing you to specify a base text that the model should modify.
You can enable predicted outputs by adding the prediction option to the providerOptions.openai object:

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI provides usage information for predicted outputs (acceptedPredictionTokens and rejectedPredictionTokens).
You can access it in the providerMetadata object.

contents.heading: predicted-outputs
contents.content:
OpenAI Predicted Outputs have several
limitations,
e.g. unsupported API parameters and no tool calling support.

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content: You can use the openai provider option to set the image input detail to high, low, original, or auto:

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content: For GPT-5.6, original preserves the input dimensions without resizing to a patch budget or pixel-dimension limit. auto and an omitted detail setting use the same sizing behavior as original, which can increase input token usage for large images.

contents.heading: image-detail
contents.content:
Because the UIMessage type (used by AI SDK UI hooks like useChat) does not
support the providerOptions property, you can use convertToModelMessages
first before passing the messages to functions like generateText or
streamText. For more details on providerOptions usage, see
here.

contents.heading: distillation
contents.content:
OpenAI supports model distillation for some models.
If you want to store a generation for use in the distillation process, you can add the store option to the providerOptions.openai object.
This will save the generation to the OpenAI platform for later use in distillation.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content:
OpenAI has introduced Prompt Caching for supported models
including gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content:
Prompt caching is automatically enabled for these models, when the prompt is 1024 tokens or longer. It does
not need to be explicitly enabled.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: You can use the response usage to access the number of prompt tokens that were a cache hit via usage.inputTokenDetails.cacheReadTokens.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For GPT-5.6 and later models, usage.inputTokenDetails.cacheWriteTokens reports tokens written to the cache.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For GPT-5.6 and later models, promptCacheOptions.ttl sets a minimum cache lifetime of 30 minutes. Earlier models generally retain in-memory prefixes for 5-10 minutes of inactivity, up to one hour.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: To improve cache hit rates, you can manually control caching using the promptCacheKey option:

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: GPT-5.6 and later models support explicit cache breakpoints on text, image, and file content blocks. Set a request-level cache key and mark the end of each reusable prefix with promptCacheBreakpoint:

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: In 'implicit' mode, OpenAI places an automatic breakpoint on the latest message and also honors explicit breakpoints. In 'explicit' mode, only marked content blocks are eligible for caching; a request without any explicit breakpoint does not use prompt caching.

contents.heading: prompt-caching
contents.content: For models before GPT-5.6 that support extended caching, you can keep cached prefixes active for up to 24 hours:

contents.heading: audio-input
contents.content: With the gpt-4o-audio-preview model, you can pass audio files to the model.

contents.heading: audio-input
contents.content:
The gpt-4o-audio-preview model is currently in preview and requires at least
some audio inputs. It will not work with non-audio data.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the OpenAI completions API using the .completion() factory method.
The first argument is the model id.
Currently only gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct is supported.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
OpenAI completion models support also some model specific settings that are not part of the standard call settings.
You can pass them as an options argument:

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: The following optional provider options are available for OpenAI completion models:

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: echo: boolean

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: Echo back the prompt in addition to the completion.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: logitBias Record<number, number>

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: Modifies the likelihood of specified tokens appearing in the completion.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Accepts a JSON object that maps tokens (specified by their token ID in
the GPT tokenizer) to an associated bias value from -100 to 100. You
can use this tokenizer tool to convert text to token IDs. Mathematically,
the bias is added to the logits generated by the model prior to sampling.
The exact effect will vary per model, but values between -1 and 1 should
decrease or increase likelihood of selection; values like -100 or 100
should result in a ban or exclusive selection of the relevant token.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
As an example, you can pass {"50256": -100} to prevent the <|endoftext|>
token from being generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: logprobs boolean | number

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Return the log probabilities of the tokens. Including logprobs will increase
the response size and can slow down response times. However, it can
be useful to better understand how the model is behaving.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Setting to true will return the log probabilities of the tokens that
were generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
Setting to a number will return the log probabilities of the top n
tokens that were generated.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: suffix string

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: The suffix that comes after a completion of inserted text.

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: completion-models
contents.content:
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help OpenAI to
monitor and detect abuse. Learn more.

contents.heading: transcription-models

The language of the input audio. Supplying the input language in ISO-639-1 format (e.g. 'en') will improve accuracy and latency.

contents.heading: transcription-models

Optional.

contents.heading: transcription-models
contents.content:

The sampling temperature, between 0 and 1. Higher values like 0.8 will make the output more random, while lower values like 0.2 will make it more focused and deterministic. If set to 0, the model will use log probability to automatically increase the temperature until certain thresholds are hit.
Defaults to 0.
Optional.

metadata.title: Perplexity
metadata.description: Learn how to use Perplexity's Sonar API with the AI SDK.

contents.content: The Perplexity provider offers access to Sonar API - a language model that uniquely combines real-time web search with natural language processing. Each response is grounded in current web data and includes detailed citations, making it ideal for research, fact-checking, and obtaining up-to-date information.
API keys can be obtained from the Perplexity Platform.

metadata.description: Learn how to use QuiverAI models with the AI SDK.

contents.content: The QuiverAI provider is available via the @ai-sdk/quiverai module. You can install it with

For more on image generation with the AI SDK see generateImage().

contents.content: Supported options:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Choose between text-to-SVG generation (generate, default) and image-to-SVG vectorization (vectorize).

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Reasoning effort for generation or vectorization. When omitted, QuiverAI uses its default.

contents.content: Requested SVG root attributes. Supports viewBox with numeric minX, minY, and positive width and height. This is separate from the unsupported size and aspectRatio options.

contents.content: When vectorizing, automatically crop the input image. Only used with operation: 'vectorize'.

contents.content: arrow-1 and arrow-1.1 accept up to 4 reference images. arrow-1.1-max accepts up to 16. For Arrow 2 and other model IDs, the provider allows the endpoint maximum of 16 references and lets the API enforce any lower model-specific limit.

contents.heading: vectorizing-a-raster-image
contents.content: Set operation to vectorize and pass a single image in prompt.images:

contents.heading: vectorizing-a-raster-image
contents.content: Vectorization returns one SVG per API request. To request multiple vectorizations with n, also set maxImagesPerCall: 1 so generateImage splits them into separate calls.

contents.heading: billing-and-usage
contents.content: Arrow 2 models return measured token counts in result.usage. Fixed-credit models may return compatibility token counts of zero; their credit charge is available in result.providerMetadata?.quiverai?.credits when supplied by the API.

contents.heading: billing-and-usage
contents.content: Model availability and supported operations depend on your organization and API key permissions. Consult QuiverAI's model catalog for current capabilities and billing. Editing, animation, and the Responses API are not yet exposed by this provider.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
You can create xAI models using a provider instance. The
first argument is the model id, e.g. grok-4.7.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: By default, xai(modelId) uses the Chat API. To use the Responses API with server-side agentic tools, explicitly use xai.responses(modelId).

contents.heading: example
contents.content: You can use xAI language models to generate text with the generateText function:

contents.heading: example
contents.content:
xAI language models can also be used in the streamText function
and support structured data generation with Output
(see AI SDK Core).

contents.heading: reasoning-effort
contents.content:
For models with configurable reasoning, you can control how much effort the
model spends thinking before responding with
providerOptions.xai.reasoningEffort. The AI SDK option accepts 'none',
'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh', but each xAI model supports a
subset.

contents.heading: reasoning-effort
contents.content:
Support and defaults are model-specific. grok-4.6 supports 'low',
'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh', defaults to 'high', and cannot disable
reasoning. grok-4.3 supports 'none', 'low', 'medium', and 'high'.
grok-4.5 supports 'low', 'medium', and 'high', defaults to 'high',
and cannot disable reasoning. The grok-4.20-reasoning and
grok-4.20-non-reasoning variants do not accept this option, and neither does
grok-build-0.1. For grok-4.20-multi-agent, 'low', 'medium', and
'high' control the number of agents instead of reasoning depth. See xAI's
reasoning
docs and
Grok 4.3 model page for
current details.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content:
xAI chat models support additional provider options that are not part of
the standard call settings. You can pass them in the providerOptions argument:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: The following optional provider options are available for xAI chat models:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: reasoningEffort 'none' | 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Control the reasoning effort for supported models. See Reasoning Effort for model-specific values and defaults.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: logprobs boolean

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Return log probabilities for output tokens.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: topLogprobs number

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Number of most likely tokens to return per token position (0-8). When set, logprobs is automatically enabled.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: parallel_function_calling boolean

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use. When true, the model can call multiple functions in parallel. When false, the model will call functions sequentially. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: priority-processing
contents.content:
providerOptions.xai.serviceTier requests higher scheduling priority, which
typically lowers time-to-first-token and speeds up inter-token latency. This
works for both the Responses API (default) and the Chat Completions API
(xai.chat()).

contents.heading: priority-processing
contents.content:
Priority requests are billed at a premium per-token rate, and xAI only charges
that rate when the response confirms the priority tier — so read the applied
tier back from providerMetadata.xai.serviceTier rather than assuming the
request you sent is the tier you got. Omitting the option is equivalent to
'default'. See xAI's priority processing
docs.

contents.heading: responses-api-agentic-tools
contents.content: You can use the xAI Responses API with the xai.responses(modelId) factory method for server-side agentic tool calling. This enables the model to autonomously orchestrate tool calls and research on xAI's servers.

contents.content: You can customize the image generation behavior with provider-specific settings via providerOptions.xai:

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: resolution '1k' | '2k'

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content:
Output resolution. 1k produces ~1024×1024 images, 2k produces ~2048×2048
images (actual dimensions vary based on aspect ratio). Available for
grok-imagine-image-pro.

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: quality 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'

contents.heading: image-provider-options
contents.content: Image quality level. Higher quality may increase generation time.

contents.content: Model
