contents.heading: video-models
contents.content:
You can create xAI video models using the .video() factory method.
For more on video generation with the AI SDK see generateVideo().

contents.heading: video-models
contents.content: This provider supports standard video generation from text prompts or image input, plus explicit video editing, video extension, and reference-to-video (R2V) operations.

contents.heading: text-to-video
contents.content: Generate videos from text prompts:

contents.heading: generation-with-image-input
contents.content: Generate videos using an image as the starting frame with an optional text prompt. This uses the standard generation path rather than a separate provider mode:

contents.heading: generation-with-image-input
contents.content: You can also pass the starting frame via the top-level frameImages option using the first_frame role. This is provider-agnostic and accepts file data (e.g. a Buffer) or a { type: 'url', url } object:

contents.heading: generation-with-image-input
contents.content:
xAI does not support first-last-frame interpolation. A last_frame entry in
frameImages is ignored with a warning — use the extend-video mode to
continue from a video's last frame instead.

contents.heading: video-editing
contents.content: Edit an existing video using a text prompt by providing a source video URL via provider options:

contents.heading: video-editing
contents.content:
Video editing accepts input videos up to 8.7 seconds long. The duration,
aspectRatio, and resolution parameters are not supported for editing - the
output matches the input video's properties (capped at 720p).

contents.heading: chaining-and-concurrent-edits
video-extension
contents.content: Extend an existing video from its last frame. The duration controls the length of the extension only, not the total output. The output inherits aspectRatio and resolution from the source video.

contents.heading: video-extension
contents.content:
Video extension does not support custom aspectRatio or resolution — the
output inherits those from the source video. duration is supported and
controls how long the extension is (not the total video length).

contents.heading: reference-to-video-r2v
contents.content: Provide reference images to guide the video's style and content. Unlike image-to-video, reference images are not used as the first frame — the model incorporates their visual elements into the generated video. Each reference image can be a public HTTPS URL or a base64 data URI.

contents.heading: reference-to-video-r2v
contents.content: Use <IMAGE_1>, <IMAGE_2>, etc. in your prompt to reference specific images. Up to 7 reference images are supported per request.

contents.heading: reference-to-video-r2v
contents.content: Alternatively, use the provider-agnostic top-level inputReferences option. Providing it automatically selects reference-to-video mode, and it accepts file data (e.g. a Buffer) or { type: 'url', url } objects:

contents.heading: reference-to-video-r2v
contents.content:
inputReferences accepts image references only. A reference with a non-image
media type (for example a video or audio clip) is ignored with a warning, and a
reference with no media type is treated as an image. If no image reference
remains, reference-to-video is not selected and no reference images are sent.

contents.heading: reference-audio
contents.content:
Reference-to-video can also give the subject a voice. referenceVoiceIds takes
up to 3 xAI preset voice ids — you cannot upload your own audio clips.
Reference the voices from the prompt with <AUDIO_0>, <AUDIO_1>, and
<AUDIO_2>, in the order the voices are passed.

contents.heading: reference-audio
contents.content:
Valid voice ids come from the xAI
text-to-speech voice roster.
Ids are case-insensitive, and an unknown id returns a 400 response listing the
available voices. referenceVoiceIds is ignored with a warning when the
resolved operation is not reference-to-video.

contents.heading: reference-audio
contents.content:
xAI documents reference audio as available in the United States only, for
trusted partners. Requests from accounts without access are rejected by the
xAI API.

contents.heading: reference-audio
contents.content:
Reference-to-video supports duration, aspectRatio, and resolution. Use
mode to select the operation — each mode is mutually exclusive. When both
are provided, frameImages takes precedence over inputReferences, and
inputReferences takes precedence over the legacy referenceImageUrls
provider option. Reference-to-video is supported by the grok-imagine-video
and grok-imagine-video-1.5 models; native 1080p requires
grok-imagine-video-1.5.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
The following provider options are available via providerOptions.xai.
You can validate the provider options using the XaiVideoModelOptions type.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: pollIntervalMs number

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: Polling interval in milliseconds for checking task status. Defaults to 5000.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: pollTimeoutMs number

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: Maximum wait time in milliseconds for video generation. Defaults to 600000 (10 minutes).

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: resolution '480p' | '720p' | '1080p'

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
Video resolution. When using the SDK's standard resolution parameter,
1920x1080 maps to 1080p, 1280x720 maps to 720p, and 854x480 maps
to 480p. Use this provider option to pass the native format directly.
1080p requires the grok-imagine-video-1.5 model and is available for
text-to-video and image-to-video; reference-to-video is capped at 720p
(a 1080p request is downgraded with a warning).

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
Optional identifier for the end user responsible for the request. xAI uses
this value for abuse monitoring. It is sent unchanged for video generation
(including reference-to-video) and video editing requests, and is omitted
when not configured. It is not sent for video extension requests. Use an
opaque stable identifier and avoid sending unnecessary personal information.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: mode 'edit-video' | 'extend-video' | 'reference-to-video'

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: Selects the explicit video operation. Each mode is mutually exclusive:

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: 'edit-video' — edit an existing video (requires videoUrl)

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: 'extend-video' — extend a video from its last frame (requires videoUrl)

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: 'reference-to-video' — generate from reference images (requires referenceImageUrls)

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: When omitted, standard generation is used. Legacy inputs are still auto-detected from fields for backward compatibility.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: videoUrl string

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
URL of a source video. Used with mode: 'edit-video' for video editing
and mode: 'extend-video' for video extension.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: referenceImageUrls string[]

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
Array of reference image URLs (1–7 images) or base64 data URIs for
reference-to-video (R2V) generation. The model incorporates visual
elements from these images without using them as the first frame. Use
<IMAGE_1>, <IMAGE_2>, etc. in the prompt to reference specific
images. Used with mode: 'reference-to-video'.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content: referenceVoiceIds string[]

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
Up to 3 xAI preset voice ids that give the subject a voice in
reference-to-video (R2V) generation. Preset voices only — audio clips
cannot be uploaded. Ids are case-insensitive and come from the
text-to-speech voice roster;
an unknown id returns a 400 listing the available voices. Use <AUDIO_0>,
<AUDIO_1>, and <AUDIO_2> tags in the prompt to reference the voices.
Ignored with a warning outside reference-to-video. Reference audio is
documented as US-only and limited to trusted partners.

contents.heading: video-provider-options
contents.content:
Video generation is an asynchronous process that can take several minutes.
Consider setting pollTimeoutMs to at least 10 minutes (600000ms) for
reliable operation. Generated video URLs are ephemeral and should be
downloaded promptly.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio-and-resolution
contents.content:
For text-to-video, you can specify both aspectRatio and resolution.
The default aspect ratio is 16:9 and the default resolution is 480p. The
grok-imagine-video-1.5 model additionally supports native 1080p for
text-to-video and image-to-video.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio-and-resolution
contents.content:
For image-to-video, the output defaults to the input image's aspect ratio.
If you specify aspectRatio, it will override this and stretch the image to the
desired ratio.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio-and-resolution
contents.content:
For video editing, the output matches the input video's aspect ratio and
resolution. Custom duration, aspectRatio, and resolution are not
supported — the output resolution is capped at 720p (e.g., a 1080p input
will be downsized to 720p).

contents.heading: aspect-ratio-and-resolution
contents.content:
For video extension, the output inherits aspectRatio and resolution
from the source video. duration is supported and controls only the
extension length.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio-and-resolution
contents.content:
For reference-to-video (R2V), you can specify duration, aspectRatio,
and resolution. Unlike text-to-video, R2V is capped at 720p — a 1080p
request is downgraded to 720p with a warning.

metadata.title: Writing a Custom Provider
metadata.description: Learn how to write a custom provider for the AI SDK

title.children: Step 1: Create the Provider Entry Point

contents.content: The AI SDK provides a Language Model Specification that enables you to create custom providers compatible with the AI SDK. This specification ensures consistency across different providers.

contents.heading: publishing-your-provider
contents.content: Please publish your custom provider in your own GitHub repository and as an NPM package. You are responsible for hosting and maintaining your provider. Once published, you can submit a PR to the AI SDK repository to add your provider to the Community Providers documentation section. Use the OpenRouter provider documentation as a template for your documentation.

contents.heading: why-the-language-model-specification
contents.content: The Language Model Specification V3 is a standardized specification for interacting with language models that provides a unified abstraction layer across all AI providers. This specification creates a consistent interface that works seamlessly with different language models, ensuring that developers can interact with any provider using the same patterns and methods. It enables:

contents.heading: why-the-language-model-specification
contents.content:
If you open-source a provider, we'd love to promote it here. Please send us a
PR to add it to the Community Providers
section.

contents.heading: understanding-the-v3-specification
contents.content: The Language Model Specification V3 creates a robust abstraction layer that works across all current and future AI providers. By establishing a standardized interface, it provides the flexibility to support emerging LLM capabilities while ensuring your application code remains provider-agnostic and future-ready.

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: At its heart, the V2 specification defines three main interfaces:

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: ProviderV3: The top-level interface that serves as a factory for different model types

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: LanguageModelV3: The primary interface for text generation models

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: EmbeddingModelV3 and ImageModelV3: Interfaces for embeddings and image generation

contents.heading: providerv3
contents.content: The ProviderV3 interface acts as the entry point:

contents.heading: languagemodelv3
contents.content: The LanguageModelV3 interface defines the methods your provider must implement:

contents.heading: languagemodelv3
contents.content: Key aspects:

contents.heading: languagemodelv3
contents.content: specificationVersion: Must be 'V3'

contents.heading: languagemodelv3
contents.content: supportedUrls: Declares which URLs (for file parts) the provider can handle natively

contents.heading: languagemodelv3
contents.content: doGenerate/doStream: methods for non-streaming and streaming generation

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: Before diving into the details, it's important to understand the distinction between two key concepts in the V3 specification:

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: LanguageModelV3Content: The specification for what the models generate

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: LanguageModelV3Prompt: The specification for what you send to the model

contents.heading: languagemodelv3content
contents.content: The V3 specification supports five distinct content types that models can generate, each designed for specific use cases:

contents.heading: text-content
contents.content: The fundamental building block for all text generation:

contents.heading: text-content
contents.content: This is used for standard model responses, system messages, and any plain text output.

contents.heading: tool-calls
contents.content: Enable models to invoke functions with structured arguments:

contents.heading: tool-calls
contents.content: The toolCallId is crucial for correlating tool results back to their calls, especially in streaming scenarios.

contents.heading: file-generation
contents.content: Support for multimodal output generation:

contents.heading: file-generation
contents.content: This enables models to generate images, audio, documents, and other file types directly.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Dedicated support for chain-of-thought reasoning (essential for models like OpenAI's o1):

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Reasoning content is tracked separately from regular text, allowing for proper token accounting and UI presentation.

contents.heading: languagemodelv3prompt
contents.content: The V3 prompt format (LanguageModelV3Prompt) is designed as a flexible message array that supports multimodal inputs:

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Each message has a specific role with allowed content types:

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: System: Model instructions (text only)

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: User: Human inputs supporting text and files

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Assistant: Model outputs with full content type support

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Tool: Results from tool executions

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Prompt parts are the building blocks of messages in the prompt structure. While LanguageModelV3Content represents the model's output content, prompt parts are specifically designed for constructing input messages. Each message role supports different types of prompt parts:

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: System messages: Only support text content

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: User messages: Support text and file parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Assistant messages: Support text, file, reasoning, and tool call parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Tool messages: Only support tool result parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Let's explore each prompt part type:

contents.heading: text-parts
contents.content: The most basic prompt part, containing plain text content:

contents.heading: reasoning-parts
contents.content: Used in assistant messages to capture the model's reasoning process:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: Enable multimodal inputs by including files in prompts:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: The data field offers flexibility:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: Uint8Array: Direct binary data

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: string: Base64-encoded data

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: URL: Reference to external content (if supported by provider via supportedUrls)

contents.heading: tool-call-parts
contents.content: Represent tool calls made by the assistant:

contents.heading: tool-result-parts
contents.content: Contain the results of executed tool calls:

contents.heading: tool-result-parts
contents.content: The optional content field enables rich tool results including images, providing more flexibility than the basic result field.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: The streaming system uses typed events for different stages:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Stream Lifecycle Events:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: stream-start: Initial event with any warnings about unsupported features

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: response-metadata: Model information and response headers

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: finish: Final event with usage statistics and finish reason

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: error: Error events that can occur at any point

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Content Events:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: All content types (text, file, reasoning, source, tool-call) stream directly

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: tool-call-delta: Incremental updates for tool call arguments

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: reasoning-part-finish: Explicit marker for reasoning section completion

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Example stream sequence:

contents.heading: usage-tracking
contents.content: Enhanced usage information:

contents.heading: tools
contents.content: The V3 specification supports two types of tools:

contents.heading: function-tools
contents.content: Standard user-defined functions with JSON Schema validation:

contents.heading: provider-defined-client-tools
contents.content: Native provider capabilities exposed as tools:

contents.heading: provider-defined-client-tools
contents.content: Tool choice can be controlled via:

contents.heading: native-url-support
contents.content: Providers can declare URLs they can access directly:

contents.heading: native-url-support
contents.content: The AI SDK checks these patterns before downloading any URL-based content.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: The specification includes a flexible system for provider-specific features without breaking the standard interface:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Provider options can be specified at multiple levels:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Call level: In LanguageModelV3CallOptions

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Message level: On individual messages

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Part level: On specific content parts (text, file, etc.)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: This layered approach allows fine-grained control while maintaining compatibility.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The V2 specification emphasizes robust error handling:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Streaming Errors: Can be emitted at any point via { type: 'error', error: unknown }

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Warnings: Non-fatal issues reported in stream-start and response objects

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Finish Reasons: Clear indication of why generation stopped:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'stop': Natural completion

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'length': Hit max tokens

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'content-filter': Safety filtering

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'tool-calls': Stopped to execute tools

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'error': Generation failed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'other': Provider-specific reasons

Unified model access: Use one API key to access hundreds of models from leading providers like Anthropic, Google, Meta, and more.
Smart provider selection: Always hit the cheapest provider, enabling fallbacks for provider uptimes and rate limits.
Simplified tracing: Monitor your LLM's performance and debug applications with Helicone observability by default, including OpenTelemetry support for logs, metrics, and traces.
Improve performance and cost: Cache responses to reduce costs and latency.
Prompt management: Handle prompt versioning and playground directly from Helicone, so you no longer depend on engineers to make changes.
Learn more about Helicone's capabilities in the Helicone Documentation.

contents.content: The Helicone provider is available in the @helicone/ai-sdk-provider package. You can install it with:

contents.heading: advanced-features

contents.heading: advanced-features

metadata.title: Hindsight
metadata.description: Learn how to use Hindsight persistent memory with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Hindsight is a persistent memory service for AI agents. The @vectorize-io/hindsight-ai-sdk package provides five AI SDK-compatible tools that give your agents long-term memory across conversations.
Features include:
Five memory tools: retain, recall, reflect, getMentalModel, and getDocument
Works with generateText, streamText, and ToolLoopAgent
Infrastructure options (budget, tags, async mode) configured at tool creation — semantic choices left to the model
Multi-user memory isolation via bankId
Full TypeScript support

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Hindsight can be run locally with Docker or used as a cloud service.

contents.heading: self-hosted-docker
contents.content: The API will be available at http://localhost:8888 and the UI at http://localhost:9999.

contents.heading: cloud
contents.content: Sign up and get your API URL from the Hindsight dashboard.

contents.heading: multi-user-memory

contents.heading: multi-user-memory
contents.content: The HindsightClient instance is shared (created once at module level), while createHindsightTools is called per-request with the current user's ID.

contents.heading: configuration
contents.content: Infrastructure options are configured at tool creation time, keeping the application in control of cost, tagging, and performance while leaving semantic choices (what to remember, what to search for) to the model.

This community provider is not yet compatible with AI SDK 5. Please wait for
the provider to be updated or consider using an AI SDK 5 compatible
provider.
LangDB is a high-performance enterprise AI gateway built in Rust, designed to govern, secure, and optimize AI traffic.
LangDB provides OpenAI-compatible APIs, enabling developers to connect with multiple LLMs by changing just two lines of code. With LangDB, you can:
Provide access to all major LLMs
Enable plug-and-play functionality using any framework like Langchain, Vercel AI SDK, CrewAI, etc., for easy adoption.
Simplify implementation of tracing and cost optimization features, ensuring streamlined operations.
Dynamically route requests to the most suitable LLM based on predefined parameters.

metadata.title: Letta
metadata.description: Learn how to use the Letta provider with the AI SDK.

contents.content: The Letta AI SDK provider allows you to use Letta agents with the AI SDK.
Features include:
Persistent and long-term memory
Access to both agent-level and model-level reasoning messages with source attribution
Support for custom agent-configured tools and MCP (Model Context Protocol)
Agent-managed filesystem operations with tool-based file access
Built-in utilities to convert between Letta and AI SDK message formats
Every Letta Send Message API feature, like Long-Running Agent Executions

contents.heading: supported-models
contents.content: See the Letta documentation for the complete list of supported models. For models not on the list, you can try configuring Letta to use OpenAI proxy.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: You can install the Letta provider with:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can import the provider instance lettaCloud or lettaLocal from @letta-ai/vercel-ai-sdk-provider:

contents.heading: basic-usage
contents.content: Get your API key from the Letta dashboard.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: You can configure Letta-specific settings using the providerOptions.letta parameter:

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: Configure agent-specific parameters for message creation. These settings apply to both streaming and non-streaming operations.

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: Available options:

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: id (string, required): The ID of your Letta agent

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: maxSteps (number): Maximum number of agent execution steps

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: includePings (boolean): Whether to include ping messages in the stream

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: streamTokens (boolean): Enable token-by-token streaming

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: background (boolean): Enable background execution for long-running operations

contents.heading: agent-configuration
contents.content: Additional parameters available in the Letta API documentation

contents.heading: timeout-configuration
contents.content: Type: number

contents.heading: timeout-configuration
contents.content: Default: 1000

contents.heading: timeout-configuration
contents.content: Set the maximum wait time (in seconds) for agent responses. This is important for long-running agent operations or when working with complex reasoning chains.

contents.heading: custom-tools-and-mcp
contents.content: Letta agents support custom tools and MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers through provider-executed tools. Once  configured on your Letta agent , you can include them in your requests using letta.tool() and Letta handles tool execution.

contents.heading: using-other-letta-client-functions
contents.content: The vercel-ai-sdk-provider extends the @letta-ai/letta-client, you can access the operations directly by using lettaCloud.client or lettaLocal.client or your custom generated letta.client

contents.heading: more-information
contents.content: For more information on the Letta API, please refer to the Letta API documentation.

metadata.title: llama.cpp
metadata.description: Learn how to use the llama.cpp provider.

This provider loads llama.cpp directly into Node.js memory, eliminating the need for an external server while providing native performance and GPU acceleration.

contents.content: Structured Output: Generate JSON objects with schema validation using Output

contents.heading: features
contents.content: Embeddings: Generate embeddings with embed and embedMany

contents.heading: features
contents.content: Chat Templates: Automatic or configurable chat template formatting (llama3, chatml, gemma, etc.)

metadata.title: MCP Sampling AI Provider
metadata.description: Learn how to use the MCP Sampling AI Provider.

title.children: Client Sampling (for clients without native support)

contents.content: The MCP Sampling AI Provider allows MCP servers to use AI models through the AI SDK by leveraging your existing client subscriptions (like VS Code Copilot). This transforms your MCP server into an agentic tool that can reason and make decisions, without requiring separate API keys or subscriptions.
The provider implements LanguageModelV2 by forwarding requests through MCP's sampling feature to the MCP client, offering unique advantages:
Server-Side AI Integration: Enable MCP servers to call language models directly through AI SDK's standard interface
No Direct Model Management: Forward AI requests to MCP clients, eliminating the need for multiple API keys
Model Flexibility: Let MCP clients decide which model to use based on preferences (cost, speed, intelligence)
Seamless AI SDK Compatibility: Support for generateText, streamText, structured output with Output, and experimental tool calling
Client Sampling Support: Add sampling capability to any MCP client with built-in helpers
Agentic Tools: Transform simple MCP tools into intelligent agents that can reason and make decisions
Learn more about MCP Sampling in the MCP Specification.

metadata.title: Neon AI Gateway
metadata.description: Learn how to use the Neon AI Gateway provider for the AI SDK.

contents.content: Neon AI Gateway is a model gateway built into Neon. A branch-scoped Neon credential gives you access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Alibaba, and other providers. The Neon provider for the AI SDK routes each model to the gateway endpoint it needs.

It supports text generation, streaming, tool calls, structured output, and image input. Models are referenced by short IDs such as gpt-5-mini or gemini-3-5-flash regardless of who hosts them, and every request is scoped to your Neon branch.

Neon AI Gateway is in beta. To use it, you need a paid Neon plan and a project
in the AWS US East (Ohio) region (aws-us-east-2). Inference is free during
the beta. Neon documents the current availability and pricing on the AI
Gateway overview.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The Neon provider is available in the @neon/ai-sdk-provider package. It requires Node.js 20.19 or later. Install it alongside AI SDK 6 with:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: In the Neon Console, open your branch and create a credential with the ai_gateway:invoke scope. Set the branch's AI Gateway URL and credential in your environment:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Use the bare branch gateway URL without an API path. The provider adds the path for each model.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: If you use the Neon CLI, neon env pull writes both variables to your .env file for the current branch.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The Neon AI Gateway quickstart explains how to create a credential and find the branch URL.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: The package exports a default neon provider. It reads NEON_AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL and NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN from the environment:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Use createNeon when you want to pass the branch URL and credential explicitly:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: createNeon also accepts custom headers and a custom fetch implementation.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: Call the provider with a Neon model ID to create a language model:

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: To switch providers, change the model ID:

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: The model ID determines which endpoint the provider uses. OpenAI models use the Responses API, Anthropic models use the Messages API, and other models use Neon's unified OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The provider accepts canonical model IDs as well as the legacy databricks- prefixed form (for example databricks-gpt-5).

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: Neon updates the model catalog as availability changes. Check the Neon model catalog before choosing a model ID. The catalog is also published as the neon provider on models.dev.

contents.heading: image-generation
contents.content: For OpenAI models that support image generation, neon.tools.imageGeneration exposes the Responses API image_generation tool. Use streamText to receive generated images as tool results:

contents.heading: image-generation
contents.content: Image generation works through a tool rather than an AI SDK image model. The provider does not support generateImage(), embed(), or embedMany().

contents.heading: branch-scoped-authentication
contents.content: Neon binds each gateway URL to a branch. A credential works on the branch where it was created and on branches descended from it. For example, preview branches forked from main can use a credential created on main. An unrelated branch cannot.

contents.heading: branch-scoped-authentication
contents.content: Model requests follow the same branch isolation as the database. The AI Gateway authentication guide covers credential creation, rotation, and branch binding.

metadata.title: Nia
metadata.description: Learn how to use Nia with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Nia by Nozomio Labs is an API for technical, up-to-date context. It lets you index docs, repos, PDFs, and datasets, then search them with AI so your agent gets real answers instead of hallucinations. The @nozomioai/nia-ai-sdk package integrates Nia with the AI SDK through tools, middleware, and direct streaming helpers.
It is designed for workflows where you want to:
Call Nia Tracer as a tool for public GitHub and documentation research
Call Nia Oracle as a tool for grounded research over indexed repositories, docs, PDFs, and datasets
Call Nia Document Agent as a tool for deep document analysis and structured extraction
Augment an existing AI SDK model with Nia-backed middleware
Stream Tracer, Oracle, or Document Agent events directly in your app
Learn more in the Nia documentation.

contents.heading: setup

contents.heading: tool-usage
contents.content: Nia works well as a set of AI SDK tools that you pass to generateText or streamText.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can pass false to any service key to disable it entirely, e.g. oracle: false if you only need Tracer. Per-service transport options (such as a separate apiKey) override the top-level ones when provided.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: The SDK also exports createTracerTool(), createOracleTool(), and createDocumentAgentTool() for when you only need a single tool.

contents.heading: middleware-usage
contents.content: Use middleware when you want Nia to enrich the last user message before your base model runs.

contents.heading: withoraclecontext

contents.heading: withoraclecontext

contents.content: The Sarvam AI Provider is a library developed to integrate with the AI SDK. This library brings Speech to Text (STT) capabilities to your applications, allowing for seamless interaction with audio and text data.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Transcribe speech to text

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: Change language_code

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
language_code specifies the language of the input audio and is required for
accurate transcription. • It is mandatory for the saarika:v1 model (this
model does not support unknown). • It is optional for the saarika:v2
model. • Use unknown when the language is not known; in that case, the API
will auto‑detect it. Available options: unknown, hi-IN, bn-IN, kn-IN,
ml-IN, mr-IN, od-IN, pa-IN, ta-IN, te-IN, en-IN, gu-IN.

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: with_timestamps?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
with_timestamps specifies whether to include start/end timestamps for each
word/token. • Type: boolean • When true, each word/token will include
start/end timestamps. • Default: false

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: with_diarization?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
with_diarization enables speaker diarization (Beta). • Type: boolean • When
true, enables speaker diarization. • Default: false

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: num_speakers?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
num_speakers sets the number of distinct speakers to detect (only when
with_diarization is true). • Type: number | null • Number of distinct
speakers to detect. • Default: null

contents.heading: document-indexing
contents.content: Before you can use the vectorstores provider, you need to define an index for your documents. An index stores document embeddings in a vector database, enabling semantic search over your content.

contents.heading: document-indexing
contents.content: An easy way to create an index is by using the VectorStoreIndex.fromDocuments function from the @vectorstores/core package. This function will automatically chunk your documents into smaller chunks, embed them, and store them in the vector database.

contents.heading: document-indexing
contents.content: To be able to embed the documents, you need an embedding model. You can use the vercelEmbedding function (see Utilities) to use any AI SDK embedding model.

contents.heading: document-indexing
contents.content: Once you have an index, you can use a retriever to find the most relevant documents based on similarity to a given query.

contents.heading: utilities

contents.heading: vercelembedding
contents.content: The vercelEmbedding function adapts any AI SDK embedding model for use with vectorstores. This enables you to use embedding providers like OpenAI or Cohere within the vectorstores ecosystem.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The following provider options are available:

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: inputType 'query' | 'document' | 'null'

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Specifies the type of input passed to the model. Defaults to 'null'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'null': When inputType is 'null', the embedding model directly converts the inputs into numerical vectors.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: For retrieval/search purposes it is recommended to use 'query' or 'document'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'query': The input is a search query, e.g., "Represent the query for retrieving supporting documents: ...".

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'document': The input is a document to be stored in a vector database, e.g., "Represent the document for retrieval: ...".

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: outputDimension number

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The number of dimensions for the resulting output embeddings. Default is 'null'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: For example, voyage-code-3 and voyage-3-large support: 2048, 1024 (default), 512, and 256.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Refer to the model documentation for supported values.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: outputDtype 'float' | 'int8' | 'uint8' | 'binary' | 'ubinary'

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The data type for the output embeddings. Defaults to 'float'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'float': 32-bit floating-point numbers (supported by all models).

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'int8', 'uint8': 8-bit integer types (supported by voyage-3-large, voyage-3.5, voyage-3.5-lite, and voyage-code-3).

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'binary', 'ubinary': Bit-packed, quantized single-bit embedding values (voyage-3-large, voyage-3.5, voyage-3.5-lite, and voyage-code-3). The returned list length is 1/8 of outputDimension. 'binary' uses offset binary encoding.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: See FAQ: Output Data Types for more details.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: truncation boolean

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Whether to truncate the input texts to fit within the model's context length. If not specified, defaults to true.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models

metadata.title: Langfuse
metadata.description: Monitor, evaluate and debug your AI SDK application with Langfuse

title.children: Group multiple executions in one trace

contents.content: Langfuse (GitHub) is an open source LLM engineering platform that helps teams to collaboratively develop, monitor, and debug AI applications. Langfuse integrates with the AI SDK to provide:
Application traces
Usage patterns
Cost data by user and model
Replay sessions to debug issues
Evaluations

contents.heading: setup
contents.content:
The AI SDK supports tracing via OpenTelemetry. With the LangfuseSpanProcessor you can collect these traces in Langfuse.
While telemetry is experimental (docs), you can enable it by setting experimental_telemetry on each request that you want to trace.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: To collect the traces in Langfuse, you need to add the LangfuseSpanProcessor to your application.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: You can set the Langfuse credentials via environment variables or directly to the LangfuseSpanProcessor constructor.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: To get your Langfuse API keys, you can self-host Langfuse or sign up for Langfuse Cloud here. Create a project in the Langfuse dashboard to get your secretKey and publicKey.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Now you need to register this span processor via the OpenTelemetry SDK.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Next.js has support for OpenTelemetry instrumentation on the framework level. Learn more about it in the Next.js OpenTelemetry guide.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Install dependencies:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Add LangfuseSpanProcessor to your instrumentation using a manual OpenTelemetry setup via NodeTracerProvider:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Install dependencies:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Add LangfuseSpanProcessor to your OpenTelemetry setup:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Done! All traces that contain AI SDK spans are automatically captured in Langfuse.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content:
Check out the sample repository (langfuse/langfuse-vercel-ai-nextjs-example) based
on the next-openai template to showcase the integration of Langfuse with Next.js and AI SDK.

contents.heading: group-multiple-executions-in-one-trace
contents.content: You can open a Langfuse trace and pass the trace ID to AI SDK calls to group multiple execution spans under one trace. The passed name in functionId will be the root span name of the respective execution.

contents.heading: group-multiple-executions-in-one-trace
contents.content: The resulting trace hierarchy will be:

contents.heading: disable-tracking-of-inputoutput
contents.content: By default, the exporter captures the input and output of each request. You can disable this behavior by setting the recordInputs and recordOutputs options to false.

contents.heading: link-langfuse-prompts-to-traces
contents.content: You can link Langfuse prompts to AI SDK generations by setting the langfusePrompt property in the metadata field:

contents.heading: link-langfuse-prompts-to-traces
contents.content: The resulting generation will have the prompt linked to the trace in Langfuse. Learn more about prompts in Langfuse here.

contents.heading: pass-custom-attributes
contents.content: All of the metadata fields are automatically captured by the exporter. You can also pass custom trace attributes to e.g. track users or sessions.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: If you deploy on Vercel, Vercel's OpenTelemetry Collector is only available on Pro and Enterprise Plans (docs).

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: You need to be on "ai": "^3.3.0" to use the telemetry feature. In case of any issues, please update to the latest version.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: On Next.js, make sure that you only have a single instrumentation file.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: If you use Sentry, make sure to either:

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: set skipOpenTelemetrySetup: true in Sentry.init

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: follow Sentry's docs on how to manually set up Sentry with OTEL

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: After setting up Langfuse Tracing for the AI SDK, you can utilize any of the other Langfuse platform features:

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Prompt Management: Collaboratively manage and iterate on prompts, use them with low-latency in production.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Evaluations: Test the application holistically in development and production using user feedback, LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, manual reviews, or custom evaluation pipelines.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Experiments: Iterate on prompts, models, and application design in a structured manner with datasets and evaluations.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: For more information, see the telemetry documentation of the AI SDK.

contents.heading: basic-concepts
contents.content: Each message triggering your LLM pipeline as a whole is captured with a Trace.

contents.heading: basic-concepts
contents.content: A Trace contains multiple Spans, which are the steps inside your pipeline.

contents.heading: basic-concepts
contents.content: A span can be an LLM call, a database query for a RAG retrieval, or a simple function transformation.

contents.content: Spans can be nested to capture the pipeline structure.

contents.heading: basic-concepts
contents.content: Traces can be grouped together on LangWatch Dashboard by having the same thread_id in their metadata, making the individual messages become part of a conversation.

contents.heading: basic-concepts

Our evaluation and observability tools help teams maintain quality, reliability, and speed throughout the AI application lifecycle. Maxim integrates with the AI SDK to provide:
Automatic Observability – Adds tracing, logging, and metadata to AI SDK calls with a simple wrapper.
Unified Model Wrapping – Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google etc. models uniformly.
Custom Metadata & Tagging – Enables attaching trace names, tags, and session IDs to track usage.
Streaming & Structured Output Support – Handles streaming responses and structured outputs seamlessly.

metadata.title: OpenAI Compatible Providers
metadata.description: Use OpenAI compatible providers with the AI SDK.

contents.content: You can use the OpenAI Compatible Provider package to use language model providers that implement the OpenAI API.
Below we focus on the general setup and provider instance creation. You can also write a custom provider package leveraging the OpenAI Compatible package.
We provide detailed documentation for the following OpenAI compatible providers:
LM Studio
NIM
ModelRush
Heroku
Clarifai
NEAR AI Cloud
The general setup and provider instance creation is the same for all of these providers.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The OpenAI Compatible provider is available via the @ai-sdk/openai-compatible module. You can install it with:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: To use an OpenAI compatible provider, you can create a custom provider instance with the createOpenAICompatible function from @ai-sdk/openai-compatible:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the provider instance:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: baseURL string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Set the URL prefix for API calls.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: apiKey string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
API key for authenticating requests. If specified, adds an Authorization
header to request headers with the value Bearer <apiKey>. This will be added
before any headers potentially specified in the headers option.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: headers Record<string,string>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Optional custom headers to include in requests. These will be added to request headers
after any headers potentially added by use of the apiKey option.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: queryParams Record<string,string>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Optional custom url query parameters to include in request urls.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: fetch (input: RequestInfo, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Custom fetch implementation.
Defaults to the global fetch function.
You can use it as a middleware to intercept requests,
or to provide a custom fetch implementation for e.g. testing.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: includeUsage boolean

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Include usage information in streaming responses. When enabled, usage data will be included in the response metadata for streaming requests. Defaults to undefined (false).

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: supportsStructuredOutputs boolean

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Set to true if the provider supports structured outputs. Only relevant for provider(), provider.chatModel(), and provider.languageModel().

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: transformRequestBody (args: Record<string, any>) => Record<string, any>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Optional function to transform the request body before sending it to the API.
This is useful for proxy providers that may require a different request format
than the official OpenAI API.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: metadataExtractor MetadataExtractor

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Optional metadata extractor to capture provider-specific metadata from API responses.
See Custom Metadata Extraction for details.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
You can create provider models using a provider instance.
The first argument is the model id, e.g. model-id.

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content: You can also use the following factory methods:

contents.content: Structured outputs - Generate JSON with schema validation (when supportsStructuredOutputs is enabled)

contents.heading: supported-capabilities
contents.content: Reasoning content - Support for models that return reasoning/thinking tokens (e.g., DeepSeek R1)

contents.heading: supported-capabilities
contents.content: System messages - Support for system prompts

contents.heading: supported-capabilities
contents.content: Multi-modal inputs - Support for images and other content types (provider-dependent)

contents.content: You can use provider language models to generate text with the generateText function:

Model Inference
API

contents.content: The following provider options are available for embedding models via providerOptions:

contents.content:
The number of dimensions the resulting output embeddings should have.

contents.content:

contents.content: The following provider options are available for completion models via providerOptions:

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content: echo boolean

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content: Echo back the prompt in addition to the completion.

contents.content: logitBias Record<string, number>

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content:
Modify the likelihood of specified tokens appearing in the completion.
Accepts a JSON object that maps tokens (specified by their token ID) to an
associated bias value from -100 to 100.

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content: The suffix that comes after a completion of inserted text.

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: completion-model-options
contents.content:
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help providers to

contents.content: The following provider options are available for chat models via providerOptions:

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: user string

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content:
A unique identifier representing your end-user, which can help the provider to

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: reasoningEffort string

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: Reasoning effort for reasoning models. The exact values depend on the provider.

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: textVerbosity string

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: Controls the verbosity of the generated text. The exact values depend on the provider.

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content: strictJsonSchema boolean

contents.heading: chat-model-options
contents.content:
Whether to use strict JSON schema validation. When true, the model uses constrained
decoding to guarantee schema compliance. Only used when the provider supports
structured outputs and a schema is provided. Defaults to true.

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: The OpenAI Compatible provider supports adding provider-specific options to the request body. These are specified with the providerOptions field in the request body.

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: For example, if you create a provider instance with the name providerName, you can add a customOption field to the request body like this:

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: Note that the providerOptions key will be in camelCase. If you set the provider name to provider-name, the options still need to be set on providerOptions.providerName.

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: The request body sent to the provider will include the customOption field with the value magic-value. This gives you an easy way to add provider-specific options to requests without having to modify the provider or AI SDK code.

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content:
The OpenAI Compatible provider supports extracting provider-specific metadata from API responses through metadata extractors.
These extractors allow you to capture additional information returned by the provider beyond the standard response format.

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content:
Metadata extractors receive the raw, unprocessed response data from the provider, giving you complete flexibility
to extract any custom fields or experimental features that the provider may include.
This is particularly useful when:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Working with providers that include non-standard response fields

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Experimenting with beta or preview features

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Capturing provider-specific metrics or debugging information

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Supporting rapid provider API evolution without SDK changes

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Metadata extractors work with both streaming and non-streaming chat completions and consist of two main components:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: A function to extract metadata from complete responses

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: A streaming extractor that can accumulate metadata across chunks in a streaming response

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Here's an example metadata extractor that captures both standard and custom provider data:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: You can provide a metadata extractor when creating your provider instance:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: The extracted metadata will be included in the response under the providerMetadata field:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: This allows you to access provider-specific information while maintaining a consistent interface across different providers.

metadata.title: Add Skills to Your Agent
metadata.description: Learn how to extend your agent with specialized capabilities loaded at runtime with Agent Skills.

title.children: Step 4: Create the Load Skill Tool

contents.content: In this guide, you will learn how to extend your agent with Agent Skills, a lightweight, open format for adding specialized knowledge and workflows that load at runtime from markdown files.
At its core, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file with metadata and instructions that tell an agent how to perform a specific task.

contents.heading: how-skills-work
contents.content: Skills use progressive disclosure to manage context efficiently:

contents.heading: how-skills-work
contents.content: Discovery: At startup, agents load only the name and description of each available skill (just enough to know when it might be relevant)

contents.heading: how-skills-work
contents.content: Activation: When a task matches a skill's description, the agent reads the full SKILL.md instructions into context

contents.heading: how-skills-work
contents.content: Execution: The agent follows the instructions, optionally loading referenced files or executing bundled code as needed

contents.heading: how-skills-work
contents.content: This approach keeps agents fast while giving them access to more context on demand.

contents.heading: the-skillmd-file
contents.content: Every skill starts with a SKILL.md file containing YAML frontmatter and Markdown instructions:

contents.heading: the-skillmd-file
contents.content: The frontmatter requires:

contents.heading: the-skillmd-file
contents.content: name: A short identifier

contents.heading: the-skillmd-file
contents.content: description: Instructions for when to use this skill

contents.heading: the-skillmd-file
contents.content: The Markdown body contains the actual skill content with no restrictions on structure or content.

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: To support skills, your agent needs:

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: Filesystem access to discover and load skill files (read files, read directories)

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: A load skill tool that reads the SKILL.md content into context

contents.heading: prerequisites
contents.content: Command execution (optional) if skills bundle scripts (e.g. a full sandbox environment)

contents.heading: step-1-define-a-sandbox-abstraction
contents.content:
This guide uses a generic sandbox abstraction for flexibility across
environments. If you're building for Node.js, you can use fs/promises and
child_process directly instead.

contents.heading: step-1-define-a-sandbox-abstraction
contents.content: Create a generic sandbox interface that provides a consistent way to interact with the filesystem. This abstraction lets you implement it differently depending on your environment (Node.js fs, a containerized sandbox, cloud storage, etc.):

contents.heading: step-2-discover-skills-at-startup
contents.content: Scan skill directories and extract metadata from each SKILL.md:

contents.heading: step-3-build-the-system-prompt
contents.content: Include discovered skills in the system prompt so the agent knows what's available:

contents.heading: step-3-build-the-system-prompt
contents.content: The agent sees only names and descriptions. Full instructions stay out of the context window until loaded.

contents.heading: step-4-create-the-load-skill-tool
contents.content: The load skill tool reads the full SKILL.md and returns the body (without frontmatter):

contents.heading: step-4-create-the-load-skill-tool
contents.content: The tool returns the skill directory path alongside the content so the agent can construct full paths to bundled resources.

contents.heading: step-5-create-the-agent
contents.content: Wire up the sandbox and skills using callOptionsSchema and prepareCall:

contents.heading: step-6-run-the-agent
contents.content: When a user asks something that matches a skill description, the agent calls loadSkill. The full instructions load into context, and the agent follows them using bash and readFile to access bundled resources.

contents.heading: accessing-bundled-resources
contents.content: Skills can reference files relative to their directory. The agent uses existing tools to access them:

contents.heading: accessing-bundled-resources
contents.content: The agent sees the skill directory path in the tool result and prepends it when accessing templates/config.json or scripts/setup.sh. No special resource loading mechanism is needed—the agent uses the same tools it uses for everything else.

metadata.title: Get started with Claude 4
metadata.description: Get started with Claude 4 using the AI SDK.

title.children: Getting Started with the AI SDK

contents.content: With the release of Claude 4, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications, particularly those that require complex reasoning capabilities and advanced intelligence.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like Claude 4 alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more.

contents.heading: claude-4
contents.content: Claude 4 is Anthropic's most advanced model family to date, offering exceptional capabilities across reasoning, instruction following, coding, and knowledge tasks. Available in two variants—Sonnet and Opus—Claude 4 delivers state-of-the-art performance with enhanced reliability and control. Claude 4 builds on the extended thinking capabilities introduced in Claude 3.7, allowing for even more sophisticated problem-solving through careful, step-by-step reasoning.

contents.heading: claude-4
contents.content: Claude 4 excels at complex reasoning, code generation and analysis, detailed content creation, and agentic capabilities, making it ideal for powering sophisticated AI workflows, customer-facing agents, and applications requiring nuanced understanding and responses. Claude Opus 4 is an excellent coding model, leading on SWE-bench (72.5%) and Terminal-bench (43.2%), with the ability to sustain performance on long-running tasks that require focused effort and thousands of steps. Claude Sonnet 4 significantly improves on Sonnet 3.7, excelling in coding with 72.7% on SWE-bench while balancing performance and efficiency.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models
contents.content: Claude 4 models respond well to clear, explicit instructions. The following best practices can help achieve optimal performance:

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models
contents.content: Provide explicit instructions: Clearly state what you want the model to do, including specific steps or formats for the response.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models
contents.content: Include context and motivation: Explain why a task is being performed to help the model better understand the underlying goals.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models
contents.content: Avoid negative examples: When providing examples, only demonstrate the behavior you want to see, not what you want to avoid.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK is the TypeScript toolkit designed to help developers build AI-powered applications with React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more. Integrating LLMs into applications is complicated and heavily dependent on the specific model provider you use.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK abstracts away the differences between model providers, eliminates boilerplate code for building chatbots, and allows you to go beyond text output to generate rich, interactive components.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: At the center of the AI SDK is AI SDK Core, which provides a unified API to call any LLM. The code snippet below is all you need to call Claude 4 Sonnet with the AI SDK:

contents.heading: reasoning-ability
contents.content: Claude 4 enhances the extended thinking capabilities first introduced in Claude 3.7 Sonnet—the ability to solve complex problems with careful, step-by-step reasoning. Additionally, both Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 can now use tools during extended thinking, allowing Claude to alternate between reasoning and tool use to improve responses. You can enable extended thinking using the thinking provider option and specifying a thinking budget in tokens. For interleaved thinking (where Claude can think in between tool calls) you'll need to enable a beta feature using the anthropic-beta header:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK Core can be paired with AI SDK UI, another powerful component of the AI SDK, to streamline the process of building chat, completion, and assistant interfaces with popular frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, and SolidStart.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK UI provides robust abstractions that simplify the complex tasks of managing chat streams and UI updates on the frontend, enabling you to develop dynamic AI-driven interfaces more efficiently.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: With three main hooks — useChat, useCompletion, and useObject — you can incorporate real-time chat capabilities, text completions, and streamed JSON into your app.

contents.content: Let's explore building a chatbot with Next.js, the AI SDK, and Claude Sonnet 4:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: Finally, update the root page (app/page.tsx) to use the useChat hook:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces

contents.heading: claude-4-model-variants
contents.content: Claude 4 is available in two variants, each optimized for different use cases:

contents.heading: claude-4-model-variants
contents.content: Claude Sonnet 4: Balanced performance suitable for most enterprise applications, with significant improvements over Sonnet 3.7.

contents.heading: claude-4-model-variants
contents.content: Claude Opus 4: Anthropic's most powerful model and the best coding model available. Excels at sustained performance on long-running tasks that require focused effort and thousands of steps, with the ability to work continuously for several hours.

metadata.title: Get started with Computer Use
metadata.description: Get started with Claude's Computer Use capabilities with the AI SDK

title.children: Getting Started with the AI SDK
Using Computer Tools with Text Generation

contents.content: With the release of Computer Use in Claude 3.5 Sonnet, you can now direct AI models to interact with computers like humans do - moving cursors, clicking buttons, and typing text. This capability enables automation of complex tasks while leveraging Claude's advanced reasoning abilities.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like Anthropic's Claude alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more. In this guide, you will learn how to integrate Computer Use into your AI SDK applications.

Computer Use is currently in beta with some  limitations
.
The feature may be error-prone at times. Anthropic recommends starting with
low-risk tasks and implementing appropriate safety measures.

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Anthropic recently released a new version of the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model which is capable of 'Computer Use'. This allows the model to interact with computer interfaces through basic actions like:

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Moving the cursor

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Clicking buttons

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Typing text

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Taking screenshots

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Reading screen content

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Computer Use enables the model to read and interact with on-screen content through a series of coordinated steps. Here's how the process works:

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Start with a prompt and tools

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Add Anthropic-defined Computer Use tools to your request and provide a task (prompt) for the model. For example: "save an image to your downloads folder."

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Select the right tool

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The model evaluates which computer tools can help accomplish the task. It then sends a formatted tool_call to use the appropriate tool.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Execute the action and return results

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The AI SDK processes Claude's request by running the selected tool. The results can then be sent back to Claude through a tool_result message.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Complete the task through iterations

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Claude analyzes each result to determine if more actions are needed. It continues requesting tool use and processing results until it completes your task or requires additional input.

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: There are three main tools available in the Computer Use API:

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Computer Tool: Enables basic computer control like mouse movement, clicking, and keyboard input

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Text Editor Tool: Provides functionality for viewing and editing text files

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Bash Tool: Allows execution of bash commands

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: Computer Use tools in the AI SDK are predefined interfaces that require your own implementation of the execution layer. While the SDK provides the type definitions and structure for these tools, you need to:

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: Set up a controlled environment for Computer Use execution

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: Implement core functionality like mouse control and keyboard input

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: Handle screenshot capture and processing

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: Set up rules and limits for how Claude can interact with your system

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: The recommended approach is to start with  Anthropic's reference implementation , which provides:

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: A containerized environment configured for safe Computer Use

contents.heading: implementation-considerations

contents.heading: implementation-considerations

contents.heading: implementation-considerations
contents.content: This reference implementation serves as a foundation to understand the requirements before building your own custom solution.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content:
If you have never used the AI SDK before, start by following the Getting
Started guide.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content:
For a working example of Computer Use implementation with Next.js and the AI
SDK, check out our AI SDK Computer Use

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: First, ensure you have the AI SDK and Anthropic AI SDK provider installed:

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: You can add Computer Use to your AI SDK applications using provider-defined-client tools. These tools accept various input parameters (like display height and width in the case of the computer tool) and then require that you define an execute function.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: Here's how you could set up the Computer Tool with the AI SDK:

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The computerTool handles two main actions: taking screenshots via getScreenshot() and executing computer actions like mouse movements and clicks through executeComputerAction(). Remember, you have to implement this execution logic (eg. the getScreenshot and executeComputerAction functions) to handle the actual computer interactions. The execute function should handle all low-level interactions with the operating system.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: Finally, to send tool results back to the model, use the toModelOutput() function to convert text and image responses into a format the model can process. The AI SDK includes experimental support for these multi-modal tool results when using Anthropic's models.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content:
Computer Use requires appropriate safety measures like using virtual machines,
limiting access to sensitive data, and implementing human oversight for
critical actions.

contents.heading: using-computer-tools-with-text-generation
contents.content: Once your tool is defined, you can use it with both the generateText and streamText functions.

contents.heading: using-computer-tools-with-text-generation
contents.content: For one-shot text generation, use generateText:

contents.heading: using-computer-tools-with-text-generation
contents.content: For streaming responses, use streamText to receive updates in real-time:

contents.heading: configure-multi-step-agentic-generations
contents.content: To allow the model to perform multiple steps without user intervention, use the stopWhen parameter. This will automatically send any tool results back to the model to trigger a subsequent generation:

contents.heading: combine-multiple-tools
contents.content: You can combine multiple tools in a single request to enable more complex workflows. The AI SDK supports all three of Claude's Computer Use tools:

contents.heading: combine-multiple-tools
contents.content:
Always implement appropriate security measures and
obtain user consent before enabling Computer Use in production applications.

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: To get the best results when using Computer Use:

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Specify simple, well-defined tasks with explicit instructions for each step

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Prompt Claude to verify outcomes through screenshots

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Use keyboard shortcuts when UI elements are difficult to manipulate

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Include example screenshots for repeatable tasks

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Provide explicit tips in system prompts for known tasks

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Remember, Computer Use is a beta feature. Please be aware that it poses unique risks that are distinct from standard API features or chat interfaces. These risks are heightened when using Computer Use to interact with the internet. To minimize risks, consider taking precautions such as:

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Use a dedicated virtual machine or container with minimal privileges to prevent direct system attacks or accidents.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Avoid giving the model access to sensitive data, such as account login information, to prevent information theft.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Limit internet access to an allowlist of domains to reduce exposure to malicious content.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Ask a human to confirm decisions that may result in meaningful real-world consequences as well as any tasks requiring affirmative consent, such as accepting cookies, executing financial transactions, or agreeing to terms of service.
