metadata.title: Backpressure
metadata.description: How to handle backpressure and cancellation when working with the AI SDK

title.children: Tying Stream Laziness to AI Responses

contents.content: This page focuses on understanding back-pressure and cancellation when working with streams. You do not need to know this information to use the AI SDK, but for those interested, it offers a deeper dive on why and how the SDK optimally streams responses.

In the following sections, we'll explore back-pressure and cancellation in the context of a simple example program. We'll discuss the issues that can arise from an eager approach and demonstrate how a lazy approach can resolve them.

contents.heading: back-pressure-and-cancellation-with-streams
contents.content: Let's begin by setting up a simple example program:

contents.heading: back-pressure-and-cancellation-with-streams
contents.content: In this example, we create an async-generator that yields positive integers, a ReadableStream that wraps our integer generator, and a reader which will read values out of our stream. Notice, too, that our integer generator logs out "yielding ${i}", and our reader logs out "read ${value}". Both take an arbitrary amount of time to process data, represented with a 100ms sleep in our generator, and a 1sec sleep in our reader.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: If you were to run this program, you'd notice something funny. We'll see roughly 10 "yield" logs for every "read" log. This might seem obvious, the generator can push values 10x faster than the reader can pull them out. But it represents a problem, our stream has to maintain an ever expanding queue of items that have been pushed in but not pulled out.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: The problem stems from the way we wrap our generator into a stream. Notice the use of for await (…) inside our start handler. This is an eager for-loop, and it is constantly running to get the next value from our generator to be enqueued in our stream. This means our stream does not respect back-pressure, the signal from the consumer to the producer that more values aren't needed yet. We've essentially spawned a thread that will perpetually push more data into the stream, one that runs as fast as possible to push new data immediately. Worse, there's no way to signal to this thread to stop running when we don't need additional data.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: To fix this, ReadableStream allows a pull handler. pull is called every time the consumer attempts to read more data from our stream (if there's no data already queued internally). But it's not enough to just move the for await(…) into pull, we also need to convert from an eager enqueuing to a lazy one. By making these 2 changes, we'll be able to react to the consumer. If they need more data, we can easily produce it, and if they don't, then we don't need to spend any time doing unnecessary work.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: Our createStream is a little more verbose now, but the new code is important. First, we need to manually call our iterator.next() method. This returns a Promise for an object with the type signature { done: boolean, value: T }. If done is true, then we know that our iterator won't yield any more values and we must close the stream (this allows the consumer to know that the stream is also finished producing values). Else, we need to enqueue our newly produced value.

contents.heading: back-pressure
contents.content: When we run this program, we see that our "yield" and "read" logs are now paired. We're no longer yielding 10x integers for every read! And, our stream now only needs to maintain 1 item in its internal buffer. We've essentially given control to the consumer, so that it's responsible for producing new values as it needs it. Neato!

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: Let's go back to our initial eager example, with 1 small edit. Now instead of reading 10,000 integers, we're only going to read 3:

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: We're back to yielding 10x the number of values read. But notice now, after we've read 3 values, we're continuing to yield new values. We know that our reader will never read another value, but our stream doesn't! The eager for await (…) will continue forever, loudly enqueuing new values into our stream's buffer and increasing our memory usage until it consumes all available program memory.

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: The fix to this is exactly the same: use pull and manual iteration. By producing values lazily, we tie the lifetime of our integer generator to the lifetime of the reader. Once the reads stop, the yields will stop too:

contents.heading: cancellation
contents.content: Since the solution is the same as implementing back-pressure, it shows that they're just 2 facets of the same problem: Pushing values into a stream should be done lazily, and doing it eagerly results in expected problems.

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: Now let's imagine you're integrating AIBot service into your product. Users will be able to prompt "count from 1 to infinity", the browser will fetch your AI API endpoint, and your servers connect to AIBot to get a response. But "infinity" is, well, infinite. The response will never end!

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: After a few seconds, the user gets bored and navigates away. Or maybe you're doing local development and a hot-module reload refreshes your page. The browser will have ended its connection to the API endpoint, but will your server end its connection with AIBot?

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: If you used the eager for await (...) approach, then the connection is still running and your server is asking for more and more data from AIBot. Our server spawned a "thread" and there's no signal when we can end the eager pulls. Eventually, the server is going to run out of memory (remember, there's no active fetch connection to read the buffering responses and free them).

contents.heading: tying-stream-laziness-to-ai-responses
contents.content: With the lazy approach, this is taken care of for you. Because the stream will only request new data from AIBot when the consumer requests it, navigating away from the page naturally frees all resources. The fetch connection aborts and the server can clean up the response. The ReadableStream tied to that response can now be garbage collected. When that happens, the connection it holds to AIBot can then be freed.

headings.content: Tying Stream Laziness to AI Responses

metadata.title: Caching
metadata.description: How to handle caching when working with the AI SDK

contents.content: Depending on the type of application you're building, you may want to cache the responses you receive from your AI provider, at least temporarily.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
The recommended approach to caching responses is using language model middleware
and the simulateReadableStream function.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
Language model middleware is a way to enhance the behavior of language models by intercepting and modifying the calls to the language model.
Let's see how you can use language model middleware to cache responses.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content:
This example uses @upstash/redis to store and retrieve the assistant's
responses but you can use any KV storage provider you would like.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: LanguageModelMiddleware has two methods: wrapGenerate and wrapStream. wrapGenerate is called when using generateText and generateObject, while wrapStream is called when using streamText and streamObject.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: For wrapGenerate, you can cache the response directly. Instead, for wrapStream, you cache an array of the stream parts, which can then be used with simulateReadableStream function to create a simulated ReadableStream that returns the cached response. In this way, the cached response is returned chunk-by-chunk as if it were being generated by the model. You can control the initial delay and delay between chunks by adjusting the initialDelayInMs and chunkDelayInMs parameters of simulateReadableStream.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware-recommended
contents.content: You can see a full example of caching with Redis in a Next.js application in our Caching Middleware Recipe.

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Alternatively, each AI SDK Core function has special lifecycle callbacks you can use. The one of interest is likely onFinish, which is called when the generation is complete. This is where you can cache the full response.

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: Here's an example of how you can implement caching using Vercel KV and Next.js to cache the OpenAI response for 1 hour:

contents.heading: using-lifecycle-callbacks
contents.content: This example uses Upstash Redis and Next.js to cache the response for 1 hour.

metadata.title: Advanced
metadata.description: Learn how to use advanced functionality within the AI SDK and RSC API.

contents.content: This section covers advanced topics and concepts for the AI SDK and RSC API. Working with LLMs often requires a different mental model compared to traditional software development.
After these concepts, you should have a better understanding of the paradigms behind the AI SDK and RSC API, and how to use them to build more AI applications.

metadata.title: Language Models as Routers
metadata.description: Generative User Interfaces and Language Models as Routers

contents.content: Since language models can render user interfaces as part of their generations, the resulting model generations are referred to as generative user interfaces.
In this section we will learn more about generative user interfaces and their impact on the way AI applications are built.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Generative user interfaces are not deterministic in nature because they depend on the model's generation output. Since these generations are probabilistic in nature, it is possible for every user query to result in a different user interface.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Users expect their experience using your application to be predictable, so non-deterministic user interfaces can sound like a bad idea at first. However, language models can be set up to limit their generations to a particular set of outputs using their ability to call functions.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: When language models are provided with a set of function definitions and instructed to execute any of them based on user query, they do either one of the following things:

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Execute a function that is most relevant to the user query.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: Not execute any function if the user query is out of bounds of the set of functions available to them.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: This way, it is possible to ensure that the generations result in deterministic outputs, while the choice a model makes still remains to be probabilistic.

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: This emergent ability exhibited by a language model to choose whether a function needs to be executed or not based on a user query is believed to be models emulating "reasoning".

contents.heading: deterministic-routes-and-probabilistic-routing
contents.content: As a result, the combination of language models being able to reason which function to execute as well as render user interfaces at the same time gives you the ability to build applications where language models can be used as a router.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Historically, developers had to write routing logic that connected different parts of an application to be navigable by a user and complete a specific task.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: In web applications today, most of the routing logic takes place in the form of routes:

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /login would navigate you to a page with a login form.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /user/john would navigate you to a page with profile details about John.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: /api/events?limit=5 would display the five most recent events from an events database.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: While routes help you build web applications that connect different parts of an application into a seamless user experience, it can also be a burden to manage them as the complexity of applications grow.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Next.js has helped reduce complexity in developing with routes by introducing:

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: File-based routing system

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Dynamic routing

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: API routes

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: Middleware

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: App router, and so on...

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: With language models becoming better at reasoning, we believe that there is a future where developers only write core application specific components while models take care of routing them based on the user's state in an application.

contents.heading: language-models-as-routers
contents.content: With generative user interfaces, the language model decides which user interface to render based on the user's state in the application, giving users the flexibility to interact with your application in a conversational manner instead of navigating through a series of predefined routes.

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: For routes like:

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /profile/[username]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /search?q=[query]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: /media/[id]

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: that have segments dependent on dynamic data, the language model can generate the correct parameters and render the user interface.

contents.heading: routing-by-parameters
contents.content: For example, when you're in a search application, you can ask the language model to search for artworks from different artists. The language model will call the search function with the artist's name as a parameter and render the search results.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: For actions that require a sequence of steps to be completed by navigating through different routes, the language model can generate the correct sequence of routes to complete in order to fulfill the user's request.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: For example, when you're in a calendar application, you can ask the language model to schedule a happy hour evening with your friends. The language model will then understand your request and will perform the right sequence of tool calls to:

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Lookup your calendar

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Lookup your friends' calendars

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Determine the best time for everyone

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Search for nearby happy hour spots

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Create an event and send out invites to your friends

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: Just by defining functions to lookup contacts, pull events from a calendar, and search for nearby locations, the model is able to sequentially navigate the routes for you.

contents.heading: routing-by-sequence
contents.content: To learn more, check out these examples using the streamUI function to stream generative user interfaces to the client based on the response from the language model.

metadata.title: Multiple Streamables
metadata.description: Learn to handle multiple streamables in your application.

contents.heading: multiple-streamable-uis
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC APIs allow you to compose and return any number of streamable UIs, along with other data, in a single request. This can be useful when you want to decouple the UI into smaller components and stream them separately.

contents.heading: multiple-streamable-uis
contents.content: The client side code is similar to the previous example, but the tool call will return the new data structure with the weather and forecast UIs. Depending on the speed of getting weather and forecast data, these two components might be updated independently.

contents.heading: nested-streamable-uis
contents.content: You can stream UI components within other UI components. This allows you to create complex UIs that are built up from smaller, reusable components. In the example below, we pass a historyChart streamable as a prop to a StockCard component. The StockCard can render the historyChart streamable, and it will automatically update as the server responds with new data.

metadata.title: Multistep Interfaces
metadata.description: Concepts behind building multistep interfaces

contents.content: Multistep interfaces refer to user interfaces that require multiple independent steps to be executed in order to complete a specific task.
In order to understand multistep interfaces, it is important to understand two concepts:
Tool composition
Application context
Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This is a powerful concept that allows you to break down complex tasks into smaller, more manageable steps.
Application context refers to the state of the application at any given point in time. This includes the user's input, the output of the language model, and any other relevant information.

When designing multistep interfaces, you need to consider how the tools in your application can be composed together to form a coherent user experience as well as how the application context changes as the user progresses through the interface.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: The application context can be thought of as the conversation history between the user and the language model. The richer the context, the more information the model has to generate relevant responses.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: In the context of multistep interfaces, the application context becomes even more important. This is because the user's input in one step may affect the output of the model in the next step.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: For example, consider a meal logging application that helps users track their daily food intake. The language model is provided with the following tools:

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: log_meal takes in parameters like the name of the food, the quantity, and the time of consumption to log a meal.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: delete_meal takes in the name of the meal to be deleted.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: When the user logs a meal, the model generates a response confirming the meal has been logged.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: Now when the user decides to delete the meal, the model should be able to reference the previous step to identify the meal to be deleted.

contents.heading: application-context
contents.content: In this example, managing the application context is important for the model to generate the correct response. The model needs to have information about the previous actions in order for it to use generate the parameters for the delete_meal tool.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This involves defining the inputs and outputs of each tool, as well as how they interact with each other.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The design of how these tools can be composed together to form a multistep interface is crucial to both the user experience of your application and the model's ability to generate the correct output.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: For example, consider a flight booking assistant that can help users book flights. The assistant can be designed to have the following tools:

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: searchFlights: Searches for flights based on the user's query.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: lookupFlight: Looks up details of a specific flight based on the flight number.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: bookFlight: Books a flight based on the user's selection.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The searchFlights tool is called when the user wants to lookup flights for a specific route. This would typically mean the tool should be able to take in parameters like the origin and destination of the flight.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The lookupFlight tool is called when the user wants to get more details about a specific flight. This would typically mean the tool should be able to take in parameters like the flight number and return information about seat availability.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The bookFlight tool is called when the user decides to book a flight. In order to identify the flight to book, the tool should be able to take in parameters like the flight number, trip date, and passenger details.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: So the conversation between the user and the model could look like this:

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: In the last tool call, the bookFlight tool does not include passenger details as it is not available in the application context. As a result, it requests the user to provide the passenger details before proceeding with the booking.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Looking up passenger information could've been another tool that the model could've called before calling the bookFlight tool assuming that the user is logged into the application. This way, the model does not have to ask the user for the passenger details and can proceed with the booking.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: The lookupContacts tool is called before the bookFlight tool to ensure that the passenger details are available in the application context when booking the flight. This way, the model can reduce the number of steps required from the user and use its ability to call tools that populate its context and use that information to complete the booking process.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: Now, let's introduce another tool called lookupBooking that can be used to show booking details by taking in the name of the passenger as parameter. This tool can be composed with the existing tools to provide a more complete user experience.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: In this example, the lookupBooking tool is used to provide the user with the status of their wife's upcoming flight. By composing this tool with the existing tools, the model is able to generate a response that includes the booking status and the departure date of the flight without requiring the user to provide additional information.

contents.heading: tool-composition
contents.content: As a result, the more tools you design that can be composed together, the more complex and powerful your application can become.

metadata.title: Prompt Engineering
metadata.description: Learn how to engineer prompts for LLMs with the AI SDK

title.children: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?

contents.heading: what-is-a-large-language-model-llm
contents.content: A Large Language Model is essentially a prediction engine that takes a sequence of words as input and aims to predict the most likely sequence to follow. It does this by assigning probabilities to potential next sequences and then selecting one. The model continues to generate sequences until it meets a specified stopping criterion.

contents.heading: what-is-a-large-language-model-llm
contents.content: These models learn by training on massive text corpuses, which means they will be better suited to some use cases than others. For example, a model trained on GitHub data would understand the probabilities of sequences in source code particularly well. However, it's crucial to understand that the generated sequences, while often seeming plausible, can sometimes be random and not grounded in reality. As these models become more accurate, many surprising abilities and applications emerge.

contents.heading: what-is-a-prompt
contents.content: Prompts are the starting points for LLMs. They are the inputs that trigger the model to generate text. The scope of prompt engineering involves not just crafting these prompts but also understanding related concepts such as hidden prompts, tokens, token limits, and the potential for prompt hacking, which includes phenomena like jailbreaks and leaks.

contents.heading: why-is-prompt-engineering-needed
contents.content: Prompt engineering currently plays a pivotal role in shaping the responses of LLMs. It allows us to tweak the model to respond more effectively to a broader range of queries. This includes the use of techniques like semantic search, command grammars, and the ReActive model architecture. The performance, context window, and cost of LLMs varies between models and model providers which adds further constraints to the mix. For example, the GPT-4 model is more expensive than GPT-3.5-turbo and significantly slower, but it can also be more effective at certain tasks. And so, like many things in software engineering, there is a trade-offs between cost and performance.

contents.heading: why-is-prompt-engineering-needed
contents.content: To assist with comparing and tweaking LLMs, we've built an AI playground that allows you to compare the performance of different models side-by-side online. When you're ready, you can even generate code with the AI SDK to quickly use your prompt and your selected model into your own applications.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Imagine you want to build a slogan generator for marketing campaigns. Creating catchy slogans isn't always straightforward!

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: First, you'll need a prompt that makes it clear what you want. Let's start with an instruction. Submit this prompt to generate your first completion.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Not bad! Now, try making your instruction more specific.

contents.heading: start-with-an-instruction
contents.content: Introducing a single descriptive term to our prompt influences the completion. Essentially, crafting your prompt is the means by which you "instruct" or "program" the model.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Clear instructions are key for quality outcomes, but that might not always be enough. Let's try to enhance your instruction further.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: These slogans are fine, but could be even better. It appears the model overlooked the 'live' part in our prompt. Let's change it slightly to generate more appropriate suggestions.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Often, it's beneficial to both demonstrate and tell the model your requirements. Incorporating examples in your prompt can aid in conveying patterns or subtleties. Test this prompt that carries a few examples.

contents.heading: include-examples
contents.content: Great! Incorporating examples of expected output for a certain input prompted the model to generate the kind of names we aimed for.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Apart from designing prompts, you can influence completions by tweaking model settings. A crucial setting is the temperature.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: You might have seen that the same prompt, when repeated, yielded the same or nearly the same completions. This happens when your temperature is at 0.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Attempt to re-submit the identical prompt a few times with temperature set to 1.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Notice the difference? With a temperature above 0, the same prompt delivers varied completions each time.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: Keep in mind that the model forecasts the text most likely to follow the preceding text. Temperature, a value from 0 to 1, essentially governs the model's confidence level in making these predictions. A lower temperature implies lesser risks, leading to more precise and deterministic completions. A higher temperature yields a broader range of completions.

contents.heading: tweak-your-settings
contents.content: For your slogan generator, you might want a large pool of name suggestions. A moderate temperature of 0.6 should serve well.

metadata.title: Rendering UI with Language Models
metadata.description: Rendering UI with Language Models

title.children: Rendering User Interfaces on the Server

contents.content: Language models generate text, so at first it may seem like you would only need to render text in your application.

Above, the language model is passed a tool called getWeather that returns the weather information as text. However, instead of returning text, if you return a JSON object that represents the weather information, you can use it to render a React component instead.
Now you can use the object returned by the getWeather function to conditionally render a React component <WeatherCard/> that displays the weather information by passing the object as props.
Here's a little preview of what that might look like.
Rendering interfaces as part of language model generations elevates the user experience of your application, allowing people to interact with language models beyond text.
They also make it easier for you to interpret sequential tool calls that take place in multiple steps and help identify and debug where the model reasoned incorrectly.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: To recap, an application has to go through the following steps to render user interfaces as part of model generations:

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The user prompts the language model.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The language model generates a response that includes a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The tool call returns a JSON object that represents the user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The response is sent to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: The client receives the response and checks if the latest message was a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: If it was a tool call, the client renders the user interface based on the JSON object returned by the tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: Most applications have multiple tools that are called by the language model, and each tool can return a different user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-multiple-user-interfaces
contents.content: For example, a tool that searches for courses can return a list of courses, while a tool that searches for people can return a list of people. As this list grows, the complexity of your application will grow as well and it can become increasingly difficult to manage these user interfaces.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC (@ai-sdk/rsc) takes advantage of RSCs to solve the problem of managing all your React components on the client side, allowing you to render React components on the server and stream them to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: Rather than conditionally rendering user interfaces on the client based on the data returned by the language model, you can directly stream them from the server during a model generation.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The createStreamableUI function belongs to the @ai-sdk/rsc module and creates a stream that can send React components to the client.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: On the server, you render the <WeatherCard/> component with the props passed to it, and then stream it to the client. On the client side, you only need to render the UI that is streamed from the server.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: Now the steps involved are simplified:

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The user prompts the language model.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The language model generates a response that includes a tool call.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The tool call renders a React component along with relevant props that represent the user interface.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: The response is streamed to the client and rendered directly.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server
contents.content: Note: You can also render text on the server and stream it to the client using React Server Components. This way, all operations from language model generation to UI rendering can be done on the server, while the client only needs to render the UI that is streamed from the server.

contents.heading: rendering-user-interfaces-on-the-server

metadata.title: Stopping Streams
metadata.description: Learn how to cancel streams with the AI SDK

contents.content:
Cancelling ongoing streams is often needed.
For example, users might want to stop a stream when they realize that the response is not what they want.
The different parts of the AI SDK support cancelling streams in different ways.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core
contents.content:
The AI SDK functions have an abortSignal argument that you can use to cancel a stream.
You would use this if you want to cancel a stream from the server side to the LLM API, e.g. by
forwarding the abortSignal from the request.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui
contents.content:
The hooks, e.g. useChat or useCompletion, provide a stop helper function that can be used to cancel a stream.
This will cancel the stream from the client side to the server.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-ui
contents.content:
Stream abort functionality is not compatible with stream resumption. If you're
using resume: true in useChat, the abort functionality will break the
resumption mechanism. Choose either abort or resume functionality, but not
both.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: When streams are aborted, you may need to perform cleanup operations such as persisting partial results or cleaning up resources. The onAbort callback provides a way to handle these scenarios on the server side.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Unlike onFinish, which is called when a stream completes normally, onAbort is specifically called when a stream is aborted via AbortSignal. This distinction allows you to handle normal completion and aborted streams differently.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content:
For UI message streams (toUIMessageStreamResponse), the onFinish callback
also receives an isAborted parameter that indicates whether the stream was
aborted. This allows you to handle both completion and abort scenarios in a
single callback.

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: The onAbort callback receives:

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: steps: Array of all completed steps before the abort occurred

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: This is particularly useful for:

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Persisting partial conversation history to database

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Saving partial progress for later continuation

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Cleaning up server-side resources or connections

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: Logging abort events for analytics

contents.heading: handling-stream-abort-cleanup
contents.content: You can also handle abort events directly in the stream using the abort stream part:

contents.heading: ui-message-streams
contents.content: When using toUIMessageStreamResponse, you need to handle stream abortion slightly differently. The onFinish callback receives an isAborted parameter, and you should pass the consumeStream function to ensure proper abort handling:

contents.heading: ui-message-streams
contents.content: The consumeStream function is necessary for proper abort handling in UI message streams. It ensures that the stream is properly consumed even when aborted, preventing potential memory leaks or hanging connections.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-rsc
contents.content: The AI SDK RSC does not currently support stopping streams.

Vercel is a platform for developers that provides the tools, workflows, and infrastructure you need to build and deploy your web apps faster, without the need for additional configuration.

Vercel allows for automatic deployments on every branch push and merges onto the production branch of your GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket projects. It is a great option for deploying your AI application.

contents.heading: stop-conditions

metadata.title: Workflow Patterns
metadata.description: Learn workflow patterns for building reliable agents with the AI SDK.

contents.content: Combine the building blocks from the overview with these patterns to add structure and reliability to your agents:
Sequential Processing - Steps executed in order
Parallel Processing - Independent tasks run simultaneously
Evaluation/Feedback Loops - Results checked and improved iteratively
Orchestration - Coordinating multiple components
Routing - Directing work based on context

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Consider these key factors:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Flexibility vs Control - How much freedom does the LLM need vs how tightly you must constrain its actions?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Error Tolerance - What are the consequences of mistakes in your use case?

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Cost Considerations - More complex systems typically mean more LLM calls and higher costs

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Maintenance - Simpler architectures are easier to debug and modify

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Start with the simplest approach that meets your needs. Add complexity only when required by:

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Breaking down tasks into clear steps

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Adding tools for specific capabilities

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Implementing feedback loops for quality control

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Introducing multiple agents for complex workflows

contents.heading: choose-your-approach
contents.content: Let's look at examples of these patterns in action.

contents.heading: patterns-with-examples
contents.content: These patterns, adapted from Anthropic's guide on building effective agents, serve as building blocks you can combine to create comprehensive workflows. Each pattern addresses specific aspects of task execution. Combine them thoughtfully to build reliable solutions for complex problems.

contents.heading: sequential-processing-chains
contents.content: The simplest workflow pattern executes steps in a predefined order. Each step's output becomes input for the next step, creating a clear chain of operations. Use this pattern for tasks with well-defined sequences, like content generation pipelines or data transformation processes.

contents.heading: routing
contents.content: This pattern lets the model decide which path to take through a workflow based on context and intermediate results. The model acts as an intelligent router, directing the flow of execution between different branches of your workflow. Use this when handling varied inputs that require different processing approaches. In the example below, the first LLM call's results determine the second call's model size and system prompt.

contents.heading: parallel-processing
contents.content: Break down tasks into independent subtasks that execute simultaneously. This pattern uses parallel execution to improve efficiency while maintaining the benefits of structured workflows. For example, analyze multiple documents or process different aspects of a single input concurrently (like code review).

contents.heading: orchestrator-worker
contents.content: A primary model (orchestrator) coordinates the execution of specialized workers. Each worker optimizes for a specific subtask, while the orchestrator maintains overall context and ensures coherent results. This pattern excels at complex tasks requiring different types of expertise or processing.

contents.heading: evaluator-optimizer
contents.content: Add quality control to workflows with dedicated evaluation steps that assess intermediate results. Based on the evaluation, the workflow proceeds, retries with adjusted parameters, or takes corrective action. This creates robust workflows capable of self-improvement and error recovery.

metadata.title: Embeddings
metadata.description: Learn how to embed values with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Embeddings are a way to represent words, phrases, or images as vectors in a high-dimensional space.
In this space, similar words are close to each other, and the distance between words can be used to measure their similarity.

contents.heading: embedding-a-single-value
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embed function to embed single values, which is useful for tasks such as finding similar words
or phrases or clustering text.
You can use it with embeddings models, e.g. openai.textEmbeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.textEmbeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
When loading data, e.g. when preparing a data store for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG),
it is often useful to embed many values at once (batch embedding).

contents.heading: embedding-many-values
contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the embedMany function for this purpose.
Similar to embed, you can use it with embeddings models,
e.g. openai.textEmbeddingModel('text-embedding-3-large') or mistral.textEmbeddingModel('mistral-embed').

contents.heading: embedding-similarity
contents.content:
After embedding values, you can calculate the similarity between them using the cosineSimilarity function.
This is useful to e.g. find similar words or phrases in a dataset.
You can also rank and filter related items based on their similarity.

contents.heading: token-usage
contents.content:
Many providers charge based on the number of tokens used to generate embeddings.
Both embed and embedMany provide token usage information in the usage property of the result object:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Embedding model settings can be configured using providerOptions for provider-specific parameters:

contents.heading: parallel-requests
contents.content: The embedMany function now supports parallel processing with configurable maxParallelCalls to optimize performance:

contents.heading: retries
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional maxRetries parameter of type number
that you can use to set the maximum number of retries for the embedding process.
It defaults to 2 retries (3 attempts in total). You can set it to 0 to disable retries.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the embedding process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
Both embed and embedMany accept an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the embedding request.

contents.heading: response-information
contents.content: Both embed and embedMany return response information that includes the raw provider response:

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.description: Learn how to handle errors in the AI SDK Core

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: Regular errors are thrown and can be handled using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-regular-errors
contents.content: See Error Types for more information on the different types of errors that may be thrown.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-simple-streams
contents.content:
When errors occur during streams that do not support error chunks,
the error is thrown as a regular error.
You can handle these errors using the try/catch block.

contents.heading: handling-streaming-errors-streaming-with-error-support
contents.content:
Full streams support error parts.
You can handle those parts similar to other parts.
It is recommended to also add a try-catch block for errors that
happen outside of the streaming.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: When streams are aborted (e.g., via chat stop button), you may want to perform cleanup operations like updating stored messages in your UI. Use the onAbort callback to handle these cases.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback is called when a stream is aborted via AbortSignal, but onFinish is not called. This ensures you can still update your UI state appropriately.

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: The onAbort callback receives:

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: steps: An array of all completed steps before the abort

contents.heading: handling-stream-aborts
contents.content: You can also handle abort events directly in the stream:

headings.content: Handling streaming errors (streaming with error support)

metadata.title: Generating Structured Data
metadata.description: Learn how to generate structured data with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
While text generation can be useful, your use case will likely call for generating structured data.
For example, you might want to extract information from text, classify data, or generate synthetic data.

Many language models are capable of generating structured data, often defined as using "JSON modes" or "tools".
However, you need to manually provide schemas and then validate the generated data as LLMs can produce incorrect or incomplete structured data.

The AI SDK standardises structured object generation across model providers
with the generateObject
and streamObject functions.
You can use both functions with different output strategies, e.g. array, object, enum, or no-schema,
and with different generation modes, e.g. auto, tool, or json.
You can use Zod schemas, Valibot, or JSON schemas to specify the shape of the data that you want,
and the AI model will generate data that conforms to that structure.

You can pass Zod objects directly to the AI SDK functions or use the
zodSchema helper function.

contents.heading: generate-object
contents.content:
The generateObject generates structured data from a prompt.
The schema is also used to validate the generated data, ensuring type safety and correctness.

contents.heading: generate-object
contents.content: See generateObject in action with these examples

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the response property:

contents.heading: stream-object
contents.content:
Given the added complexity of returning structured data, model response time can be unacceptable for your interactive use case.
With the streamObject function, you can stream the model's response as it is generated.

contents.heading: stream-object
contents.content: You can use streamObject to stream generated UIs in combination with React Server Components (see Generative UI)) or the useObject hook.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content:
streamObject immediately starts streaming.
Errors become part of the stream and are not thrown to prevent e.g. servers from crashing.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content: To log errors, you can provide an onError callback that is triggered when an error occurs.

contents.heading: output-strategy
contents.content: You can use both functions with different output strategies, e.g. array, object, enum, or no-schema.

contents.heading: object
contents.content:
The default output strategy is object, which returns the generated data as an object.
You don't need to specify the output strategy if you want to use the default.

contents.heading: array
contents.content:
If you want to generate an array of objects, you can set the output strategy to array.
When you use the array output strategy, the schema specifies the shape of an array element.
With streamObject, you can also stream the generated array elements using elementStream.

contents.heading: enum
contents.content:
If you want to generate a specific enum value, e.g. for classification tasks,
you can set the output strategy to enum
and provide a list of possible values in the enum parameter.

contents.heading: no-schema
contents.content:
In some cases, you might not want to use a schema,
for example when the data is a dynamic user request.
You can use the output setting to set the output format to no-schema in those cases
and omit the schema parameter.

contents.heading: schema-name-and-description
contents.content: You can optionally specify a name and description for the schema. These are used by some providers for additional LLM guidance, e.g. via tool or schema name.

contents.heading: accessing-reasoning
contents.content: You can access the reasoning used by the language model to generate the object via the reasoning property on the result. This property contains a string with the model's thought process, if available.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: When generateObject cannot generate a valid object, it throws a AI_NoObjectGeneratedError.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate a parsable object that conforms to the schema.
It can arise due to the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be validated against the schema.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: text: The text that was generated by the model. This can be the raw text or the tool call text, depending on the object generation mode.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: response: Metadata about the language model response, including response id, timestamp, and model.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: usage: Request token usage.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error (e.g. a JSON parsing error). You can use this for more detailed error handling.

contents.heading: repairing-invalid-or-malformed-json
contents.content: The repairText function is experimental and may change in the future.

contents.heading: repairing-invalid-or-malformed-json
contents.content:
Sometimes the model will generate invalid or malformed JSON.
You can use the repairText function to attempt to repair the JSON.

contents.heading: repairing-invalid-or-malformed-json
contents.content:
It receives the error, either a JSONParseError or a TypeValidationError,
and the text that was generated by the model.
You can then attempt to repair the text and return the repaired text.

contents.heading: structured-outputs-with-generatetext-and-streamtext
contents.content: You can generate structured data with generateText and streamText by using the experimental_output setting.

contents.heading: structured-outputs-with-generatetext-and-streamtext
contents.content:
Some models, e.g. those by OpenAI, support structured outputs and tool calling
at the same time. This is only possible with generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: structured-outputs-with-generatetext-and-streamtext
contents.content:
Structured output generation with generateText and streamText is
experimental and may change in the future.

contents.heading: more-examples
contents.content: You can see generateObject and streamObject in action using various frameworks in the following examples:

headings.content: Structured outputs with generateText and streamText

metadata.title: Generating Text
metadata.description: Learn how to generate text with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate text in response to a prompt, which can contain instructions and information to process.
For example, you can ask a model to come up with a recipe, draft an email, or summarize a document.
The AI SDK Core provides two functions to generate text and stream it from LLMs:
generateText: Generates text for a given prompt and model.
streamText: Streams text from a given prompt and model.
Advanced LLM features such as tool calling and structured data generation are built on top of text generation.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can generate text using the generateText function. This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: You can use more advanced prompts to generate text with more complex instructions and content:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: The result object of generateText contains several promises that resolve when all required data is available:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.reasoning: The full reasoning that the model has generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.reasoningText: The reasoning text of the model (only available for some models).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.files: The files that were generated in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in the last step (only available for some models).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that were made in the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The results of the tool calls from the last step.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.usage: The usage of the model during the final step of text generation.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.totalUsage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.request: Additional request information.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.response: Additional response information, including response messages and body.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.providerMetadata: Additional provider-specific metadata.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: result.experimental_output: The generated structured output using the experimental_output specification.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content:
Sometimes you need access to the full response from the model provider,
e.g. to access some provider-specific headers or body content.

contents.heading: accessing-response-headers--body
contents.content: You can access the raw response headers and body using the response property:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: Depending on your model and prompt, it can take a large language model (LLM) up to a minute to finish generating its response. This delay can be unacceptable for interactive use cases such as chatbots or real-time applications, where users expect immediate responses.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: AI SDK Core provides the streamText function which simplifies streaming text from LLMs:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.textStream is both a ReadableStream and an AsyncIterable.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming and suppresses errors to prevent
server crashes. Use the onError callback to log errors.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
You can use streamText on its own or in combination with AI SDK
UI and AI SDK
RSC.
The result object contains several helper functions to make the integration into AI SDK UI easier:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toUIMessageStreamResponse(): Creates a UI Message stream HTTP response (with tool calls etc.) that can be used in a Next.js App Router API route.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse(): Writes UI Message stream delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toTextStreamResponse(): Creates a simple text stream HTTP response.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.pipeTextStreamToResponse(): Writes text delta output to a Node.js response-like object.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content:
streamText is using backpressure and only generates tokens as they are
requested. You need to consume the stream in order for it to finish.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: It also provides several promises that resolve when the stream is finished:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.content: The content that was generated in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.text: The generated text.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.reasoning: The full reasoning that the model has generated.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.reasoningText: The reasoning text of the model (only available for some models).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.files: Files that have been generated by the model in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.sources: Sources that have been used as references in the last step (only available for some models).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolCalls: The tool calls that have been executed in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.toolResults: The tool results that have been generated in the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.finishReason: The reason the model finished generating text.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.usage: The usage of the model during the final step of text generation.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.totalUsage: The total usage across all steps (for multi-step generations).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.warnings: Warnings from the model provider (e.g. unsupported settings).

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.steps: Details for all steps, useful for getting information about intermediate steps.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.request: Additional request information from the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.response: Additional response information from the last step.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: result.providerMetadata: Additional provider-specific metadata from the last step.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content:
streamText immediately starts streaming to enable sending data without waiting for the model.
Errors become part of the stream and are not thrown to prevent e.g. servers from crashing.

contents.heading: onerror-callback
contents.content: To log errors, you can provide an onError callback that is triggered when an error occurs.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: When using streamText, you can provide an onChunk callback that is triggered for each chunk of the stream.

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: It receives the following chunk types:

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: text

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: reasoning

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: source

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-call

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-input-start

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-input-delta

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: tool-result

contents.heading: onchunk-callback
contents.content: raw

contents.heading: onfinish-callback
contents.content:
When using streamText, you can provide an onFinish callback that is triggered when the stream is finished (
API Reference
).
It contains the text, usage information, finish reason, messages, steps, total usage, and more:

contents.heading: fullstream-property
contents.content:
You can read a stream with all events using the fullStream property.
This can be useful if you want to implement your own UI or handle the stream in a different way.
Here is an example of how to use the fullStream property:

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
You can use the experimental_transform option to transform the stream.
This is useful for e.g. filtering, changing, or smoothing the text stream.

contents.heading: stream-transformation
contents.content:
The transformations are applied before the callbacks are invoked and the promises are resolved.
If you e.g. have a transformation that changes all text to uppercase, the onFinish callback will receive the transformed text.

contents.heading: smoothing-streams
contents.content:
The AI SDK Core provides a smoothStream function that
can be used to smooth out text streaming.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also implement your own custom transformations.
The transformation function receives the tools that are available to the model,
and returns a function that is used to transform the stream.
Tools can either be generic or limited to the tools that you are using.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
Here is an example of how to implement a custom transformation that converts
all text to uppercase:

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
You can also stop the stream using the stopStream function.
This is e.g. useful if you want to stop the stream when model guardrails are violated, e.g. by generating inappropriate content.

contents.heading: custom-transformations
contents.content:
When you invoke stopStream, it is important to simulate the step-finish and finish events to guarantee that a well-formed stream is returned
and all callbacks are invoked.

contents.heading: multiple-transformations
contents.content: You can also provide multiple transformations. They are applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Some providers such as Perplexity and
Google Generative AI include sources in the response.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content:
Currently sources are limited to web pages that ground the response.
You can access them using the sources property of the result.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: Each url source contains the following properties:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: id: The ID of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: url: The URL of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: title: The optional title of the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: providerMetadata: Provider metadata for the source.

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use generateText, you can access the sources using the sources property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: When you use streamText, you can access the sources using the fullStream property:

contents.heading: sources
contents.content: The sources are also available in the result.sources promise.

contents.heading: examples
contents.content: You can see generateText and streamText in action using various frameworks in the following examples:

metadata.title: Image Generation
metadata.description: Learn how to generate images with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the generateImage
function to generate images based on a given prompt using an image model.
You can access the image data using the base64 or uint8Array properties:

contents.heading: size-and-aspect-ratio
contents.content: Depending on the model, you can either specify the size or the aspect ratio.

contents.heading: size
contents.content:
The size is specified as a string in the format {width}x{height}.
Models only support a few sizes, and the supported sizes are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: aspect-ratio
contents.content:
The aspect ratio is specified as a string in the format {width}:{height}.
Models only support a few aspect ratios, and the supported aspect ratios are different for each model and provider.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: generateImage also supports generating multiple images at once:

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content:
generateImage will automatically call the model as often as needed (in
parallel) to generate the requested number of images.

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: Each image model has an internal limit on how many images it can generate in a single API call. The AI SDK manages this automatically by batching requests appropriately when you request multiple images using the n parameter. By default, the SDK uses provider-documented limits (for example, DALL-E 3 can only generate 1 image per call, while DALL-E 2 supports up to 10).

contents.heading: generating-multiple-images
contents.content: If needed, you can override this behavior using the maxImagesPerCall setting when generating your image. This is particularly useful when working with new or custom models where the default batch size might not be optimal:

contents.heading: providing-a-seed
contents.content:
You can provide a seed to the generateImage function to control the output of the image generation process.
If supported by the model, the same seed will always produce the same image.

contents.heading: provider-specific-settings
contents.content:
Image models often have provider- or even model-specific settings.
You can pass such settings to the generateImage function
using the providerOptions parameter. The options for the provider
(openai in the example below) become request body properties.

contents.heading: abort-signals-and-timeouts
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional abortSignal parameter of
type AbortSignal
that you can use to abort the image generation process or set a timeout.

contents.heading: custom-headers
contents.content:
generateImage accepts an optional headers parameter of type Record<string, string>
that you can use to add custom headers to the image generation request.

contents.heading: warnings
contents.content: If the model returns warnings, e.g. for unsupported parameters, they will be available in the warnings property of the response.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-meta-data
contents.content: Some providers expose additional meta data for the result overall or per image.

contents.heading: additional-provider-specific-meta-data
contents.content: The outer key of the returned providerMetadata is the provider name. The inner values are the metadata. An images key is always present in the metadata and is an array with the same length as the top level images key.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content:
When generateImage cannot generate a valid image, it throws a AI_NoImageGeneratedError.
Unclassified empty image responses are retried according to maxRetries before this error is thrown.
Providers can classify terminal empty responses, such as moderation blocks, with isRetryable: false; these responses are not retried.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: This error occurs when the AI provider fails to generate an image. It can arise due to the following reasons:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model failed to generate a response

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The model generated a response that could not be parsed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The error preserves the following information to help you log the issue:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: responses: Metadata about the image model responses, including timestamp, model, and headers.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: cause: The cause of the error. You can use this for more detailed error handling

contents.heading: generating-images-with-language-models
contents.content:
Some language models such as Google gemini-2.5-flash-image-preview support multi-modal outputs including images.
With such models, you can access the generated images using the files property of the response.

metadata.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
metadata.description: Learn how to connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and use their tools with AI SDK Core.

contents.content: The MCP tools feature is experimental and may change in the future.

The AI SDK supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to access their tools, resources, and prompts.
This enables your AI applications to discover and use capabilities across various services through a standardized interface.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: We recommend using HTTP transport (like StreamableHTTPClientTransport) for production deployments. The stdio transport should only be used for connecting to local servers as it cannot be deployed to production environments.

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: Create an MCP client using one of the following transport options:

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: HTTP transport (Recommended): Either configure HTTP directly via the client using transport: { type: 'http', ... }, or use MCP's official TypeScript SDK StreamableHTTPClientTransport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: SSE (Server-Sent Events): An alternative HTTP-based transport

contents.heading: initializing-an-mcp-client
contents.content: stdio: For local development only. Uses standard input/output streams for local MCP servers

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: For production deployments, we recommend using the HTTP transport. You can configure it directly on the client:

contents.heading: http-transport-recommended
contents.content: Alternatively, you can use StreamableHTTPClientTransport from MCP's official TypeScript SDK:

contents.heading: sse-transport
contents.content: SSE provides an alternative HTTP-based transport option. Configure it with a type and url property. You can also provide an authProvider for OAuth:

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The stdio transport should only be used for local servers.

contents.heading: stdio-transport-local-servers
contents.content: The Stdio transport can be imported from either the MCP SDK or the AI SDK:

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content: You can also bring your own transport by implementing the MCPTransport interface for specific requirements not covered by the standard transports.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
The client returned by the experimental_createMCPClient function is a
lightweight client intended for use in tool conversion. It currently does not
support all features of the full MCP client, such as: session
management, resumable streams, and receiving notifications.

contents.heading: custom-transport
contents.content:
Authorization via OAuth is supported when using the AI SDK MCP HTTP or SSE
transports by providing an authProvider.

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: After initialization, you should close the MCP client based on your usage pattern:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For short-lived usage (e.g., single requests), close the client when the response is finished

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: For long-running clients (e.g., command line apps), keep the client open but ensure it's closed when the application terminates

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When streaming responses, you can close the client when the LLM response has finished. For example, when using streamText, you should use the onFinish callback:

contents.heading: closing-the-mcp-client
contents.content: When generating responses without streaming, you can use try/finally or cleanup functions in your framework:

contents.heading: using-mcp-tools
contents.content: The client's tools method acts as an adapter between MCP tools and AI SDK tools. It supports two approaches for working with tool schemas:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: With schema discovery, all tools offered by the server are automatically listed, and input parameter types are inferred based on the schemas provided by the server:

contents.heading: schema-discovery
contents.content: This approach is simpler to implement and automatically stays in sync with server changes. However, you won't have TypeScript type safety during development, and all tools from the server will be loaded

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: For better type safety and control, you can define the tools and their input schemas explicitly in your client code:

contents.heading: schema-definition
contents.content: This approach provides full TypeScript type safety and IDE autocompletion, letting you catch parameter mismatches during development. When you define schemas, the client only pulls the explicitly defined tools, keeping your application focused on the tools it needs

contents.heading: using-mcp-resources
contents.content: According to the MCP specification, resources are application-driven data sources that provide context to the model. Unlike tools (which are model-controlled), your application decides when to fetch and pass resources as context.

contents.heading: using-mcp-resources
contents.content: The MCP client provides three methods for working with resources:

contents.heading: listing-resources
contents.content: List all available resources from the MCP server:

contents.heading: reading-resource-contents
contents.content: Read the contents of a specific resource by its URI:

contents.heading: listing-resource-templates
contents.content: Resource templates are dynamic URI patterns that allow flexible queries. List all available templates:

contents.heading: using-mcp-prompts
contents.content: According to the MCP specification, prompts are user-controlled templates that servers expose for clients to list and retrieve with optional arguments.

contents.heading: getting-a-prompt
contents.content: Retrieve prompt messages, optionally passing arguments defined by the server:

contents.heading: handling-elicitation-requests
contents.content: Elicitation is a mechanism where MCP servers can request additional information from the client during tool execution. For example, a server might need user input to complete a registration form or confirmation for a sensitive operation.

contents.heading: handling-elicitation-requests
contents.content:
It is up to the client application to handle elicitation requests properly.
The MCP client simply surfaces these requests from the server to your
application code.

contents.heading: enabling-elicitation-support
contents.content: To enable elicitation, you need to advertise the capability when creating the MCP client:

contents.heading: registering-an-elicitation-handler
contents.content: Use the onElicitationRequest method to register a handler that will be called when the server requests input:

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: Your handler must return an object with an action field that can be one of:

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'accept': User provided the requested information. Must include content with the data.

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'decline': User chose not to provide the information.

contents.heading: elicitation-response-actions
contents.content: 'cancel': User cancelled the operation entirely.
