contents.content: You can see MCP in action in the following examples:

metadata.title: Language Model Middleware
metadata.description: Learn how to use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models

contents.content:
Language model middleware is a way to enhance the behavior of language models
by intercepting and modifying the calls to the language model.

It can be used to add features like guardrails, RAG, caching, and logging
in a language model agnostic way. Such middleware can be developed and
distributed independently from the language models that they are applied to.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
You can use language model middleware with the wrapLanguageModel function.
It takes a language model and a language model middleware and returns a new
language model that incorporates the middleware.

contents.heading: using-language-model-middleware
contents.content: The wrapped language model can be used just like any other language model, e.g. in streamText:

contents.heading: multiple-middlewares
contents.content:
You can provide multiple middlewares to the wrapLanguageModel function.
The middlewares will be applied in the order they are provided.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK comes with several built-in middlewares that you can use to configure language models:

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: extractReasoningMiddleware: Extracts reasoning information from the generated text and exposes it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: simulateStreamingMiddleware: Simulates streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.

contents.heading: built-in-middleware
contents.content: defaultSettingsMiddleware: Applies default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
Some providers and models expose reasoning information in the generated text using special tags,
e.g. <think> and </think>.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: The extractReasoningMiddleware function can be used to extract this reasoning information and expose it as a reasoning property on the result.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content: You can then use that enhanced model in functions like generateText and streamText.

contents.heading: extract-reasoning
contents.content:
The extractReasoningMiddleware function also includes a startWithReasoning option.
When set to true, the reasoning tag will be prepended to the generated text.
This is useful for models that do not include the reasoning tag at the beginning of the response.
For more details, see the DeepSeek R1 guide.

contents.heading: simulate-streaming
contents.content:
The simulateStreamingMiddleware function can be used to simulate streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models.
This is useful when you want to maintain a consistent streaming interface even when using models that only provide complete responses.

contents.heading: default-settings
contents.content: The defaultSettingsMiddleware function can be used to apply default settings to a language model.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: The AI SDK provides a Language Model Middleware specification. Community members can develop middleware that adheres to this specification, making it compatible with the AI SDK ecosystem.

contents.heading: community-middleware
contents.content: Here are some community middlewares that you can explore:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The Custom tool call parser middleware extends tool call capabilities to models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style tools parameter. This includes many self-hosted and third-party models that lack native function calling features.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content:
Using this middleware on models that support native function calls may result
in unintended performance degradation, so check whether your model supports
native function calls before deciding to use it.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: This middleware enables function calling capabilities by converting function schemas into prompt instructions and parsing the model's responses into structured function calls. It works by transforming the JSON function definitions into natural language instructions the model can understand, then analyzing the generated text to extract function call attempts. This approach allows developers to use the same function calling API across different model providers, even with models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style function calling format, providing a consistent function calling experience regardless of the underlying model implementation.

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: The @ai-sdk-tool/parser package offers three middleware variants:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: createToolMiddleware: A flexible function for creating custom tool call middleware tailored to specific models

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: hermesToolMiddleware: Ready-to-use middleware for Hermes & Qwen format function calls

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: gemmaToolMiddleware: Pre-configured middleware for Gemma 3 model series function call format

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Here's how you can enable function calls with Gemma models that don't support them natively:

contents.heading: custom-tool-call-parser
contents.content: Find more examples at this link.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
Implementing language model middleware is advanced functionality and requires
a solid understanding of the language model
specification.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: You can implement any of the following three function to modify the behavior of the language model:

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: transformParams: Transforms the parameters before they are passed to the language model, for both doGenerate and doStream.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapGenerate: Wraps the doGenerate method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content:
wrapStream: Wraps the doStream method of the language model.
You can modify the parameters, call the language model, and modify the result.

contents.heading: implementing-language-model-middleware
contents.content: Here are some examples of how to implement language model middleware:

contents.heading: examples
contents.content:
These examples are not meant to be used in production. They are just to show
how you can use middleware to enhance the behavior of language models.

contents.heading: logging
contents.content: This example shows how to log the parameters and generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: caching
contents.content: This example shows how to build a simple cache for the generated text of a language model call.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content: This example shows how to use RAG as middleware.

contents.heading: retrieval-augmented-generation-rag
contents.content:
Helper functions like getLastUserMessageText and findSources are not part
of the AI SDK. They are just used in this example to illustrate the concept of
RAG.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
Guard rails are a way to ensure that the generated text of a language model call
is safe and appropriate. This example shows how to use guardrails as middleware.

contents.heading: guardrails
contents.content:
The streaming example buffers each text block until text-end so matches
split across text-delta chunks cannot leak through. This delays output and
uses memory proportional to the text block size. Do not redact each delta
independently. An incremental implementation must retain every possible
incomplete match, and a fixed-size buffer alone is not safe for unbounded
variable-length patterns.

contents.heading: configuring-per-request-custom-metadata
contents.content: To send and access custom metadata in Middleware, you can use providerOptions. This is useful when building logging middleware where you want to pass additional context like user IDs, timestamps, or other contextual data that can help with tracking and debugging.

metadata.title: Overview
metadata.description: An overview of AI SDK Core.

contents.content:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced programs that can understand, create, and engage with human language on a large scale.
They are trained on vast amounts of written material to recognize patterns in language and predict what might come next in a given piece of text.

AI SDK Core simplifies working with LLMs by offering a standardized way of integrating them into your app - so you can focus on building great AI applications for your users, not waste time on technical details.
For example, here’s how you can generate text with various models using the AI SDK:

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
AI SDK Core has various functions designed for text generation, structured data generation, and tool usage.
These functions take a standardized approach to setting up prompts and settings, making it easier to work with different models.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
generateText: Generates text and tool calls.
This function is ideal for non-interactive use cases such as automation tasks where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
streamText: Stream text and tool calls.
You can use the streamText function for interactive use cases such as chat bots and content streaming.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
generateObject: Generates a typed, structured object that matches a Zod schema.
You can use this function to force the language model to return structured data, e.g. for information extraction, synthetic data generation, or classification tasks.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-core-functions
contents.content:
streamObject: Stream a structured object that matches a Zod schema.
You can use this function to stream generated UIs.

contents.heading: api-reference
contents.content: Please check out the AI SDK Core API Reference for more details on each function.

metadata.title: Prompt Engineering
metadata.description: Learn how to develop prompts with AI SDK Core.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When you create prompts that include tools, getting good results can be tricky as the number and complexity of your tools increases.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Here are a few tips to help you get the best results:

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use a model that is strong at tool calling, such as gpt-5 or gpt-4.1. Weaker models will often struggle to call tools effectively and flawlessly.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the number of tools low, e.g. to 5 or less.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Keep the complexity of the tool parameters low. Complex Zod schemas with many nested and optional elements, unions, etc. can be challenging for the model to work with.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Use semantically meaningful names for your tools, parameters, parameter properties, etc. The more information you pass to the model, the better it can understand what you want.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: Add .describe("...") to your Zod schema properties to give the model hints about what a particular property is for.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: When the output of a tool might be unclear to the model and there are dependencies between tools, use the description field of a tool to provide information about the output of the tool execution.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: You can include example input/outputs of tool calls in your prompt to help the model understand how to use the tools. Keep in mind that the tools work with JSON objects, so the examples should use JSON.

contents.heading: prompts-for-tools
contents.content: In general, the goal should be to give the model all information it needs in a clear way.

contents.heading: tool--structured-data-schemas
contents.content: The mapping from Zod schemas to LLM inputs (typically JSON schema) is not always straightforward, since the mapping is not one-to-one.

contents.heading: zod-dates
contents.content:
Zod expects JavaScript Date objects, but models return dates as strings.
You can specify and validate the date format using z.string().datetime() or z.string().date(),
and then use a Zod transformer to convert the string to a Date object.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: When working with tools that have optional parameters, you may encounter compatibility issues with certain providers that use strict schema validation.

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content:
This is particularly relevant for OpenAI models with structured outputs
(strict mode).

contents.heading: optional-parameters
contents.content: For maximum compatibility, optional parameters should use .nullable() instead of .optional():

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: For tool calls and object generation, it's recommended to use temperature: 0 to ensure deterministic and consistent results:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Lower temperature values reduce randomness in model outputs, which is particularly important when the model needs to:

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Generate structured data with specific formats

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Make precise tool calls with correct parameters

contents.heading: temperature-settings
contents.content: Follow strict schemas consistently

contents.heading: inspecting-warnings
contents.content:
Not all providers support all AI SDK features.
Providers either throw exceptions or return warnings when they do not support a feature.
To check if your prompt, tools, and settings are handled correctly by the provider, you can check the call warnings:

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content:
You can inspect the raw HTTP request bodies for models that expose them, e.g. OpenAI.
This allows you to inspect the exact payload that is sent to the model provider in the provider-specific way.

contents.heading: http-request-bodies
contents.content: Request bodies are available via the request.body property of the response:

metadata.title: Provider & Model Management
metadata.description: Learn how to work with multiple providers and models

title.children: Combining Custom Providers, Provider Registry, and Middleware

contents.content:
When you work with multiple providers and models, it is often desirable to manage them in a central place
and access the models through simple string ids.

The AI SDK offers custom providers and
a provider registry for this purpose:

With custom providers, you can pre-configure model settings, provide model name aliases,
and limit the available models.
The provider registry lets you mix multiple providers and access them through simple string ids.
You can mix and match custom providers, the provider registry, and middleware in your application.

contents.heading: custom-providers
contents.content: You can create a custom provider using customProvider.

contents.heading: example-custom-model-settings
contents.content:
You might want to override the default model settings for a provider or provide model name aliases
with pre-configured settings.

contents.heading: example-model-name-alias
contents.content: You can also provide model name aliases, so you can update the model version in one place in the future:

contents.heading: example-limit-available-models
contents.content: You can limit the available models in the system, even if you have multiple providers.

contents.heading: provider-registry
contents.content: You can create a provider registry with multiple providers and models using createProviderRegistry.

contents.heading: setup-with-custom-separator
contents.content: By default, the registry uses : as the separator between provider and model IDs. You can customize this separator:

contents.heading: example-use-language-models
contents.content:
You can access language models by using the languageModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-text-embedding-models
contents.content:
You can access text embedding models by using the textEmbeddingModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: example-use-image-models
contents.content:
You can access image models by using the imageModel method on the registry.
The provider id will become the prefix of the model id: providerId:modelId.

contents.heading: combining-custom-providers-provider-registry-and-middleware
contents.content:

metadata.title: Settings
metadata.description: Learn how to configure the AI SDK.

contents.content: Large language models (LLMs) typically provide settings to augment their output.
All AI SDK functions support the following common settings in addition to the model, the prompt, and additional provider-specific settings:

Some providers do not support all common settings. If you use a setting with a
provider that does not support it, a warning will be generated. You can check
the warnings property in the result object to see if any warnings were
generated.

contents.heading: maxoutputtokens
contents.content: Maximum number of tokens to generate.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content: Temperature setting.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means almost deterministic results, and higher values mean more randomness.

contents.heading: temperature
contents.content: It is recommended to set either temperature or topP, but not both.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content: Nucleus sampling.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, nucleus sampling is a number between 0 and 1.
E.g. 0.1 would mean that only tokens with the top 10% probability mass are considered.

contents.heading: topp
contents.content: It is recommended to set either temperature or topP, but not both.

contents.heading: topk
contents.content: Only sample from the top K options for each subsequent token.

contents.heading: topk
contents.content:
Used to remove "long tail" low probability responses.
Recommended for advanced use cases only. You usually only need to use temperature.

contents.heading: presencepenalty
contents.content: The presence penalty affects the likelihood of the model to repeat information that is already in the prompt.

contents.heading: presencepenalty
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means no penalty.

contents.heading: frequencypenalty
contents.content: The frequency penalty affects the likelihood of the model to repeatedly use the same words or phrases.

contents.heading: frequencypenalty
contents.content:
The value is passed through to the provider. The range depends on the provider and model.
For most providers, 0 means no penalty.

contents.heading: stopsequences
contents.content: The stop sequences to use for stopping the text generation.

contents.heading: stopsequences
contents.content:
If set, the model will stop generating text when one of the stop sequences is generated.
Providers may have limits on the number of stop sequences.

contents.heading: seed
contents.content:
It is the seed (integer) to use for random sampling.
If set and supported by the model, calls will generate deterministic results.

contents.heading: maxretries
contents.content: Maximum number of retries. Set to 0 to disable retries. Default: 2.

contents.heading: abortsignal
contents.content: An optional abort signal that can be used to cancel the call.

contents.heading: abortsignal
contents.content:
The abort signal can e.g. be forwarded from a user interface to cancel the call,
or to define a timeout.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content: Additional HTTP headers to be sent with the request. Only applicable for HTTP-based providers.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content:
You can use the request headers to provide additional information to the provider,
depending on what the provider supports. For example, some observability providers support
headers such as Prompt-Id.

contents.heading: headers
contents.content:
The headers setting is for request-specific headers. You can also set
headers in the provider configuration. These headers will be sent with every
request made by the provider.

contents.content:
The AI SDK provides the generateSpeech

To access the generated audio:

metadata.title: Telemetry
metadata.description: Using OpenTelemetry with AI SDK Core

contents.content: AI SDK Telemetry is experimental and may change in the future.

The AI SDK uses OpenTelemetry to collect telemetry data.
OpenTelemetry is an open-source observability framework designed to provide
standardized instrumentation for collecting telemetry data.

Check out the AI SDK Observability Integrations
to see providers that offer monitoring and tracing for AI SDK applications.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: For Next.js applications, please follow the Next.js OpenTelemetry guide to enable telemetry first.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: You can then use the experimental_telemetry option to enable telemetry on specific function calls while the feature is experimental:

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content:
When telemetry is enabled, you can also control if you want to record the input values and the output values for the function.
By default, both are enabled. You can disable them by setting the recordInputs and recordOutputs options to false.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content:
Disabling the recording of inputs and outputs can be useful for privacy, data transfer, and performance reasons.
You might for example want to disable recording inputs if they contain sensitive information.

contents.heading: telemetry-metadata
contents.content:
You can provide a functionId to identify the function that the telemetry data is for,
and metadata to include additional information in the telemetry data.

contents.heading: custom-tracer
contents.content:
You may provide a tracer which must return an OpenTelemetry Tracer. This is useful in situations where
you want your traces to use a TracerProvider other than the one provided by the @opentelemetry/api singleton.

metadata.title: Testing
metadata.description: Learn how to use AI SDK Core mock providers for testing.

contents.content:
Testing language models can be challenging, because they are non-deterministic
and calling them is slow and expensive.

To enable you to unit test your code that uses the AI SDK, the AI SDK Core
includes mock providers and test helpers. You can import the following helpers from ai/test:
MockEmbeddingModelV2: A mock embedding model using the embedding model v2 specification.
MockLanguageModelV2: A mock language model using the language model v2 specification.
mockId: Provides an incrementing integer ID.
mockValues: Iterates over an array of values with each call. Returns the last value when the array is exhausted.
simulateReadableStream: Simulates a readable stream with delays.

With mock providers and test helpers, you can control the output of the AI SDK
and test your code in a repeatable and deterministic way without actually calling
a language model provider.

metadata.title: Tool Calling
metadata.description: Learn about tool calling and multi-step calls (using stopWhen) with AI SDK Core.

title.children: Example: Extract tool results from all steps
Message Modification for Longer Agentic Loops
Example: Use a model with structured outputs for repair
Example: Use the re-ask strategy for repair
AI SDK Tools vs MCP Tools

contents.content:
As covered under Foundations, tools are objects that can be called by the model to perform a specific task.
AI SDK Core tools contain three elements:
description: An optional description of the tool that can influence when the tool is picked.
inputSchema: A Zod schema or a JSON schema that defines the input parameters. The schema is consumed by the LLM, and also used to validate the LLM tool calls.

execute: An optional async function that is called with the inputs from the tool call. It produces a value of type RESULT (generic type). It is optional because you might want to forward tool calls to the client or to a queue instead of executing them in the same process.

You can use the tool helper function to
infer the types of the execute parameters.
The tools parameter of generateText and streamText is an object that has the tool names as keys and the tools as values:

When a model uses a tool, it is called a "tool call" and the output of the
tool is called a "tool result".

Tool calling is not restricted to only text generation.
You can also use it to render user interfaces (Generative UI).

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: With the stopWhen setting, you can enable multi-step calls in generateText and streamText. When stopWhen is set and the model generates a tool call, the AI SDK will trigger a new generation passing in the tool result until there are no further tool calls or the stopping condition is met.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content:
The stopWhen conditions are only evaluated when the last step contains tool
results.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: By default, when you use generateText or streamText, it triggers a single generation. This works well for many use cases where you can rely on the model's training data to generate a response. However, when you provide tools, the model now has the choice to either generate a normal text response, or generate a tool call. If the model generates a tool call, it's generation is complete and that step is finished.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: You may want the model to generate text after the tool has been executed, either to summarize the tool results in the context of the users query. In many cases, you may also want the model to use multiple tools in a single response. This is where multi-step calls come in.

contents.heading: multi-step-calls-using-stopwhen
contents.content: You can think of multi-step calls in a similar way to a conversation with a human. When you ask a question, if the person does not have the requisite knowledge in their common knowledge (a model's training data), the person may need to look up information (use a tool) before they can provide you with an answer. In the same way, the model may need to call a tool to get the information it needs to answer your question where each generation (tool call or text generation) is a step.

contents.heading: steps
contents.content:
To access intermediate tool calls and results, you can use the steps property in the result object
or the streamText onFinish callback.
It contains all the text, tool calls, tool results, and more from each step.

contents.heading: onstepfinish-callback
contents.content:
When using generateText or streamText, you can provide an onStepFinish callback that
is triggered when a step is finished,
i.e. all text deltas, tool calls, and tool results for the step are available.
When you have multiple steps, the callback is triggered for each step.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: The prepareStep callback is called before a step is started.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: It is called with the following parameters:

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: model: The model that was passed into generateText.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: stepNumber: The number of the step that is being executed.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: steps: The steps that have been executed so far.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: messages: The messages that will be sent to the model for the current step.

contents.heading: preparestep-callback
contents.content: You can use it to provide different settings for a step, including modifying the input messages.

contents.heading: message-modification-for-longer-agentic-loops
contents.content: In longer agentic loops, you can use the messages parameter to modify the input messages for each step. This is particularly useful for prompt compression:

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content:
Adding the generated assistant and tool messages to your conversation history is a common task,
especially if you are using multi-step tool calls.

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content:
Both generateText and streamText have a response.messages property that you can use to
add the assistant and tool messages to your conversation history.
It is also available in the onFinish callback of streamText.

contents.heading: response-messages
contents.content: The response.messages property contains an array of ModelMessage objects that you can add to your conversation history:

contents.content: AI SDK Core supports dynamic tools for scenarios where tool schemas are not known at compile time. This is useful for:

You can return an AsyncIterable over multiple results.
In this case, the last value from the iterable is the final tool result.

contents.heading: preliminary-tool-results

This can be used in combination with generator functions to e.g. stream status information
during the tool execution:

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content:
You can use the toolChoice setting to influence when a tool is selected.
It supports the following settings:

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: auto (default): the model can choose whether and which tools to call.

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: required: the model must call a tool. It can choose which tool to call.

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: none: the model must not call tools

contents.heading: tool-choice
contents.content: { type: 'tool', toolName: string (typed) }: the model must call the specified tool

contents.heading: tool-execution-options
contents.content: When tools are called, they receive additional options as a second parameter.

contents.heading: tool-call-id
contents.content:
The ID of the tool call is forwarded to the tool execution.
You can use it e.g. when sending tool-call related information with stream data.

contents.heading: messages
contents.content:
The messages that were sent to the language model to initiate the response that contained the tool call are forwarded to the tool execution.
You can access them in the second parameter of the execute function.
In multi-step calls, the messages contain the text, tool calls, and tool results from all previous steps.

contents.heading: abort-signals
contents.content:
The abort signals from generateText and streamText are forwarded to the tool execution.
You can access them in the second parameter of the execute function and e.g. abort long-running computations or forward them to fetch calls inside tools.

contents.heading: context-experimental
contents.content:
You can pass in arbitrary context from generateText or streamText via the experimental_context setting.
This context is available in the experimental_context tool execution option.

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: The following tool input lifecycle hooks are available:

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputStart: Called when the model starts generating the input (arguments) for the tool call

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputDelta: Called for each chunk of text as the input is streamed

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputAvailable: Called when the complete input is available and validated

contents.heading: tool-input-lifecycle-hooks
contents.content: onInputStart is always called before onInputAvailable, including when using generateText. onInputDelta is only called in streaming contexts (when using streamText).

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
Modularizing your code often requires defining types to ensure type safety and reusability.
To enable this, the AI SDK provides several helper types for tools, tool calls, and tool results.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
You can use them to strongly type your variables, function parameters, and return types
in parts of the code that are not directly related to streamText or generateText.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
Each tool call is typed with ToolCall<NAME extends string, ARGS>, depending
on the tool that has been invoked.
Similarly, the tool results are typed with ToolResult<NAME extends string, ARGS, RESULT>.

contents.heading: types
contents.content:
The tools in streamText and generateText are defined as a ToolSet.
The type inference helpers TypedToolCall<TOOLS extends ToolSet>
and TypedToolResult<TOOLS extends ToolSet> can be used to
extract the tool call and tool result types from the tools.

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: The AI SDK has three tool-call related errors:

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: NoSuchToolError: the model tries to call a tool that is not defined in the tools object

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: InvalidToolInputError: the model calls a tool with inputs that do not match the tool's input schema

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: ToolCallRepairError: an error that occurred during tool call repair

contents.heading: handling-errors
contents.content: When tool execution fails (errors thrown by your tool's execute function), the AI SDK adds them as tool-error content parts to enable automated LLM roundtrips in multi-step scenarios.

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: generateText throws errors for tool schema validation issues and other errors, and can be handled using a try/catch block. Tool execution errors appear as tool-error parts in the result steps:

contents.heading: generatetext
contents.content: Tool execution errors are available in the result steps:

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: streamText sends errors as part of the full stream. Tool execution errors appear as tool-error parts, while other errors appear as error parts.

contents.heading: streamtext
contents.content: When using toUIMessageStreamResponse, you can pass an onError function to extract the error message from the error part and forward it as part of the stream response:

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: The tool call repair feature is experimental and may change in the future.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
Language models sometimes fail to generate valid tool calls,
especially when the input schema is complex or the model is smaller.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
If you use multiple steps, those failed tool calls will be sent back to the LLM
in the next step to give it an opportunity to fix it.
However, you may want to control how invalid tool calls are repaired without requiring
additional steps that pollute the message history.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content:
You can use the experimental_repairToolCall function to attempt to repair the tool call
with a custom function.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: You can use different strategies to repair the tool call:

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Use a model with structured outputs to generate the inputs.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Send the messages, system prompt, and tool schema to a stronger model to generate the inputs.

contents.heading: tool-call-repair
contents.content: Provide more specific repair instructions based on which tool was called.

contents.heading: active-tools
contents.content:
Language models can only handle a limited number of tools at a time, depending on the model.
To allow for static typing using a large number of tools and limiting the available tools to the model at the same time,
the AI SDK provides the activeTools property.

contents.heading: active-tools
contents.content:
It is an array of tool names that are currently active.
By default, the value is undefined and all tools are active.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
Multi-modal tool results are experimental and supported by Anthropic, OpenAI,
and Google (Gemini 3 models).

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
For Google, use base64 media parts (image-data / file-data) or base64
data: URLs in URL-style parts. Remote HTTP(S) URLs in tool-result URL parts
are not supported.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
In order to send multi-modal tool results, e.g. screenshots, back to the model,
they need to be converted into a specific format.

contents.heading: multi-modal-tool-results
contents.content:
AI SDK Core tools have an optional toModelOutput function
that converts the tool result into a content part.

contents.content: Here is an example for converting a screenshot into a content part:

contents.content:
Once you start having many tools, you might want to extract them into separate files.
The tool helper function is crucial for this, because it ensures correct type inference.

contents.heading: extracting-tools
contents.content: Here is an example of an extracted tool:

contents.heading: mcp-tools
contents.content:
The AI SDK supports connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to access their tools.
MCP enables your AI applications to discover and use tools across various services through a standardized interface.

contents.heading: mcp-tools
contents.content: For detailed information about MCP tools, including initialization, transport options, and usage patterns, see the MCP Tools documentation.

contents.heading: ai-sdk-tools-vs-mcp-tools
contents.content: In most cases, you should define your own AI SDK tools for production applications. They provide full control, type safety, and optimal performance. MCP tools are best suited for rapid development iteration and scenarios where users bring their own tools.

metadata.title: Handling Authentication
metadata.description: Learn how to authenticate with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
The RSC API makes extensive use of Server Actions to power streaming values and UI from the server.

Server Actions are exposed as public, unprotected endpoints. As a result, you should treat Server Actions as you would public-facing API endpoints and ensure that the user is authorized to perform the action before returning any data.

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.description: Learn how to handle errors with the AI SDK.

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
Two categories of errors can occur when working with the RSC API: errors while streaming user interfaces and errors while streaming other values.

contents.heading: handling-ui-errors
contents.content: To handle errors while generating UI, the streamableUI object exposes an error() method.

contents.heading: handling-ui-errors
contents.content: With this method, you can catch any error with the stream, and return relevant UI. On the client, you can also use a React Error Boundary to wrap the streamed component and catch any additional errors.

contents.heading: handling-other-errors
contents.content: To handle other errors while streaming, you can return an error object that the receiver can use to determine why the failure occurred.

metadata.title: Managing Generative UI State
metadata.description: Overview of the AI and UI states

title.children: What is AI and UI State?
Calling Server Actions from the Client

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

State is an essential part of any application. State is particularly important in AI applications as it is passed to large language models (LLMs) on each request to ensure they have the necessary context to produce a great generation. Traditional chatbots are text-based and have a structure that mirrors that of any chat application.
For example, in a chatbot, state is an array of messages where each message has:
id: a unique identifier
role: who sent the message (user/assistant/system/tool)
content: the content of the message
This state can be rendered in the UI and sent to the model without any modifications.

With Generative UI, the model can now return a React component, rather than a plain text message. The client can render that component without issue, but that state can't be sent back to the model because React components aren't serialisable. So, what can you do?
The solution is to split the state in two, where one (AI State) becomes a proxy for the other (UI State).

One way to understand this concept is through a Lego analogy. Imagine a 10,000 piece Lego model that, once built, cannot be easily transported because it is fragile. By taking the model apart, it can be easily transported, and then rebuilt following the steps outlined in the instructions pamphlet. In this way, the instructions pamphlet is a proxy to the physical structure. Similarly, AI State provides a serialisable (JSON) representation of your UI that can be passed back and forth to the model.

contents.heading: what-is-ai-and-ui-state
contents.content: The RSC API simplifies how you manage AI State and UI State, providing a robust way to keep them in sync between your database, server and client.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content: AI State refers to the state of your application in a serialisable format that will be used on the server and can be shared with the language model.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content: For a chat app, the AI State is the conversation history (messages) between the user and the assistant. Components generated by the model would be represented in a JSON format as a tool alongside any necessary props. AI State can also be used to store other values and meta information such as createdAt for each message and chatId for each conversation. The LLM reads this history so it can generate the next message. This state serves as the source of truth for the current application state.

contents.heading: ai-state
contents.content:
Note: AI state can be accessed/modified from both the server and the
client.

contents.heading: ui-state
contents.content: UI State refers to the state of your application that is rendered on the client. It is a fully client-side state (similar to useState) that can store anything from Javascript values to React elements. UI state is a list of actual UI elements that are rendered on the client.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: AI SDK RSC simplifies managing AI and UI state across your application by providing several hooks. These hooks are powered by  React context  under the hood.

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: Notably, this means you do not have to pass the message history to the server explicitly for each request. You also can access and update your application state in any child component of the context provider. As you begin building multistep generative interfaces, this will be particularly helpful.

contents.content: To use @ai-sdk/rsc to manage AI and UI State in your application, you can create a React context using createAI:

contents.heading: creating-the-ai-context
contents.content: Next, wrap your application with your newly created context. With that, you can get and set AI and UI State across your entire application.

contents.heading: reading-ui-state-in-client
contents.content: The UI state can be accessed in Client Components using the useUIState hook provided by the RSC API. The hook returns the current UI state and a function to update the UI state like React's useState.

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-in-client
contents.content: The AI state can be accessed in Client Components using the useAIState hook provided by the RSC API. The hook returns the current AI state.

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-on-server
contents.content: The AI State can be accessed within any Server Action provided to the createAI context using the getAIState function. It returns the current AI state as a read-only value:

contents.heading: reading-ai-state-on-server

Remember, you can only access state within actions that have been passed to
the createAI context within the actions key.

contents.heading: updating-ai-state-on-server
contents.content: The AI State can also be updated from within your Server Action with the getMutableAIState function. This function is similar to getAIState, but it returns the state with methods to read and update it:

contents.heading: updating-ai-state-on-server
contents.content:
It is important to update the AI State with new responses using .update()
and .done() to keep the conversation history in sync.

contents.content: To call the sendMessage action from the client, you can use the useActions hook. The hook returns all the available Actions that were provided to createAI:

contents.heading: calling-server-actions-from-the-client
contents.content: When the user submits a message, the sendMessage action is called with the message content. The response from the action is then added to the UI state, updating the displayed messages.

contents.content:
Important! Don't forget to update the UI State after you call your Server
Action otherwise the streamed component will not show in the UI.

metadata.title: Handling Loading State
metadata.description: Overview of handling loading state with AI SDK RSC

title.children: Handling Loading State on the Client
Streaming Loading State from the Server

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.

Given that responses from language models can often take a while to complete, it's crucial to be able to show loading state to users. This provides visual feedback that the system is working on their request and helps maintain a positive user experience.
There are three approaches you can take to handle loading state with the AI SDK RSC:
Managing loading state similar to how you would in a traditional Next.js application. This involves setting a loading state variable in the client and updating it when the response is received.
Streaming loading state from the server to the client. This approach allows you to track loading state on a more granular level and provide more detailed feedback to the user.
Streaming loading component from the server to the client. This approach allows you to stream a React Server Component to the client while awaiting the model's response.

contents.heading: client
contents.content: Let's create a simple Next.js page that will call the generateResponse function when the form is submitted. The function will take in the user's prompt (input) and then generate a response (response). To handle the loading state, use the loading state variable. When the form is submitted, set loading to true, and when the response is received, set it back to false. While the response is being streamed, the input field will be disabled.

contents.heading: server
contents.content: Now let's implement the generateResponse function. Use the streamText function to generate a response to the input.

contents.heading: streaming-loading-state-from-the-server
contents.content: If you are looking to track loading state on a more granular level, you can create a new streamable value to store a custom variable and then read this on the frontend. Let's update the example to create a new streamable value for tracking loading state:

contents.heading: client-1
contents.content: This allows you to provide more detailed feedback about the generation process to your users.

contents.heading: streaming-loading-components-with-streamui
contents.content: If you are using the  streamUI  function, you can stream the loading state to the client in the form of a React component. streamUI supports the usage of  JavaScript generator functions , which allow you to yield some value (in this case a React component) while some other blocking work completes.

contents.content: This guide helps you migrate from AI SDK RSC to AI SDK UI.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: The AI SDK has two packages that help you build the frontend for your applications – AI SDK UI and AI SDK RSC.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: We introduced support for using React Server Components (RSC) within the AI SDK to simplify building generative user interfaces for frameworks that support RSC.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: However, given we're pushing the boundaries of this technology, AI SDK RSC currently faces significant limitations that make it unsuitable for stable production use.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: It is not possible to abort a stream using server actions. This will be improved in future releases of React and Next.js (1122).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: When using createStreamableUI and streamUI, components remount on .done(), causing them to flicker (2939).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Many suspense boundaries can lead to crashes (2843).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Using createStreamableUI can lead to quadratic data transfer. You can avoid this using createStreamableValue instead, and rendering the component client-side.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Closed RSC streams cause update issues (3007).

contents.heading: background
contents.content: Due to these limitations, AI SDK RSC is marked as experimental, and we do not recommend using it for stable production environments.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: As a result, we strongly recommend migrating to AI SDK UI, which has undergone extensive development to provide a more stable and production grade experience.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: In building v0, we have invested considerable time exploring how to create the best chat experience on the web. AI SDK UI ships with many of these best practices and commonly used patterns like language model middleware, multi-step tool calls, attachments, telemetry, provider registry, and many more. These features have been considerately designed into a neat abstraction that you can use to reliably integrate AI into your applications.

contents.heading: basic-setup
contents.content: The streamUI function executes as part of a server action as illustrated below.

contents.heading: before-call-server-action-and-update-ui-state
contents.content: The chat interface calls the server action. The response is then saved using the useUIState hook.

contents.heading: before-call-server-action-and-update-ui-state
contents.content: The streamUI function combines generating text and rendering the user interface. To migrate to AI SDK UI, you need to separate these concerns – streaming generations with streamText and rendering the UI with useChat.

contents.heading: after-replace-server-action-with-route-handler
contents.content: The streamText function executes as part of a route handler and streams the response to the client. The useChat hook on the client decodes this stream and renders the response within the chat interface.

contents.heading: parallel-tool-calls
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, streamUI does not support parallel tool calls. You will have to use a combination of streamText, createStreamableUI and createStreamableValue.

contents.heading: parallel-tool-calls
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, useChat comes with built-in support for parallel tool calls. You can define multiple tools in the streamText and have them called them in parallel. The useChat hook will then handle the parallel tool calls for you automatically.

contents.heading: multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, streamUI does not support multi-step tool calls. You will have to use a combination of streamText, createStreamableUI and createStreamableValue.

contents.heading: multi-step-tool-calls
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, useChat comes with built-in support for multi-step tool calls. You can set maxSteps in the streamText function to define the number of steps the language model can make in a single call. The useChat hook will then handle the multi-step tool calls for you automatically.

contents.heading: generative-user-interfaces
contents.content: The streamUI function uses tools as a way to execute functions based on user input and renders React components based on the function output to go beyond text in the chat interface.

contents.heading: before-render-components-within-the-server-action-and-stream-to-client
contents.content: As mentioned earlier, streamUI generates text and renders the React component in a single server action call.

contents.heading: after-replace-with-route-handler-and-stream-props-data-to-client
contents.content: The streamText function streams the props data as response to the client, while useChat decode the stream as toolInvocations and renders the chat interface.

contents.heading: handling-client-interactions
contents.content: With AI SDK RSC, components streamed to the client can trigger subsequent generations by calling the relevant server action using the useActions hooks. This is possible as long as the component is a descendant of the <AI/> context provider.

contents.heading: after-use-another-chat-hook-with-same-id-from-the-component
contents.content: After switching to AI SDK UI, these messages are synced by initializing the useChat hook in the component with the same id as the parent component.

contents.heading: loading-indicators
contents.content: In AI SDK RSC, you can use the initial parameter of streamUI to define the component to display while the generation is in progress.

contents.heading: before-use-loading-to-show-loading-indicator
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, you can use the tool invocation state to show a loading indicator while the tool is executing.

contents.heading: saving-chats
contents.content: Before implementing streamUI as a server action, you should create an <AI/> provider and wrap your application at the root layout to sync the AI and UI states. During initialization, you typically use the onSetAIState callback function to track updates to the AI state and save it to the database when done(...) is called.

contents.heading: after-save-chats-using-callback-function-of-streamtext
contents.content: With AI SDK UI, you will save chats using the onFinish callback function of streamText in your route handler.

contents.heading: restoring-chats
contents.content: When using AI SDK RSC, the useUIState hook contains the UI state of the chat. When restoring a previously saved chat, the UI state needs to be loaded with messages.

contents.heading: restoring-chats
contents.content: Similar to how you typically save chats in AI SDK RSC, you should use the onGetUIState callback function to retrieve the chat from the database, convert it into UI state, and return it to be accessible through useUIState.

contents.heading: before-load-chat-from-database-using-callback-function-of-context-provider
contents.content: AI SDK UI uses the messages field of useChat to store messages. To load messages when useChat is mounted, you should use initialMessages.

contents.heading: before-load-chat-from-database-using-callback-function-of-context-provider
contents.content: As messages are typically loaded from the database, we can use a server actions inside a Page component to fetch an older chat from the database during static generation and pass the messages as props to the <Chat/> component.

contents.heading: streaming-object-generation
contents.content: The createStreamableValue function streams any serializable data from the server to the client. As a result, this function allows you to stream object generations from the server to the client when paired with streamObject.

contents.heading: before-read-streamable-value-and-update-object
contents.content: To migrate to AI SDK UI, you should use the useObject hook and implement streamObject within your route handler.

metadata.title: Multistep Interfaces
metadata.description: Overview of Building Multistep Interfaces with AI SDK RSC

contents.content:
AI SDK RSC is currently experimental. We recommend using AI SDK
UI for production. For guidance on migrating from
RSC to UI, see our migration guide.
Multistep interfaces refer to user interfaces that require multiple independent steps to be executed in order to complete a specific task.
For example, if you wanted to build a Generative UI chatbot capable of booking flights, it could have three steps:
Search all flights
Pick flight
Check availability
To build this kind of application you will leverage two concepts, tool composition and application context.

Tool composition is the process of combining multiple tools to create a new tool. This is a powerful concept that allows you to break down complex tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. In the example above, "search all flights", "pick flight", and "check availability" come together to create a holistic "book flight" tool.

Application context refers to the state of the application at any given point in time. This includes the user's input, the output of the language model, and any other relevant information. In the example above, the flight selected in "pick flight" would be used as context necessary to complete the "check availability" task.

contents.content: The turn-by-turn implementation is the simplest form of multistep interfaces. In this implementation, the user and the model take turns during the conversation. For every user input, the model generates a response, and the conversation continues in this turn-by-turn fashion.
