metadata.description: Learn how to write a custom provider for the AI SDK

title.children: Step 1: Create the Provider Entry Point

contents.content: The AI SDK provides a Language Model Specification that enables you to create custom providers compatible with the AI SDK. This specification ensures consistency across different providers.

contents.heading: publishing-your-provider
contents.content: Please publish your custom provider in your own GitHub repository and as an NPM package. You are responsible for hosting and maintaining your provider. Once published, you can submit a PR to the AI SDK repository to add your provider to the Community Providers documentation section. Use the OpenRouter provider documentation as a template for your documentation.

contents.heading: why-the-language-model-specification
contents.content: The Language Model Specification V2 is a standardized specification for interacting with language models that provides a unified abstraction layer across all AI providers. This specification creates a consistent interface that works seamlessly with different language models, ensuring that developers can interact with any provider using the same patterns and methods. It enables:

contents.heading: why-the-language-model-specification
contents.content:
If you open-source a provider, we'd love to promote it here. Please send us a
PR to add it to the Community Providers
section.

contents.heading: understanding-the-v2-specification
contents.content: The Language Model Specification V2 creates a robust abstraction layer that works across all current and future AI providers. By establishing a standardized interface, it provides the flexibility to support emerging LLM capabilities while ensuring your application code remains provider-agnostic and future-ready.

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: At its heart, the V2 specification defines three main interfaces:

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: ProviderV2: The top-level interface that serves as a factory for different model types

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: LanguageModelV2: The primary interface for text generation models

contents.heading: architecture
contents.content: EmbeddingModelV2 and ImageModelV2: Interfaces for embeddings and image generation

contents.heading: providerv2
contents.content: The ProviderV2 interface acts as the entry point:

contents.heading: languagemodelv2
contents.content: The LanguageModelV2 interface defines the methods your provider must implement:

contents.heading: languagemodelv2
contents.content: Key aspects:

contents.heading: languagemodelv2
contents.content: specificationVersion: Must be 'V2'

contents.heading: languagemodelv2
contents.content: supportedUrls: Declares which URLs (for file parts) the provider can handle natively

contents.heading: languagemodelv2
contents.content: doGenerate/doStream: methods for non-streaming and streaming generation

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: Before diving into the details, it's important to understand the distinction between two key concepts in the V2 specification:

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: LanguageModelV2Content: The specification for what the models generate

contents.heading: understanding-input-vs-output
contents.content: LanguageModelV2Prompt: The specification for what you send to the model

contents.heading: languagemodelv2content
contents.content: The V2 specification supports five distinct content types that models can generate, each designed for specific use cases:

contents.heading: text-content
contents.content: The fundamental building block for all text generation:

contents.heading: text-content
contents.content: This is used for standard model responses, system messages, and any plain text output.

contents.heading: tool-calls
contents.content: Enable models to invoke functions with structured arguments:

contents.heading: tool-calls
contents.content: The toolCallId is crucial for correlating tool results back to their calls, especially in streaming scenarios.

contents.heading: file-generation
contents.content: Support for multimodal output generation:

contents.heading: file-generation
contents.content: This enables models to generate images, audio, documents, and other file types directly.

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Dedicated support for chain-of-thought reasoning (essential for models like OpenAI's o1):

contents.heading: reasoning
contents.content: Reasoning content is tracked separately from regular text, allowing for proper token accounting and UI presentation.

contents.heading: languagemodelv2prompt
contents.content: The V2 prompt format (LanguageModelV2Prompt) is designed as a flexible message array that supports multimodal inputs:

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Each message has a specific role with allowed content types:

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: System: Model instructions (text only)

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: User: Human inputs supporting text and files

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Assistant: Model outputs with full content type support

contents.heading: message-roles
contents.content: Tool: Results from tool executions

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Prompt parts are the building blocks of messages in the prompt structure. While LanguageModelV2Content represents the model's output content, prompt parts are specifically designed for constructing input messages. Each message role supports different types of prompt parts:

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: System messages: Only support text content

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: User messages: Support text and file parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Assistant messages: Support text, file, reasoning, and tool call parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Tool messages: Only support tool result parts

contents.heading: prompt-parts
contents.content: Let's explore each prompt part type:

contents.heading: text-parts
contents.content: The most basic prompt part, containing plain text content:

contents.heading: reasoning-parts
contents.content: Used in assistant messages to capture the model's reasoning process:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: Enable multimodal inputs by including files in prompts:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: The data field offers flexibility:

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: Uint8Array: Direct binary data

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: string: Base64-encoded data

contents.heading: file-parts
contents.content: URL: Reference to external content (if supported by provider via supportedUrls)

contents.heading: tool-call-parts
contents.content: Represent tool calls made by the assistant:

contents.heading: tool-result-parts
contents.content: Contain the results of executed tool calls:

contents.heading: tool-result-parts
contents.content: The optional content field enables rich tool results including images, providing more flexibility than the basic result field.

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: The streaming system uses typed events for different stages:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Stream Lifecycle Events:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: stream-start: Initial event with any warnings about unsupported features

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: response-metadata: Model information and response headers

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: finish: Final event with usage statistics and finish reason

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: error: Error events that can occur at any point

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Content Events:

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: All content types (text, file, reasoning, source, tool-call) stream directly

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: tool-call-delta: Incremental updates for tool call arguments

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: reasoning-part-finish: Explicit marker for reasoning section completion

contents.heading: stream-parts
contents.content: Example stream sequence:

contents.heading: usage-tracking
contents.content: Enhanced usage information:

contents.heading: tools
contents.content: The V2 specification supports two types of tools:

contents.heading: function-tools
contents.content: Standard user-defined functions with JSON Schema validation:

contents.heading: provider-defined-client-tools
contents.content: Native provider capabilities exposed as tools:

contents.heading: provider-defined-client-tools
contents.content: Tool choice can be controlled via:

contents.heading: native-url-support
contents.content: Providers can declare URLs they can access directly:

contents.heading: native-url-support
contents.content: The AI SDK checks these patterns before downloading any URL-based content.

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: The specification includes a flexible system for provider-specific features without breaking the standard interface:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Provider options can be specified at multiple levels:

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Call level: In LanguageModelV2CallOptions

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Message level: On individual messages

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: Part level: On specific content parts (text, file, etc.)

contents.heading: provider-options
contents.content: This layered approach allows fine-grained control while maintaining compatibility.

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: The V2 specification emphasizes robust error handling:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Streaming Errors: Can be emitted at any point via { type: 'error', error: unknown }

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Warnings: Non-fatal issues reported in stream-start and response objects

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: Finish Reasons: Clear indication of why generation stopped:

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'stop': Natural completion

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'length': Hit max tokens

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'content-filter': Safety filtering

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'tool-calls': Stopped to execute tools

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'error': Generation failed

contents.heading: error-handling
contents.content: 'other': Provider-specific reasons

contents.content: To implement a custom language model provider, you'll need to install the required packages:

title.children: Client Sampling (for clients without native support)

contents.content: The MCP Sampling AI Provider allows MCP servers to use AI models through the AI SDK by leveraging your existing client subscriptions (like VS Code Copilot). This transforms your MCP server into an agentic tool that can reason and make decisions, without requiring separate API keys or subscriptions.
The provider implements LanguageModelV2 by forwarding requests through MCP's sampling feature to the MCP client, offering unique advantages:
Server-Side AI Integration: Enable MCP servers to call language models directly through AI SDK's standard interface
No Direct Model Management: Forward AI requests to MCP clients, eliminating the need for multiple API keys
Model Flexibility: Let MCP clients decide which model to use based on preferences (cost, speed, intelligence)
Seamless AI SDK Compatibility: Support for generateText, streamText, generateObject, and experimental tool calling
Client Sampling Support: Add sampling capability to any MCP client with built-in helpers
Agentic Tools: Transform simple MCP tools into intelligent agents that can reason and make decisions
Learn more about MCP Sampling in the MCP Specification.

contents.content: Change language_code

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
language_code specifies the language of the input audio and is required for
accurate transcription. • It is mandatory for the saarika:v1 model (this
model does not support unknown). • It is optional for the saarika:v2
model. • Use unknown when the language is not known; in that case, the API
will auto‑detect it. Available options: unknown, hi-IN, bn-IN, kn-IN,
ml-IN, mr-IN, od-IN, pa-IN, ta-IN, te-IN, en-IN, gu-IN.

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: with_timestamps?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
with_timestamps specifies whether to include start/end timestamps for each
word/token. • Type: boolean • When true, each word/token will include
start/end timestamps. • Default: false

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: with_diarization?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
with_diarization enables speaker diarization (Beta). • Type: boolean • When
true, enables speaker diarization. • Default: false

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content: num_speakers?

contents.heading: changing-parameters
contents.content:
num_speakers sets the number of distinct speakers to detect (only when
with_diarization is true). • Type: number | null • Number of distinct
speakers to detect. • Default: null

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content:
You can create models that call the Voyage embeddings API

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: You can use Voyage embedding models to generate embeddings with the embed or embedMany function:

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Voyage embedding models support additional provider options that can be passed via providerOptions.voyage:

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The following provider options are available:

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: inputType 'query' | 'document' | 'null'

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Specifies the type of input passed to the model. Defaults to 'null'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'null': When inputType is 'null', the embedding model directly converts the inputs into numerical vectors.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: For retrieval/search purposes it is recommended to use 'query' or 'document'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'query': The input is a search query, e.g., "Represent the query for retrieving supporting documents: ...".

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'document': The input is a document to be stored in a vector database, e.g., "Represent the document for retrieval: ...".

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: outputDimension number

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The number of dimensions for the resulting output embeddings. Default is 'null'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: For example, voyage-code-3 and voyage-3-large support: 2048, 1024 (default), 512, and 256.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Refer to the model documentation for supported values.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: outputDtype 'float' | 'int8' | 'uint8' | 'binary' | 'ubinary'

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: The data type for the output embeddings. Defaults to 'float'.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'float': 32-bit floating-point numbers (supported by all models).

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'int8', 'uint8': 8-bit integer types (supported by voyage-3-large, voyage-3.5, voyage-3.5-lite, and voyage-code-3).

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: 'binary', 'ubinary': Bit-packed, quantized single-bit embedding values (voyage-3-large, voyage-3.5, voyage-3.5-lite, and voyage-code-3). The returned list length is 1/8 of outputDimension. 'binary' uses offset binary encoding.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: See FAQ: Output Data Types for more details.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: truncation boolean

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: Whether to truncate the input texts to fit within the model's context length. If not specified, defaults to true.

contents.heading: text-embedding-models
contents.content: You can find more models on the Voyage Library homepage.

contents.heading: example-2-embed-multiple-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content:
If you get an image URL not found error, convert the image to base64 and pass the
base64 data URL in the image array. The value should be a Base64-encoded image in the
data URL format data:[mediatype];base64,<data>. Supported media types: image/png,
image/jpeg, image/webp, and image/gif.

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: The following constraints apply to the values list:

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: The list must not contain more than 1,000 values.

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: Each image must not contain more than 16 million pixels or be larger than 20 MB in size.

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: With every 560 pixels of an image being counted as a token, each input in the list must not exceed 32,000 tokens, and the total number of tokens across all inputs must not exceed 320,000.

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: Voyage multimodal embedding models support additional provider options that can be passed via providerOptions.voyage:

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: The following provider options are available:

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: inputType 'query' | 'document'

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: Specifies the type of input passed to the model. Defaults to 'query'.

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: When inputType is specified as 'query' or 'document', Voyage automatically prepends a prompt to your inputs before vectorizing them, creating vectors tailored for retrieval/search tasks:

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: 'query': Prepends "Represent the query for retrieving supporting documents: "

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: 'document': Prepends "Represent the document for retrieval: "

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: outputEncoding 'base64'

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: The data encoding for the resulting output embeddings. Defaults to null (list of 32-bit floats).

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: If null, embeddings are returned as a list of floating-point numbers (float32).

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding
contents.content: If 'base64', embeddings are returned as a Base64-encoded NumPy array of single-precision floats.

contents.content: See FAQ: Output Data Types for more details.

contents.content: truncation boolean

contents.heading: example-1-embed-multiple-texts-and-images-as-single-embedding

metadata.title: Langfuse
metadata.description: Monitor, evaluate and debug your AI SDK application with Langfuse

title.children: Group multiple executions in one trace

contents.content: Langfuse (GitHub) is an open source LLM engineering platform that helps teams to collaboratively develop, monitor, and debug AI applications. Langfuse integrates with the AI SDK to provide:
Application traces
Usage patterns
Cost data by user and model
Replay sessions to debug issues
Evaluations

contents.heading: setup
contents.content:
The AI SDK supports tracing via OpenTelemetry. With the LangfuseExporter you can collect these traces in Langfuse.
While telemetry is experimental (docs), you can enable it by setting experimental_telemetry on each request that you want to trace.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: To collect the traces in Langfuse, you need to add the LangfuseExporter to your application.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: You can set the Langfuse credentials via environment variables or directly to the LangfuseExporter constructor.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: To get your Langfuse API keys, you can self-host Langfuse or sign up for Langfuse Cloud here. Create a project in the Langfuse dashboard to get your secretKey and publicKey.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Now you need to register this exporter via the OpenTelemetry SDK.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Next.js has support for OpenTelemetry instrumentation on the framework level. Learn more about it in the Next.js OpenTelemetry guide.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Install dependencies:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Add LangfuseExporter to your instrumentation:

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: Done! All traces that contain AI SDK spans are automatically captured in Langfuse.

contents.heading: example-application
contents.content:
Check out the sample repository (langfuse/langfuse-vercel-ai-nextjs-example) based
on the next-openai template to showcase the integration of Langfuse with Next.js and AI SDK.

contents.heading: group-multiple-executions-in-one-trace
contents.content: You can open a Langfuse trace and pass the trace ID to AI SDK calls to group multiple execution spans under one trace. The passed name in functionId will be the root span name of the respective execution.

contents.heading: group-multiple-executions-in-one-trace
contents.content: The resulting trace hierarchy will be:

contents.heading: disable-tracking-of-inputoutput
contents.content: By default, the exporter captures the input and output of each request. You can disable this behavior by setting the recordInputs and recordOutputs options to false.

contents.heading: link-langfuse-prompts-to-traces
contents.content: You can link Langfuse prompts to AI SDK generations by setting the langfusePrompt property in the metadata field:

contents.heading: link-langfuse-prompts-to-traces
contents.content: The resulting generation will have the prompt linked to the trace in Langfuse. Learn more about prompts in Langfuse here.

contents.heading: pass-custom-attributes
contents.content: All of the metadata fields are automatically captured by the exporter. You can also pass custom trace attributes to e.g. track users or sessions.

contents.heading: debugging
contents.content: Enable the debug option to see the logs of the exporter.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: If you deploy on Vercel, Vercel's OpenTelemetry Collector is only available on Pro and Enterprise Plans (docs).

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: You need to be on "ai": "^3.3.0" to use the telemetry feature. In case of any issues, please update to the latest version.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: On NextJS, make sure that you only have a single instrumentation file.

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: If you use Sentry, make sure to either:

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: set skipOpenTelemetrySetup: true in Sentry.init

contents.heading: troubleshooting
contents.content: follow Sentry's docs on how to manually set up Sentry with OTEL

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: After setting up Langfuse Tracing for the AI SDK, you can utilize any of the other Langfuse platform features:

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Prompt Management: Collaboratively manage and iterate on prompts, use them with low-latency in production.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Evaluations: Test the application holistically in development and production using user feedback, LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, manual reviews, or custom evaluation pipelines.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: Experiments: Iterate on prompts, models, and application design in a structured manner with datasets and evaluations.

contents.heading: learn-more
contents.content: For more information, see the telemetry documentation of the AI SDK.

contents.heading: basic-concepts
contents.content: Each message triggering your LLM pipeline as a whole is captured with a Trace.

contents.content: A Trace contains multiple Spans, which are the steps inside your pipeline.

contents.content: SigNoz is a single tool for all your monitoring and observability needs. Here are a few reasons why you should choose SigNoz:
Single tool for observability(logs, metrics, and traces)
Built on top of OpenTelemetry, the open-source standard which frees you from any type of vendor lock-in
Correlated logs, metrics and traces for much richer context while debugging
Uses ClickHouse (used by likes of Uber & Cloudflare) as datastore - an extremely fast and highly optimized storage for observability data
DIY Query builder, PromQL, and ClickHouse queries to fulfill all your use-cases around querying observability data

contents.heading: enable-telemetry-for-vercel-ai-sdk
contents.content: The Vercel AI SDK uses OpenTelemetry to collect telemetry data. OpenTelemetry is an open-source observability framework designed to provide standardized instrumentation for collecting telemetry data.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: Check out more detailed information about Vercel AI SDK’s telemetry options visit here.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: You can then use the experimental_telemetry option to enable telemetry on specific function calls while the feature is experimental:

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: When telemetry is enabled, you can also control whether you want to record the input values and the output values for the function. By default, both are enabled. You can disable them by setting the recordInputs and recordOutputs options to false.

contents.heading: enabling-telemetry
contents.content: Disabling the recording of inputs and outputs can be useful for privacy, data transfer, and performance reasons. You might, for example, want to disable recording inputs if they contain sensitive information.

contents.heading: telemetry-metadata
contents.content: You can provide a functionId to identify the function that the telemetry data is for, and metadata to include additional information in the telemetry data.

contents.heading: custom-tracer
contents.content: You may provide a tracer which must return an OpenTelemetry Tracer. This is useful in situations where you want your traces to use a TracerProvider other than the one provided by the @opentelemetry/api singleton.

contents.heading: custom-tracer
contents.content: Your Vercel AI SDK commands should now automatically emit traces, spans, and events. You can find more details on the types of spans and events generated here.

contents.heading: custom-tracer
contents.content: Finally, you should be able to view this data in Signoz Cloud under the traces tab.

metadata.title: OpenAI Compatible Providers
metadata.description: Use OpenAI compatible providers with the AI SDK.

contents.content: You can use the OpenAI Compatible Provider package to use language model providers that implement the OpenAI API.
Below we focus on the general setup and provider instance creation. You can also write a custom provider package leveraging the OpenAI Compatible package.
We provide detailed documentation for the following OpenAI compatible providers:
LM Studio
NIM
ModelRush
Heroku
Clarifai
The general setup and provider instance creation is the same for all of these providers.

contents.heading: setup
contents.content: The OpenAI Compatible provider is available via the @ai-sdk/openai-compatible module. You can install it with:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: To use an OpenAI compatible provider, you can create a custom provider instance with the createOpenAICompatible function from @ai-sdk/openai-compatible:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: You can use the following optional settings to customize the provider instance:

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: baseURL string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Set the URL prefix for API calls.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: apiKey string

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
API key for authenticating requests. If specified, adds an Authorization
header to request headers with the value Bearer <apiKey>. This will be added
before any headers potentially specified in the headers option.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: headers Record<string,string>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Optional custom headers to include in requests. These will be added to request headers
after any headers potentially added by use of the apiKey option.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: queryParams Record<string,string>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Optional custom url query parameters to include in request urls.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: fetch (input: RequestInfo, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content:
Custom fetch implementation.
Defaults to the global fetch function.
You can use it as a middleware to intercept requests,
or to provide a custom fetch implementation for e.g. testing.

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: includeUsage boolean

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Include usage information in streaming responses. When enabled, usage data will be included in the response metadata for streaming requests. Defaults to undefined (false).

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: supportsStructuredOutputs boolean

contents.heading: provider-instance
contents.content: Set to true if the provider supports structured outputs. Only relevant for provider(), provider.chatModel(), and provider.languageModel().

contents.heading: language-models
contents.content:
You can create provider models using a provider instance.
The first argument is the model id, e.g. model-id.

contents.heading: example
contents.content: You can use provider language models to generate text with the generateText function:

contents.heading: custom-query-parameters
contents.content:
Some providers may require custom query parameters. An example is the Azure AI
Model Inference
API
which requires an api-version query parameter.

contents.heading: custom-query-parameters
contents.content:
You can set these via the optional queryParams provider setting. These will be
added to all requests made by the provider.

contents.heading: custom-query-parameters
contents.content:
For example, with the above configuration, API requests would include the query parameter in the URL like:
https://api.provider.com/v1/chat/completions?api-version=1.0.0.

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: The OpenAI Compatible provider supports adding provider-specific options to the request body. These are specified with the providerOptions field in the request body.

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: For example, if you create a provider instance with the name provider-name, you can add a custom-option field to the request body like this:

contents.heading: provider-specific-options
contents.content: The request body sent to the provider will include the customOption field with the value magic-value. This gives you an easy way to add provider-specific options to requests without having to modify the provider or AI SDK code.

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content:
The OpenAI Compatible provider supports extracting provider-specific metadata from API responses through metadata extractors.
These extractors allow you to capture additional information returned by the provider beyond the standard response format.

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content:
Metadata extractors receive the raw, unprocessed response data from the provider, giving you complete flexibility
to extract any custom fields or experimental features that the provider may include.
This is particularly useful when:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Working with providers that include non-standard response fields

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Experimenting with beta or preview features

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Capturing provider-specific metrics or debugging information

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Supporting rapid provider API evolution without SDK changes

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Metadata extractors work with both streaming and non-streaming chat completions and consist of two main components:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: A function to extract metadata from complete responses

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: A streaming extractor that can accumulate metadata across chunks in a streaming response

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: Here's an example metadata extractor that captures both standard and custom provider data:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: You can provide a metadata extractor when creating your provider instance:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: The extracted metadata will be included in the response under the providerMetadata field:

contents.heading: custom-metadata-extraction
contents.content: This allows you to access provider-specific information while maintaining a consistent interface across different providers.

contents.content: With the release of Claude 4, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications, particularly those that require complex reasoning capabilities and advanced intelligence.

contents.heading: claude-4
contents.content: Claude 4 is Anthropic's most advanced model family to date, offering exceptional capabilities across reasoning, instruction following, coding, and knowledge tasks. Available in two variants—Sonnet and Opus—Claude 4 delivers state-of-the-art performance with enhanced reliability and control. Claude 4 builds on the extended thinking capabilities introduced in Claude 3.7, allowing for even more sophisticated problem-solving through careful, step-by-step reasoning.

contents.heading: claude-4
contents.content: Claude 4 excels at complex reasoning, code generation and analysis, detailed content creation, and agentic capabilities, making it ideal for powering sophisticated AI workflows, customer-facing agents, and applications requiring nuanced understanding and responses. Claude Opus 4 is an excellent coding model, leading on SWE-bench (72.5%) and Terminal-bench (43.2%), with the ability to sustain performance on long-running tasks that require focused effort and thousands of steps. Claude Sonnet 4 significantly improves on Sonnet 3.7, excelling in coding with 72.7% on SWE-bench while balancing performance and efficiency.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-claude-4-models
contents.content: Avoid negative examples: When providing examples, only demonstrate the behavior you want to see, not what you want to avoid.

contents.content: With the release of Computer Use in Claude 3.5 Sonnet, you can now direct AI models to interact with computers like humans do - moving cursors, clicking buttons, and typing text. This capability enables automation of complex tasks while leveraging Claude's advanced reasoning abilities.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like Anthropic's Claude alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more. In this guide, you will learn how to integrate Computer Use into your AI SDK applications.

Computer Use is currently in beta with some  limitations
.
The feature may be error-prone at times. Anthropic recommends starting with
low-risk tasks and implementing appropriate safety measures.

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Anthropic recently released a new version of the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model which is capable of 'Computer Use'. This allows the model to interact with computer interfaces through basic actions like:

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Moving the cursor

contents.heading: computer-use

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Typing text

contents.content: Taking screenshots

contents.heading: computer-use
contents.content: Reading screen content

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Computer Use enables the model to read and interact with on-screen content through a series of coordinated steps. Here's how the process works:

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Start with a prompt and tools

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Add Anthropic-defined Computer Use tools to your request and provide a task (prompt) for the model. For example: "save an image to your downloads folder."

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Select the right tool

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The model evaluates which computer tools can help accomplish the task. It then sends a formatted tool_call to use the appropriate tool.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Execute the action and return results

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The AI SDK processes Claude's request by running the selected tool. The results can then be sent back to Claude through a tool_result message.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Complete the task through iterations

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Claude analyzes each result to determine if more actions are needed. It continues requesting tool use and processing results until it completes your task or requires additional input.

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: There are three main tools available in the Computer Use API:

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Computer Tool: Enables basic computer control like mouse movement, clicking, and keyboard input

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Text Editor Tool: Provides functionality for viewing and editing text files

contents.heading: available-tools
contents.content: Bash Tool: Allows execution of bash commands

contents.content: For one-shot text generation, use generateText:

contents.content: You can combine multiple tools in a single request to enable more complex workflows. The AI SDK supports all three of Claude's Computer Use tools:

contents.content:
Always implement appropriate security measures and

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: To get the best results when using Computer Use:

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Specify simple, well-defined tasks with explicit instructions for each step

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Prompt Claude to verify outcomes through screenshots

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Use keyboard shortcuts when UI elements are difficult to manipulate

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Include example screenshots for repeatable tasks

contents.heading: best-practices-for-computer-use
contents.content: Provide explicit tips in system prompts for known tasks

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Remember, Computer Use is a beta feature. Please be aware that it poses unique risks that are distinct from standard API features or chat interfaces. These risks are heightened when using Computer Use to interact with the internet. To minimize risks, consider taking precautions such as:

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Use a dedicated virtual machine or container with minimal privileges to prevent direct system attacks or accidents.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Avoid giving the model access to sensitive data, such as account login information, to prevent information theft.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Limit internet access to an allowlist of domains to reduce exposure to malicious content.

contents.heading: security-measures
contents.content: Ask a human to confirm decisions that may result in meaningful real-world consequences as well as any tasks requiring affirmative consent, such as accepting cookies, executing financial transactions, or agreeing to terms of service.

With the release of Llama 3.1, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI application with large language models (LLMs) like Llama 3.1 alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more

contents.heading: llama-31
contents.content: The release of Meta's Llama 3.1 is an important moment in AI development. As the first state-of-the-art open weight AI model, Llama 3.1 is helping accelerate developers building AI apps. Available in 8B, 70B, and 405B sizes, these instruction-tuned models work well for tasks like dialogue generation, translation, reasoning, and code generation.

contents.heading: benchmarks
contents.content: Llama 3.1 surpasses most available open-source chat models on common industry benchmarks and even outperforms some closed-source models, offering superior performance in language nuances, contextual understanding, and complex multi-step tasks. The models' refined post-training processes significantly improve response alignment, reduce false refusal rates, and enhance answer diversity, making Llama 3.1 a powerful and accessible tool for building generative AI applications.

contents.heading: benchmarks
contents.content: Source: Meta AI - Llama 3.1 Model Card

contents.heading: choosing-model-size
contents.content: Llama 3.1 includes a new 405B parameter model, becoming the largest open-source model available today. This model is designed to handle the most complex and demanding tasks.

contents.heading: choosing-model-size
contents.content: When choosing between the different sizes of Llama 3.1 models (405B, 70B, 8B), consider the trade-off between performance and computational requirements. The 405B model offers the highest accuracy and capability for complex tasks but requires significant computational resources. The 70B model provides a good balance of performance and efficiency for most applications, while the 8B model is suitable for simpler tasks or resource-constrained environments where speed and lower computational overhead are priorities.

contents.heading: tools
contents.content: While LLMs have incredible generation capabilities, they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather). The solution: tools, which are like programs that you provide to the model, which it can choose to call as necessary.

contents.heading: using-tools-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK supports tool usage across several of its functions, including generateText and streamUI. By passing one or more tools to the tools parameter, you can extend the capabilities of LLMs, allowing them to perform discrete tasks and interact with external systems.

contents.heading: agents

contents.content: While the Llama 3.1 family of models are powerful out-of-the-box, their performance can be enhanced through effective prompt engineering and fine-tuning techniques.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering
contents.content: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting input prompts to elicit desired outputs from language models. It involves structuring and phrasing prompts in ways that guide the model towards producing more accurate, relevant, and coherent responses.

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: As a reminder, this application will have three main features:

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: Generate SQL queries from natural language

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: Create a chart from the query results

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: Explain SQL queries in plain English

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: For each of these features, you'll use the AI SDK via  Server Actions  to interact with OpenAI's GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini models. Server Actions are a powerful React Server Component feature that allows you to call server-side functions directly from your frontend code.

contents.heading: building-the-application
contents.content: Let's start with generating a SQL query from natural language.

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: For the model to generate accurate SQL queries, it needs context about your database schema, tables, and relationships. You will communicate this information through a prompt that should include:

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Schema information

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Example data formats

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Available SQL operations

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Best practices for query structure

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Nuanced advice for specific fields

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Let's write a prompt that includes all of this information:

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: There are several important elements of this prompt:

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Schema description helps the model understand exactly what data fields to work with

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Includes rules for handling queries based on common SQL patterns - for example, always using ILIKE for case-insensitive string matching

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Explains how to handle edge cases in the dataset, like dealing with the comma-separated investors field and ensuring whitespace is properly handled

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Instead of having the model guess at industry categories, it provides the exact list that exists in the data, helping avoid mismatches

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: The prompt helps standardize data transformations - like knowing to interpret "10b" as "10.0" billion dollars, or that rates should be decimal values

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: Clear rules ensure the query output will be chart-friendly by always including at least two columns of data that can be plotted

contents.heading: providing-context
contents.content: This prompt structure provides a strong foundation for query generation, but you should experiment and iterate based on your specific needs and the model you're using.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action
contents.content: With the prompt done, let's create a Server Action.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action
contents.content: Open app/actions.ts. You should see one action already defined (runGeneratedSQLQuery).

contents.heading: create-a-server-action
contents.content: Add a new action. This action should be asynchronous and take in one parameter - the natural language query.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action
contents.content: In this action, you'll use the generateObject function from the AI SDK which allows you to constrain the model's output to a pre-defined schema. This process, sometimes called structured output, ensures the model returns only the SQL query without any additional prefixes, explanations, or formatting that would require manual parsing.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action
contents.content: Note, you are constraining the output to a single string field called query using zod, a TypeScript schema validation library. This will ensure the model only returns the SQL query itself. The resulting generated query will then be returned.

contents.heading: update-the-frontend
contents.content: With the Server Action in place, you can now update the frontend to call this action when the user submits a natural language query. In the root page (app/page.tsx), you should see a handleSubmit function that is called when the user submits a query.

contents.heading: update-the-frontend
contents.content: Import the generateQuery function and call it with the user's input.

contents.heading: update-the-frontend
contents.content: Now, when the user submits a natural language query (ie. "how many unicorns are from San Francisco?"), that question will be sent to your newly created Server Action. The Server Action will call the model, passing in your system prompt and the users query, and return the generated SQL query in a structured format. This query is then passed to the runGeneratedSQLQuery action to run the query against your database. The results are then saved in local state and displayed to the user.

contents.heading: update-the-frontend
contents.content: Save the file, make sure the dev server is running, and then head to localhost:3000 in your browser. Try submitting a natural language query and see the generated SQL query and results. You should see a SQL query generated and displayed under the input field. You should also see the results of the query displayed in a table below the input field.

contents.heading: update-the-frontend
contents.content: Try clicking the SQL query to see the full query if it's too long to display in the input field. You should see a button on the right side of the input field with a question mark icon. Clicking this button currently does nothing, but you'll add the "explain query" functionality to it in the next step.

contents.heading: explain-sql-queries
contents.content:
Next, let's add the ability to explain SQL queries in plain English. This feature helps users understand how the generated SQL query works by breaking it down into logical sections.
As with the SQL query generation, you'll need a prompt to guide the model when explaining queries.

contents.heading: explain-sql-queries
contents.content: Let's craft a prompt for the explain query functionality:

contents.heading: explain-sql-queries
contents.content: Like the prompt for generating SQL queries, you provide the model with the schema of the database. Additionally, you provide an example of what each section of the query might look like. This helps the model understand the structure of the query and how to break it down into logical sections.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content: Add a new Server Action to generate explanations for SQL queries.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content: This action takes two parameters - the original natural language input and the generated SQL query.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content: This action uses the generateObject function again. However, you haven't defined the schema yet. Let's define it in another file so it can also be used as a type in your components.

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content: Update your lib/types.ts file to include the schema for the explanations:

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content: This schema defines the structure of the explanation that the model will generate. Each explanation will have a section and an explanation. The section is the part of the query being explained, and the explanation is the plain English explanation of that section. Go back to your actions.ts file and import and use the explanationSchema:

contents.heading: create-a-server-action-1
contents.content:
You can use output: "array" to indicate to the model that you expect an
array of objects matching the schema to be returned.

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: Next, update the query-viewer.tsx component to display these explanations. The handleExplainQuery function is called every time the user clicks the question icon button on the right side of the query. Let's update this function to use the new explainQuery action:

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: Now when users click the explanation button (the question mark icon), the component will:

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: Show a loading state

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: Send the active SQL query and the users natural language query to your Server Action

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: The model will generate an array of explanations

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: The explanations will be set in the component state and rendered in the UI

contents.heading: update-query-viewer
contents.content: Submit a new query and then click the explanation button. Hover over different elements of the query. You should see the explanations for each section!

contents.heading: visualizing-query-results
contents.content: Finally, let's render the query results visually in a chart. There are two approaches you could take:

contents.heading: visualizing-query-results
contents.content: Send both the query and data to the model and ask it to return the data in a visualization-ready format. While this provides complete control over the visualization, it requires the model to send back all of the data, which significantly increases latency and costs.

contents.heading: visualizing-query-results
contents.content: Send the query and data to the model and ask it to generate a chart configuration (fixed-size and not many tokens) that maps your data appropriately. This configuration specifies how to visualize the information while delivering the insights from your natural language query. Importantly, this is done without requiring the model return the full dataset.

contents.heading: visualizing-query-results
contents.content: Since you don't know the SQL query or data shape beforehand, let's use the second approach to dynamically generate chart configurations based on the query results and user intent.

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: For this feature, you'll create a Server Action that takes the query results and the user's original natural language query to determine the best visualization approach. Your application is already set up to use shadcn charts (which uses Recharts under the hood) so the model will need to generate:

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Chart type (bar, line, area, or pie)

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Axis mappings

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Visual styling

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Let's start by defining the schema for the chart configuration in lib/types.ts:

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Replace the existing export type Config = any; type with the new one.

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: This schema makes extensive use of Zod's .describe() function to give the model extra context about each of the key's you are expecting in the chart configuration. This will help the model understand the purpose of each key and generate more accurate results.

contents.heading: generate-the-chart-configuration
contents.content: Another important technique to note here is that you are defining description and takeaway fields. Not only are these useful for the user to quickly understand what the chart means and what they should take away from it, but they also force the model to generate a description of the data first, before it attempts to generate configuration attributes like axis and columns. This will help the model generate more accurate and relevant chart configurations.

contents.heading: create-the-server-action
contents.content: Create a new action in app/actions.ts:

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: With the action in place, you'll want to trigger it automatically after receiving query results. This ensures the visualization appears almost immediately after data loads.

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Update the handleSubmit function in your root page (app/page.tsx) to generate and set the chart configuration after running the query:

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Now when users submit queries, the application will:

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Generate and run the SQL query

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Display the table results

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Generate a chart configuration for the results

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Allow toggling between table and chart views

contents.heading: update-the-chart-component
contents.content: Head back to the browser and test the application with a few queries. You should see the chart visualization appear after the table results.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: You've built an AI-powered SQL analysis tool that can convert natural language to SQL queries, visualize query results, and explain SQL queries in plain English.

contents.heading: next-steps
contents.content: You could, for example, extend the application to use your own data sources or add more advanced features like customizing the chart configuration schema to support more chart types and options. You could also add more complex SQL query generation capabilities.

title.children: Getting Started with the AI SDK
Using Tools with the AI SDK

contents.content: With the release of OpenAI's o1 series models, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications, particularly those that require complex reasoning capabilities.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI o1 alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more.

contents.heading: openai-o1
contents.content: OpenAI released a series of AI models designed to spend more time thinking before responding. They can reason through complex tasks and solve harder problems than previous models in science, coding, and math. These models, named the o1 series, are trained with reinforcement learning and can "think before they answer". As a result, they are able to produce a long internal chain of thought before responding to a prompt.

contents.heading: openai-o1
contents.content: The main reasoning model available in the API is:

contents.heading: openai-o1
contents.content: o1: Designed to reason about hard problems using broad general knowledge about the world.

contents.heading: benchmarks
contents.content: OpenAI o1 models excel in scientific reasoning, with impressive performance across various domains:

contents.heading: benchmarks
contents.content: Ranking in the 89th percentile on competitive programming questions (Codeforces)

contents.heading: benchmarks
contents.content: Placing among the top 500 students in the US in a qualifier for the USA Math Olympiad (AIME)

contents.heading: benchmarks

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o1-models
contents.content: The o1 models perform best with straightforward prompts. Some prompt engineering techniques, like few-shot prompting or instructing the model to "think step by step," may not enhance performance and can sometimes hinder it. Here are some best practices:

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o1-models
contents.content: Keep prompts simple and direct: The models excel at understanding and responding to brief, clear instructions without the need for extensive guidance.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o1-models
contents.content: Avoid chain-of-thought prompts: Since these models perform reasoning internally, prompting them to "think step by step" or "explain your reasoning" is unnecessary.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o1-models
contents.content: Use delimiters for clarity: Use delimiters like triple quotation marks, XML tags, or section titles to clearly indicate distinct parts of the input, helping the model interpret different sections appropriately.

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o1-models
contents.content: Limit additional context in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): When providing additional context or documents, include only the most relevant information to prevent the model from overcomplicating its response.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK is the TypeScript toolkit designed to help developers build AI-powered applications with React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more. Integrating LLMs into applications is complicated and heavily dependent on the specific model provider you use.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK abstracts away the differences between model providers, eliminates boilerplate code for building chatbots, and allows you to go beyond text output to generate rich, interactive components.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: At the center of the AI SDK is AI SDK Core, which provides a unified API to call any LLM. The code snippet below is all you need to call OpenAI o1 with the AI SDK:

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content:
To use the o1 model, you must either be using @ai-sdk/openai version 0.0.59 or
greater, or set temperature: 1.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: AI SDK Core abstracts away the differences between model providers, allowing you to focus on building great applications. The unified interface also means that you can easily switch between models by changing just one line of code.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: System messages are automatically converted to OpenAI developer messages.

contents.heading: refining-reasoning-effort
contents.content:
You can control the amount of reasoning effort expended by o1 through the reasoningEffort parameter.
This parameter can be set to 'low', 'medium', or 'high' to adjust how much time and computation the model spends on internal reasoning before producing a response.

contents.heading: refining-reasoning-effort
contents.content:
The reasoningEffort parameter is only supported by o1 and has no effect on
other models.

contents.heading: generating-structured-data
contents.content: While text generation can be useful, you might want to generate structured JSON data. For example, you might want to extract information from text, classify data, or generate synthetic data. AI SDK Core provides two functions (generateObject and streamObject) to generate structured data, allowing you to constrain model outputs to a specific schema.

contents.heading: generating-structured-data
contents.content: This code snippet will generate a type-safe recipe that conforms to the specified zod schema.

contents.heading: tools
contents.content: While LLMs have incredible generation capabilities, they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather). The solution: tools, which are like programs that you provide to the model, which it can choose to call as necessary.

contents.heading: using-tools-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK supports tool usage across several of its functions, like generateText and streamText. By passing one or more tools to the tools parameter, you can extend the capabilities of LLMs, allowing them to perform discrete tasks and interact with external systems.

contents.heading: using-tools-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: Here's an example of how you can use a tool with the AI SDK and o1:

contents.heading: using-tools-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: In this example, the getWeather tool allows the model to fetch real-time weather data (simulated for simplicity), enhancing its ability to provide accurate and up-to-date information.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK Core can be paired with AI SDK UI, another powerful component of the AI SDK, to streamline the process of building chat, completion, and assistant interfaces with popular frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and SvelteKit.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK UI provides robust abstractions that simplify the complex tasks of managing chat streams and UI updates on the frontend, enabling you to develop dynamic AI-driven interfaces more efficiently.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: With four main hooks — useChat, useCompletion, and useObject — you can incorporate real-time chat capabilities, text completions, streamed JSON, and interactive assistant features into your app.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: Let's explore building a chatbot with Next.js, the AI SDK, and OpenAI o1:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: The useChat hook on your root page (app/page.tsx) will make a request to your AI provider endpoint (app/api/chat/route.ts) whenever the user submits a message. The messages are then displayed in the chat UI.

contents.content: Ready to get started? Here's how you can dive in:

contents.heading: get-started
contents.content: Explore the documentation at ai-sdk.dev/docs to understand the full capabilities of the AI SDK.

contents.heading: get-started

contents.heading: get-started
contents.content: Dive deeper with advanced guides on topics like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and multi-modal chat at ai-sdk.dev/docs/guides.

Using Tools with the AI SDK

contents.content: With the release of OpenAI's o3-mini model, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications, particularly those that require complex STEM reasoning capabilities.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI o3-mini alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more.

contents.heading: openai-o3-mini
contents.content: OpenAI recently released a new AI model optimized for STEM reasoning that excels in science, math, and coding tasks. o3-mini matches o1's performance in these domains while delivering faster responses and lower costs. The model supports tool calling, structured outputs, and system messages, making it a great option for a wide range of applications.

contents.heading: openai-o3-mini
contents.content: o3-mini offers three reasoning effort levels:

contents.heading: openai-o3-mini
contents.content: [Low]: Optimized for speed while maintaining solid reasoning capabilities

contents.heading: openai-o3-mini
contents.content: [Medium]: Balanced approach matching o1's performance levels

contents.heading: openai-o3-mini
contents.content: [High]: Enhanced reasoning power exceeding o1 in many STEM domains

contents.heading: prompt-engineering-for-o3-mini
contents.content: Use delimiters for clarity: Use delimiters like triple quotation marks, XML tags, or section titles to clearly indicate distinct parts of the input.

metadata.title: RAG Agent
metadata.description: Learn how to build a RAG Agent with the AI SDK and Next.js

contents.content: In this guide, you will learn how to build a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent.
Before we dive in, let's look at what RAG is, and why we would want to use it.

contents.heading: what-is-rag
contents.content: RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. In simple terms, RAG is the process of providing a Large Language Model (LLM) with specific information relevant to the prompt.

contents.heading: why-is-rag-important
contents.content: While LLMs are powerful, the information they can reason on is restricted to the data they were trained on. This problem becomes apparent when asking an LLM for information outside of their training data, like proprietary data or common knowledge that has occurred after the model’s training cutoff. RAG solves this problem by fetching information relevant to the prompt and then passing that to the model as context.

contents.heading: why-is-rag-important
contents.content: To illustrate with a basic example, imagine asking the model for your favorite food:

contents.heading: why-is-rag-important
contents.content: Not surprisingly, the model doesn’t know. But imagine, alongside your prompt, the model received some extra context:

contents.heading: why-is-rag-important
contents.content: Just like that, you have augmented the model’s generation by providing relevant information to the query. Assuming the model has the appropriate information, it is now highly likely to return an accurate response to the users query. But how does it retrieve the relevant information? The answer relies on a concept called embedding.

contents.heading: why-is-rag-important
contents.content:
You could fetch any context for your RAG application (eg. Google search).
Embeddings and Vector Databases are just a specific retrieval approach to
achieve semantic search.

contents.heading: embedding
contents.content: Embeddings are a way to represent words, phrases, or images as vectors in a high-dimensional space. In this space, similar words are close to each other, and the distance between words can be used to measure their similarity.

contents.heading: embedding
contents.content: In practice, this means that if you embedded the words cat and dog, you would expect them to be plotted close to each other in vector space. The process of calculating the similarity between two vectors is called ‘cosine similarity’ where a value of 1 would indicate high similarity and a value of -1 would indicate high opposition.

contents.heading: embedding
contents.content:
Don’t worry if this seems complicated. a high level understanding is all you
need to get started! For a more in-depth introduction to embeddings, check out
this guide.

contents.heading: embedding
contents.content: As mentioned above, embeddings are a way to represent the semantic meaning of words and phrases. The implication here is that the larger the input to your embedding, the lower quality the embedding will be. So how would you approach embedding content longer than a simple phrase?

contents.heading: chunking
contents.content: Chunking refers to the process of breaking down a particular source material into smaller pieces. There are many different approaches to chunking and it’s worth experimenting as the most effective approach can differ by use case. A simple and common approach to chunking (and what you will be using in this guide) is separating written content by sentences.

contents.heading: chunking
contents.content: Once your source material is appropriately chunked, you can embed each one and then store the embedding and the chunk together in a database. Embeddings can be stored in any database that supports vectors. For this tutorial, you will be using Postgres alongside the pgvector plugin.

contents.heading: all-together-now
contents.content: Combining all of this together, RAG is the process of enabling the model to respond with information outside of it’s training data by embedding a users query, retrieving the relevant source material (chunks) with the highest semantic similarity, and then passing them alongside the initial query as context. Going back to the example where you ask the model for your favorite food, the prompt preparation process would look like this.

contents.heading: all-together-now
contents.content: By passing the appropriate context and refining the model’s objective, you are able to fully leverage its strengths as a reasoning machine.

contents.heading: all-together-now
contents.content: Onto the project!

contents.heading: create-embeddings-table

contents.heading: create-embeddings-table

contents.heading: create-embeddings-table

contents.content: Now that you have a table to store embeddings, it’s time to write the logic to create the embeddings.

contents.content: Create a file with the following command:

contents.content: Remember, to create an embedding, you will start with a piece of source material (unknown length), break it down into smaller chunks, embed each chunk, and then save the chunk to the database. Let’s start by creating a function to break the source material into small chunks.

contents.heading: generate-chunks
contents.content: This function will take an input string and split it by periods, filtering out any empty items. This will return an array of strings. It is worth experimenting with different chunking techniques in your projects as the best technique will vary.

contents.content: You will use the AI SDK to create embeddings. This will require two more dependencies, which you can install by running the following command:

contents.content:
The AI SDK is designed to be a unified interface to interact with any large
language model. This means that you can change model and providers with just
one line of code! Learn more about available providers and
building custom providers

contents.heading: generate-embeddings
contents.content: Let’s add a function to generate embeddings. Copy the following code into your lib/ai/embedding.ts file.

contents.heading: generate-embeddings
contents.content: In this code, you first define the model you want to use for the embeddings. In this example, you are using OpenAI’s text-embedding-ada-002 embedding model.

contents.heading: generate-embeddings
contents.content: Next, you create an asynchronous function called generateEmbeddings. This function will take in the source material (value) as an input and return a promise of an array of objects, each containing an embedding and content. Within the function, you first generate chunks for the input. Then, you pass those chunks to the embedMany function imported from the AI SDK which will return embeddings of the chunks you passed in. Finally, you map over and return the embeddings in a format that is ready to save in the database.

contents.heading: update-server-action
contents.content: Open the file at lib/actions/resources.ts. This file has one function, createResource, which, as the name implies, allows you to create a resource.

contents.heading: update-server-action
contents.content: This function is a Server Action, as denoted by the “use server”; directive at the top of the file. This means that it can be called anywhere in your Next.js application. This function will take an input, run it through a Zod schema to ensure it adheres to the correct schema, and then creates a new resource in the database. By default, useChat will send a POST request to the /api/chat endpoint with the messages as the request body.

contents.heading: create-api-route
contents.content: In Next.js, you can create custom request handlers for a given route using Route Handlers. Route Handlers are defined in a route.ts file and can export HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, PATCH etc.
