contents.heading: create-api-route
contents.content: Head back to the browser and try to send a message again. You should see a response from the model streamed directly in!

contents.heading: refining-your-prompt
contents.content: While you now have a working agent, it isn't doing anything special.

contents.heading: refining-your-prompt
contents.content: Let’s add system instructions to refine and restrict the model’s behavior. In this case, you want the model to only use information it has retrieved to generate responses. Update your route handler with the following code:

contents.heading: refining-your-prompt
contents.content: Head back to the browser and try to ask the model what your favorite food is. The model should now respond exactly as you instructed above (“Sorry, I don’t know”) given it doesn’t have any relevant information.

contents.heading: refining-your-prompt
contents.content: In its current form, your agent is now, well, useless. How do you give the model the ability to add and query information?

contents.heading: using-tools
contents.content: A tool is a function that can be called by the model to perform a specific task. You can think of a tool like a program you give to the model that it can run as and when it deems necessary.

contents.heading: using-tools
contents.content: Let’s see how you can create a tool to give the model the ability to create, embed and save a resource to your agents’ knowledge base.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: Update your route handler with the following code:

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: In this code, you define a tool called addResource. This tool has three elements:

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: description: description of the tool that will influence when the tool is picked.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: inputSchema: Zod schema that defines the input necessary for the tool to run.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: execute: An asynchronous function that is called with the arguments from the tool call.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: In simple terms, on each generation, the model will decide whether it should call the tool. If it deems it should call the tool, it will extract the input and then append a new message to the messages array of type tool-call. The AI SDK will then run the execute function with the parameters provided by the tool-call message.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: Head back to the browser and tell the model your favorite food. You should see an empty response in the UI. Did anything happen? Let’s see. Run the following command in a new terminal window.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: This will start Drizzle Studio where we can view the rows in our database. You should see a new row in both the embeddings and resources table with your favorite food!

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: Let’s make a few changes in the UI to communicate to the user when a tool has been called. Head back to your root page (app/page.tsx) and add the following code:

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: With this change, you now conditionally render the tool that has been called directly in the UI. Save the file and head back to browser. Tell the model your favorite movie. You should see which tool is called in place of the model’s typical text response.

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: Don't worry about the tool-getInformation tool case in the switch statement

contents.heading: add-resource-tool
contents.content: we'll add that tool in a later section.

contents.heading: improving-ux-with-multi-step-calls
contents.content: It would be nice if the model could summarize the action too. However, technically, once the model calls a tool, it has completed its generation as it ‘generated’ a tool call. How could you achieve this desired behaviour?

contents.heading: improving-ux-with-multi-step-calls
contents.content: The AI SDK has a feature called stopWhen which allows stopping conditions when the model generates a tool call. If those stopping conditions haven't been hit, the AI SDK will automatically send tool call results back to the model!

contents.content: Open your root page (api/chat/route.ts) and add the following key to the streamText configuration object:

contents.heading: improving-ux-with-multi-step-calls
contents.content: Head back to the browser and tell the model your favorite pizza topping (note: pineapple is not an option). You should see a follow-up response from the model confirming the action.

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: The model can now add and embed arbitrary information to your knowledge base. However, it still isn’t able to query it. Let’s create a new tool to allow the model to answer questions by finding relevant information in your knowledge base.

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: To find similar content, you will need to embed the users query, search the database for semantic similarities, then pass those items to the model as context alongside the query. To achieve this, let’s update your embedding logic file (lib/ai/embedding.ts):

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: In this code, you add two functions:

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: generateEmbedding: generate a single embedding from an input string

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: findRelevantContent: embeds the user’s query, searches the database for similar items, then returns relevant items

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: With that done, it’s onto the final step: creating the tool.

contents.content: Go back to your route handler (api/chat/route.ts) and add a new tool called getInformation:

contents.heading: retrieve-resource-tool
contents.content: Head back to the browser, refresh the page, and ask for your favorite food. You should see the model call the getInformation tool, and then use the relevant information to formulate a response!

contents.heading: conclusion
contents.content: Congratulations, you have successfully built an AI agent that can dynamically add and retrieve information to and from a knowledge base. Throughout this guide, you learned how to create and store embeddings, set up server actions to manage resources, and use tools to extend the capabilities of your agent.

contents.heading: event-handler
contents.content: First, let's take a look at our API route (api/events.ts):

contents.heading: event-handler
contents.content: This file defines a POST function that handles incoming requests from Slack. First, you check the request type to see if it's a URL verification request. If it is, you respond with the challenge string provided by Slack. If it's an event callback, you verify the request and then have access to the event data. This is where you can implement your event handling logic.

contents.heading: event-handler
contents.content: You then handle three types of events: app_mention, assistant_thread_started, and message:

contents.heading: event-handler

contents.heading: event-handler

contents.heading: event-handler
contents.content: For message, you call handleNewAssistantMessage with the event and the bot user ID.

contents.heading: event-handler

contents.heading: the-waituntil-function
contents.content: Slack expects a response within 3 seconds to confirm the request is being handled. However, generating AI responses can take longer. If you don't respond to the Slack request within 3 seconds, Slack will send another request, leading to another invocation of your API route, another call to the LLM, and ultimately another response to the user. To solve this, you can use the waitUntil function, which allows you to run your AI logic after the response is sent, without blocking the response itself.

contents.content: This means, your API endpoint will:

contents.heading: the-waituntil-function

contents.heading: the-waituntil-function

contents.heading: the-waituntil-function

contents.content: The real power of the AI SDK comes from tools that enable your bot to perform actions. Let's add two useful tools:

contents.content: In this updated implementation:

metadata.title: Get started with Claude 3.7 Sonnet

title.children: Getting Started with the AI SDK

contents.content: With the release of Claude 3.7 Sonnet, there has never been a better time to start building AI applications, particularly those that require complex reasoning capabilities.

The AI SDK is a powerful TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications with large language models (LLMs) like Claude 3.7 Sonnet alongside popular frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more.

contents.heading: claude-37-sonnet
contents.content: Claude 3.7 Sonnet is Anthropic's most intelligent model to date and the first Claude model to offer extended thinking—the ability to solve complex problems with careful, step-by-step reasoning. With Claude 3.7 Sonnet, you can balance speed and quality by choosing between standard thinking for near-instant responses or extended thinking or advanced reasoning. Claude 3.7 Sonnet is state-of-the-art for coding, and delivers advancements in computer use, agentic capabilities, complex reasoning, and content generation. With frontier performance and more control over speed, Claude 3.7 Sonnet is a great choice for powering AI agents, especially customer-facing agents, and complex AI workflows.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK is the TypeScript toolkit designed to help developers build AI-powered applications with React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Node.js, and more. Integrating LLMs into applications is complicated and heavily dependent on the specific model provider you use.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The AI SDK abstracts away the differences between model providers, eliminates boilerplate code for building chatbots, and allows you to go beyond text output to generate rich, interactive components.

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: At the center of the AI SDK is AI SDK Core, which provides a unified API to call any LLM. The code snippet below is all you need to call Claude 3.7 Sonnet with the AI SDK:

contents.heading: getting-started-with-the-ai-sdk
contents.content: The unified interface also means that you can easily switch between providers by changing just two lines of code. For example, to use Claude 3.7 Sonnet via Amazon Bedrock:

contents.heading: reasoning-ability
contents.content: Claude 3.7 Sonnet introduces a new extended thinking—the ability to solve complex problems with careful, step-by-step reasoning. You can enable it using the thinking provider option and specifying a thinking budget in tokens:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK Core can be paired with AI SDK UI, another powerful component of the AI SDK, to streamline the process of building chat, completion, and assistant interfaces with popular frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and SvelteKit.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: AI SDK UI provides robust abstractions that simplify the complex tasks of managing chat streams and UI updates on the frontend, enabling you to develop dynamic AI-driven interfaces more efficiently.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: With four main hooks — useChat, useCompletion, and useObject — you can incorporate real-time chat capabilities, text completions, streamed JSON, and interactive assistant features into your app.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: Let's explore building a chatbot with Next.js, the AI SDK, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: In a new Next.js application, first install the AI SDK and the Anthropic provider:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces

contents.content:
You can forward the model's reasoning tokens to the client with
sendReasoning: true in the toUIMessageStreamResponse method.

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: Finally, update the root page (app/page.tsx) to use the useChat hook:

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces

You can access the model's reasoning tokens with the reasoning part on the

contents.heading: building-interactive-interfaces
contents.content: The useChat hook on your root page (app/page.tsx) will make a request to your LLM provider endpoint (app/api/chat/route.ts) whenever the user submits a message. The messages are then displayed in the chat UI.

metadata.title: Caching Middleware
metadata.description: Learn how to create a caching middleware with Next.js and KV.

metadata.description: Add a human approval step to your agentic system with Next.js and the AI SDK

title.children: Forward Tool Call To The Client
Move tool declarations to their own file

contents.content: When building agentic systems, it's important to add human-in-the-loop (HITL) functionality to ensure that users can approve actions before the system executes them. This recipe will describe how to build a low-level solution and then provide an example abstraction you could implement and customise based on your needs.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: To understand how to implement this functionality, let's look at how tool calling works in a simple Next.js chatbot application with the AI SDK.

contents.heading: background

Within the execute function of createUIMessageStream, call streamText and pass in the converted messages (sent from the client). Finally, merge the resulting generation into the UIMessageStream.

contents.heading: background
contents.content: What happens if you ask the LLM for the weather in New York?

contents.heading: background
contents.content: The LLM has one tool available, weather, which requires a location to run. This tool will, as stated in the tool's description, "show the weather in a given city to the user". If the LLM decides that the weather tool could answer the user's query, it would generate a ToolCall, extracting the location from the context. The AI SDK would then run the associated execute function, passing in the location parameter, and finally returning a tool result.

contents.heading: background

contents.heading: adding-a-confirmation-step
contents.content: If confirmed, execute the tool and update the result

contents.heading: adding-a-confirmation-step
contents.content: If declined, update the result with an error message

contents.heading: adding-a-confirmation-step
contents.content: Send the updated tool result back to the client to maintain state consistency

contents.heading: forward-tool-call-to-the-client
contents.content: To implement HITL functionality, you start by omitting the execute function from the tool definition. This allows the frontend to intercept the tool call and handle the responsibility of adding the final tool result to the tool call.

contents.heading: forward-tool-call-to-the-client
contents.content:
Each tool call must have a corresponding tool result. If you do not add a tool
result, all subsequent generations will fail.

contents.heading: intercept-tool-call
contents.content: On the frontend, you map through the messages, either rendering the message content or checking for tool invocations and rendering custom UI.

contents.heading: intercept-tool-call
contents.content: You can check if the tool requiring confirmation has been called and, if so, present options to either confirm or deny the proposed tool call. This confirmation is done using the addToolOutput function to create a tool result and append it to the associated tool call.

contents.heading: intercept-tool-call
contents.content:
The sendMessage() function after addToolOutput will trigger a call to your
route handler.

contents.heading: handle-confirmation-response
contents.content: Adding a tool result and sending the message will trigger another call to your route handler. Before sending the new messages to the language model, you pull out the last message and map through the message parts to see if the tool requiring confirmation was called and whether it's in a "result" state. If those conditions are met, you check the confirmation state (the tool result state that you set on the frontend with the addToolOutput function).

contents.heading: handle-confirmation-response
contents.content: In this implementation, you use simple strings like "Yes, the user confirmed" or "No, the user declined" as states. If confirmed, you execute the tool. If declined, you do not execute the tool. In both cases, you update the tool result from the arbitrary data you sent with the addToolOutput function to either the result of the execute function or an "Execution declined" statement. You send the updated tool result back to the frontend to maintain state synchronization.

contents.heading: handle-confirmation-response
contents.content: After handling the tool result, your API route continues. This triggers another generation with the updated tool result, allowing the LLM to continue attempting to solve the query.

metadata.title: Markdown Chatbot with Memoization
metadata.description: Build a chatbot that renders and memoizes Markdown responses with Next.js and the AI SDK.

contents.content: When building a chatbot with Next.js and the AI SDK, you'll likely want to render the model's responses in Markdown format using a library like react-markdown. However, this can have negative performance implications as the Markdown is re-rendered on each new token received from the streaming response.
As conversations get longer and more complex, this performance impact becomes exponentially worse since the entire conversation history is re-rendered with each new token.

This recipe uses memoization - a performance optimization technique where the results of expensive function calls are cached and reused to avoid unnecessary re-computation. In this case, parsed Markdown blocks are memoized to prevent them from being re-parsed and re-rendered on each token update, which means that once a block is fully parsed, it's cached and reused rather than being regenerated. This approach significantly improves rendering performance for long conversations by eliminating redundant parsing and rendering operations.

contents.content: Next, create a memoized markdown component that will take in raw Markdown text into blocks and only updates when the content actually changes. This component splits Markdown content into blocks using the marked library to identify discrete Markdown elements, then uses React's memoization features to optimize re-rendering by only updating blocks that have actually changed.

contents.heading: client
contents.content: Finally, on the client, use the useChat hook to manage the chat state and render the chat interface. You can use the MemoizedMarkdown component to render the message contents in Markdown format without compromising on performance. Additionally, you can render the form in its own component so as to not trigger unnecessary re-renders of the chat messages. You can also use the experimental_throttle option that will throttle data updates to a specified interval, helping to manage rendering performance.

contents.content:
Some models allow developers to provide a list of tools that can be called at any time during a generation.
This is useful for extending the capabilities of a language model to either use logic or data to interact with systems external to the model.

contents.heading: accessing-tool-calls-and-tool-results
contents.content: If the model decides to call a tool, it will generate a tool call. You can access the tool call by checking the toolCalls property on the result.

contents.heading: accessing-tool-results
contents.content: You can access the result of a tool call by checking the toolResults property on the result.

contents.heading: accessing-tool-results
contents.content: toolResults will only be available if the tool has an execute function.

contents.heading: model-response
contents.content:
When using tools, it's important to note that the model won't respond with the tool call results by default.
This is because the model has technically already generated its response to the prompt: the tool call.
Many use cases will require the model to summarise the results of the tool call within the context of the original prompt automatically.
You can achieve this by using stopWhen
which will automatically send toolResults to the model to trigger another generation.

metadata.title: Embed Text in Batch
metadata.description: Learn how to embed multiple text using the AI SDK and Node

contents.content: When working with large datasets or multiple pieces of text, processing embeddings one at a time can be inefficient. Batch embedding allows you to convert multiple text inputs into embeddings simultaneously, significantly improving performance and reducing API calls. This is particularly useful when processing documents, chat messages, or any collection of text that needs to be vectorized.

This example shows how to embed multiple text inputs in a single operation using the AI SDK. For single text embedding, see our Embed Text example, or for a practical application, check out our RAG example which demonstrates how batch embeddings can be used in a document retrieval system.

metadata.title: Embed Text
metadata.description: Learn how to embed text using the AI SDK and Node

contents.content: Text embeddings are numerical representations of text that capture semantic meaning, allowing machines to understand and process language in a mathematical way. These vector representations are crucial for many AI applications, as they enable tasks like semantic search, document similarity comparison, and content recommendation.

This example demonstrates how to convert text into embeddings using a text embedding model. The resulting embedding is a high-dimensional vector that represents the semantic meaning of the input text. For a more practical application of embeddings, check out our RAG example which shows how embeddings can be used for document retrieval.

metadata.title: Generate Object with a Reasoning Model
metadata.description: Learn how to generate structured data with a reasoning model using the AI SDK and Node

contents.content:
Reasoning models, like DeepSeek's R1, are gaining popularity due to their ability to understand and generate better responses to complex queries than non-reasoning models.
You may want to use these models to generate structured data. However, most (like R1 and OpenAI's o1) do not support tool-calling or structured outputs.

One solution is to pass the output from a reasoning model through a smaller model that can output structured data (like gpt-4o-mini). These lightweight models can efficiently extract the structured data while adding very little overhead in terms of speed and cost.

metadata.title: Generate Object
metadata.description: Learn how to generate structured data using the AI SDK and Node

contents.content: Earlier functions like generateText and streamText gave us the ability to generate unstructured text. However, if you want to generate structured data like JSON, you can provide a schema that describes the structure of your desired object to the generateObject function.

The function requires you to provide a schema using zod, a library for defining schemas for JavaScript objects. By using zod, you can also use it to validate the generated object and ensure that it conforms to the specified structure.

A chat completion allows you to generate text based on a series of messages. This series of messages can be any series of interactions between any number of systems, but the most popular and relatable use case has been a series of messages that represent a conversation between a user and a model.

metadata.title: Intercepting Fetch Requests
metadata.description: Learn how to intercept fetch requests using the AI SDK and Node

contents.content: Many providers support setting a custom fetch function using the fetch argument in their factory function.

A custom fetch function can be used to intercept and modify requests before they are sent to the provider's API,

Adding authentication headers
Modifying request bodies
Caching responses
Using a custom HTTP client

metadata.title: Local Caching Middleware
metadata.description: Learn how to create a caching middleware for local development.

contents.content: When developing AI applications, you'll often find yourself repeatedly making the same API calls during development. This can lead to increased costs and slower development cycles. A caching middleware allows you to store responses locally and reuse them when the same inputs are provided.
This approach is particularly useful in two scenarios:
Iterating on UI/UX - When you're focused on styling and user experience, you don't want to regenerate AI responses for every code change.
Working on evals - When developing evals, you need to repeatedly test the same prompts, but don't need new generations each time.

contents.heading: implementation
contents.content: In this implementation, you create a JSON file to store responses. When a request is made, you first check if you have already seen this exact request. If you have, you return the cached response immediately (as a one-off generation or chunks of tokens). If not, you trigger the generation, save the response, and return it.

contents.heading: implementation
contents.content:
Make sure to add the path of your local cache to your .gitignore so you do
not commit it.

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: For regular generations, you store and retrieve complete responses. Instead, the streaming implementation captures each token as it arrives, stores the full sequence, and on cache hits uses the SDK's simulateReadableStream utility to recreate the token-by-token streaming experience at a controlled speed (defaults to 10ms between chunks).

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: This approach gives you the best of both worlds:

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Instant responses for repeated queries

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: Preserved streaming behavior for UI development

contents.heading: how-it-works
contents.content: The middleware handles all transformations needed to make cached responses indistinguishable from fresh ones, including normalizing tool calls and fixing timestamp formats.

contents.heading: using-the-middleware
contents.content: The middleware can be easily integrated into your existing AI SDK setup:

contents.heading: considerations
contents.content: When using this caching middleware, keep these points in mind:

contents.heading: considerations
contents.content: Development Only - This approach is intended for local development, not production environments

contents.heading: considerations
contents.content: Cache Invalidation - You'll need to clear the cache (delete the cache file) when you want fresh responses

contents.heading: considerations
contents.content: Multi-Step Flows - When using stopWhen, be aware that caching occurs at the individual language model response level, not across the entire execution flow. This means that while the model's generation is cached, the tool call is not and will run on each generation.

metadata.title: Web Search Agent
metadata.description: Learn how to build an agent that has access to web with the AI SDK and Node

contents.content: There are two approaches you can take to building a web search agent with the AI SDK:
Use a model that has native web-searching capabilities
Use a tool to access the web and return search results.

Both approaches have their advantages and disadvantages. Models with native search capabilities tend to be faster and there is no additional cost to make the search. The disadvantage is that you have less control over what is being searched, and the functionality is limited to models that support it.

instead, by using a tool, you can achieve more flexibility and greater control over your search queries. It allows you to customize your search strategy, specify search parameters, and you can use it with any LLM that supports tool calling. This approach will incur additional costs for the search API you use, but gives you complete control over the search experience.

contents.heading: using-native-web-search
contents.content: There are several models that offer native web-searching capabilities (Perplexity, OpenAI, Gemini). Let's look at how you could build a Web Search Agent across providers.

contents.heading: openai-responses-api
contents.content: OpenAI's Responses API has a built-in web search tool that can be used to search the web and return search results. This tool is called web_search and is accessed via the openai provider.

contents.heading: perplexity
contents.content: Perplexity's Sonar models combines real-time web search with natural language processing. Each response is grounded in current web data and includes detailed citations.

contents.heading: gemini
contents.content: With compatible Gemini models, you can enable search grounding to give the model access to the latest information using Google search.

contents.heading: using-tools
contents.content: When using tools for web search, you have two options: use ready-made tools that integrate directly with the AI SDK, or build custom tools tailored to your specific needs.

contents.heading: using-tools
contents.content: Unlike the native web search examples where searching is built into the model, using web search tools requires multiple steps. The language model will make two generations - the first to call the relevant web search tool (extracting search queries from the context), and the second to process the results and generate a response. This multi-step process is handled automatically when you set stopWhen: stepCountIs(n) to a value greater than 1.

contents.heading: using-tools
contents.content:
By using stopWhen, you can automatically send tool results back to the
language model alongside the original question, enabling the model to respond
with information relevant to the user's query based on the search results.
This creates a seamless experience where the agent can search the web and
incorporate those findings into its response.

contents.content: Let's create a simple React component that will call the generate function when a button is clicked. The generate function will call the streamText function, which will then generate text based on the input prompt. To consume the stream of text in the client, we will use the readStreamableValue function from the @ai-sdk/rsc module.

contents.heading: server
contents.content: On the server side, we need to implement the generate function, which will call the streamText function. The streamText function will generate text based on the input prompt. In order to stream the text generation to the client, we will use createStreamableValue that can wrap any changeable value and stream it to the client.

contents.heading: server
contents.content: Using DevTools, we can see the text generation being streamed to the client in real-time.

metadata.title: Record Token Usage after Streaming User Interfaces
metadata.description: Learn how to record token usage after streaming user interfaces using the AI SDK and React Server Components

contents.content:
When you're streaming structured data with streamUI,
you may want to record the token usage for billing purposes.

contents.heading: onfinish-callback
contents.content:
You can use the onFinish callback to record token usage.
It is called when the stream is finished.

metadata.title: Stream Updates to Visual Interfaces
metadata.description: Learn how to generate text using the AI SDK and React Server Components.

contents.content: In our previous example we've been streaming react components from the server to the client. By streaming the components, we open up the possibility to update these components based on state changes that occur in the server.
